column14: MAX in-app bidding mediation commands ~70-80% share in mobile gaming, imposing high SDK migration friction and A/B revenue-loss risk on publishers, while coupling MAX auction clearing-price visibility with the AXON ML recommendation engine creates a potent two-sided data network effect. Empirical proof: 5Y median GAAP ROIC exceeds 12% (~14-18%; financials baseline 18.5%), surging from ~3.3% (FY21) and -0.8% (FY22) to ~12.5-14.9% (FY23), ~31-42% (FY24), and ~82-95% (FY25) with >100% tangible operating ROIC and operating margins expanding to 75.8% (FY25) and ~76-78% (2026). Performance auctions capture nominal ad-spend inflation ad valorem. Primary erosion threats: unilateral Apple iOS / Google Android OS privacy and attribution policy changes, EU GDPR litigation, and rival ML ad-bidding convergence from vertically integrated walled gardens (Meta, Alphabet, Amazon) and Unity LevelPlay.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While AppLovin possesses an elite near-term mediation switching-cost and ML auction flywheel (MAX + AXON) with extraordinary 2024-2026 economics, it fails the 15-year Mauboussin predictability and Munger disruption bar. Starting from a Tier 3 software/ad-tech baseline (CAP 10-15Y), Step 2 deducts 5 years under Macrotrend #1 (Automation & Cognitive Tech) and structural platform dependency: unlike vertically integrated AI hegemons owning consumer surfaces and OS infrastructure (Alphabet, Meta, Apple), AppLovin owns neither the mobile OS, app store, nor first-party consumer apps (having divested its Apps unit in June 2025). Its ~76-78% GAAP operating margins rely on third-party cross-app behavioral modeling inside Apple/Google walled gardens (which previously triggered the FY22 ATT margin collapse and ongoing EU GDPR class-action scrutiny) and face long-term AI bidding replication and agentic-commerce shifts away from mobile-game interstitials. With its pure-play AXON 2.0/e-commerce profit regime barely ~3 years old, 15+ year margin persistence is unassured. Ineligible for Calamity Tier because Anchor Gate 4 fails. Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.
column21: Multi-cycle financial record (SEC 10-K/10-Q; April 2021 IPO; FY23 continuing ops restated for Apps divestiture): FY21 rev $2,793.1M, op inc $150.0M, NI $35.3M, FCF ~$359.3M (GAAP ROIC ~3.3%); FY22 post-ATT slump rev $2,817.1M, op loss $(47.8)M, NI $(192.9)M, FCF ~$388.4M (ROIC ~-0.8%); FY23 continuing ops rev $1,842.0M (vs $3.28B pre-restatement), op inc $772.4M (41.9% margin), NI $356.7M, FCF $1,037.1M (ROIC ~12.5-14.9%); FY24 rev $3,224.1M, op inc $1,911.0M (59.3% margin), NI $1,580.0M, FCF $2,073.4M (ROIC ~31-42%); FY25 rev $5,480.7M (+70% YoY; 51.6% US / 48.4% RoW), op inc $4,151.9M (75.8% margin), NI $3,333.8M ($3,433M cont. ops), FCF $3,951.9M (118.5% FCF/NI conversion; ROIC ~82-95%). 9M 2026 momentum continued with rev $5,951M (+56% YoY; Q3 2026 >$2.18B) and NI $3,911M (~66% net margin). Portfolio & M&A history: Acquired Machine Zone (2020, ~$329-500M), Adjust (2021, ~$968M), MoPub (Jan 2022, $1.05B cash), and Wurl (Apr 2022, ~$430M); failed $17.5B unsolicited Unity bid (2022). On June 30, 2025, divested its low-margin mobile Apps studio unit to Tripledot Studios ($400M cash + ~20% equity), becoming a pure-play ad-tech platform, and launched self-serve Axon Ads Manager broadly to global e-commerce advertisers in June 2026. Balance sheet & capital allocation: Q3 2026 cash $3,173.7M vs LT debt $3,516.1M (senior notes due 2029-2054 at 5.125-5.950%; 9M26 interest $153.4M, >20x coverage), goodwill $1,516.4M; CEO Adam Foroughi holds ~11% beneficial stake and buyback authorization reached $3.6B cumulative by late 2026 (net shrinking share count despite $210.4M FY25 / ~$84M Q3 2026 SBC). Regulatory & platform risk: While the SEC closed its Oct 2025 probe on Aug 5, 2026 with no enforcement action and CapitalWatch retracted money-laundering claims with an apology in Feb 2026, AppLovin remains exposed to EU GDPR class-action litigation (The Privacy Collective / Amnesty International Netherlands), state privacy laws, and unilateral iOS/Android OS identifier/attribution rules.

column14: No durable structural moat or pricing power. Global media-buying scale, Omni/Acxiom data workflows, and multi-year MSAs create only modest administrative switching friction; clients re-pitch accounts every 3-5 years across Publicis, WPP, and boutiques, while Meta/Google/Amazon own the true ad-tech toll booths. Pre-IPG 12-14% GAAP ROIC (14.2% historical median) relied on negative media-payable working capital rather than pricing power—standalone revenue stagnated from $15.13B (FY15) to $15.69B (FY24, +0.4% nominal CAGR), far below inflation—before FY25 GAAP ROIC collapsed to ~1.9% (~9% mid-2026) post-IPG merger. Primary erosion threats: AI creative/media disintermediation, walled-garden self-serve ad suites, client in-housing, and chronic procurement fee deflation masked by principal media arbitrage.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (REJECT). Advertising holding company model lacks a defensible structural moat (3a = None) and fails Gate 3b on pricing power >= inflation and incremental return on capital. Standalone revenue was stagnant over a decade ($15.13B in FY15 to $15.69B in FY24, ~0.4% nominal CAGR), while client procurement fee pressure and generative AI execution deflation forced OMC into a defensive $13.5B all-stock IPG merger (targeting $1.5B cost cuts) and opaque principal media markups. Post-IPG GAAP ROIC fell to ~1.9% in FY25 (~9% in mid-2026) on $23.35B of goodwill/intangibles. Calamity Tier is inapplicable as both 3a fails and agency workflows face terminal Macrotrend #1 AI disintermediation. Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.
column21: Multi-cycle financial record: Pre-merger standalone revenue grew only 3.7% cumulative over nine years from $15,134.4M in FY15 (operating income $2,003.5M, 13.2% margin; diluted EPS $4.41) to $14,954.1M in FY19 ($2,126.8M EBIT; $5.86 EPS) and $15,689.1M in FY24 ($2,274.6M EBIT, 14.5% margin; $1,480.6M net income; $7.46 EPS; 5.2% organic growth), after dipping -11.9% organically in FY20. Pre-IPG 10Y median ROIC of 14.2% (12.5-13.3% in FY23-24) reflected asset-light human capital and media-payable float, while real pricing power lagged inflation as walled gardens (Google, Meta, Amazon) captured global digital ad growth. Following the Nov 26, 2025 all-stock acquisition of IPG (~$13B-$13.5B equity value plus ~$2.95B assumed senior notes), FY25 reported revenue rose to $17,271.9M (including ~1 month of IPG), but ~$1.8B-$2.1B of restructuring/severance/transaction charges and $547.1M disposition losses reduced GAAP operating income to $444.7M (2.57% margin), generating a GAAP net loss of $(54.5)M ($(0.27) EPS) and compressing FY25 ROIC to ~1.86% (Non-GAAP adj. net income ~$1.8B, $8.65 adj. EPS; OCF $2,938.2M, capex $149.8M, FCF ~$2.79B). Capital allocation and balance sheet: OMC deployed capital into bolt-ons (Flywheel Digital in 2024) and the transformational IPG merger while executing $3.21B in 9M 2026 share buybacks and $703.3M dividends; as of Sept 30, 2026, balance sheet carried $18,608.8M goodwill and $4,743.2M net intangibles ($23.35B total vs $9,950.8M equity, -$13.4B tangible equity), $9,389.5M long-term debt vs $3,796.4M cash, and $375.0M 9M 2026 interest expense (up from $182.1M in 9M25), with trailing ROIC recovering only toward ~9%.

column21: Public Track Record & Restructuring: SpaceX filed Form S-1 on May 20, 2026 and completed its Nasdaq IPO (SPCX) on June 12, 2026 at $135/share (~$75B gross / ~$85.7B net proceeds; market cap ~$1.85T as of Nov 2026), providing <5 months of public trading history and only two Form 10-Q reports (Q2 and Q3 2026). Effective Feb 2, 2026, SpaceX absorbed X.AI Holdings Corp. (which had acquired X Holdings / Twitter on Mar 28, 2025) under common-control accounting (ASC 805-50), retrospectively recasting FY2023-FY2025 statements, and subsequently closed the acquisition of Cursor on Aug 14, 2026. Multi-Year Financial Track Record: Consolidated FY2023 revenue $10,387M (EBIT -$3,298M, Net Income -$4,628M, OCF $4,520M, CapEx $4,415M, Owner FCF $1,206M); FY2024 revenue $14,015M (EBIT $1,822M, Net Income $21M, OCF $5,776M, CapEx $11,163M, Owner FCF $1,168M, GAAP ROIC 5.17%, Tangible ROIC 11.29%); FY2025 revenue $18,674M (EBIT -$2,274M, Net Income -$4,937M, OCF $6,785M, CapEx $20,906M, Owner FCF -$1,863M, GAAP ROIC -5.41%, Tangible ROIC -9.90%; 5Y median GAAP ROIC -0.12%). In Q2 2026, revenue reached $7.8B with -$541M GAAP net loss and $18.37B capex ($15.83B AI infra). In Q3 2026, revenue surged to $14,575M with $2,791M operating income and $4,404M GAAP net income (aided by ~$1.0B net other/investment income and tax benefits), but CapEx hit $19,593M ($16.44B AI infra), leaving 9M 2026 OCF of ~$13.10B against $48.07B CapEx (-$34.97B 9M FCF). Post-IPO cash/marketable securities stand near ~$89.9B-$100B vs ~$38.8B-$39.4B total debt and finance leases (up from FY2025 pre-IPO $24.75B cash / $21.97B debt). Rapidly Shifting Segment Mix & Unproven Bets: FY2025 revenue split was Connectivity/Starlink $11.39B (61%, $4.42B operating profit), Space/Launch $4.09B (22%, -$0.66B operating loss), and AI/xAI+X $3.20B (17%, -$6.36B operating loss). By Q3 2026, Super Intelligence (SI) jumped ~830% YoY to $7.56B (~51.9% of total revenue, including $608M post-close from Cursor and 1.7 GW Colossus compute scaling), overtaking Connectivity/Starlink ($5.25B, 13.6M consumer subscribers, $2.4B operating profit) and Space/Launch ($1.80B, -$7M operating loss). Growth assumptions depend heavily on uncommercialized Starship full reusability and orbital refueling plus an FCC filing for up to 1M orbital AI data-center satellites that the S-1 acknowledges have never been operated or tested in space. Governance & Related-Party Opacity: Elon Musk holds ~85.1% voting power via 10-vote Class B shares alongside ~42% equity; SpaceX uses Nasdaq's controlled-company exemption (no independent board majority), Texas incorporation (3% ownership bar for derivative suits), mandatory binding arbitration waiving investor class actions, and confirmed Oct 2026 independent-committee talks regarding a potential ~$3.5T Tesla-SpaceX merger.

column14: Fox possesses genuine brand and spectrum intangibles (Fox News Media's #1 US cable news franchise generating 42% Cable Network EBITDA margins, 29 FCC-licensed O&O local TV stations, Tubi's 110M+ MAU FAST platform, and Roku's ~100M-household North American CTV OS acquired Nov 6, 2026). However, it fails Gate 3b on both pricing power and incremental capital returns: (1) per-subscriber affiliate/retrans fee hikes (~+9-10% distribution revenue growth) cannot preserve volume in a shrinking traditional pay-TV bundle (~35% US penetration, eroding ~6-8% annually); (2) Fox rents rather than owns marquee live sports rights (~$33B in contractual commitments, ~$2.25B/yr NFL contract with 2029/2030 opt-out), allowing leagues to extract most broadcast surplus (Television EBITDA margin only 10-15%) and compressing standalone consolidated EBIT margins from 21-23% (FY16-18) to 14-16% in non-election/non-Super-Bowl years; (3) Tubi/Roku CTV ads face brutal auction pricing against YouTube, Amazon, Meta, and Netflix; and (4) the ~$22B EV Roku acquisition (~25x+ forward EBITDA, ~$10.4B new debt, ~26% Class A equity dilution) yields only ~3.5-4.5% estimated Year-1/Year-2 incremental ROIIC even with $400M planned synergies, diluting pro-forma GAAP ROIC from 14.8% down to ~8-9% (<12% hurdle).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT). Fox News and live broadcast sports confer narrow legacy bundle leverage, but the business lacks inflation-beating pricing power without customer attrition and surrenders economic rents to monopolistic sports leagues ($33B contractual commitments) while digital CTV/AVOD ads (Tubi, Roku) remain auction-priced. Critically, the Nov 6, 2026 close of the ~$22B EV Roku acquisition deploys ~140% of prior invested capital at ~3.5-4.5% post-synergy incremental ROIIC, pulling pro-forma GAAP ROIC down to ~8-9% (below the 12% proof-of-moat bar) while adding $10.4B of acquisition debt ($8.4B 364-day bridge + $2.0B term loan) and ~26% equity dilution. Calamity Tier does not apply because Anchor Gate 4 would independently fail (CAP <= 10 due to Macrotrend #1 linear TV cord-cutting/Big Tech sports bidding/CTV OS rivalry and Macrotrend #2 aging ~69-70 median Fox News audience). column21: Standalone historical financials (SEC EDGAR / FY2025-FY2026 Form 10-K, fiscal year ended June 30): FY2026 revenue reached $17,126M (+5.1% YoY vs $16,300M in FY2025), with Cable Network Programming generating $7,348M revenue ($4,662M distribution, $1,687M ads, $999M content/other) and $3,099M Segment EBITDA (42.2% margin), while Television (FOX broadcast, 29 O&O stations, Tubi) generated $9,666M revenue and $1,438M Segment EBITDA (14.9% margin; vs $945M / 10.1% in FY2025). Standalone 5Y median GAAP ROIC (14.79%, range 11.69%-19.80%) and Tangible ROIC (28.77%) passed standalone hurdles with 105.9% 5Y Owner FCF conversion ($1,428M Owner FCF / $1,468M OCF-less-capex in FY2026; $2,858M Owner FCF in FY2025), and Q1 FY2027 (ended Sept 30, 2026) posted $4,571M revenue (+22% YoY on World Cup/political ads) and +9% distribution revenue ($2.08B) aided by Fox One. However, consolidated EBIT margins compressed ~600 bps over the decade from 21.3%-22.8% (FY16-18) to 14.0%-15.6% in normal non-election/non-Super-Bowl years (FY21, FY22, FY26) under ~$33B-$35B sports rights obligations. On Nov 6, 2026, Fox closed the ~$22B EV acquisition of Roku ($95.30 cash + 0.9799 FOXA Class A shares per Roku share; legacy Fox holders ~74%, Roku ~26%; Murdoch LGC Holdco retains ~36.2% Class B voting control post-Sept 2025 trust settlement). Roku reported $4,737M revenue, $88.4M GAAP NI, $420.5M Adj EBITDA in FY2025 and $164.1M operating income ($795.7M TTM FCF) in Q3 2026; even with $400M planned Year-2 synergies, ~$675M-$830M estimated post-synergy NOPAT on ~$19.3B net EV (~$22B less Roku's $2.72B cash) equals ~3.5%-4.3% incremental ROIIC and drags pro-forma GAAP ROIC to ~8-9%. Pro-forma gross debt jumps from $6.61B (Sept 30, 2026) to ~$17.0B (including $8.4B 364-day bridge loan + $2.0B term loan), pushing S&P adjusted leverage to ~3.3x (BBB Stable) alongside unresolved $2.7B Smartmatic defamation litigation following the $787.5M Dominion settlement.

column14: Last-mile HFC network passing 70M+ homes post-Cox (Aug 2026) and bundled Spectrum Mobile (>13.5M lines) create local switching friction, but the moat fails both empirical Gate 3b hurdles. GAAP ROIC has stayed well below 12% across the cycle (~6.9%-9.0% in 2021-2025; 10Y median 7.2%; TTM mid-2026 ~5.7%-6.8%), and incremental ROIIC on $43.4B of 2022-2025 CapEx has stalled as EBIT slipped from $13.12B (2024) to $12.91B (2025) and pro forma EBITDA fell 4.0% YoY in Q3 2026. Pricing power >= inflation is absent: dual-front competition from FTTH overbuilders (>60% US fiber overlap) and 5G Fixed Wireless Access (17M+ US connections) forces price-locks and promotional mobile/streaming bundles while core internet customers erode (-400k in 2025, -172k standalone in Q2 2026, -233k pro forma in Q3 2026), culminating in a $6.33B Legacy Charter franchise impairment in Q3 2026.

column14: Comcast's local HFC/fiber plant passing 63M+ US premises, converged Xfinity Mobile bundle (10.6M lines at Q3 2026), and Universal Studios/theme park IP create regional scale barriers, but the business fails both empirical Gate 3b hurdles. GAAP ROIC has remained consistently below the 12% threshold across the cycle (7.7% in 2021, 5.3%-6.3% in 2022, 7.4%-9.4% in 2023, 8.4%-10.8% in 2024, 6.7%-8.4% in 2025, and 6.3%-6.8% TTM Q3 2026; 10Y median 8.5%), and incremental ROIIC is negligible: ~$66B of cumulative CapEx over 2020-2025 yielded lower FY2025 Operating Income ($20.67B) than FY2019 ($21.13B), with 9M 2026 EBIT falling 15% YoY to $14.62B. While stripping all $143.3B of YE 2025 goodwill, franchise rights, and intangibles mathematically lowers tangible capital to ~$43.3B, franchise rights ($59.4B) reflect paid-for network access and ex-goodwill invested capital (~$125B) still earns only ~12.6% with zero incremental EBIT compounding. Crucially, pricing power >= inflation has broken down: broadband price hikes triggered accelerating churn (-411k total domestic broadband subs in 2024; -711k in 2025) to FTTH fiber overbuilders and 5G Fixed Wireless Access, forcing a 2025-2026 pivot to lower everyday pricing, multi-year price locks, and free wireless lines that turned residential broadband ARPU negative (-3.1% Q1 2026, -3.8% Q2 2026, -2.9% Q3 2026) while still losing subscribers (-376k residential broadband subs across Q1-Q3 2026).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT). column21: Consolidated revenue plateaued from $121.43B (2022) to $121.57B (2023), $123.73B (2024), and $123.71B (2025), before declining 6.1% YoY reported in Q3 2026 to $29.30B (+0.5% pro forma; 9M 2026 revenue $90.70B) following the January 2026 spin-off of cable networks into Versant (VSNT). Domestic broadband total subscribers fell from ~32.25M (YE23) to 31.84M (YE24, -411k) and 31.26M (YE25, -711k), with residential broadband declining to ~28.34M by Q3 2026 (-65k Q1, -167k Q2, -144k Q3 2026) and ARPU reversing to -3.1%, -3.8%, and -2.9% YoY despite Xfinity Mobile reaching 10.6M lines. YE2025 balance sheet carried $98.94B total debt, $9.48B cash, $96.90B Comcast equity ($97.15B total), $65.68B net PP&E, $61.50B goodwill, $59.37B franchise rights, $22.47B other intangibles, and $27.79B deferred tax liabilities; by Q3 2026 total debt declined to ~$87.37B ($76.6B net debt), interest expense ran $4.41B in FY2025 and $3.11B in 9M 2026 (~4.7x EBIT/interest), share buybacks were suspended starting Q3 2026, and Brian Roberts retains nondilutable 33.3% Class B voting control on ~1% economic equity.

column14: Nationwide licensed wireless spectrum ($128.1B net licenses at FY25 plus $23B EchoStar spectrum closed Jul 2026) and dense fiber infrastructure (39.7M passings at Q3 2026, expanding via $5.75B Lumen fiber assets) deter a fourth facilities-based national entrant (shown by EchoStar's MNO exit). However, AT&T fails Proof of Moat decisively: 5Y median GAAP ROIC is 6.41% (10Y range -1.28% to 8.72%; FY25 8.72%) and 5Y median ex-goodwill tangible ROIC is 8.92% even before including $128B+ spectrum licenses in operating capital, while ~$94.1B of FY21-FY25 capex generated flat-to-negative EBIT ($25.9B in FY21 vs $24.2B in FY25). Pricing power >= inflation also fails: nominal $1-$2 wireless plan increases are eroded by 36-month $1,000+ handset promotional bill-credit subsidies (FY25 Mobility service revenue +3.1%, Q3 2026 postpaid phone ARPU $58.90), while Business Wireline revenue fell 8.4% to $17.2B with an $(816)M operating loss. Primary threats: 3-way MNO promotional churn rivalry (T-Mobile, Verizon), cable MVNO bundling (Charter/Comcast), fixed wireless/LEO satellite competition, legacy enterprise wireline decay, and perpetual 5G/fiber capex absorption.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT – G3 Moat & Pricing). While AT&T owns hard-to-replicate US wireless spectrum and fiber assets serving essential daily connectivity (passing Gates 1 and 2), its 5Y median GAAP ROIC of 6.41% (8.92% ex-goodwill tangible ROIC before $128B+ spectrum licenses) and low-single-digit incremental ROIIC fall far short of the >=12% GAAP / >=15% tangible Proof of Moat bar. Three-player wireless competition forces heavy 36-month smartphone subsidies that neutralize nominal plan hikes, while legacy Business Wireline is shrinking into operating losses ($(816)M in FY25). column21: Business model & revenue mix: Founded 2005 and listed March 21, 2024 ($34 IPO). Revenue is ~94% digital advertising ($847M of $895M in Q3 2026) and ~6% AI data licensing/other ($140.0M in FY25; $48M in Q3 2026, anchored by ~$60M/yr Google and ~$70M/yr OpenAI deals), concentrated 81.1% in the U.S. ($1,785.6M) and 18.9% international ($417.0M) in FY25. Multi-year financial history (FY21–9M 2026): FY21 revenue $484.9M / -$127.2M op loss / -$127.9M net loss; FY22 $666.7M / -$172.2M op loss / -$158.6M net loss / -$94.0M OCF; FY23 $804.0M / -$140.2M op loss / -$90.8M net loss / -$75.1M OCF; FY24 $1,300.4M / -$560.6M op loss / -$484.3M net loss (including $801.7M IPO-triggered SBC) / $222.1M OCF / ~$215.8M FCF / 90.5% gross margin; FY25 $2,202.5M (+69% YoY) / $442.0M op income / $529.7M net income / $690.9M OCF / $684.2M FCF ($6.7M capex) / $343.2M SBC / 91.2% gross margin / ~61.1% FY25 ROIC. 2026 YTD scaled to Q1 $663M rev ($204M NI), Q2 $805M rev ($253M NI), and Q3 2026 $895M rev (+53% YoY), 91.5% gross margin, $283M NI ($1.40 diluted EPS), $364M OCF, $363M FCF ($1M capex), and $402M Adj. EBITDA (45% margin), with Q4 2026 revenue guided at $1.00B–$1.03B. Balance sheet & capital allocation: $3,033.4M cash & marketable securities as of Sept 30, 2026 ($2,476.8M at YE25), negligible debt (~$21–25M), $42.2M goodwill, $3.58B equity, and $340.0M repurchased across 2.19M shares in 9M 2026 under a $1B Feb 2026 authorization (0.1% YTD net dilution; 206.3M diluted shares), offset by dual-class voting control (Advance Publications / CEO Steve Huffman), Tencent stake, $322.1M 9M 2026 SBC (~15% of Q3 rev), and ongoing Rule 10b5-1 insider sales. Gate 2 & corroborating structural risks: Australia included Reddit in its late-2025 under-16 social media ban (Reddit is suing in the High Court in Nov 2026) alongside UK Online Safety Act, EU DSA, and US FTC/state AG minor-safety inquiries. Beyond Gate 2, 4 of 5 years (2021–2024) were GAAP loss-making (negative historical ROIC, lacking multi-cycle >=12% proof and prior-cycle EPS peak), while Google AI Overviews/AI Mode zero-click summaries cannibalize search discovery—U.S. DAUq fell 2% YoY to 50.7M in Q3 2026 (vs 51.6M in Q3 2025; global DAUq flat QoQ at 130.3M) with management flagging potential low-double-digit sequential DAUq declines in Q4 2026 amid search traffic drops and login-wall tests, compounded by unpaid volunteer moderator friction and AI bot/GEO spam threatening forum authenticity.

column11: 57% of segment operating income ($10.0B of $17.55B in FY25; 54% in Q3 FY26) derives from Experiences—heavily weighted to big-ticket destination theme park vacations, resorts, and Disney Cruise Line voyages ($7.82B Parks/Cruises OI; $60B 10-year capex commitment)—which Gate 2 explicitly rejects as deferrable, discretionary leisure cyclicals rather than essential needs or everyday habits.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). While Disney owns iconic multi-generational family IP and a profitable streaming bundle (Disney+/Hulu DTC generated $1.33B FY25 OI, 7.6% of total segment profit), its dominant economic engine and capital sink is discretionary destination leisure: Experiences accounts for 57.0% of FY25 segment operating income ($9.995B of $17.551B; 54.3% in Q3 FY26) and absorbs the bulk of a ~$60B 10-year park and cruise-ship expansion plan. Big-ticket family park vacations and cruise voyages are deferrable discretionary outlays (Parks & Resorts OI fell 30.5% peak-to-trough during FY09-FY10, and 2025-2026 middle-class pricing fatigue forced renewed ticket/resort discounting). Anchor Gate 2 is non-waivable under Calamity Tier (and structurally DIS also fails Gate 3b on sub-hurdle 3.8% 5Y median GAAP ROIC / 10.7% tangible ROIC and Gate 4 on linear cord-cutting, sports-rights inflation, and UGC/AI attention fragmentation). Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.
column21: FY2025 10-K segment mix ($94,425M consolidated revenue; $17,551M total segment OI; $13,013M GAAP EBIT): Experiences $36,156M rev / $9,995M OI (Domestic Parks & Experiences $25,191M rev / $6,375M OI; International $6,520M rev / $1,442M OI; Consumer Products $4,445M rev / $2,178M OI); Entertainment $42,466M rev / $4,674M OI (Linear Networks $9,364M rev / $2,955M OI, down 14% YoY after falling 21% in FY23 and 16% in FY24; DTC $24,614M rev / $1,327M OI; Content Sales/Licensing $8,488M rev / $392M OI); Sports $17,672M rev / $2,882M OI. Q3 FY2026 (ended June 27, 2026): revenue $25.25B (+7% YoY), segment OI $5.56B (+21% YoY), with Experiences at $9.97B rev / $3.02B OI (54.3% of segment OI), Entertainment $11.35B rev / $1.68B OI (SVOD $5.53B rev / $712M OI, 12.9% margin), and Sports $858M OI (-17% YoY). Cyclicality proof: during the Great Recession, Parks & Resorts OI fell 25% in FY09 ($1,897M to $1,418M) and 7% in FY10 ($1,318M) amid attendance and rate discounting; in 2025-2026, consumer wallet fatigue and Universal Epic Universe competition prompted expanded promotional park/resort deals. Multi-cycle capital efficiency & cash flow: following the $71.3B 21st Century Fox acquisition (FY19) and ~$11B cumulative DTC streaming losses (FY19-FY24), FY21-FY25 GAAP ROIC (at 21% statutory tax on GAAP EBIT) ran 1.8%, 3.8%, 3.0%, 4.5%, and 6.8% (5Y median 3.8%; third-party TTM mid-2026 ~7.6%-7.8%; 10Y ref 7.2%), while Tangible Operating ROIC (excluding $73.29B goodwill and $9.27B net intangibles in FY25) ran 6.5%, 12.0%, 8.7%, 10.7%, and 15.0% (5Y median 10.7%). OCF / CapEx / FCF progressed from $5.57B / $3.58B / $1.99B (FY21) and $6.00B / $4.94B / $1.06B (FY22) to $13.97B / $5.41B / $8.56B (FY24) and $18.10B / $8.02B / $10.08B (FY25); 9M FY26 OCF was $12.52B with ~$6.8B CapEx and $5.74B FCF. FY25 GAAP Net Income ($12.40B vs FY18 peak $12.60B) included a one-time $3,277M non-cash Hulu tax benefit (~$9.13B underlying). Strategic & balance sheet commitments: ~$60B 10-year Experiences/cruise CapEx plan, NBA ($2.6B-$2.8B/yr, 2025-2036) and NFL ($2.7B/yr plus 10% ESPN equity traded for NFL Network/RedZone) rights inflation, ~$9B total Hulu 33% buyout (closed June 2025), Star India / Reliance JioStar JV (37% stake, $1.5B+ FY24 impairments), Fubo / Hulu+Live TV 70% merger (Oct 2025), and $1.5B Epic Games stake. Q3 FY26 borrowings stood at $46.04B ($8.63B current, $37.41B long-term) against $5.19B cash ($40.86B net debt; FY21-FY25 EBIT/net interest covered 2.1x, 4.7x, 4.2x, 6.6x, 10.0x) while targeting >=$9B FY26 buybacks ($7.2B completed in 9M26) and paying $0.75/sh semi-annual dividends. Governance: Experiences Chairman Josh D'Amaro succeeded Bob Iger as CEO on March 18, 2026 (Dana Walden appointed President & CCO; Iger senior advisor through Dec 2026).

column11: Discretionary out-of-home live entertainment easily deferred in recessions or halted in public-health shocks, combined with acute societal, legislative, and antitrust hostility targeting its core Ticketing profit engine (April 2026 federal jury monopolization verdict with 33 states seeking Ticketmaster divestiture, plus ongoing FTC junk-fee/BOTS Act litigation).
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Concert promotion and festival attendance are episodic, big-ticket discretionary outlays—not an essential Western necessity or high-frequency everyday habit—and face extreme societal, legislative, and antitrust ruin risk against the Ticketmaster fee engine (~48% of consolidated AOI). Following the DOJ's March 2026 behavioral settlement (15% primary fee cap, open marketplace, 13 amphitheater booking divestitures), 33 state AGs plus D.C. won an April 15, 2026 federal jury verdict finding illegal monopolization on all counts ($1.72/ticket overcharge) and are pursuing a forced structural breakup of Ticketmaster before Judge Arun Subramanian, alongside an FTC deceptive-fee/BOTS Act lawsuit that survived dismissal in September 2026. Calamity Tier is ineligible because Anchor Gate 2 fails non-waivably, and even downstream Gates 3b, 4, 5, and 6 exhibit chronic structural flaws (~8.5%-10% multi-cycle GAAP ROIC, breakup runway risk, $60M/yr CEO pay amid consumer backlash, 3.96x FY25 EBIT interest coverage, $9.75B total debt at Q3 2026, and $550.8M FY25 redeemable NCI accretion leaving negative -$0.24 diluted EPS available to common). Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.
column21: Business & Segment Economics (FY2024-FY2025 10-K & Q3 2026 10-Q): FY2025 consolidated revenue reached $25.20B (+8.8% YoY from $23.16B in FY24 and $22.73B in FY23, vs $11.55B in FY19 and pandemic trough $6.27B in FY21). Segment mix shows a capital-heavy, razor-thin promotion funnel supporting fee extraction: Concerts generated $20.86B revenue (82.8% of total) but only $687M AOI (3.3% margin), whereas Ticketing ($3.08B revenue, ~$1.14B AOI) and Sponsorship & Advertising ($1.33B revenue, $845M AOI) supplied ~84% of consolidated AOI ($2.37B). Q3 2026 revenue grew 19% YoY to $10.11B with Q3 operating income of $892.0M. Capital Efficiency & Earnings Quality: Reported 10Y avg ROIC in LYV.json is 8.5% (2021-2025 GAAP ROIC medians ~7.3%-10.3%). On FY2025 GAAP EBIT of $1,251.2M ($824.5M in FY24 after $454.9M Astroworld contingencies; $1,084.9M in FY23), after-tax NOPAT (~$839M-$938M) over net invested capital excluding third-party client cash ($1.6B FY25; $2.67B Q3 2026) and unearned event-related deferred revenue ($3.98B FY25; $3.82B Q3 2026) yields ~8%-9% GAAP ROIC; third-party screens claiming >35% ROIC treat fan ticket prepayments as excess corporate cash. Consolidated net income was $690.7M in FY25 ($1,131.1M in FY24 aided by a $601.2M tax valuation allowance release), with $496.0M attributable to Live Nation; however, accretion of redeemable noncontrolling interests ($550.8M in FY25 vs $258.1M in FY24 and $247.4M in FY23) turned FY25 net income available to common stockholders negative at $(54.8)M ($(0.24) diluted EPS vs $2.74 in FY24). Cash Flow, Balance Sheet & Governance: FY25 OCF of $1,395.3M minus $1,061.7M CapEx (up from $646.6M FY24 and $438.6M FY23; $1.1B-$1.2B guided for FY26) and $251.0M NCI distributions left just $82.6M in common FCF, despite management highlighting $1,298.2M Adjusted FCF. Total debt climbed from $8.20B at YE25 to $9.75B at Q3 2026 ($1.86B current + $7.89B LT) plus $2.20B PV of operating lease liabilities and $924.5M redeemable NCI (YE25), against $8.26B total cash ($2.67B client cash; $3.82B event deferred revenue, leaving ~$1.77B unencumbered corporate cash) and $456.8M Live Nation stockholders' equity (negative tangible equity given $2.89B goodwill and $1.45B intangibles at YE25). EBIT interest coverage was 3.96x in FY25 ($1,251.2M / $316.0M), 2.53x in FY24, and 3.10x in FY23. Liberty Media spun off its ~29.7% stake into Liberty Live Holdings in Dec 2025; CEO Michael Rapino earned ~$32.6M in FY25 and signed a 2026 extension through 2031 at a $60M/yr target package plus $20M upfront RSUs. Legal/Regulatory: March 2026 DOJ settlement ($280M fund, 15% primary fee cap, open ticketing marketplace, 13 amphitheater booking divestitures under Tunney Act review); April 15, 2026 jury liability verdict in favor of 33 states + D.C. pursuing forced Ticketmaster breakup; September 2026 denial of LYV's motion to dismiss the FTC/7-state BOTS Act and hidden junk-fee (up to 44%) lawsuit.

column14: Global #1 paid SVOD scale (325M+ paying households at end-2025, ~$51.1B FY2026E revenue) amortizes ~$17-20B/yr in cash content spend across roughly 3-5x more paying subscribers than pure-play SVOD peers, delivering low cost-per-hour-watched to consumers while generating ~29.5-31.5% operating margins. Empirical proof of moat: 5Y median GAAP ROIC ~16-17% (FY2021-FY2025, troughing at ~12.1-13.7% in FY2022 and expanding to ~25.7-26.9% in FY2025 and ~28-30.6% TTM in 2026) with zero goodwill and >50% incremental ROIIC; US Standard ad-free pricing stepped up from $9.99 (2015) to $19.99/mo (Mar 2026) with ~2% or lower churn. Primary erosion threats: zero contractual switching costs (1-click cancel), attention substitution toward free/UGC video (YouTube/TikTok), generative AI lowering video creation barriers, live sports rights cost inflation, and Paramount-Skydance-WBD consolidation.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Netflix is the undisputed SVOD scale leader today (325M+ households, ~26-30% ROIC, $19.99/mo pricing power, fortress net debt <0.7x earnings), it fails the 15+ year Munger runway bar under the Tier 3 Media/Entertainment base rate (10-15Y CAP) combined with a -5Y haircut on Macrotrend #1 (Automation & Cognitive Tech / AI Disruption). Unlike full-stack AI hegemons (Alphabet/YouTube) or physical-world monopolies, Netflix has zero contractual switching costs and relies on a ~$20B/yr depreciating content treadmill. Generative AI video (Veo, Sora) compresses studio production barriers for creator platforms—where YouTube already commands ~15.8% of US TV viewing vs. Netflix's ~7.7-8%—while 2026 saw flattening watch-time growth, a cut in 2026 ad-revenue guidance ($3.0B to $2.7B), ~1,000 layoffs (6% of staff) with top content leadership exits, escalating live sports rights commitments, a newly consolidated $111B Paramount-Skydance-WBD rival, and Netflix's own Dec 2025 $82.7B defensive bid for Warner Bros. (before walking away in Feb 2026). Not eligible for Calamity Pass because Gate 4 is non-waivable. Downstream Gates 5-6 bypassed per waterfall.
column21: Multi-cycle financial record (FY2016-FY2025 & 9M 2026): Revenue scaled from $20.16B (FY19) to $39.00B (FY24), $45.18B (FY25, +15.9% YoY), and $51.1B guided for FY26 (+13% YoY; Q1 $12.25B, Q2 $12.56B, Q3 $12.87B). Operating margin expanded from 4.3% (FY16) and 17.8% (FY22) to 26.7% (FY24), 29.5% (FY25, $13.33B EBIT), and 31.5% FY26 guidance (9M 2026 EBIT $12.61B; Q3 2026 34.6% margin, Q4 guided 26.0% incl. ~120 bps layoff/severance drag). GAAP Net Income rose from $187M (FY16) and $4.49B (FY22) to $8.71B (FY24), $10.98B (FY25), and $12.35B in 9M 2026 (incl. $2.8B pre-tax WBD breakup fee). After negative FCF during the 2016-2019 buildout (-$1.66B to -$3.14B) and -$0.13B in FY21, post-inflection FCF reached $6.93B (FY23), $6.92B (FY24), and $9.46B (FY25; cumulative FY23-25 FCF conversion 92.9% of GAAP NI), with FY26 FCF guided to ~$12.0B (~$9.2B organic ex-$2.8B WBD fee) after $14.93B in 9M 2026 cash content additions (~$20B/yr pace). ROIC improved from ~7.5% (FY16) and ~12.1-13.7% (FY22) to ~22.6% (FY24), ~26.9% (FY25), and ~28-30.6% TTM (2026), with $0 goodwill. Footprint & pricing: 325M+ paid memberships (UCAN ~40-43% of revenue, EMEA largest sub base, LATAM double-digit growth, APAC volume engine); US Standard rose from $9.99 (2015-17) to $19.99/mo (Mar 2026), Ad-tier $8.99/mo (~47% of new sign-ups in key markets), Premium $26.99/mo, with churn ~2% or under. M&A & balance sheet context: Dec 2025 agreed to buy Warner Bros. studios/HBO Max for ~$82.7B EV (amended to ~$83B all-cash Jan 2026) before walking away Feb 26, 2026 when Paramount Skydance bid $111B, collecting a $2.8B termination fee (and incurring ~$85M financing termination amortization); resumed aggressive buybacks ($10.7B in 9M 2026, $4.8B in Q3 2026; SBC only $134M in Q3). Q3 2026 balance sheet holds $8.22B cash/ST investments vs. $15.13B gross debt ($6.91B net debt, <0.7x FY25 NI), $26.62B equity, 17.2x FY25 / 20.3x 9M26 EBIT interest coverage, and A2/A credit ratings. Gate 4 disruption basis: Nielsen The Gauge shows YouTube at ~15.8% US TV share (~2x Netflix's ~7.7-8%); generative AI video (Veo, Sora) fuels creator ecosystems while Netflix's 2026 total viewing-hour growth flattened, FY26 ad-revenue guidance fell from $3.0B to $2.7B, ~1,000 staff (6%) were laid off alongside CCO/Film chief departures, live sports rights outlays (WWE $500M/yr, NFL, FIFA) rose, and Paramount-Skydance-WBD consolidated.

column14: Owns premier Hollywood IP and broadcast intangibles (Warner Bros., Paramount Pictures, HBO, DC, Harry Potter, Top Gun, Star Trek, CBS, CNN, TNT Sports, and 203M combined DTC subscribers), which prevent exact duplication. However, these intangibles fail empirical proof of moat and net pricing power: Paramount Global's 10Y median ROIC is 4.5% (GAAP ROIC never reached 12% in 2019-2025, turning negative in 2024-2025), WBD's 2023-2025 ROIC ran ~2-3%, and standalone 9M 2026 Paramount Skydance annualized Tangible Operating ROIC (~8%) and GAAP ROIC (~5.7%) remain well below the 12%/15% hurdles. Primary erosion threats: secular pay-TV cord-cutting shrinking the core linear profit pool (-7% YoY at Paramount TV Media in Q3 2026; -12% YoY revenue / -21% YoY EBITDA at WBD Linear in FY25), economic rent extraction by creative talent and sports leagues (NFL, NCAA, UFC; WBD's loss of US NBA rights), and fierce DTC streaming competition (Netflix, YouTube, Disney, Amazon, Apple) forcing heavy content reinvestment and bundle discounting.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT). Passes Gate 1 (established studio/TV/streaming model) and Gate 2 under the v6.19+ 'likely to' staple household entertainment standard (CBS live sports/news, HBO/Paramount+ household streaming, studio content). While iconic IP franchises support an Intangibles archetype (3a), the combined Paramount-Skydance-WBD business fails Gate 3b structurally: multi-cycle GAAP and tangible ROIC sit persistently in the low-to-mid single digits (well below 12%), economic rents are captured by sports leagues and talent, and linear TV cord-cutting destroys net pricing power across the legacy cash-cow segment. Ineligible for v6.25 Calamity Tier because Gate 3b failure is chronic rather than a temporary blip on an intact >=12-15% ROIC engine, and Anchor Gate 4 (CAP < 15Y) would also fail under secular linear decay, digital/AI attention fragmentation, and $87B gross debt refinancing risk. Downstream Gates 4-6 left null per strict sequential waterfall.
column21: Multi-cycle financial history demonstrates structural capital destruction rather than compounder economics. Pre-merger Paramount Global posted 10Y median ROIC of 4.5% (2019-2024 ROIC: 9.64%, 9.07%, 11.41%, 3.23%, ~3-4%, and negative/-13.0% GAAP in 2024), operating margins sliding from 18.2% (2021) to 4.2% (2022), -4.2% (2023), -21.1% (2024), and -0.1% (2025, -$35M operating income on $29.03B revenue), and FCF falling from ~$1.2-1.3B (2022) to ~$308M (2025). Pre-acquisition WBD saw revenue contract from $41.32B (2023) to $39.32B (2024) and $37.30B (2025), with FCF halving from $6.16B (2023) to $3.09B (2025), FY25 operating income of just $738M (against $2,085M net interest expense), and ~2-3% ROIC; WBD Global Linear Networks revenue fell 12% YoY to $17.66B and Adjusted EBITDA fell 21% YoY to $6.41B in FY25 (vs $2.55B Studios and $1.37B Streaming). Standalone Q3 2026 Paramount Skydance (reported Nov 9, 2026) generated $7.03B revenue (+5% YoY), $368M operating income ($1.5B 9M26), $1.0B Adjusted EBITDA, $73M GAAP net earnings, and $353M 9M26 FCF ($101M Q3 ex-restructuring; $31M reported net of $174M transformation costs): TV Media ($3.0B Q3 rev, -7% YoY; $3.1B 9M26 Adj. EBITDA) still supplies the overwhelming majority of segment profit vs DTC ($2.5B Q3 rev, $225M Adj. EBITDA; 82.2M Paramount+ subs) and Studios ($1.5B Q3 rev, $329M 9M26 Adj. EBITDA). Even after Skydance purchase-accounting write-downs (Q2 2026 goodwill $2.03B, intangibles $5.65B), 9M26 annualized EBIT of ~$2.0B (~$1.5B NOPAT) on ~$18.7B standalone tangible invested capital yields only ~8.0% Tangible ROIC (~5.7% GAAP ROIC). On Oct 6, 2026, Paramount Skydance closed the $110.9B EV ($31/sh) WBD buyout using $47B non-voting Class B equity (incl. ~$24B Gulf SWFs: PIF, L'imad, QIA) and $57B new secured debt, leaving ~$87B pro forma gross debt (~$77-80B net debt, >6x-7.8x leverage, S&P/Fitch BB / Moody's Ba3), dual-class control (<1% Class A shares holding 100% votes via Ellison family/RedBird), a $200M Q4 2026 Warner Bros. film slate EBITDA headwind, and unproven reliance on $6B 3-year cost synergies.

column11: Discretionary combat sports, scripted wrestling, and big-ticket VIP event hospitality (IMG/On Location ~29% of FY25 revenue) rather than an essential Western need or universal daily habit; compounded by antitrust litigation (UFC $375M settlement & active Johnson v. Zuffa spoliation hearings), Saudi sovereign site-fee/JV concentration, and sports-betting/regulatory exposure.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Despite strong UFC and WWE broadcast rights step-ups (Paramount+, Netflix, ESPN), TKO monetizes discretionary spectator entertainment and cyclical big-ticket VIP corporate hospitality/agency services (IMG/On Location, ~29% of FY25 revenue, which posted $(48)M Adj. EBITDA in FY24) rather than an essential Western need or low-risk daily consumer staple. Zuffa with Oct 2026 spoliation hearings), Muhammad Ali Act reform lobbying for Zuffa Boxing, growing revenue reliance on Saudi sovereign payouts (GEA/Sela), and legacy WWE misconduct litigation. column21: Model & Segment Breakdown: TKO combines UFC, WWE, and (via the Feb 28, 2025 $3.25B all-stock common-control acquisition from parent Endeavor) IMG, On Location, and PBR. FY25 consolidated revenue was $4,735.2M (vs ~$4,884.2M FY24): WWE $1,709.4M ($896.5M Adj. EBITDA, 52.4% margin), UFC $1,502.2M ($851.0M Adj. EBITDA, 56.7% margin), and IMG/On Location $1,367.3M (28.9% of revenue; $160.0M Adj. EBITDA in FY25 vs $(48.0)M loss in FY24 due to Paris Olympics hospitality losses). Multi-year rights include WWE Raw on Netflix (10-yr), WWE PLEs on ESPN DTC ($1.6B/5-yr starting 2026), and UFC US rights on Paramount+/CBS ($7.7B/7-yr starting 2026, ending traditional PPV). Capital Efficiency & Earnings: Consolidated GAAP Operating Income was $376-$447M (FY23), $30.9M (FY24, restated), $835.0M (FY25), and $1,145.8M (9M 2026); GAAP ROIC was ~3.4% (FY23), ~0.2% (FY24), and ~5.7% (FY25) against $11,773M combined goodwill ($8,445M) and other intangibles ($3,328M) and $9,215.7M total equity/NCI (v1 median ROIC 11.5%). FY25 Consolidated Net Income was $546.2M ($195.4M attributable to TKO Class A; FY24 $(246.0)M loss); 9M 2026 Net Income was ~$831.6M ($289.6M Class A). Cash Flow & Leverage: FY25 OCF $1,285.7M and FCF $1,159.0M; 9M 2026 OCF $1,540.6M and FCF $1,474.0M (boosted by ~$604.0M net On Location FIFA World Cup 2026 escrow prepayments; CapEx $66.6M). Gross debt expanded from $3,724.1M (YE25; $831.1M cash; 4.1x FY25 EBIT/interest) to $4,647M (Sept 30, 2026; $630.9M unrestricted cash; 5.7x 9M26 coverage), followed by pricing $1.0B of 6.500% Senior Secured Notes due 2031 in Nov 2026 to fund share repurchases (>$1.6B returned YTD Q3 2026). Governance & Legal Risks: Up-C structure controlled (~59%) by private Endeavor/Silver Lake; CEO Ari Emanuel ($67M+ reported pay, ~71% 2024 Say-on-Pay support); $375M Le v. Zuffa antitrust settlement (approved Feb 2025); active Johnson v. Zuffa class action (Oct 2026 spoliation sanction hearings); Zuffa Boxing JV with Saudi PIF-backed Sela; and legacy Vince McMahon/Janel Grant litigation (transitioned to arbitration mid-2026).

column14: Crown jewels Dow Jones (WSJ Lindy brand, B2B Risk & Compliance, and OPIS energy/chemical benchmarks with >90% retention) and 61%-owned REA Group (~61% EBITDA margin Australian property portal network effect) generate ~77% of pre-corporate Segment EBITDA ($1,404M of $1,830M in FY2026). However, News Corp fails Gate 3b empirically on both consolidated capital efficiency and group-wide pricing power: (1) 10-year GAAP ROIC ranged from 2.84% to 7.82% (FY2022-FY2026 5Y median 5.90%), reaching only ~7.8%-8.2% in peak FY2026 even after divesting Foxtel (April 2025); (2) continuing EBIT barely moved from $981M (FY2022) to $1,029M (FY2026) despite ~$1.45B spent on OPIS/Base Chemicals (2022) and ~$407M-$426M annual CapEx, showing weak incremental ROIIC; and (3) ~57% of FY2026 revenue ($5,125M across News Media $2,227M, Book Publishing $2,288M, and Move/Realtor.com $610M) lacks pricing power >= inflation without volume/share loss. Primary erosion threats: secular print circulation and ad decay plus AI search disintermediation in News Media; Amazon buyer power in trade books; and intensifying property portal rivalry via CoStar's Aug 2025 A$3.0B Domain acquisition, Homes.com in the US, and REA Group's Sept 2026 ACCC enforceable undertaking eliminating restrictive agent bundle clauses.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT). column20: Fails Gate 1 (REJECT). column21: Historical operating performance prior to the 2026 restructuring failed compounder standards: following the Dec 31, 2023 all-stock merger with DISH Network, consolidated revenue contracted sequentially from ~$18.63B (FY22) and ~$17.02B (FY23) to ~$15.8B (FY24) and $15.00B (FY25), while operating losses persisted (~-$304M in FY24; -$91.1M operating loss, -$17.6B non-cash impairments, and -$14.50B GAAP net loss in FY25), FY25 FCF was -$1.07B, and historical median ROIC sat at 2.5% (TTM ~0.7%-2.8%, well below WACC). column14: National 5G macro tower network and $98.0B of scarce FCC-licensed wireless spectrum (led by 2.5 GHz mid-band, 600 MHz low-band, and C-band/UScellular holdings) create a high physical and regulatory barrier against greenfield fourth-carrier entry. Pricing power is constrained by number portability, promotional handset subsidies from AT&T and Verizon, cable MVNO fixed-mobile bundles (Comcast, Charter, Optimum), elevated ~1.09% postpaid phone churn and Price Lock arbitration pushback on 2024-2026 legacy plan hikes, and emerging SpaceX/Starlink hybrid D2D competition following its 800 MHz and EchoStar spectrum deals.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (3b = N, REJECT). column21: Multi-cycle SEC EDGAR financials (FY2016-2025): Revenue scaled from $37.5B (FY2016) to $68.4B (FY2020 Sprint merger) and $88.3B (FY2025; service revenue $71.3B, +8% YoY). Growth relied heavily on international/Mainland China expansion while core U.S. revenue stagnated/dipped ~3% against Alo Yoga, Vuori, and dupe competition. Leadership instability further compounded product execution misses: CEO Calvin McDonald stepped down effective Jan 31, 2026 amid founder Chip Wilson criticism, with CFO Meghan Frank and CCO André Maestrini serving as interim co-CEOs and Marti Morfitt as Executive Chair.

column14: Iconic global intangible equity (Swoosh, Jordan Brand), Air/ZoomX footwear IP, unmatched pro-league and athlete endorsement scale ($46.4B revenue), and demand-creation budget prevent direct arbitrage by generic makers. Empirical proof across the cycle holds via 21.5% 10Y median ROIC (moderating to ~15% in FY25 and ~11.8%-18.7% in FY26 trough) and ~42.7%-42.9% trough gross margins, with selective FY26 tariff-offset price increases lifting gross margin +20 bps. Primary erosion threats are severe: global footwear share contracted from high-20s% toward low-20s% as On (>60% GM), Hoka, and Adidas captured running and lifestyle demand, while retro franchise over-supply and wholesale reset depressed FY25-FY26 net income ~45% below prior peaks.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Nike passes Gates 1-3 on transparent asset-light economics, entrenched everyday footwear/sportswear habits in Western markets, and multi-cycle intangible brand ROIC (21.5% historical median), it fails the 15-year CAP and 5-Macrotrend Secular Resilience bar. Outside View: branded athletic footwear is Consumer Discretionary with 3-7 year style and running-innovation cycles and shared Asian contract factories, allowing agile insurgents (On, Hoka) and resurgent peers (Adidas, Anta/Li-Ning) to erode share rapidly—stalling FY26 revenue at $46.40B (+0.2%) and shrinking Net Income further to $3.11B (-3.4%) nearly two years into CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround. Inside View: active, unhedged Macrotrend [3] (Geopolitical Realignment & Supply Chain Reshoring) headwind—FY26 10-K shows 95% of NIKE Brand footwear is manufactured in Vietnam (52%), Indonesia (27%), and China (16%), leaving margins directly exposed to U.S. tariffs and US-China friction alongside persistent Greater China demand weakness.
column21: Multi-cycle financial record: Historical 10Y median ROIC is 21.5%. In FY25 (ended May 31, 2025), revenue dropped ~10% YoY (-9% currency-neutral) to $46,309M, gross profit fell 14% to $19,790M (~42.7% GM), Net Income fell ~44% to $3,219M, OCF was $3,698M (~$2.4B FCF), and ROIC moderated to ~15%. In FY26 (ended May 31, 2026), turnaround stabilization remained elusive: revenue was flat at $46,398M (+0.2% YoY), Net Income declined another ~3.4% to $3,108M, FCF slipped to ~$2.1B-$2.2B, and ROIC ranged ~11.8%-18.7% depending on capital adjustments, though gross margin edged up +20 bps to ~42.9% via selective pricing and inventory cleanup. Channel & regional mix: NIKE Direct fell from $18.8B (FY25) to $17.7B (FY26) as CEO Elliott Hill's 'Win Now' and 'Pace' plans re-engaged wholesale partners (Foot Locker, Dick's, JD Sports, specialty running), lifting North America wholesale at the cost of structurally lower wholesale unit gross margins while Greater China and EMEA remained soft. Supply chain & geopolitical concentration (FY25/FY26 10-Ks): 100% independent contract manufacturing; NIKE Brand footwear concentrated ~52% in Vietnam (51% FY25), ~27% in Indonesia (28% FY25), and ~16% in China (17% FY25), with 4 vendors representing ~59%-60% of footwear volume; apparel spanned 34 countries across 321 factories (303 in FY25). Balance sheet remained healthy at FY26 end ($9,030M cash & short-term investments vs $7,941M total debt), but structural fashion-cycle fade, specialty running share loss to On/Hoka, and unhedged Asian tariff/supply-chain exposure cap CAP at 10 years.

column11: Discretionary aspirational apparel and lifestyle goods easily deferred or traded down during downturns; lacks the essential necessity, daily habit, or supply-constrained ultra-luxury scarcity (Hermès, LVMH, Ferrari) required under Munger's 'likely to spend' standard.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). column21: Multi-cycle trajectory: Net revenue moved from ~$7.62B (FY2015) to ~$6.16B (FY2020) and ~$6.63B (FY2024) before accelerating to ~$7.08B in FY2025 (+7% YoY) and ~$8.11B in FY2026 (+14.6% YoY reported, +12% constant currency). Governance & capital allocation: Dual-class voting structure (Class B 10 votes/share held largely by the Lauren family; Executive Chairman Ralph Lauren and CEO Patrice Louvet since 2017 executing Next Great Chapter) with consistent dividends and Class A share buybacks.

column11: Accessible-luxury fashion handbags and leather accessories are deferrable discretionary purchases exposed to fashion-trend cyclicality and middle-class spending pullbacks, not essential needs, everyday staple rituals, or ultra-affluent Lindy scarcity luxury.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need, REJECT). While Coach is enjoying a strong FY25-FY26 brand resurgence (77.8% consolidated gross margin, $8.00B FY26 revenue), Tapestry's accessible-luxury handbags and accessories remain non-essential, easily deferred discretionary fashion goods rather than functional necessities, daily habits, or Lindy ultra-luxury scarcity franchises like Hermes or Ferrari. (0.9% GAAP) in 2025—far below AZO/ORLY's 18-20%—with adjusted EPS falling two consecutive years ($9.33 in 2023 -> $8.16 in 2024 -> $7.37 in 2025). column21: Multi-cycle financial history (SEC EDGAR FY2016-FY2025): Revenue grew from $15,339.7M (2016) to $23,090.6M (2023), $23,486.6M (2024), and $24,300.1M (2025), but GAAP EBIT barely moved from $1,229.3M (8.01% margin in 2016; $1,430.5M / 8.50% in 2018) to $1,272.8M (5.42% in 2024) and collapsed to $215.7M (0.89%) in 2025 on a ~$741.9M US pension settlement charge plus restructuring/credit charges. Even on an adjusted basis, 2025 net income fell to ~$1.0B ($7.37 EPS vs. $8.16 in 2024 and $9.33 peak Owner EPS in 2023) despite $175M of realized restructuring savings. GAAP ROIC averaged ~19-21% in 2021-2023 (5Y median 19.07%; 10Y median 17.95%) before compressing to 13.54% (2024) and 2.27% (2025), while 2016-2024 Net Invested Capital rose from $3,500.8M to $7,600.0M (+$4,099.2M) for +$43.5M EBIT (1.1% pre-tax ROIIC) and +$216.9M Net Income (5.3% ROIIC). Segments & 2025-2026 separation: Global Automotive (NAPA/AAG/Repco, >$15B sales, ~75-80% DIFM commercial, ~8-9% EBITDA margins) lags pure-play retail/commercial peers AZO and ORLY (~50-53% gross, 18-20% EBIT margins), whereas Motion Industries (~$9B sales, ~12-13% EBITDA margins, +6%+ YoY 2026 growth) is being carved out into an independent public company in Q1 2027 following Elliott Management's >$1B activist stake. Capital allocation & balance sheet: Serial M&A inflated Goodwill & Intangibles from $1,574.7M (2016) to $5,044.5M (2025) against $4,423.0M equity (negative tangible equity of -$621.5M) and expanded debt from $550.0M (2016) to $3,498.4M (2025; net debt $3,021.2M), pushing interest expense from $64.5M (2023) to $163.5M (2025; 1.32x GAAP EBIT coverage). Cumulative 2021-2025 Owner FCF conversion was 97.5% ($4,258.5M vs. $4,368.0M NI), but FY2025 Owner FCF ($372.1M) fell short of Dividend King payouts ($563.8M).

column14: Brand equity and proprietary footwear design IP across UGG ($2.74B FY26 sales) and HOKA ($2.59B FY26 sales), reinforced by strict wholesale allocation and full-price selling discipline. Empirically verified by 28.5% historical median ROIC (30-35%+ in FY25-FY26), 57.9% FY25 gross margin, and 23.1%-23.7% operating margins even amid promotional industry discounting. Primary erosion threats: zero customer switching costs, fashion/silhouette cyclicality, and surging running rivals (On Holding, Salomon, Nike, Adidas).
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While UGG and HOKA generate elite current ROIC (30-35%+) and ~23% operating margins via brand intangibles and full-price discipline, branded footwear has zero switching costs and high Mauboussin fade risk (Tier 3 baseline <=15Y) as HOKA normalizes against On Holding, Salomon, Nike, and Adidas and UGG faces fashion-cycle rotation. Deductive -5Y Macrotrend [3] haircut applies for heavy reliance on outsourced Vietnam/Asian manufacturing hit by ~20%+ U.S. tariffs, which labor-intensive shoe assembly (Macrotrend [2]) cannot economically reshore.
column21: FY25 net sales rose 16.3% to $4.986B (UGG $2.531B +13.1%, HOKA $2.233B +23.6%, Other $221.2M -8.6%) with gross margin expanding to 57.9% (from 55.6% in FY24) and operating income of $1.183B (~23.7% margin). FY26 net sales rose 9.8% to $5.472B (UGG $2.74B +8.2%, HOKA $2.59B +15.9%, non-core labels streamlined including Sanuk divestiture/exit) with operating income of $1.263B (~23.1% margin) and FCF above $1.1B. Historical median ROIC is 28.5% (30-35%+ recently). Management (CEO Stefano Caroti, CFO Steve Fasching) enforces full-price selling to protect brand equity despite U.S. DTC volume friction, operates essentially debt-free with $1.6B-$1.9B cash, repurchased 10.5M shares for $1.075B in FY26, and raised buyback authorization by $3.5B in May 2026 (~$5B total). Fails 15Y Munger runway bar due to zero switching costs, HOKA growth normalization amidst fierce competition, and Vietnam/SE Asia tariff concentration.

column14: Dominant North American home-improvement duopoly (~2x Lowe's revenue with far higher sales per sq ft) creates unmatched supplier purchasing scale, proprietary/exclusive brands (Ryobi, Husky, HDX, Behr), and an integrated store plus Pro flatbed/branch network (augmented by SRS Distribution and GMS) that smaller chains and parcel e-commerce cannot profitably match on heavy, immediate-need building materials. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 41.5% (27.1% GAAP / 56.7% tangible in FY25 post-M&A; company-reported FY25 Adjusted ROIC 25.7%), positive full-cycle incremental ROIIC (>15% after tax even including $23B+ of recent M&A at a housing trough), and gross margins held steady at ~33.0%-33.7% through lumber, tariff, and wholesale-mix pressures. Primary erosion threats: structural margin and ROIC dilution as lower-margin specialty Pro wholesale distribution grows in mix, prolonged high mortgage rates suppressing big-ticket remodel turnover, and e-commerce encroachment in lighter hardware SKUs.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. North America's indispensable home-improvement retail and Pro building-materials leader, anchored by scale economies shared across ~2,300 big-box stores and >1,250 SRS/GMS specialty trade branches serving continuous repair/maintenance on an aging housing stock. Physically insulated from AI disruption and online parcel economics, with diversified sourcing managing tariffs and high-rate housing turnover muting growth cyclically rather than terminally. CAP set conservatively at 15Y to reflect US store saturation and ROIC/margin fade toward wholesale Pro distribution. Balance sheet passes baseline hurdles (3.49x LT debt/NI, 3.39x net debt/NI, 8.66x EBIT/interest at cycle trough, 91.6% 5Y FCF conversion), with buybacks prudently paused since March 2024 to pay down M&A debt and commercial paper, though $32.7B of goodwill leaves negative tangible book equity and post-dividend deleveraging warrants monitoring. [5-10Y g: R&R/Pro volume 2.5% + pricing/ticket 2.0% + SRS/GMS cross-sell mix 1.0% - wholesale mix/tariff drag 0.5% + normalized buybacks 1.5%]
column21: 10-year SEC EDGAR financials (FY2016-FY2025) and 2026 interim filings verify exceptional multi-cycle capital efficiency and cash conversion despite a frozen US housing turnover backdrop. Revenue compounded from $94,595M (FY16) to $164,683M (FY25), dipping only 3.0% from the FY22 pandemic peak ($157,403M) to FY23 ($152,669M) before rebounding via Pro expansion and turning positive organically in 1H 2026 (Q1 2026 sales $41.8B, comps +0.6%; Q2 2026 sales $47.9B, comps +1.7%). Operating margins ranged from 13.8%-15.3% pre-2024 before stepping down to 13.49% (FY24) and 12.69% (FY25) due to lower-margin SRS/GMS wholesale mix, M&A intangible amortization, and housing turnover deleverage; consolidated gross margin held tightly near ~33.0%-33.7% across 2025-1H 2026. GAAP ROIC ranged from 34.9%-55.7% across FY16-FY24 and printed 27.14% in FY25 (5Y median 41.53%; company Adjusted ROIC 25.7% in FY25, 25.4% in interim 2026), while tangible operating ROIC remained 56.74% in FY25. Owner FCF totaled $126,804M across FY16-FY25 against $129,459M Net Income (97.9% 10Y conversion; 91.6% 5Y conversion), with capital-light maintenance needs (FY25 capex $3,679M vs D&A $3,514M, ~2.2% of sales) and minimal SBC ($522M, 0.3% of sales). Owner EPS compounded at 6.84% over 10 years ($6.73 in FY16 to $16.69 FY22 peak; $14.23 in FY25 trough), with clear peak-to-peak recovery visibility as turnover normalizes and SRS/GMS synergies scale. Following major Pro acquisitions—HD Supply (2020), SRS Distribution (2024), and GMS Inc. (FY25, ~$5.5B EV)—goodwill/intangibles rose from $12,061M (FY23) to $32,673M (FY25) (yielding -$19,860M tangible equity despite GAAP equity rebounding to $12,813M), and LT debt peaked at $51,365M (FY24) before declining to $49,397M (FY25) ($1,389M cash; 3.49x LT debt/NI; 8.66x EBIT/interest). Management kept share buybacks paused from March 2024 through 1H 2026 to prioritize dividend stability ($9,152M in FY25) and commercial paper/debt reduction; CEO Ted Decker took a temporary medical leave in August 2026 with tenured insiders Ann-Marie Campbell and CFO Richard McPhail assuming interim oversight.

column14: #2 position in the US big-box home improvement duopoly behind Home Depot, backed by $86B-$92B purchasing scale, supply-chain density, private-label depth, and physical store/distribution reach for bulky and urgent building materials. Historical 10Y median ROIC is 28.5% with FY2026 trailing ROIC of ~24.8%-26.8% (though optically elevated by $(9.9B)-$(14.2B) shareholders' deficit from buybacks) and 11.2%-12.5% operating margins. Fails Gate 3b on autonomous pricing power >= inflation and recent incremental returns: #2 price-follower with a DIY-heavy mix facing transparent SKU price competition from Home Depot, Amazon, and regional chains plus commodity pass-through dynamics in lumber/building supplies. In FY2024-2026, inflation-adjusted pricing/volume power stalled (FY2026 comparable sales guided flat after +0.6% Q1 and +0.2% Q2) while GAAP operating margin compressed from 12.5% (FY2024) to 11.8% (FY2025) to 11.2% guidance (FY2026E), and ~$10B of 2025 Pro wholesale/installation M&A (ADG >$1B; FBM $8.8B) diluted margins with flat-to-lower GAAP EBIT ($10.47B FY24 vs ~$10.30B FY26E).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT – G3 Moat & Pricing). Although Lowe's passes Gates 1-2 as an essential US home-maintenance retailer and holds #2 scale economies in the home-improvement duopoly (3a = Scale economies shared), it lacks autonomous pricing power >= inflation and exhibits deteriorating incremental returns. Heavily DIY-skewed and trailing Home Depot in Pro share, Lowe's acts largely as a retail price-follower on cross-shopped tools/appliances and a pass-through merchant on commodity building materials. Amid sticky inflation, comparable sales have stalled (FY2026 guidance cut to flat after +0.6% Q1 and +0.2% Q2) while GAAP operating margins compressed from 12.5% (FY2024) to 11.8% (FY2025) to 11.2% guidance (FY2026E), with ~$10B of debt-funded 2025 Pro acquisitions (ADG and FBM) diluting margins and failing to lift GAAP EBIT above FY2024 levels.
column21: Financial Track Record & Cash Conversion: FY2024 net sales $83,674M, GAAP operating income $10,466M (12.51% margin), net earnings $6,957M, operating cash flow $9,625M less CapEx $1,927M = ~$7,698M FCF (~111% conversion). FY2025 (ended Jan 30, 2026) net sales $86,286M, GAAP operating income $10,153M (11.77% margin), net earnings $6,654M, non-GAAP FCF ~$7.7B (~116% conversion). FY2026 guidance (updated post-Q2 after Q1 +0.6% comps on $23.1B sales and Q2 +0.2% comps on $26.0B sales): ~$92.0B sales (down from $92B-$94B), flat comps (down from flat to +2%), 11.2% GAAP operating margin (11.6% adjusted), ~$1.6B net interest expense, ~$11.75 GAAP EPS ($12.25 adjusted), and up to $2.5B CapEx. Capital Efficiency & Pricing Power: Workbook 10Y median ROIC is 28.5% and 2026 trailing ROIC hovers near ~24.8%-26.8%, though book invested capital is shrunk by shareholders' deficit ($(14,231)M in FY2024; $(9,917)M in FY2025) from prior buybacks. Pricing power is constrained by #2 DIY-heavy positioning behind Home Depot, cross-retailer price transparency, housing turnover lock-in, and commodity pass-through dynamics, yielding flat nominal FY2026 comps and ~130 bps of GAAP margin compression since FY2024. M&A, Capital Allocation & Balance Sheet: Seeking catch-up penetration in the $250B Pro market, Lowe's deployed ~$10B in 2025 on Artisan Design Group (>$1B, mid-2025; builder interior finishes installation) and Foundation Building Materials ($8.8B cash, closed Oct 2025 via $9.0B bridge facility and debt; >370 interior building product branches), diluting operating margins and lifting long-term debt (excl. current) from $32,901M (FY24) to $37,490M (FY25) — 5.63x FY25 net earnings, with FY26E GAAP EBIT/interest coverage tightening to ~6.4x.

column11: Cyclical merchant homebuilder selling big-ticket, mortgage-rate-sensitive discretionary homes that buyers readily defer during interest rate spikes or economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). While shelter is a basic necessity, purchasing a newly built single-family home from a merchant homebuilder is a big-ticket, mortgage-rate-sensitive, deferrable cyclical purchase rather than a non-deferrable necessity or entrenched everyday habit. Elevated mortgage rates and affordability constraints in FY25–FY26 forced D.R. Horton to rely on sales incentives and rate buydowns, shrinking consolidated revenue from $36.80B (FY24) to $33.0B (FY26), compressing home sales gross margins from 23.5% (FY24) to 19.5% (Q4 FY26), and cutting net income from $4.76B to $2.9B. Fails the Munger 'likely to spend' standard.
column21: Business & Segments: Largest US homebuilder by volume (IPO 1992), operating across core Homebuilding (84,202 homes closed and $30.6B home sales revenue in FY26 ended Sep 30, 2026), Rental operations ($1.2B revenue; 2,073 single-family rental homes and 2,737 multi-family units sold in FY26), majority-owned Forestar lot development (13,545 lots sold in FY26), and Financial Services. Historical & Recent Cycle Performance: Dossier 10Y median ROIC of 18.2% (v1 workbook), yet multi-year results show classic housing cyclicality. Consolidated revenue fell from $36.80B in FY24 to $34.25B in FY25 (-6.9%) and $33.0B in FY26 (-4%), while net income declined from $4.76B ($14.34 diluted EPS) in FY24 to $3.59B in FY25 and $2.9B ($10.11 diluted EPS) in FY26 (FY26 ROE 12.2%, ROA 8.2%). Home sales gross margin compressed from 23.5% in FY24 to 21.5% in FY25, 20.7% in Q3 FY26, and 19.5% in Q4 FY26 (with early FY27 guided to 18.0%–18.5%) amid mortgage rate buydowns, sales incentives, pricing adjustments, and warranty/litigation costs, alongside $91.4M in Q4 FY26 rental inventory impairments. Cash Flow & Capital Structure: Operating cash flow was $2.19B in FY24, $3.42B in FY25 (~$3.28B FCF), and $3.51B in FY26. Ended FY26 with $2.12B cash and restricted cash ($7.2B total liquidity) and 20.8% debt-to-total-capital (subsequently repaying $600M of 1.3% senior notes in Oct 2026; FY25 notes payable $5.97B vs. $2.99B cash), while returning $4.1B in FY26 via $3.6B buybacks (24.0M shares) and $513.3M dividends. Despite conservative leverage and national scale, demand and pricing remain hostage to mortgage affordability and deferrable buyer spending.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket cyclical homebuilder; new-home purchases are deferrable when mortgage rates rise or macro conditions soften, forcing heavy price cuts and rate-buydown incentives.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need, REJECT). Lennar passes Gate 1 as a well-established, transparent US homebuilder, but fails Gate 2 because new-home purchases are big-ticket, financing-sensitive, deferrable cyclicals explicitly disqualified under the Munger 'likely to spend' bar. Stubborn ~6.8%-7% mortgage rates across 2025-2026 required 12%-14.1% sales incentives to sustain volume, compressing home sales gross margin from 21.8% (Q1 2024) to 15.2%-15.8% (Q1-Q3 2026) and compressing TTM ROIC to ~4.5%-4.8% (down from 15%-18% at the 2021-2022 peak). Calamity Tier does not apply because Gate 2 fails.
column21: Multi-cycle financial record demonstrates acute cyclicality rather than steady compounding: while Lennar's v1 10-year average ROIC stood at 16.5% (boosted by the 2021-2022 housing boom when ROIC reached 15%-18%), ROIC fell to ~5%-7% in the 2018 slowdown, 7.55% in FY2025 (ROE 8.21%), and ~4.5%-4.8% TTM as of Q3 2026 (period ended Aug 31, 2026). Revenue declined from $35.4B in FY2024 (net income $3.9B; operating cash flow ~$2.4B) to $34.2B in FY2025 (net income $2.1B, including a $156M Millrose exchange-offer loss; operating cash flow $216.8M amid Millrose spin-off inventory/capital realignments). In FY2026, Q3 revenue fell 9.2% YoY to $8.0B on 20,840 deliveries (-3% YoY), new orders declined 9% YoY to 20,879, Q3 net earnings fell to $284M ($1.19 EPS vs. $2.29 prior year), and FY2026 delivery guidance was cut to 80,000-81,000 homes. Home sales gross margin contracted from 21.8% (Q1 2024) to 18.7% (Q1 2025), 17.5% (Q3 2025), 15.2% (Q1 2026), and 15.8% (Q3 2026) as Lennar relied on ~14% sales incentives (late 2025-Q1 2026) and ~12% incentives (Q3 2026) via mortgage-rate buydowns and price cuts to protect its 'Even-Flow' manufacturing cadence (116-122 day cycle times). Strategically, Lennar spun off Millrose Properties in Feb 2025 (1:2 distribution) and retired 8.0M LEN shares in a Nov 2025 Millrose share-exchange offer, reaching ~98% option-controlled homesites. Balance sheet leverage remains conservative: Q3 2026 homebuilding cash was $1.2B ($3.6B total liquidity, $650M drawn on its $3.1B revolver), homebuilding debt was ~$4.3B (~$5.9B-$6.0B consolidated debt), homebuilding debt-to-capital was 16.6% (12.7% net), $400M of 5.25% senior notes were redeemed without revolver draws, and $256M (3M shares) was repurchased in Q3 2026.

column11: Pure-play cyclical homebuilder selling big-ticket, mortgage-rate-sensitive, deferrable residential housing purchases rather than a recurring essential necessity or entrenched everyday habit.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need & Entrenched Habits, REJECT). While NVR operates a best-in-class, asset-light finished-lot option model with a net cash balance sheet and disciplined buybacks, it remains a pure-play cyclical US homebuilder explicitly excluded under Gate 2. Buying a newly constructed home is a large, mortgage-financed, easily deferrable big-ticket purchase, as demonstrated by FY2025 new orders falling 10% YoY, ending backlog falling 15% YoY, FY2025 net income declining 20% YoY to $1.34B, and Q3 2026 net income dropping 27.5% YoY to $248.6M amid affordability and rate headwinds.
column21: Gate 1 passes: NVR has a >30-year post-1993 public operating record with transparent disclosure of lot purchase option deposits, pre-sold backlog, settlements, and captive originate-to-sell mortgage banking (Ryan Homes, NVHomes, Heartland Homes, NVR Mortgage Finance). Financial & multi-cycle record: NVR's asset-light land-option and pre-sold construction model generates elite capital efficiency (32.5% historical median ROIC in dossier; ~93.6% FY2022 peak, ~63.8% FY2024, ~49.8% FY2025, normalizing to ~25%-34% TTM in mid-2026) and enabled profitable survival through the 2008 GFC by walking away from option deposits rather than taking raw-land impairments. Balance sheet & cash flow: As of Dec 31, 2025, NVR held ~$1.88B in homebuilding cash (~$1.92B total cash) vs $909.2M in senior notes (zero credit facility borrowings) and $3.86B equity; FY2025 FCF was ~$1.1B (~82% conversion of $1.34B net income) while shrinking share count via buybacks (FY2025 EPS -14% to $436.55 vs -20% net income). By Sep 30, 2026, homebuilding cash stood at $1,091.3M vs $907.7M senior notes and $3,435.0M equity. Gate 2 rejection mechanism: Despite superior capital structure and capital allocation, end-market demand is fundamentally cyclical and deferrable. In FY2025, revenue fell ~2% to ~$10.3B, settlements slipped 4% to 21,915 units, new orders dropped 10% to 20,410 units, backlog declined 15% to 8,448 units, and homebuilding gross profit compressed from $2.44B to $2.14B. Cyclical pressure deepened in 2026, with Q2 2026 net income at $236.5M (~$2.32B revenue) and Q3 2026 revenue down 8% YoY to $2.40B with net income down 27.5% YoY to $248.6M. Because Gate 2 is an Anchor Gate, Calamity Tier does not apply and evaluation halts at Gate 2.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket cyclical homebuilder; new-home purchases are deferrable during elevated mortgage rates and economic downturns, driving cyclical swings in volume, incentives, and margins.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need, REJECT). Cyclical US production homebuilder (Pulte, Centex, Del Webb, DiVosta, John Wieland) whose big-ticket residential sales are highly deferrable and interest-rate sensitive. While management maintains solid land-option discipline (~55% optioned lots) and low net leverage (~3% net debt-to-capital in Q3 2026), softening affordability and ~7.5% mortgage rates drove FY2025 net income down ~30% YoY ($2.17B vs. $3.08B in FY2024), compressed home sale gross margins from ~27.5% (FY2024) to ~24.7% (FY2025) and 24.8% (Q3 2026), and lifted incentives to 10.4% of home sale revenue in Q3 2026 (up from 8.9% a year earlier). Fails Munger's non-deferrable everyday-need standard.
column21: Business Model & Segments: US S&P 500 homebuilder generating >96% of revenue from single-family attached/detached home sales across first-time, move-up, and active-adult segments (FY2024 total revenue $17.9B / home sales $17.3B; FY2025 total revenue $17.3B / home sales $16.7B on 29,572 closings), supplemented by ancillary mortgage/title financial services. Multi-Cycle Financial Track Record: Prior dossier data reports a 17.8% 10-year median ROIC, with FY2024 ROE of 27.5% and peak GAAP net income of $3.083B ($14.69/diluted share) at a ~27.5% home sale gross margin. As mortgage rates remained elevated into 2025-2026, FY2025 net income fell ~30% to ~$2.17B (~$10.49/share) and gross margin compressed to ~24.7% (including ~80 bps of land impairment charges). In Q3 2026, home sale revenues fell 9% YoY to $3.9B, net income declined 19% YoY to $476M ($2.53/share vs. $2.96/share), community foot traffic fell 14% YoY, gross margin slid to 24.8% (vs. 26.2% YoY, including $26M / ~70 bps land impairments), and backlog stood at 10,298 homes ($6.4B, +3% YoY) with a ~10% cancellation rate. Cash Flow & Capital Allocation: FY2024 operating cash flow was $1.681B (FCF ~$1.56B after ~$118.5M CapEx) and FY2025 operating cash flow was $1.871B (FCF ~$1.75B after ~$122.7M CapEx), supporting $1.2B of FY2025 share repurchases ($350M in Q3 2026) and $5.2B of FY2025 land investment (~$4B YTD through Q3 2026). Balance Sheet & Pricing Dynamics: Conservative balance sheet with $1.6B senior notes principal in FY2024-2025 (zero revolver borrowings) and ~$1.4B cash, 12.1% debt-to-capital, and ~3% net debt-to-capital as of Q3 2026. Of ~224,000 lots under control in Q3 2026, ~55% were optioned (PHM walked away from ~8,000 option lots in Q3 2026). Despite improved asset-light discipline, transactional pricing power relies on rate buydowns and concessions—sales incentives reached 10.4% of home sale revenue in Q3 2026 (up 150 bps YoY)—underscoring cyclical deferrability rather than recurring customer lock-in.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket furniture, home decor, and specialty kitchenware purchases (Pottery Barn, West Elm, Williams Sonoma) are deferrable in recessions and tied to housing turnover rather than essential daily needs or high-frequency habits.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT – G2 Essential Need). Despite elite retail execution under CEO Laura Alber (18.1% FY25 operating margin, 42.3% GAAP / 51.6% adjusted FY25 ROIC, $1.0B cash with no funded revolver debt), Williams-Sonoma's core banners (Pottery Barn, West Elm, Williams Sonoma) sell discretionary, big-ticket furniture, home decor, and upscale kitchenware that households easily defer during downturns or low housing turnover. Following the >$8.6B FY22 peak, revenue normalized to ~$7.77B-$7.8B across FY24-FY25 (-1.6% FY24 comps), confirming cyclical demand deferrability outside essential daily needs or high-frequency habits.
column21: Multi-cycle & recent financial profile: Revenue scaled from ~$4.9B-$5.1B c. 2015-2016 (net income ~$250M-$300M) to a pandemic peak >$8.6B in FY22 before normalizing to ~$7.77B-$7.8B in FY24 (-1.6% comps) and $7.8B in FY25 (+1.24% YoY, +3.5% comps), with dossier 10Y median ROIC at 22.4%. Operating execution has been exceptionally strong: FY24 operating margin reached 17.9% (~$1.39B EBIT, ~$1.5B FCF on ~$1.7B OCF and ~$221.6M capex, $1.2B cash, zero revolver debt, 54.0% ROIC) and FY25 operating margin expanded to 18.1% ($1.42B EBIT, $1.3B OCF, $1.0B cash, no material funded debt, 42.3% ROIC / 51.6% adjusted ROIC), with >$1B annual net income and >$1.3B TTM FCF. In FY26, management raised full-year guidance assuming zero housing recovery (Q1 +4.8% and Q2 +6.2% comps across Pottery Barn, West Elm, Williams Sonoma, B2B, and emerging banners Rejuvenation/Mark and Graham/GreenRow), while navigating ~230 bps tariff margin drag and ~$200M IEEPA tariff refunds ($47.5M vendor reimbursements, $10M employee 401(k) contributions) alongside multi-country sourcing shifts across China, Vietnam, and India. Gate 1 passes (transparent omni-channel retail/DTC model public for decades), but Gate 2 rejects on core demand nature: furniture, furnishings, and specialty cookware are big-ticket, deferrable discretionary durables exposed to housing cycles rather than essential necessities or entrenched daily rituals.

column11: Discretionary leisure travel and vacation lodging are infrequent, deferrable consumer expenditures rather than essential needs or daily habits, compounded by escalating municipal and EU short-term rental restrictions over residential housing.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Despite strong asset-light marketplace economics, ~22% ROIC, and ~$8.7B net cash, Airbnb operates in discretionary, deferrable leisure travel (Hotels, Resorts & Cruise Lines) rather than an essential Western necessity or entrenched everyday ritual, and faces persistent societal and legislative hostility in dense urban markets (e.g., NYC Local Law 18 and tightening European short-term rental caps/registrations).
column21: Gate 1 (Y): Transparent, asset-light two-sided lodging marketplace (Dec 2020 IPO; FY2024 revenue $11.102B, FY2025 revenue $12.241B +10.3% YoY, 533M Nights & Seats Booked +8% YoY; FY2025 Net Income $2.511B, FCF ~$4.6B; ~$11.0B cash vs ~$2.27B total debt; 22.4% median ROIC, ~21-25% operating margins; Q3 2026 revenue +19% YoY with $12B Nov 2026 buyback authorization; SBC up ~13% YoY in FY2025; dual-class Class B 20-vote founder control). Gate 2 (N): Fails Munger 'likely to spend' essential/everyday-habit and low-societal-risk criteria. Leisure vacation rentals are discretionary and deferrable in downturns alongside airlines and cruise lines, while core urban supply faces durable political/housing-affordability backlash (NYC Local Law 18 banning most unhosted stays under 30 days; EU Short-Term Rental Data Regulation plus local caps/taxes in Spain, Italy, France, and Greece, prompting a pivot toward suburban stays and boutique hotels). Strict waterfall leaves Gates 3-6 null; calamity tier inapplicable since Anchor Gate 2 fails.

column11: Predominantly discretionary leisure travel and vacation lodging (1.235B room nights in FY2025, ~36% alternative accommodations/vacation rentals), which are episodic, big-ticket, and deferrable in downturns rather than an essential functional necessity or daily habit.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need & Entrenched Habits, REJECT). Although Booking Holdings operates a transparent, asset-light OTA marketplace (passing Gate 1), its $186.1B in gross bookings are overwhelmingly driven by discretionary consumer leisure travel and vacation lodging (including ~36% alternative accommodations), placing it alongside explicitly rejected travel cyclicals (airlines, cruise lines). Travel spending is episodic and deferrable during recessions or geopolitical disruptions, evidenced by the 54.9% revenue collapse and negative EBIT (-$631M) in FY2020 and Q4 2026 guidance moderating to 1-3% room-night growth amid softer international travel and Middle East disruptions, failing the Munger 'likely to spend' staple/necessity bar.
column21: Multi-cycle financials (FY2016-FY2025 SEC EDGAR): Sales compounded from $10,743M (FY16) to $15,066M (FY19), collapsed 54.9% to $6,796M in FY20 (EBIT -$631M, Owner FCF -$434M), and rebounded to $26,917M in FY25 (+13.4% YoY; EBIT $8,825M, 32.8% margin; GAAP NI $5,404M; OCF $9,409M; CapEx $322M; SBC $613M; Owner FCF $8,474M, 156.8% FCF/NI; FY25 reported FCF $9.1B; 5Y median GAAP ROIC 82.1% with negative book equity since FY23). FY2025 revenue model breakdown: Merchant $17,755M (66.0%, +25.5% YoY), Agency $7,968M (29.6%, -6.5% YoY), and Advertising/Other (KAYAK, OpenTable) $1,194M (4.4%) on $186.1B gross bookings (+12%) and 1.235B room nights (+8%; ~55% direct channel, ~36% alternative accommodations; SEC filings do not separately quantify leisure vs. business travel but confirm predominantly leisure orientation). 9M 2026 operating trajectory: Q1 rev $5.53B (+16%), Q2 rev $7.35B (+8%), Q3 GAAP rev $8.89B (-1.3% due to a discrete $900M FTC-related revenue charge at Priceline; ~+9% ex-charge), Q3 room nights 345M (+7%), Q4 room-night growth guided to 1-3%. Moat & regulatory context: Two-sided lodging supply network faces EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) gatekeeper designation removing wide/narrow EEA rate parity clauses, alongside emerging agentic-AI travel disintermediation risk.
