Capital allocation & balance sheet: 25-for-1 stock split effective April 2026; FY25 dividends $1,248M and 9M 2026 share buybacks ~$9.5B drove negative GAAP equity (-$5,578M at FY25, goodwill/intangibles $3,587M), supported by $17,203M cash vs. $16,856M LT debt ($347M net cash) and 5.46x FY25 EBIT/interest coverage ($8,825M / $1,617M).

column11: Discretionary big-ticket leisure cruise vacations that are easily deferred in economic downturns, inflationary squeezes, or travel shocks, with abundant land-based vacation substitutes; neither an essential Western need nor an entrenched everyday habit (cruise lines are an explicit Gate 2 reject category).
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need & Everyday Habits, REJECT). Carnival passes Gate 1 as a transparent, long-established global cruise operator, but fails Gate 2 because multi-day leisure cruises are deferrable, big-ticket discretionary travel rather than an essential necessity or high-frequency everyday habit. Despite strong post-pandemic cyclical recovery and rational industry supply dynamics, demand remains vulnerable to macro downturns and consumers have abundant land-based resort/hotel substitutes, while the operating model remains capital-intensive, fuel-exposed, and structurally scarred by past crisis leverage and equity dilution. Gate 2 is an anchor gate, so Calamity Tier does not apply.
column21: Historical capital efficiency is weak across cycles, with a 10-year median ROIC of 6.5% (screener financials_csv) reflecting severe pandemic shutdown losses alongside heavy ongoing fleet capex. Post-pandemic recovery drove record FY2025 (ended Nov 30, 2025) revenue of $26.6B, operating income of $4.5B (+25% YoY), GAAP net income of $2.76B (adjusted $3.1B), operating cash flow of $6.22B, CapEx of $3.61B, FCF of $2.61B, and adjusted ROIC exceeding 13%. Momentum continued in 2026: Q1 revenue $6.2B (though surging Brent crude/fuel inflation created a >$500M earnings headwind), Q2 revenue $6.7B with record $9.0B customer deposits and unification under a single Bermuda-incorporated entity, and Q3 revenue $8.44B with $1.92B net income ($5.303B 9M operating cash flow) while trailing ROIC hovered near 11-11.5%+. Total debt fell from a ~$35B post-pandemic peak to $24.04B at FY2025 end (cash $1.928B; net interest expense $1.3B vs $1.8B in FY2024 and ~$251M in FY2019) and $23.9B by Q3 2026, eliminating all secured debt, regaining investment-grade ratings (Fitch and S&P), and resuming dividends and ~$1.2B YTD share buybacks against 1,402M FY2025 diluted shares after severe 2020-2022 equity dilution. Despite operational repair, the underlying cruise business remains cyclical, capital-heavy, and discretionary.

column11: Discretionary, big-ticket leisure travel and vacation lodging bookings (hotels, Vrbo rentals, flights, packages) are deferrable in recessions and macro shocks rather than essential needs or entrenched everyday habits.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need & Everyday Habits). Expedia Group operates a discretionary leisure travel and lodging marketplace (Expedia, Hotels.com, Vrbo, and B2B travel distribution) in the Hotels, Resorts & Cruise Lines sub-industry. Vacation lodging, holiday rentals, and air travel are infrequent, big-ticket, deferrable expenditures that consumers curtail during recessions and macro shocks rather than essential needs or daily habits. Even on downstream metrics, Expedia trails Booking.com and Airbnb with sub-hurdle historical ROIC (~8-11.5% vs 12% threshold) and top-of-funnel dependence on Google and emerging AI search channels.
column21: Gate 1 passes: established US public online travel platform since 2005 with transparent 10-K reporting across B2C brands (Expedia, Hotels.com, Vrbo unified under One Key loyalty) and B2B white-label/partner distribution. Gate 2 fails: gross bookings ($119.6B in FY25) and revenues remain fundamentally tied to cyclical, discretionary leisure travel and vacation lodging rather than functional necessities or high-frequency everyday habits. Financial track record: FY24 revenue $13,691M, GAAP operating income $1,319M (~9.6% margin), GAAP net income $1,224M ($1,234M attributable), FCF $2,329M ($3,085M CFO minus $756M capex), LT debt $5,223M (total debt ~$6.53B-$6.57B). FY25 revenue rose 8% YoY to $14,733M, GAAP operating income rose 42% YoY to $1,871M (~12.7% margin), GAAP net income $1,301M ($1,294M attributable), FCF $3,110M ($3,880M CFO), LT debt $4,470M (total debt ~$6.42B, or ~4.9x FY25 GAAP net income and ~2.1x FCF). FY26 guidance targets $131.4B-$131.9B gross bookings, double-digit revenue growth, and 180-200 bps Adjusted EBITDA margin expansion, led by B2B growth and autonomous partner onboarding. Historical capital efficiency remains sub-hurdle (11.5% 10Y median ROIC in financials_csv; ~8-10% recent range vs ~10% WACC). Capital allocation prioritizes buybacks (~9M shares for $1.7B-$1.93B in FY25; ~$788M in Q1 2026) and a $0.48 quarterly dividend, while competitive positioning relies on defending traffic via Google AI Mode, Meta Muse, and OpenAI ad integrations against Booking.com and Airbnb.

column11: Lodging demand relies on deferrable discretionary leisure travel and cyclically cuttable corporate travel/conferences (Hotels, Resorts & Cruise Lines) rather than an essential necessity or high-frequency everyday habit; revenue fell 54.4% and EBIT turned negative (-$418M) in FY2020.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Despite an asset-light franchise and management fee model, Hilton sits in Hotels, Resorts & Cruise Lines and remains fundamentally tied to discretionary leisure vacations and cyclical corporate travel budgets that are readily deferred in downturns (FY2020 revenue -54.4% to $4,307M, EBIT -$418M, NI -$715M; FY2025 comparable RevPAR stalled at +0.4%). Lodging is neither a non-deferrable functional necessity nor a high-frequency daily habit under Munger's standard.
column21: Business & Segment Model: Pure-play asset-light global hotel franchisor and manager (>9,150 properties at FY2025 year-end; 240M+ Hilton Honors loyalty members; 2017 spin-offs of Park Hotels & Resorts and Hilton Grand Vacations). Core profits stem from management, franchise, and licensing fees (franchise/licensing fees $815M in Q3 2026; management and franchise fees +9.5% YoY) earned as a percentage of third-party hotel room revenues, alongside pass-through cost reimbursements and minimal owned/leased properties. System expansion remains strong with 6.7% net unit growth in FY2025 (~97,000 gross room openings) and a 6.0%-7.0% NUG target in 2026 backed by a record 543,100-room pipeline as of Q3 2026. Multi-Cycle Demand & Financials (FY2016-2026): Revenue rose from $6,576M (FY2016) to $9,452M (FY2019), collapsed -54.4% to $4,307M in FY2020 (EBIT -$418M, NI -$715M, GAAP ROIC -5.15%), and rebounded to $8,773M (FY2022), $10,235M (FY2023), $11,174M (FY2024), and $12,039M (FY2025, +7.7% YoY; EBIT $2,693M, NI $1,457M). System-wide currency-neutral RevPAR decelerated to +0.4% in FY2025 before accelerating to +5.8% YoY in Q3 2026 (75.8% occupancy, +3.9% ADR; FY2026 RevPAR guidance 4.0%-4.5%; FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance $4,060M-$4,080M). Capital Efficiency & Cash Flow: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 24.42% (FY2021-FY2025 range: 12.05%-35.32%), with 113.7% multi-year FCF conversion (FY2025 Owner FCF $1,858M on OCF $2,129M, CapEx $101M, SBC $170M; cumulative FY2022-FY2025 Owner FCF $6,709M vs. GAAP NI $5,388M) and 10.26% peak-to-peak Owner EPS CAGR ($3.95 in FY2019 to $6.44 in FY2025; FY2017 $1,084M NI excluded as non-cash spike). Capital Allocation & Leverage: Under CEO Christopher Nassetta, capital returns (~$3.3B in FY2025; ~$3.5B FY2026 outlook, $2.9B YTD Oct 2026) have consistently exceeded Owner FCF via incremental borrowing at elevated valuation multiples (30.86x-57.51x Owner EPS), pushing long-term debt from $7,956M (FY2019) to $12,338M (FY2025, $918M cash, 8.47x LT debt/NI, 4.34x EBIT/interest) and $13,453M total debt ($12,623M net debt) at Q3 2026, while driving book equity to -$5,388M (tangible equity -$10,916M).

column11: Lodging and resort demand relies heavily on discretionary leisure vacations and deferrable corporate travel rather than an essential functional necessity or high-frequency everyday habit.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need, REJECT). Global hotel, resort, and timeshare/lodging demand depends on discretionary consumer travel and deferrable corporate T&E budgets that contract sharply in downturns (FY2020 revenue fell 50% YoY, EBIT dropped 95% to $84M, and net income turned negative at -$267M). While its asset-light franchise and Bonvoy credit card fee engine is high-margin, underlying customer demand is episodic and cyclical rather than an essential need or entrenched daily habit.
column21: Business & Scale: World's largest hotel franchisor/manager with 9,805 properties and 1,779,936 rooms across 145 countries/territories at YE2025 (pipeline ~4,100 properties / >618k rooms). Asset-light model collects base management, incentive management, franchise, and Chase/Amex co-branded credit card fees tied to Marriott Bonvoy (~271M members driving ~75% of U.S./Canada and ~68% of global room nights); GAAP revenue ($26,186M in FY2025) includes large zero-margin pass-through cost reimbursements. Multi-Cycle Financials & ROIC: Pre-COVID GAAP ROIC ranged 14.8% (2016) to 25.7% (2019), and reported FY2025 ROIC was ~21.4%. Cyclical shock exposed in FY2020 as sales fell from $20,972M (2019) to $10,571M, EBIT fell from $1,800M to $84M, and Owner EPS fell from $3.79 to -$0.25. Recovery peaked at $10.18 Owner EPS in FY2023 ($3,083M NI), followed by FY2025 revenue $26,186M, EBIT $4,141M, NI $2,601M, Owner FCF $2,518M (86.7% multi-year FCF conversion), and 2026 global RevPAR +6.5% YoY (4.5%-5% full-year outlook). Capital Allocation & Balance Sheet: Led by CEO Anthony Capuano and CFO Jen Mason (succeeding Leeny Oberg). 2016 Starwood deal created $19,243M of goodwill/intangibles. Returned >$4.0B via buybacks and dividends in FY2025, driving GAAP book equity negative (-$682M in 2023, -$2,992M in 2024, -$3,771M in 2025). Per FY2025 10-K, actual long-term debt is $14,990M and total debt is ~$16.2B (undercounted at $23M in XBRL financials_csv) vs $358M cash, implying ~5.8x LT debt/NI and 5.1x EBIT/interest coverage ($809M interest) with a BBB S&P rating.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket leisure travel easily deferred in recessions or external shocks; cruise lines are explicitly excluded from essential Western needs and everyday staple habits.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Cruise vacations are big-ticket, deferrable discretionary leisure purchases rather than an essential Western necessity or entrenched everyday habit, exposing demand to severe cyclical and shock-driven contractions (as demonstrated by pandemic shutdowns and >2x share dilution since FY2019). Even structurally, the business operates with sub-hurdle capital returns (5.5% 10Y median ROIC; ~5.9%–9.8% in FY2025 and ~9.1%–9.2% in 2026 TTM), negative FY2025 GAAP FCF (~-$1.2B amid $3.26B shipbuild capex), and heavy leverage ($14.83B net debt, 5.5x Adjusted EBITDA as of Q3 2026), failing the Munger compounding bar.
column21: Business Model & Demand Profile: Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings operates cruise lines (including Norwegian Cruise Line and Oceania Cruises) selling discretionary leisure vacations—an explicit Gate 2 non-essential, deferrable cyclical category. Historical Capital Efficiency & Earnings: 10Y median workbook ROIC is 5.5%, with FY2025 ROIC reported between 5.87% and 9.83% and 2026 TTM tracking ~9.1%–9.2% (below the 12% hurdle). FY2024 revenue of $9.45B produced $1,560.9M operating income and $910.3M GAAP net income; FY2025 revenue grew ~3.7% to $9.8B with $1,592.3M operating income, while GAAP net income fell to $423.2M ($1.045B adjusted) weighed down by $953.5M net interest expense (including $272.5M debt extinguishment/modification costs). Q3 2026 revenue flattened YoY at $2.95B with $491.5M quarterly net income (vs. $419.3M in Q3 2025). Cash Flow, Capex & Balance Sheet: Capital intensity from newbuild ship deliveries (including Norwegian Aqua and Oceania's Allura) drove capex (additions to property and equipment, net) to $2,750.4M in FY2023, $1,211.0M in FY2024, and $3,259.6M in FY2025, resulting in roughly -$1.2B GAAP FCF in FY2025. As of September 30, 2026 (Q3 2026), total debt stood at $15.09B against $256.5M cash ($14.83B net debt; 5.5x net leverage vs. ~$2.55B FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance), alongside ongoing refinancings including $950M senior unsecured notes due 2031 issued in October 2026. Share Dilution: Sustaining liquidity through the COVID-19 shock required heavy equity and convertible issuances, expanding basic weighted-average shares from 213.9M in FY2019 to 448.5M in FY2025 and 458.3M in 9M 2026 (diluted weighted-average shares rose from 216.5M in FY2019 to 463.7M in 9M 2026).

column11: Discretionary big-ticket vacation purchase deferrable in recessions; cruise lines are non-essential leisure spending rather than an everyday Western habit or functional necessity.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need, REJECT). Royal Caribbean Group operates capital-intensive cruise lines, an explicitly discretionary, big-ticket, and deferrable leisure category rather than an essential Western necessity or entrenched everyday habit. Although post-pandemic cyclical demand is strong, cruise spending collapses severely in downturns or travel disruptions (generating over $13B in cumulative GAAP net losses across 2020-2022), failing the Munger 'likely to spend' durability standard. Because Gate 2 is an Anchor Gate, Calamity Tier does not apply.
column21: Royal Caribbean Group operates global cruise vacations across Royal Caribbean International, Celebrity Cruises, Silversea Cruises, private destinations, and joint venture interests (including TUI Cruises), deriving revenue from passenger tickets and onboard spending. Multi-cycle financials underscore severe demand cyclicality and capital intensity: the dossier records a 10-year median ROIC of 8.2% (below the 12% hurdle), and from 2020 to 2025 annual revenue swung from $2.21B (2020) and $1.53B (2021) to $8.84B (2022), $13.90B (2023), $16.48B (2024), and $17.94B (2025). GAAP net income swung from losses of $(5.80)B in 2020, $(5.26)B in 2021, and $(2.16)B in 2022 to profits of $1.70B (2023), $2.88B (2024), and $4.27B (2025; $15.61 diluted EPS). Standard ROIC recovered from -11.80% (2020), -10.30% (2021), and -1.97% (2022) to 6.96% (2023), 9.36% (2024), and 9.98% (2025), while company-reported ROIC reached 18.0% in FY2025. Strong cyclical momentum continued across Q1-Q3 2026 (Q1 revenue ~$4.5B, adj. EPS $3.60, ~$1.1B returned via buybacks and dividends; Q2 revenue $4.83B, net income $1.13B, 110.2% load factor; Q3 revenue $5.59B, net income $1.73B, 112.4% load factor; FY2026 adj. EPS guidance raised to $17.85-$17.95). Despite cyclical strength and 2026 deleveraging below 3x with ~$6.9B liquidity, FY2025 operating cash flow of ~$6.47B required ~$5.23B of capex (leaving ~$1.24B FCF, ~29% of GAAP net income) and year-end 2025 total debt remained $21.3B ($17.61B mid-2025 long-term debt) after peaking at $23.4B in 2022, confirming high discretionary cyclicality and heavy capital demands.

column11: Non-essential discretionary leisure products (>50% traditional Consumer Products toys and ~46.5% Wizards hobbyist trading cards/digital gaming) easily deferred or displaced by digital screens rather than serving an essential need or broad everyday household habit, evidenced by -12% (FY24) and -4% (FY25) Consumer Products revenue declines and a ~$1.02B Q2 2025 goodwill impairment.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need & Entrenched Habits, REJECT). Over half of Hasbro's revenue remains seasonal, hit-driven physical toys (Nerf, Transformers, licensed action figures, board games) that families readily defer or replace with digital screen entertainment, as shown by -12% (2024) and -4% (2025) Consumer Products revenue drops and a ~$1.02B goodwill impairment in 2025. While Wizards of the Coast ($2.19B in FY25, 46% operating margin) is a powerful niche hobbyist IP engine via Magic: The Gathering and digital licensing, collectible trading cards and casual gaming are discretionary leisure spending rather than an essential Western necessity or universal everyday staple under Munger's bar.
column21: Multi-cycle capital returns remain sub-hurdle (10Y median ROIC 9.5% in financials_csv; FY15-25 consolidated sales roughly flat from ~$4.5B to $4.71B). FY2024 revenue was $4.14B (-17% reported, -7% ex-eOne), GAAP operating profit $690M (16.7% margin; $839M / 20.3% adjusted), GAAP net earnings $394.4M ($386M attributable), OCF $847.4M, and FCF ~$649.9M (after ~$197.5M PPE & software CapEx). In FY2025, total revenue rose 13.7% to $4.71B, led by Wizards of the Coast & Digital Gaming surging 44.7% to $2.19B (~46.5% of sales) and $1,006.8M operating profit (46.0% margin) on +59% Magic: The Gathering growth (including Universes Beyond crossovers like Avatar: The Last Airbender) and $168M from Monopoly Go! licensing. However, Consumer Products (>50% of revenue) fell 4% YoY (after -12% in FY24, though rebounding +7% in Q4 2025) and incurred a ~$1.02B Q2 2025 non-cash goodwill impairment from macro and tariff pressures, dragging consolidated FY25 GAAP operating profit to $11.1M (0.2% margin; $1,140M / 24.2% adjusted) and GAAP net income to $(318.2)M ($5.54 adjusted EPS), despite OCF of $893.2M and FCF of ~$694.9M (expanding toward ~$1.1B TTM in mid-2026). Consumer Products faces high customer concentration with mass retailers (Walmart, Target, Amazon) and weak toy pricing power, contrasting with WotC's strong collector pricing power. Capital allocation bears scars from the ~$4B eOne acquisition and subsequent loss-making divestiture of core film/TV operations to Lionsgate, though management shifted to asset-light IP licensing, paid down $225M of debt in FY25 to reduce long-term debt from $3,380.8M (FY24) to $2,767.9M (FY25, vs. $695M year-end 2024 cash), guided FY26 revenue +3-5% constant currency and $1.40B-$1.45B adjusted EBITDA, and authorized a $1.0B buyback program.

column14: Rural store density and farm-savvy customer service create local convenience switching barriers in secondary/tertiary markets, but TSCO lacks structural pricing power above inflation. Passing on price increases leads directly to unit volume contractions, traffic declines, and customer cross-shopping at Walmart, dollar stores, local farm co-ops, and e-commerce (Chewy/Amazon).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT – G3 Moat & Pricing). Specialty rural lifestyle retailer with strong brand recognition and high ROIC (~14-18%), but lacks genuine pricing power above inflation. Unit volumes and transaction counts stall when prices rise, as seen in flat comparable store sales (+0.1% FY24, +1.2% FY25, -1.0% to 0% FY26 guidance) and stagnant net income plateaued at ~$1.10B across 2022-2025. Operating margins compressed to 8.0-8.3% due to rural wage inflation and SG&A pressures.
column21: FY2024 revenue of $14.88B and net income of $1.10B; FY2025 revenue of $15.52B and net income of $1.10B (zero net income growth across 4 consecutive years). Comp store sales moderated from pandemic highs to +0.1% in FY24, +1.2% in FY25, and guided -1.0% to flat in FY26 (Q3 2026 at +0.4%). Free cash flow conversion remains weak at ~58% in FY24 ($637M FCF / $1,101M NI) and ~68% in FY25 ($741M FCF / $1,096M NI), well below the 80% threshold due to $675M-$700M annual capex. Balance sheet carries $1.83B in long-term debt plus >$3.5B in operating lease liabilities across 2,390+ stores.

column11: Non-essential / easily forgone product or service.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Specialty beauty retailer selling cosmetics, fragrances, prestige skincare, and salon services. Products are discretionary and easily forgone, deferred, or substituted during consumer belt-tightening; lacks the non-discretionary deprivation or Lindy pricing power of true staples. Third-party retail distribution faces intense competitive pressure from Sephora (including its Kohl's expansion), Amazon, and brand direct-to-consumer channels.
column21: Ulta operates ~1,400 specialty stores across the US. While historically achieving high ROIC (>20%) driven by store expansion and its 44M+ member Ultamate Rewards loyalty program, its product offering remains discretionary. Operating margins compressed from 15.0% in FY24 to 13.9% in FY25 and ~12.4% in FY26 due to heightened promotional activity and aggressive suburban competition from Sephora at Kohl's and Amazon. Zero consumer switching costs and lack of proprietary brand ownership leave it vulnerable to retail disintermediation and spending cycles.

column14: Scale economies shared via massive direct procurement of fresh, responsibly sourced ingredients and industry-leading restaurant throughput ($3.2M+ AUV across 4,000+ company-owned locations). Insurmountable unit cost advantages allow CMG to deliver high-protein, 1.5-lb+ entrees at accessible price points that fragmented fast-casual peers cannot replicate at scale. Moat proved by multi-year GAAP ROIC consistently exceeding 20% (and operating ROIC >45%) alongside successful cumulative price realization passing through ingredient and wage inflation. Primary erosion threats: brand fatigue / portion perception backlash, unit-level labor cost escalation, and aggressive copycat fast-casual concepts.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Chipotle has built an exceptional fast-casual brand with high throughput and unit volumes, it operates an entirely company-owned restaurant footprint of 4,000+ units employing ~120,000 hourly workers without a franchise royalty buffer. The business faces an unhedged terminal headwind under Macrotrend 2 (Demographic Aging & Labor Scarcity), where structural food-service wage inflation and labor shortages compress restaurant-level margins (falling from 27.4% to 23.3% in 2026). Under the Mauboussin Rule of Secular Resilience, an active headwind on manual labor intensity caps the competitive advantage period at CAP <= 10 years, failing the 15-year Munger longevity threshold.
column21: Chipotle grew revenue from $6.0B in 2020 to $11.3B in 2024 and $11.9B in 2025, with operating income of $1.94B (16.2% operating margin). High capital efficiency is demonstrated by multi-year GAAP ROIC of 20-47%, supported by $3.2M+ average unit volumes (AUV) and sub-2-year cash payback on new builds across 4,042 restaurants. Pristine balance sheet with zero funded debt (only operating lease liabilities of $5.1B) and ~$1B+ in cash and short-term investments. FCF conversion tracks 80-85% of net income ($1.15B FCF on $1.4B net income). However, the 100% company-operated store model leaves Chipotle directly exposed to accelerating hourly labor inflation (e.g. California AB 1228 $20/hr minimum wage), requiring continuous labor investments that compressed restaurant-level margins from 27.4% to 23.3% in 2026. Executive leadership transition to CEO Scott Boatwright in late 2024 has necessitated deliberate margin concessions to protect transaction traffic and resolve consumer portion-size pushback, underscoring secular labor and consumer sensitivity limits.

column14: Domino's operates an entrenched scale economies shared moat: high store density ('fortressing') cuts delivery radiuses and transit times, while vertically integrated regional supply chain dough/ingredient centers pass procurement efficiencies to franchisees. National scale funds an advertising powerhouse (6% royalty/ad contribution) and digital dominance (37M+ active loyalty members). Empirical proof: historical ROIC consistently 30-50%+ and ability to lift core promotional pricing ($5.99 to $6.99) while maintaining positive order counts. Primary erosion threats: third-party delivery aggregators (DoorDash, Uber Eats) disintermediating customer relationships and fast-food discounting wars.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT). While Domino's franchise economic engine is highly cash generative (FY2025 FCF of ~$672M, >110% GAAP net income conversion) and interest coverage is 5.27x, it fails Munger's peace-of-mind fortress balance sheet test. Decades of debt-funded share repurchases and whole-business securitizations have driven book equity into a -$3.90B deficit (negative tangible equity, triggering an automatic Gate 6 red flag) with $4.81B in long-term debt against FY2025 net income of $601.7M (8.0x net debt / net income, double the <= 4.0x ceiling). The capital structure relies continuously on the kindness of debt markets to roll over securitized tranches, leaving equity vulnerable to credit freezes.
column21: FY2025 operating results demonstrate strong underlying unit economics: Total revenues of $4,940.0M (+5.0% YoY), operating income of $954.0M (+8.5% YoY), and GAAP net income of $601.7M (+3.0% YoY). Free cash flow converted cleanly at ~$671.5M-$680.1M (Operating cash flow $792.1M less capex of $120.6M, representing ~112% of net income). Historical ROIC exceeds 35-40% across cycles driven by asset-light franchising (over 20,000 stores globally, ~98% franchised) and cost-plus supply chain centers. However, capital structure violates Gate 6 balance sheet standards: Long-term debt stood at $4,810.7M at FY2025 year-end (up from $3,825.7M in FY2024), resulting in Net Debt / Net Income of ~8.0x (far above the <= 4.0x ceiling). Total liabilities exceed total assets by $3.90B, leaving stockholders' deficit at -$3.90B due to cumulative leveraged share repurchases. Annual interest expense of $181.1M yields interest coverage of 5.27x, offering minimal safety margin during economic or credit downturns. Because this high-leverage recapitalized structure is permanent management policy rather than a temporary shock, Calamity Tier is inapplicable.

column11: Full-service casual and fine dining (Olive Garden, LongHorn Steakhouse, Ruth's Chris) is discretionary and easily deferrable or substituted with home cooking during economic downturns; it fails the Munger/Buffett essential need or high-frequency everyday habit standard.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Darden is the largest full-service restaurant operator in the US, but casual dining and steakhouse concepts are deferrable discretionary spending categories rather than essential needs or entrenched everyday habits. Traffic remains vulnerable to disposable income contractions and consumer trade-down pressures.
column21: Operates over 2,000 full-service restaurants across brands including Olive Garden (flagship casual Italian), LongHorn Steakhouse, Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen, Yard House, and Ruth's Chris Steak House (acquired FY24). Despite purchasing scale efficiencies and FY24-FY25 revenue exceeding $11B-$13B with steady 11-14% ROIC, casual dining lacks switching costs, faces intense fragmented competition from independent eateries and fast-casual alternatives, and suffers guest count contraction during consumer discretionary belt-tightening.

column14: Supply chain and global marketing purchasing power create insurmountable scale economies shared with franchisees, enabling unmatched value menu pricing (e.g. $5 Meal Deal, McValue) while extracting 15%+ percentage rent and royalty tollbooths on top-line sales. Competitors cannot replicate McDonald's prime corner-lot physical real-estate footprint or supply contracts. Empirical proof: 10-year median ROIC of 30.3% and consistent >45% operating margins across cycles. Primary erosion risk: low-income consumer traffic sensitivity to cumulative post-COVID menu inflation and QSR value price wars.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Irreplaceable global QSR real-estate and franchise royalty tollbooth operating 40,000+ locations across 100+ countries. Massive supply chain scale economies shared with franchisees enable unmatched value pricing while collecting contractually formula-indexed percentage rents and royalties (>45% operating margin). Insulated from macrotrends via localized sourcing, kiosk/mobile automation (210M+ digital loyalty users), and inflation-indexed rent streams. Balance sheet structured for peace of mind: $40B debt is supported by 7.8x interest coverage and non-displaceable commercial real-estate cash flows; negative book equity is an artifact of cumulative historical buybacks that is steadily normalizing. [5-10Y g: net unit growth 2.0% + comparable sales/price 2.5% + mix/digital 1.0% - franchisee support margin drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 30.3% and operating ROIC of 33.7%, consistently exceeding 23% in all years since 2016 (peaking at 34.1% in 2021). Multi-year FCF conversion of 90.6% (2025 Owner FCF of $8.19B vs Net Income of $8.56B). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS compounded at 8.7% CAGR from $5.44 in 2016 to a record $11.95 in 2025. Systemwide sales exceed $139B across 40,000+ restaurants (approx. 95% franchised). High-margin franchise royalties and property rental income generate operating margins >45% ($12.39B EBIT in 2025). Long-term debt of $39.97B is supported by 7.83x interest coverage (EBIT $12.39B / Interest $1.58B) and contractual real-estate rental agreements. Negative accounting equity (-$1.79B in 2025) is an artifact of historical treasury share repurchases and has narrowed from -$8.21B in 2019 without external solvency risk.

column14: Global store density, proprietary ethical coffee sourcing/roasting infrastructure, and the Starbucks Rewards digital ecosystem (~34M+ active US members with substantial prepaid stored-value float) create high customer repeat frequency and scale advantages over independent cafes. Empirical proof includes a 10-year median ROIC of 22.8% and gross margins near 68-70%. Primary erosion threats include value-conscious customer pushback on premium pricing, beverage preparation complexity eroding throughput, rapid low-cost automated rivals in international markets (e.g. Luckin in China), and store-level labor friction.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Starbucks commands an iconic global beverage brand and habitual daily ritual, it faces severe structural headwinds under the 5-Macrotrend filter. Demographic aging and labor scarcity (Pillar 2) create persistent operational bottlenecks and wage inflation across its ~400,000 store workers that cannot be automated without degrading the handcrafted coffeehouse proposition. Furthermore, geopolitical and low-cost competitive displacement in China (Pillar 3) broke its primary international growth vector, forcing a retreat to a licensed JV model. Combined with balance sheet fragility (-$8.1B shareholders' deficit from historic debt-funded buybacks and ~$15B in long-term debt), Starbucks fails the Munger durability bar for a 15+ year predictable compounding runway.
column21: FY2025 revenue was $37.2B with operating income compressing to $2.9B (7.9% operating margin) before recovering toward $2.5B+ net income in FY2026 under Brian Niccol's 'Back to Starbucks' turnaround. 10-year median ROIC is 22.8%, proving historical brand power and returns on capital. However, traffic declines in 2024-2025 demonstrated pricing elasticity limits for $7+ handcrafted drinks. In China, relentless low-cost competition from Luckin Coffee forced a structural conversion of retail operations into a licensed JV in 2026. The balance sheet carries ~$14.6B-$15.0B in long-term debt against net income of $1.86B-$2.53B (debt/net income ~5.8x-7.8x) and a total stockholders' deficit of $(8.1B) resulting from aggressive debt-funded share repurchases.

column14: Global franchisor scale advantage (~98% franchised across ~60,000 restaurants) anchored by iconic Lindy consumer brands (KFC, Taco Bell). Massive collective marketing budgets ($1B+) and supply chain purchasing power create high barriers against independent restaurant operators. Empirical proof of moat: 5-year median ROIC of 24%+ (reaching 37-46% on net invested capital) and continuous system sales expansion. Demonstrated pricing power through menu price hikes and digital upsells outpacing food-away-from-home CPI without volume destruction. Primary erosion threats include fast-casual competition, third-party delivery fee friction, and franchisee margin compression from minimum-wage inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Balance Sheet, REJECT). While Yum! Brands possesses high-quality franchise economics across KFC and Taco Bell with excellent cash conversion (FCF >95% of NI), its capital structure fails Munger peace-of-mind standards: long-term net debt of ~$10.5B represents ~6.7x normal owner earnings ($1.56B FY2025 net income, well above the <=4.0x threshold), interest coverage is thin at ~4.4x EBIT/interest (below the >5.0x minimum), and multi-year debt-funded share repurchases have created a -$6.17B stockholders' deficit (severely negative tangible equity), triggering the disqualifying financial engineering red flag.
column21: FY2024 revenue of $7.55B, operating profit of $2.40B, net income of $1.49B, and FCF of ~$1.43B. FY2025 revenue of $8.21B (+9%), operating profit of $2.57B (+7%), net income of $1.56B (+5%), and FCF of ~$1.64B (operating cash flow $2.01B minus capex ~$370M). In mid-2026, completed the strategic divestiture of Pizza Hut for ~$2.4B total net proceeds ($1.7B one-time pre-tax gain, temporarily elevating TTM net income to $3.44B), sharpening focus on KFC (35,000+ units) and Taco Bell. Repaid $675M credit facility with proceeds but returned $1.8B to shareholders via buybacks and dividends in 9M 2026, maintaining long-term debt at ~$10.5B against cash of ~$450M. Stockholders' deficit stands at -$6.17B due to a deliberate, permanent policy of maintaining ~4.0x Net Debt/EBITDA leverage via debt-funded repurchases. Interest expense of ~$580M results in 4.4x EBIT interest coverage.

column14: Dominant US on-demand local delivery network (~67% market share) demonstrating clear pricing power via take-rate expansion from 11% to over 13.5% through DashPass subscription scale (18M+ members) and high-margin merchant advertising without losing customer volume.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet, REJECT). While DoorDash possesses a dominant US food delivery network effect (~67% market share) and pricing power via take-rate expansion, reported cash flows are an accounting mirage heavily distorted by massive stock-based compensation ($1.10B in FY24, $1.05B in FY25, exceeding cumulative GAAP net income). The company lacks a multi-cycle peak-to-peak earnings track record (GAAP profitable only since FY24) and has taken on $3.3B in debt to fund aggressive cross-border and software acquisitions (Deliveroo, SevenRooms), failing Munger's real cash conversion and balance sheet standards.
column21: FY24 revenue $10.72B (+24%), operating loss $(38)M, GAAP net income $123M, FCF ~$1.8B, SBC $1.10B. FY25 revenue $13.72B (+28%), operating income $723M, GAAP net income $935M, FCF ~$1.8B, SBC $1.05B. Multi-year GAAP net income totals $1.06B against $2.15B in stock-based compensation, meaning real Owner FCF after dilutive employee compensation is negative to negligible. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~8.2% (FY25 ROIC ~6.5%), below the 12% hurdle. Balance sheet holds $5.98B in cash and short-term investments against $3.30B in total debt following the $1.2B SevenRooms acquisition and £2.9B ($3.9B) Deliveroo acquisition.

column14: Massive global origination, crushing, and logistics network provides operational scale, but products are fungible commodities traded on global exchanges. ADM is a price-taker on commodity crush margins (soybean crush, corn wet milling, ethanol) and cannot raise prices independently of global market supply and demand. 5-year median ROIC (~5-7%) and 10-year median ROIC (9.5%) consistently fail the 12% threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% and lack of pricing power, REJECT). Agribusiness processor and commodity price-taker whose operating margins (1.8-4.3%) and returns on capital fluctuate with cyclical global crush margins. 5-year median ROIC of ~5.4% and 10-year median ROIC of 9.5% fail the 12% compounding hurdle. Structurally lacks pricing power above inflation.
column21: Historical ROIC: 2020: 3.9%, 2021: 5.4%, 2022: 7.2%, 2023: 7.3%, 2024: 3.7%, 2025: ~2.8%; 10-year median ROIC is 9.5%, consistently failing the 12% hurdle. Operating margins range from 1.8% to 4.3% across the cycle. While ADM generates substantial revenue ($85B-$100B+) and operates an essential global agricultural logistics network, profits are fundamentally tied to spot crush margins and grain supply dynamics rather than proprietary pricing power. FCF is highly volatile due to massive working capital swings tied to commodity price cycles ($1.2B in 2024 vs $4.2B in 2025). Furthermore, internal control material weaknesses and SEC/DOJ investigations over intersegment profit shifting to mask Nutrition segment underperformance resulted in a $40M SEC settlement in January 2026.

column14: Global oilseed processing and grain origination network provides physical scale and logistics presence, but offers no structural pricing power. Operates as a pure commodity price-taker whose operating margins (2-3%) and ROIC (10Y avg ~7%, FY24 7.1%, FY25 3.6%) are governed by volatile, cyclical soybean and softseed crush spreads rather than proprietary economic rents. Return on capital consistently falls below the 12% hurdle across the cycle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Global agricultural processor and merchandiser operating as a commodity price-taker. Despite vast origination and crushing scale enhanced by the Viterra acquisition, Bunge lacks pricing power over fungible agricultural commodities. Operating margins average 2-3% and multi-cycle ROIC (~7% 10-year average, falling to ~3.6% in 2025) fails the 12% hurdle. Margins remain hostage to industry crush spreads and volatile working-capital swings.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record shows 10-year average ROIC of ~6.95% (5-year median ~10.2%, dropping to ~7.09% in FY2024 and ~3.62% in FY2025), failing the 12% hurdle. Gross margins are paper-thin at 4.5%-6.5% and operating margins average 2%-3%, occasionally turning negative during agricultural down-cycles (e.g. 2019). July 2025 acquisition of Viterra ($10.6B total consideration including $5.34B stock and $3.55B debt absorption) expands scale in grain handling and origination but increases capital intensity and leverage while leaving the core price-taking commodity economics unchanged. Bunge cannot unilaterally raise prices above global market-clearing levels without immediate customer defection.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Understandability, REJECT). Recent spin-off (separated from Corteva on October 1, 2026) lacking a standalone multi-cycle public operating record. Complex carve-out capitalization with ~$5.58B in borrowings, credit facilities, and a $3.5B upstream cash distribution to historical DuPont entity EIDP. Standalone capital allocation, corporate governance, and through-cycle ROIC remain unproven through an agricultural downturn.
column21: Vylor (VYLR) was spun off from Corteva (CTVA) on October 1, 2026, housing the Pioneer and Brevant seed and traits genetics businesses. While Pioneer has storied heritage assets, Vylor has traded publicly for only ~6 weeks as of November 2026 and lacks an independent, multi-cycle public operating and capital allocation record through an agricultural downturn. Carved-out financial history indicates sub-hurdle capital efficiency with median GAAP ROIC of 4.85% (FY24 GAAP ROIC 5.65%, FY25 GAAP ROIC 4.06%), with EBIT contracting from $1,118M in FY24 to $671M in FY25. Balance sheet at separation was structured with ~$5.58B in debt and facilities, used in part to fund a $3.5B upstream transfer to legacy DuPont entity EIDP amid lingering litigation scrutiny. Under Munger's default-reject mandate, unseasoned corporate spin-offs lacking standalone multi-cycle history fail Gate 1.

column14: Unrivaled scale economies shared flywheel: low SKU count (~4,000) generates immense purchasing power and supplier volume discounts, capped markups (14-15%) pass savings to members, driving negative working capital and rapid inventory turns (>12x). Proven by 38-44% GAAP ROIC and consistent 92%+ renewal rates with regular membership fee increases (raised to $65/$130 in Sep 2024 with zero churn). Erosion risks from warehouse club competitors or digital delivery are mitigated by bulk physical handling advantages and Kirkland Signature value.
column20: A quintessential Munger masterpiece and global archetype of scale economies shared. Unbroken peak-to-peak EPS compounding over 10+ years, 92%+ membership renewal across 84M+ members, and a fortress balance sheet with >$16B in net cash and 80x+ interest coverage. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends. [5-10Y g: comp store volume 4.0% + pricing/fee increases 1.5% + warehouse expansion 2.5% + digital/Kirkland mix 0.5% - wage/capex reinvestment drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: 10-year track record of peak-to-peak EPS compounding from $6.08 in FY17 to $20.76 in FY26 (13% CAGR). Median GAAP ROIC of 38.8% (tangible/operating ROIC >41%). FCF conversion consistently >100% (FY26 Owner FCF $12.2B vs NI $9.2B, fcf_conv 1.18x) aided by negative working capital cycle. Total cash and ST investments of $20.2B vastly exceed LT debt of $3.9B ($16.3B net cash). EBIT/Interest coverage of 80.6x. Membership fee revenue grew to $5.91B in FY26 following the Sep 2024 fee hike to $65/$130, with US/Canada renewal rates holding at 92.3%.

column14: Rural small-format store density (~20,000 locations) provides convenience in small towns, but the company lacks pricing power against Walmart and branded CPG suppliers. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has fallen to ~9.2% (6-8% in FY24-FY25), well below the 12% threshold, with negative incremental ROIIC over the last cycle. Primary erosion threats include Walmart's superior scale/omnichannel reach, hard discounters (Aldi, Dollar Tree), shift toward low-margin consumables, and inflation squeezing core low-income consumers.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Rural discount retailer lacks pricing power above inflation; selling branded packaged goods to financially stretched low-income consumers forces severe margin compression when input costs rise. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has deteriorated to ~9.2% (FY24-FY25 ROIC ~6-8%), well below the 12% threshold, with negative incremental ROIIC over the past cycle as $2B+ in invested capital yielded lower operating profit ($2.2B vs $3.2B in FY21). Intense everyday low price competition from Walmart and hard discounters prevents sustained economic profit compounding.
column21: Dollar General operates ~20,000 small-format stores across 47 US states, serving rural areas where 75% of Americans live within 5 miles of a store. However, consumables represent over 80% of net sales, leaving the company exposed to low gross margin items (~20-25%) while higher-margin seasonal/home merchandise has lagged. Operating margin compressed from 8.6% in FY21 to 4.2% in FY24 before recovering modestly to ~5.1% in FY25 ($2.2B operating profit on $42.7B sales). 5-year GAAP ROIC has dropped below the 12% hurdle (FY21: ~14.5%, FY22: ~13.5%, FY23: ~9.2%, FY24: ~6.1%, FY25: ~6.8%, 5-year median: ~9.2%). Incremental ROIIC across the 2021-2025 cycle is negative. The business model possesses neither pricing power >= inflation nor defensible excess returns above cost of capital.

column14: Dollar Tree attempts a scale economies shared model in small-box discount retail, but lacks an insurmountable cost advantage against Walmart (over 30x larger scale) and cross-border ultra-discount platforms (Temu, Shein). Proof of moat fails: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.5% (against the 12% hurdle). The company lacks pricing power >= inflation: breaking its $1.00 price point to $1.25 triggered traffic drag, while multi-price tiering ($3-$7) directly exposes it to fierce competition from Walmart everyday low prices with zero defensible barriers.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 8.5% < 12%, REJECT). Discount variety retailer lacks structural pricing power and fails empirical proof of moat. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 8.5% falls well short of the 12% threshold. Moving away from its signature $1.00 fixed-price format to $1.25 alienated core budget shoppers, while the multi-price expansion ($3, $5, $7) directly collides with retail behemoths (Walmart) and cross-border ultra-discount platforms (Temu, Shein) without an insurmountable cost advantage.
column21: Financial Track Record: 10-year / 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.5%, consistently failing the 12% hurdle. Operating margins historically hovered around 5-8%, expanding slightly to ~8.3-8.5% on continuing operations post-Family Dollar separation. FCF generation historically fluctuated ($1.1B in FY2025 on continuing operations) but burdened by continuous store renovation, multi-price format conversions (Dollar Tree 3.0), and lease obligations. Segments & Business Model: Following the July 2025 sale of Family Dollar to Brigade Capital and Macellum Capital for $1.007B in cash (a staggering loss on the $8.5B paid in 2015), the company operates primarily the Dollar Tree banner (>8,000 stores). Assortment is roughly 45-50% consumables (food, snacks, health and beauty, cleaning supplies) and 50-55% variety/seasonal merchandise. Pricing Power & Moat Dynamics: Dollar Tree possesses zero switching costs and no pricing power above inflation. The breaking of the $1.00 price point to $1.25 in 2021-2022 generated customer resistance and foot traffic declines. The multi-price expansion ($3-$7) strips away the format's simplicity and brings Dollar Tree into direct competition with Walmart, Dollar General, and factory-direct cross-border e-commerce (Temu, Shein). M&A & Capital Allocation: The 2015 debt-funded acquisition of Family Dollar for $8.5B destroyed billions of dollars in shareholder value through massive goodwill impairments, operational dysfunction, and eventual fire-sale divestiture in 2025 for $1.007B. Even on standalone operations, capital reinvestment yields sub-hurdle returns.

column11: Discretionary-heavy general merchandise mix (~50% apparel, home furnishings, hardlines); consumer shopping trips are deferrable and easily forgone during economic downturns, lacking staple grocery indispensability.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Discretionary-heavy general merchandise retailer (~50% sales in apparel, home furnishings, and hardlines) whose curated 'cheap chic' shopping trips are deferrable during inflationary pressures. Lacks essential grocery staple indispensability and exhibits zero customer deprivation if vanished, with traffic consistently lost to Walmart and Amazon.
column21: FY2024–FY2025 performance underscored structural vulnerability: comparable sales contracted -2.6% in FY2025 due to consumer discretionary pullback. Operating margin compressed to ~4.9% (vs 8.4% peak in FY2021). While Food & Beverage ($24.1B) and Household Essentials ($18.0B) drive frequency, discretionary categories (Apparel ~$15.8B, Home Furnishings $15.6B, Hardlines $15.8B) drive higher-margin profitability but suffer severe deferral when consumer budgets tighten. Long-term debt stands at ~$16.5B against ~$11.8B net debt.

column14: Unrivaled scale economies shared: $713B+ top-line volume creates unbeatable purchasing leverage over suppliers, passing cost savings to consumers via Everyday Low Prices (EDLP). High-margin retail media (Walmart Connect, $6.4B run-rate) and marketplace fees increasingly subsidize core retail pricing. Proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 18.9% and operating ROIC of 25.7%. Primary erosion risks include Amazon digital delivery density, deep discounter expansion (Aldi), and distribution center wage inflation.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Dominant omnichannel grocery and general merchandise retailer benefiting from scale economies shared. Secular insulation across all 5 macrotrends driven by supply chain robotics automation, private label resilience, and high-margin retail media growth. Fortress balance sheet with net debt / net income ~1.1x and >12x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: traffic and volume 2.0% + pricing/inflation pass-through 1.5% + retail media and marketplace mix 1.5% - digital supply chain capex drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: Multi-cycle compounding demonstrated by 10-year revenue growth from $486B to $713B and peak owner EPS rising from $1.46 (FY16) to $2.73 (FY25). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 18.9% (operating ROIC 25.7%), well above the 12% hurdle. Cash generation is robust with FCF conversion of 115.5% (FY25 OCF of $41.6B easily funding $26.6B capex). Balance sheet leverage is modest with $34.6B long-term debt offset by $10.7B cash against $21.9B net income (net debt repayable in ~1.1 years; interest coverage of 12.86x). Prudent capital allocation: disciplined exits of lower-return international units (Asda, Seiyu) while scaling high-growth omnichannel assets (Flipkart, PhonePe, Walmart Connect, Symbotic automation partnership).

column14: Centuries-old brand equity of Jack Daniel's (#1 American whiskey globally), Woodford Reserve, and Old Forester protected by proprietary cooperages and multi-year aged whiskey inventory barriers (4-7+ year maturation lead times) that cannot be replicated by capital alone. Multi-cycle proof demonstrated by 10-year median ROIC of ~16.2% and stable gross margins near 60%. Key erosion risks include younger cohort alcohol moderation, GLP-1 appetite suppression headwinds, retaliatory import tariffs, and premium tequila/RTD competitive intensity.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global spirits leader anchored by iconic Jack Daniel's trademark, aged barrel inventory moat, and pricing power offsetting input cost inflation. While spirits face secular volume headwinds from GLP-1 adoption and Gen Z moderation, premiumization, international expansion, and RTD co-branding (Jack & Coke) support steady compounding. Balance sheet is conservative with net debt under 3x net income and interest coverage exceeding 11x. [5-10Y g: global volume 1.0% + price/mix 2.5% + RTD expansion 1.0% - tariff/input margin drag 0.5% + share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: 10-year historical GAAP ROIC median of 16.2%, consistently exceeding the 12% hurdle. Gross margins steady between 59% and 62%; operating margins consistently in the 26-33% range. FY2024 operating income was $1.40B and FY2025 operating income was $1.09B, with net interest expense of $97M yielding >11x EBIT/interest coverage. Total debt reduced to ~$2.7B in FY2025 (debt/net income ~3.1x, well below 4.0x threshold) following repayment of $300M senior notes. Multi-year FCF conversion averages 80-100% normalized across barrel inventory aging cycles. Brown family dual-class ownership structure maintains multi-decade stewardship and over 40 consecutive years of dividend increases (Dividend Aristocrat).

column14: Exclusive perpetual US commercial rights to Modelo Especial, Corona Extra, and Pacifico coupled with massive brewery scale in Mexico (Nava, Obregón, Veracruz) and deep US distributor lock-in. Beer segment yields ~38% operating margins. However, consolidated 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 10.5% (failing the 12% threshold) due to heavy brewery capex, $13B+ acquired intangibles, and catastrophic capital allocation (>$4B Canopy Growth write-off and $1.5B–$2.5B FY25 wine impairment). Primary threats include 100% Mexican brewing single-source exposure to US-Mexico tariffs, category volume maturation, and demographic/immigration headwinds.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Despite possessing a strong consumer brand intangible moat in imported Mexican beers (Modelo Especial, Corona Extra, Pacifico), Constellation fails the empirical proof-of-moat hurdle with a 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~10.5%, persistently below the 12% threshold. Capital efficiency is structurally diluted by high capital intensity in Mexican brewery buildouts, massive acquired intangibles, and catastrophic capital misallocation (including the >$4B Canopy Growth write-off and $1.5B–$2.5B FY25 wine goodwill impairment). Downstream, the business also faces severe single-source foreign manufacturing exposure with 100% of beer brewed in Mexico subject to cross-border tariff risks.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 10.5%, failing the Gate 3b hurdle (>= 12%). While Constellation's beer division generates robust operating margins (~38%) and owns the #1 dollar-share US beer brand (Modelo Especial), consolidated returns on capital have been chronically dragged down by non-beer operations and value-destructive capital allocation. The company invested over $4B into Canopy Growth which resulted in near-total write-downs, followed by a $1.5B–$2.5B goodwill impairment on Wine & Spirits in FY25. Free cash flow conversion has historically been constrained by continuous multi-hundred-million-dollar Mexican brewery capital expenditures ($800M–$1B+/year). Long-term debt remains around $11B–$12B with leverage near 3.0x EBITDA. With 100% of beer production located in Mexico, the core earnings engine is directly vulnerable to US-Mexico trade policy, tariffs, and border friction.

column14: Unrivaled North American distribution scale and local route density provide insurmountable per-stop logistics cost advantages over regional competitors. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 18.2% and gross margin remains steady at ~18.3%. Food inflation is reliably passed through via cost-plus contract mechanisms and dynamic independent pricing. Primary erosion threats include independent restaurant distress and driver wage inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Market leader in foodservice distribution with scale economies shared and high ROIC (18.2% median), but structurally violates Gate 6 balance sheet peace-of-mind. Total debt of $12.3B against $1.76B net income yields lt_debt/NI of 7.0x (net debt/NI of 6.0x), far exceeding the 4.0x ceiling. Interest coverage of ~4.9x falls below the 5.0x minimum, and debt-funded share buybacks have resulted in negative tangible equity of -$3.5B.
column21: FY2025 revenue of $84.6B, operating income (EBIT) of $3,095M, net income of $1,757M, and OCF of $2,638M against capex of $700M (FCF conversion 104%). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 18.16% and operating tangible ROIC exceeds 34%. However, long-term debt is $12,315M against cash of $1,786M (net debt $10,529M, or 6.0x net income). FY2025 cash interest paid of $629M yields EBIT/interest coverage of 4.92x (below the 5.0x hurdle). Stockholders' equity of $2,666M minus $6,177M goodwill/intangibles leaves negative tangible equity of -$3,511M, reflecting aggressive debt-funded buybacks rather than a fortress balance sheet.

column14: Rural geographic monopoly where ~50% of stores operate in towns with <5,000 residents lacking restaurant or grocery competition. 5th largest US pizza chain with ~60% prepared food gross margins and proven pricing power above inflation; 5Y median GAAP ROIC of 12.7% and tangible ROIC of 15.1%-17.8%. Primary erosion threats are long-term EV fleet adoption dampening fuel trips and rural population stagnation.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Dominant rural Midwest and Southern convenience hub operating as a local geographic monopoly where ~50% of stores reside in towns with populations under 5,000 lacking restaurant or grocery competition. High-margin prepared food (5th largest US pizza chain with ~60% gross margins) provides resilient pricing power above inflation. Insulated from AI disruption and structurally cushioned against rapid EV transition by rural driving dynamics and heavy fee-simple store ownership (~90%). Fortress balance sheet with 10.7x interest coverage and net debt repayable in 2.5 years of net income. [5-10Y g: store count growth 3.0% + inside traffic volume 1.5% + prepared food pricing 2.5% + mix shift 1.0% - fuel volume drag 0.5% + share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: Owner EPS compounded at 18.0% CAGR from $4.48 in FY2016 to $19.16 in FY2025. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 12.71% and FY2025 tangible operating ROIC reached 17.83%. 10-year cumulative Owner FCF of $4.42B represents 115.5% conversion of GAAP Net Income ($3.83B), with TTM FCF conversion at 116.7%. Pristine balance sheet despite November 2024 acquisition of Fikes/CEFCO (198 stores, $1.15B): FY2025 Net Debt of $1.81B is 2.53x Net Income ($714.4M) and EBIT interest coverage is 10.7x ($1,033.7M EBIT vs $96.6M interest). Network of ~2,900 stores supported by self-distribution logistics (~75% inside goods) and over 9 million Casey's Rewards loyalty members.

column14: Conventional grocery retail model lacks pricing power and defensible economic barriers against Walmart, Costco, and Aldi. 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~9.2% against a 12% minimum hurdle, and GAAP operating margins remain compressed at 2.0–2.6%. The company cannot raise prices above food inflation without immediately forfeiting market share to non-union discounters, and its attempt to achieve defensive scale via the $24.6B Albertsons merger was blocked by federal and state antitrust injunctions in late 2024 and terminated.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Traditional supermarket chain structurally unable to clear capital efficiency hurdles, with a 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~9.2% (below 12% hurdle) and thin 2.0–2.6% operating margins. Lacks independent pricing power against non-union retail giants (Walmart, Costco) and hard discounters (Aldi). The attempted $24.6B merger with Albertsons was permanently blocked by federal and state antitrust courts in December 2024 and terminated.
column21: 10-year historical GAAP ROIC averages 8–9% (median ~9.2%), consistently below the 12% threshold. Operating margins remain thin at 2.06% in FY24 ($3.1B EBIT on $148B sales) and 2.62% in FY25 ($3.85B EBIT on $147B sales). Cash generation is absorbed by heavy ongoing store remodel capex and digital fulfillment investments. Balance sheet is burdened by $17.6B in long-term debt and finance leases ($25B+ total obligations) along with multi-employer pension commitments. In December 2024, federal and state courts granted injunctions blocking the $24.6B Albertsons merger, which was subsequently abandoned and triggered multi-billion dollar breach-of-contract litigation from Albertsons. Kroger remains a structural price-taker relative to Walmart (>20% US grocery share) and Costco.

column14: Entrenched niche brand leadership across consumer staple categories (Arm & Hammer, Trojan, First Response, Batiste, Waterpik, TheraBreath) where #1/#2 market shares and retail shelf space deter direct competition from conglomerates. Demonstrated pricing power through raw material inflation cycles with gross margins sustained around 44-45% and 10-year median ROIC ~16.8% (FY24-FY25 GAAP ROIC ~13.5-14.0%). Key erosion risks include private-label penetration in value laundry and retail customer concentration.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Resilient consumer staples portfolio of focused #1/#2 brands anchored by Arm & Hammer. Pricing power demonstrated across inflationary cycles with gross margins at 44-45%. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends with FCF conversion >100% and conservative ~2.7x net debt to net income. [5-10Y g: volume 1.5% + price 1.5% + mix/reinvestment 2.0% - margin drags 0.0% + buybacks 1.5%]
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 16.8% (FY24 ~14.0%, FY25 ~13.8%). FY25 net sales reached $6.20B with operating income of $1.17B (18.9% margin) and FCF of ~$1.1B on net income of $741.5M (>140% FCF conversion). Net debt of ~$2.0B easily serviceable via ~2.7 years of net income with interest coverage at ~12.3x.

column14: Colgate commands a dominant ~41.4% global value share in toothpaste and ~32.4% in manual toothbrushes across 200+ countries, reinforced by massive Lindy brand awareness, ubiquitous shelf-space distribution, and strong dental professional endorsements. Hill's Pet Nutrition adds a high-margin science-based moat driven by veterinarian recommendations and therapeutic formulas. Demonstrated pricing power through repeated mid-single digit price increases passing through commodity inflation while maintaining or expanding market share. Empirical moat proof: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 35.6%, operating ROIC exceeding 100%, and gross margins near 60%. Primary erosion risks include private label encroachment in basic tiers and retail channel consolidation.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Unrivaled global oral care franchise commanding >41% worldwide toothpaste market share alongside Hill's high-margin science-based pet nutrition. Demonstrated pricing power across multiple inflationary cycles with multi-year GAAP ROIC averaging >35%. Fully insulated from 5 macrotrends with local supply chains and non-discretionary daily consumable habits. Robust balance sheet with 12x+ interest coverage and Net Debt repayable in <1.6 years of Owner FCF. [5-10Y g: volume 1.5% + price 2.0% + mix/reinvestment 1.5% - input cost drag 0.5% + buybacks 1.0%]
column21: 10-year financial history demonstrates extraordinary capital efficiency: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 35.6% (operating ROIC >100%), gross margins consistently 59-60%, and Owner FCF conversion averages >120% of GAAP Net Income ($3.48B Owner FCF vs $2.13B GAAP NI in 2025). As of Q3 2026, organic sales grew 3.6% (+1.7% volume, +2.0% price) with Hill's organic sales up 5.7% and toothpaste global value share steady at 41.4%. Balance sheet carries $6.87B long-term debt against $1.29B cash (net debt $5.58B), generating $3.31B EBIT with $267M interest expense for 12.4x interest coverage, well above safety thresholds. 62 consecutive years of dividend increases.

column14: Category leadership and Lindy brand recognition across core staples (Clorox bleach, Pine-Sol, Glad, Kingsford, Hidden Valley). Multi-cycle median ROIC of 18.2% and gross margin recovery back to ~44.5% demonstrate brand pricing power, but commoditized chemical formulations face persistent private-label substitution pressure (Great Value, Kirkland).
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Mature, heavily US-centric household staples portfolio with flat-to-negative multi-year organic volume growth and severe private-label substitutability across core categories (bleach, trash bags, cat litter). Under Macrotrend 5 (Structural Inflation & Cost of Capital), persistent commodity input cost volatility (resin, chlor-alkali) and elevated refinancing costs on ~$4.0B of debt collide with private-label price ceilings, capping the competitive advantage period below the 15-year hurdle.
column21: 10-year median ROIC ~18.2%. Revenue has compounded at <2% CAGR over FY15-FY25, with organic volume frequently flat to negative. Gross margin collapsed from 45% to ~36% during the 2021-2023 inflationary shock, requiring aggressive pricing actions to recover to 44.5%, which triggered volume elasticity and trade-downs to store brands. Over 80% of sales remain concentrated in the saturated domestic US market, leaving limited runway for value-accretive capital deployment. Failed M&A diversification in vitamins/supplements (RenewLife/VMS) resulted in major goodwill write-downs and subsequent divestment.

column14: No structural moat archetype. Kimberly-Clark operates in commoditized consumer tissue and personal care categories with zero customer switching costs and high private-label retailer penetration. The company cannot sustain price hikes above raw material (wood pulp, polymer resins) inflation without volume erosion and market share loss to store brands, exemplified by its complete exit from the Canadian consumer Kleenex business in 2023. Top-line 10-year revenue CAGR of under 1% significantly lags cumulative inflation.
column20: Rejected at Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing). Kimberly-Clark lacks a defensible moat archetype ('None') and fails pricing power ('N'). In commoditized tissue and personal care categories with zero switching barriers, price increases to recover volatile raw material (pulp, resin) costs trigger volume losses to lower-priced private label and store brands. 10-year sales CAGR (<1%) severely trails inflation, and margins remain cyclical to input cost spikes.
column21: 10-year net sales hovered between $18B and $20B (CAGR <1% from 2015 to 2025), failing to keep pace with >30% cumulative inflation and reflecting chronic real volume stagnation. Gross margins are volatile and exposed to commodity cycles, falling from ~37% in 2020 to ~30.5% in 2021-2022 during input cost inflation. Complete exit from the Canadian consumer facial tissue market (discontinuing Kleenex) in 2023 demonstrated inability to pass through costs against private label. Infant care (Huggies) faces long-term demographic volume headwinds from declining birth rates alongside fierce competition from Procter & Gamble and retailer store brands.

column14: Lindy brand power and grocery shelf real estate across North America Retail (Cheerios, Pillsbury, Betty Crocker, Nature Valley) and Pet (Blue Buffalo). However, brand equity has steadily commoditized against aggressive private-label store brands, fresh perimeter alternatives, and price-sensitive consumer defection, preventing price realization above inflation without severe volume loss.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). General Mills lacks pricing power >= inflation: price increases during post-pandemic inflation triggered sustained organic pound volume contractions and market share losses to private-label alternatives across cereal, snacks, and refrigerated dough. To defend volume in FY25-FY26, management was forced to step up trade promotions and consumer value investments, causing organic net sales to contract (-2% in FY26) and ROIC to moderate below the 12% threshold (9.3%-11.3% in FY25-FY26).
column21: FY24-FY26 financial results demonstrate structural pricing elasticity constraints: FY24 reported net sales down 1% with negative volume; FY25 organic sales flat to down with heavy promotional discounting; FY26 organic sales down 2% and reported net sales down 5% to $18.4B. ROIC moderated from 11.3%-12.3% in FY24 to 9.3%-11.3% in FY25, failing the sustained >= 12% cycle hurdle. Free cash flow contracted from $2.53B in FY24 to $2.29B in FY25 and $1.63B in FY26. Blue Buffalo pet food segment has slowed from premiumization tailwinds to category normalization, failing to offset center-aisle grocery volume declines.

column14: Brand equity in staple packaged protein and shelf-stable foods (SPAM, Skippy, Jennie-O, Planters, Hormel Black Label) creates shelf presence, but lacks pricing power to outrun commodity cost swings. Competitors and private-label store brands readily arbitrage shelf space in packaged meats and nuts. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has deteriorated to ~8% (FY21 10.1%, FY22 9.5%, FY23 7.7%, FY24 8.5%, FY25 6.1%), well below the 12% hurdle. Pricing actions trigger retail volume elasticity and market share erosion.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% and lack of pricing power >= inflation, REJECT). While Hormel possesses recognizable consumer protein and pantry brands (SPAM, Skippy, Planters, Jennie-O), it operates as a price-sensitive packaged food processor unable to pass through sustained input cost inflation without suffering volume declines. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has sunk to ~8% (dropping to 6.1% in FY25), well below the 12% threshold. Capital allocation was further impaired by the debt-financed $3.4B Planters acquisition, which diluted returns on capital and triggered $234M in non-cash impairments in FY25.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates structural capital efficiency erosion: GAAP ROIC steadily fell from 13.1% in FY20 to 10.1% in FY21, 9.5% in FY22, 7.7% in FY23, 8.5% in FY24, and 6.1% in FY25 (5-year median ~8.1%, far below the 12% Munger hurdle). Operating margins compressed from ~10.3% in FY21 to 5.48% GAAP (8.4% adjusted) in FY25. In FY21, Hormel acquired Planters from Kraft Heinz for $3.4B funded by ~$3.2B in senior notes, expanding long-term debt from negligible levels to $2.8B-$2.9B. The acquisition diluted corporate returns and required $234M in Q4 FY25 non-cash asset impairment charges. Attempts to raise prices across Retail triggered consumer pushback and elasticity-related volume contractions, proving absence of pricing power ahead of inflation. Jennie-O turkey operations remain subject to biological and commodity cycles (avian influenza). FCF conversion has fluctuated widely ($762M in FY20, $1.01B in FY24, and dropping to $535M in FY25).

column14: Iconic century-old confectionery brands (Reese's, Hershey's, Kisses, Kit Kat US license) command ~45% US chocolate confectionery market share and entrenched checkout-lane front-end shelf placement that competitors cannot economically displace. Proven pricing power with multi-year high single-digit price realizations absorbing historic cocoa shocks; 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 21.2% well above the 12% hurdle. Primary erosion threats include GLP-1 weight-loss adoption reducing impulse snacking, extreme raw cocoa input volatility, and retailer private-label encroachment in salty snacks.
column20: Passes all 6 gates into funnel. Dominant US confectionery franchise with ~45% chocolate market share and iconic Lindy brands (Reese's, Hershey's, Kisses). Strong pricing power has consistently countered severe agricultural cost shocks. Balance sheet remains conservative with net debt/EBITDA ~2.0x, interest coverage >7.5x even at cyclical cocoa troughs, and FCF conversion >100%. [5-10Y g: snack volume 1.0% + brand pricing 2.0% + product mix 1.0% - input cost drag 0.5% + share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 10-year average ROIC exceeds 20% (5-year median GAAP ROIC ~21.2%), remaining resilient through economic cycles and troughing near ~10% only during unprecedented 2024-2025 cocoa commodity spikes. Operating cash flow of $1.7B-$1.9B reliably generates FCF conversion >100% of net income ($1.7B-$1.9B FCF vs $1.1B-$1.8B NI). FY2025 operating income of $1.44B covers net interest expense of $190M by 7.6x (17.5x in FY2024), and net debt (~$3.6B) is repayable in ~2.0 years of normal owner earnings. Reese's remains the #1 confection brand in the US, supporting dominant front-end retail checkout placement and category-leading gross margins.

column14: While Kraft Heinz holds iconic brand intangibles across condiments, cheese, and packaged meals (Heinz, Kraft, Philadelphia, Oscar Mayer), the economic moat fails empirical verification. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~5.2-6.8% falls dramatically short of the 12% hurdle (and tangible ROIC fails the 15% threshold). Pricing power above inflation is absent: price increases across 2022-2024 resulted in severe volume contraction (-2.1% volume/mix in FY2024, -3.4% organic sales in FY2025) as price-sensitive consumers migrated to private-label store brands, forcing heavy promotional rollbacks and marketing reinvestments. Structural moat erosion is compounded by retailer bargaining power (Walmart, Kroger, Aldi) and center-aisle grocery disintermediation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 5.2-6.8% < 12%, lack of pricing power; REJECT). Despite possessing household heritage food brands (Heinz, Kraft, Philadelphia), Kraft Heinz fails the empirical proof-of-moat test with multi-year GAAP ROIC severely below the 12% hurdle. Attempts to pass through input cost inflation via list price hikes triggered immediate volume contractions (-2.1% in FY2024, -3.4% organic sales in FY2025) and private-label market share losses in core center-store categories, disproving pricing power.
column21: Financial Track Record: 10-year median ROIC is 6.8%, with 2023-2025 annual ROIC lingering between 4.9% and 5.7%, well below the 12% cost of capital benchmark. In FY2024, net sales fell 3.0% (organic sales -2.1%) with persistent negative volume/mix across North American retail. In FY2025, organic net sales contracted -3.4%, driven by consumer pushback and private-label share gains in cheese, meats, and shelf-stable meals. FCF generation remained positive ($2.96B in 2023, $3.16B in 2024, ~$3.7B in 2025), but capital returns remain depressed by a legacy goodwill and intangible base that suffered a $15.4B write-down in 2019 and recurring subsequent impairments. Balance Sheet & Leverage: Net debt stands at ~$17.5B-$18.5B ($21.2B total debt vs $3.7B cash in FY2025), representing ~4.7x net debt to normalized net income, exceeding the conservative fortress threshold. Competitive Dynamics: Private label penetration in US center-aisle grocery exceeded 20-23% in 2024-2025, as major grocery retailers (Walmart Great Value, Kroger, Aldi) narrowed the quality gap and expanded price differentials, stripping Kraft Heinz of pricing independence.

column14: Global Lindy snack brand portfolio (Oreo, Cadbury, Milka, Ritz, LU, Toblerone) backed by massive direct-store delivery and global retail distribution networks. However, proof of moat fails empirical hurdles: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7-10.8% (consistently below the 12.0% hurdle) due to a heavy invested capital base burdened by $24.0B+ of goodwill and $16.0B+ of acquired intangibles. Furthermore, steep cocoa and packaging cost inflation highlighted clear pricing power boundaries, as aggressive price increases induced volume/mix contraction (-1.0% in FY24 with sustained volume elasticity in FY25) and retail pushback.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (REJECT). Proof of Moat fails empirical hurdle: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 10.8% in workbook data and ~6-9% on reported GAAP figures across 2020-2025, consistently missing the mandatory 12.0% threshold. Heavy goodwill and intangibles from historical acquisitions (Kraft spin-off, Cadbury, Clif Bar, Chipita) dilute returns on capital. Furthermore, pricing actions to pass through 50-year-high cocoa costs led to negative volume elasticity (-1.0% volume/mix in FY24 and persistent volume pressure in FY25), proving pricing power cannot outpace severe input cost spikes without customer volume loss. Downstream gates bypassed per strict waterfall.
column21: Mondelez International generates over $36B in net revenue from iconic snack food brands (Oreo, Cadbury, Milka, Ritz, belVita, Philadelphia). Despite strong brand recognition, historical GAAP ROIC has consistently trended between 5% and 11% (2020: ~6.5%, 2021: ~7.3%, 2022: ~5.2%, 2023: ~8.9%, 2024: ~9.2%, 2025: ~5.4%), yielding a 5-year median of 10.8% (or lower on reported GAAP), failing the mandatory 12.0% hurdle. Invested capital (~$45B) is heavily weighted by $24.0B of goodwill and over $16B of other intangibles. In FY24 and FY25, organic revenue growth (+4.3%) was driven entirely by pricing, while volume/mix turned negative (-1.0% in FY24 with continued elasticity in FY25). FY25 reported operating income dropped ~44% to $3,548M and net income declined to $2,451M under peak cocoa cost pressures. Total debt stands at $21.2B ($19.1B net debt), representing ~7.8x FY25 net earnings.

column14: Category-captain shelf dominance and iconic heritage brands (McCormick, Frank's RedHot, French's, Cholula) create formidable intangible barriers. Supermarket retailers rely on McCormick to design, stock, and manage entire spice aisles. Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 100% (GAAP ROIC ~9.6-10% reflects $8.6B goodwill/intangibles from RB Foods and Cholula acquisitions). Successfully passed through 20%+ cumulative pricing over 2021-2024 with volumes recovering to positive growth in 2024-2025. Primary erosion risks are private-label trade-down in commoditized basic spices if retail price gaps widen excessively, and customer consolidation in quick-service restaurant B2B solutions.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global leader in spices, seasonings, and flavors with unmatched grocery category captaincy and iconic brands (McCormick, Frank's RedHot, French's, Cholula). Proved pricing power through 20%+ cumulative price realization during the 2021-2024 inflation cycle. Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 100%, and balance sheet deleveraging continues steadily (Net Debt / NI = 3.8x, interest coverage 5.5x). Fully insulated from AI and technology disruption. [5-10Y g: organic volume 1.5% + price/mix 2.0% + margin expansion/deleveraging 1.5% + bolt-on M&A/buybacks 0.5%]
column21: FY2025 revenue reached $6.84B with operating income of $1.07B (15.7% operating margin). Tangible ROIC consistently exceeds 100%, while GAAP ROIC median is 9.6% due to $8.6B of acquired goodwill/intangibles. 2025 Owner EPS reached a new peak of $2.97 (surpassing prior peak of $2.80 in 2021 and $2.62 in 2019), confirming peak-to-peak compounding. Free cash flow conversion averaged 89.3% in FY2025 ($694M Owner FCF vs $789M Net Income) and >90% over 5 years. Total long-term debt reduced from $4.44B post-RB Foods acquisition in 2017 to $3.11B in 2025. Net debt of $3.01B is repayable in 3.81 years of net income, and EBIT/interest coverage is 5.46x. 40 consecutive years of dividend increases.

column14: Brand intangibles across US grocery shelf staples (Jif peanut butter #1, Folgers coffee #1 retail ground, Milk-Bone #1 dog treat, Smucker's fruit spreads, Uncrustables) provide widespread retail distribution, but fail to generate economic moat protection. Pricing power is severely constrained by intense private-label store brand competition in spreads and coffee, acute customer concentration with retail giants (Walmart accounts for roughly 33% of sales), and direct exposure to volatile green coffee bean commodity cycles. Capital efficiency is chronically sub-hurdle, with 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~8.5% (and recent GAAP ROIC <2%), well below the required 12% threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~8.5% (and low-single-digit ROIC following the $5.6B Hostess acquisition) falls far short of the mandatory 12% hurdle across the cycle. Despite leadership in pantry staples (Jif, Folgers) and pet snacks (Milk-Bone), the business lacks true pricing power above inflation due to severe customer concentration (Walmart represents roughly one-third of sales), intense private-label competition in spreads and coffee, and volatile green coffee input commodity swings. The massive ~$2.9B goodwill/intangible impairment on Hostess Brands underscores chronic value destruction and inability to compound capital at high incremental returns.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates structurally inadequate capital efficiency: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~8.5%, with peak pandemic-era ROIC reaching only ~7.0% (FY2021) and falling to low single digits (~1.8% or negative) in FY2025-FY2026 following $2.9B in non-cash goodwill and trademark impairments on Hostess Brands. Operating margins historically range between 12-14% during normal periods but experience significant volatility from commodity costs (green coffee, peanuts) and supply chain shocks. Revenue concentration is acute, with Walmart accounting for approximately 33% of total net sales, limiting bargaining leverage. The $5.6B Hostess acquisition completed in FY2024 increased debt to ~$7.0B (debt/EBITDA ~4.4x post-deal) with subsequent multi-billion impairment charges confirming significant capital misallocation and inability to generate >12% incremental ROIIC.

column14: Commodity protein processor lacking structural barriers to entry or customer switching costs. Operating margins and returns are dictated by cyclical livestock availability (US cattle herd liquidation cycle) and feed costs rather than proprietary pricing power. 10-year historical ROIC (~7.2%) and recent ROIC (2-4%) consistently fail the 12% hurdle. High buyer power from concentrated grocery retailers (Walmart ~18% of revenue) limits pricing power.
