column20: Fails Gate 3 (Gate 3a Moat Archetype: None; Gate 3b ROIC < 12% and zero pricing power). Tyson Foods is a commodity protein processor (beef, chicken, pork) operating as a price-taker subject to volatile livestock cycles, feed grain costs, and concentrated retail buyer power (Walmart ~18%). 10-year historical average ROIC of ~7.2% and recent ROIC of 2-4% fall far short of the 12% hurdle.
column21: 10-year historical average ROIC is ~7.2% (FY2023-FY2025 ROIC depressed at 2.4%-4.2%), failing the 12% multi-cycle hurdle. FY2023 FCF was -$187M, recovering to $1.46B in FY2024 and $1.18B in FY2025. Beef segment (~50% of sales) is burdened by multi-decade low US cattle herd inventories and severe margin compression. Massive retail customer bargaining power (Walmart represents ~18% of revenue) and undifferentiated commodity protein prevent sustained pricing power above cost inflation. Past antitrust settlements regarding broiler chicken price-fixing further illustrate lack of organic pricing power.

column14: Global prestige beauty leader with entrenched brand intangibles (Estée Lauder, Clinique, La Mer, MAC, Tom Ford, Le Labo) and prime department store and travel retail counter real estate. Gross margin expanded 230 bps to 74.0% during the sales downturn, confirming underlying pricing power, but multi-year ROIC fell below the 12% hurdle due to the Asia travel retail destocking crisis and $911M in brand impairment write-downs.
column19: Identifiable, temporary, fixable calamity across gates {3b, 5, 6}. Broken metrics: 5-year median GAAP ROIC compressed to ~7.9% (trough ~5.5% in FY2025 with -$1.13B net loss) following the China/Asia travel retail inventory glut and $911M non-cash impairments (Tom Ford, Too Faced); peak-to-peak EPS broken; net debt escalated to $9.5B (Debt/EBITDA > 4.5x) forcing a dividend cut; and capital allocation scored 0 due to former CEO Freda's peak-cycle M&A and daigou channel stuffing. Intact moat proof: Gross margin expanded 230 bps to 74.0% in FY2025, demonstrating resilient pricing power; core prestige brands maintained leading positions; and FY2026 results verified recovery with Mainland China organic sales up +9% and global net sales up +5% (+3% organic) to $15B as channel destocking concluded. Fix catalyst & kill-switch: New CEO Stéphane de La Faverie (effective Jan 2025) executing 'Beauty Reimagined' and PRGP structural cost savings to restore operating margins to mid-teens and deleverage debt. Kill-switch: Exit if organic sales contract past FY2027, gross margin falls below 70%, or Net Debt / EBITDA fails to decline below 3.0x by FY2028.
column20: Calamity pass tier. Enduring prestige beauty intangibles with 74% gross margin and zero terminal macrotrend headwinds, recovering from an acute Asia travel retail inventory shock. While depressed ROIC, balance sheet leverage, and prior capital allocation missteps trigger failures at Gates 3b, 5, and 6, FY2026 operational turnaround under CEO Stéphane de La Faverie confirms the calamity is temporary and fixable. [5-10Y g: prestige volume 3.0% + price 2.0% + luxury mix 1.0% - restructuring & marketing drag 0.5% + net buybacks 0.5%]
column21: FY2021/2022 peak net sales of $17.7B and operating income of $3.17B (ROIC 16.6%) collapsed during the post-COVID Asia travel retail destocking to FY2024 ($15.61B) and FY2025 ($14.33B, -$1.13B net loss from $911M non-cash impairments on Tom Ford and Too Faced). Despite volume contraction, gross margin expanded to 74.0% in FY2025. FY2026 results confirmed stabilization and recovery: net sales rose 5% to $15.0B (3% organic) with Mainland China organic sales up 9%. Total debt stands at ~$9.5B (Debt/EBITDA > 4.5x), prompting a dividend cut to conserve cash. Portfolio spans Skin Care (~50%), Makeup (~30%), Fragrance (~16%), Hair Care (~4%) across Lindy prestige brands (La Mer, Clinique, Estée Lauder, MAC, Le Labo).

column14: (1) Brand equity, consumer trust, and global retail shelf-space distribution across OTC healthcare (Tylenol, Motrin, Benadryl, Zyrtec), oral care (Listerine), and skincare (Neutrogena, Aveeno, Band-Aid) provide entry barriers against de novo consumer brands. (2) However, historical capital efficiency fails the quality threshold: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 11.2% (below the 12% hurdle), and post-JNJ spin-off GAAP ROIC sits at sub-10% due to an asset-heavy balance sheet loaded with ~$20B in carved-out intangibles/goodwill and ~$8.5B in debt. (3) Primary erosion threats include pervasive private-label substitution across chemically identical OTC drug monographs (store-brand acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and cetirizine sold at steep discounts by mass retailers), severe market share erosion in Skin Health to clinical dermatological brands (CeraVe, La Roche-Posay), volume contraction whenever list prices are increased, and corporate absorption via acquisition by Kimberly-Clark in November 2026.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC 11.2% < 12% hurdle & negative price elasticity, REJECT). While Kenvue possesses iconic, household-name OTC and personal care brands (Tylenol, Listerine, Neutrogena), its underlying economic engine fails the Munger quality hurdle. Spun off from Johnson & Johnson encumbered with ~$8.5B in debt and massive capitalized intangibles, standalone GAAP ROIC has tracked persistently below 12%. When enacting price hikes in 2023–2025 to offset inflation, organic volumes turned negative across Self Care and Skin Health as consumers traded down to chemically identical private-label OTC generics or shifted to dermatologist-recommended skincare alternatives (CeraVe), confirming the absence of true pricing power without volume sacrifice. Acquired by Kimberly-Clark for $48.7B EV (completed November 2026).
column21: Historical 10-year median ROIC is 11.2% (dossier), strictly failing the 12% Gate 3b minimum standard; post-spin standalone GAAP ROIC remained depressed at ~8-10% on ~$20B+ invested capital. Kenvue's operations span Self Care (~40% of revenue; Tylenol, Motrin, Zyrtec), Skin Health & Beauty (~30%; Neutrogena, Aveeno), and Essential Health (~30%; Listerine, Band-Aid, Johnson's). FY2024-2025 sales stagnated around $15.4B-$15.7B as 1-3% price/mix realization was neutralized by -1% to -2% volume declines, reflecting consumer elasticity and share losses to private label and clinical skincare rivals. Balance sheet at year-end 2025 carried $8.5B in debt against $1.1B in cash (net debt ~$7.4B, ~4.4x net income of ~$1.7B). While FCF reached $1.7B in 2025, capital efficiency remained structurally sub-hurdle. Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue on November 2, 2026 in a cash-and-stock merger valued at $48.7B EV ($3.50 cash + 0.14625 KMB shares per KVUE share), delisting the equity from public markets.

column14: Unrivaled scale economies across global distribution, $8B+ annual advertising, and retail shelf space dominance combined with Lindy brand equity across 20+ billion-dollar brands (Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest, Dawn). Proved pricing power through recent inflation cycles with cumulative price increases defending 23%+ ROIC and 23% operating margins. Primary threat is private-label trade-down during severe economic contractions.
column20: Archetypal global consumer staples fortress with 23% median ROIC, 97% Owner FCF conversion, and an AA-rated balance sheet with 1.4x debt/OE and 22.5x interest coverage. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends with local-for-local manufacturing and essential daily use habits. Primary risk is private-label trade-down in severe economic recessions. [5-10Y g: organic volume 2.0% + price/mix 2.0% + margin expansion 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
column21:
Procter & Gamble demonstrates multi-decade compounding excellence across 5 core segments: Fabric & Home Care (~35% of sales, Tide/Ariel/Dawn/Bounty), Baby, Feminine & Family Care (~25%, Pampers/Always/Charmin), Beauty (~18%, Head & Shoulders/Pantene/Olay), Health Care (~14%, Crest/Oral-B/Vicks), and Grooming (~8%, Gillette/Venus).
1. Capital Efficiency: 10-year GAAP ROIC median of 23.2% (excluding non-cash 2018 Gillette impairment, ROIC has stayed between 22% and 26% every year since FY2019). Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 100%. Operating margin expanded from ~20% in 2016 to ~23% in 2025.
2. Pricing Power: Demonstrated sustained pricing power through the 2021-2024 inflationary surge, achieving mid-single-digit price realization annually with minimal volume elasticity and defending gross margins above 50%.
3. Cash Flow Conversion: FCF conversion over 10 years averages 95-100% of GAAP Net Income (FY2025 Owner FCF of $15.9B on $16.0B Net Income). Capex remains low and disciplined at 4-5% of net sales.
4. Capital Allocation & Balance Sheet: Total debt of $22.8B against $9.9B cash (net debt of $12.9B is <0.8x Net Income). Interest coverage of 22.5x ($19.7B EBIT / $877M interest). 68-year track record of consecutive annual dividend increases with steady counter-cyclical share repurchases shrinking share count ~1-2% annually. Following the 2015-2016 Coty divestitures and restructuring into 6 focused business units, management has maintained exceptional capital discipline under Jon Moeller and successor Shailesh Jejurikar.

column14: Moat anchored in massive Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD) bottling/distribution network reaching ~90% of US retail doors, combined with the Keurig single-serve brewer installed base in ~40M households and iconic brand equity (Dr Pepper, Canada Dry, Snapple). Competitors cannot easily replicate the national direct store distribution footprint, enabling KDP to distribute third-party partner brands (Evian, C4, Ghost, Polar) with high route density. Proof of moat: Tangible ROIC >50% on low physical capital base ($2.5B PP&E) and stable gross margins of 54-56%, with Dr Pepper taking volume share to reach #2 CSD status while realizing mid-single-digit price hikes. Erosion threats: Post-patent pod commoditization, proliferation of compatible third-party and private-label K-cups, plateauing brewer household penetration, and raw coffee commodity volatility.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Dr Pepper and refreshment beverages possess strong brand equity and DSD scale, the at-home coffee platform (Keurig) faces structural maturation, pod volume stagnation, and post-patent private label competition. Unhedged agricultural exposure to volatile green coffee prices (Macrotrend 4) and severe capital structure strain from the €15.7B debt-funded JDE Peet's acquisition in a higher-rate regime (Macrotrend 5) truncate competitive advantage longevity below the 15-year threshold. Downstream Gates 5 and 6 left null under strict waterfall.
column21: Financials: 5Y median GAAP ROIC is 5-6% (suppressed by ~$44B in merger goodwill/intangibles), though tangible ROIC exceeds 50% on $2.5B PP&E. Gross margins have held steady at ~54-56%, with operating margins of ~21-23%. Pricing power demonstrated in US Refreshment Beverages where Dr Pepper achieved #2 CSD market share while realizing 6-10% price/mix. However, US Coffee segment has struggled with flat-to-declining pod volumes and brewer shipment declines post-COVID as US household penetration plateaued at ~38-40M homes. Balance sheet carries $13.0B in long-term debt against $2.1B GAAP net income (Net Debt/NI ~6x), which balloons significantly with the €15.7B ($17.4B) acquisition of JDE Peet's in 2025/2026, violating conservative debt-to-earnings thresholds.

column14: Global bottler ecosystem of ~200 independent partners serving over 30 million retail outlets creates unmatchable distribution scale, high route density, and pervasive cold-drink placement. Empirical moat proof: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 17.5%, tangible operating ROIC of 26.0%, and gross margins consistently maintained at 58-61%. Demonstrated consistent pricing power via incidence-based concentrate pricing contracts with price/mix gains of 11% (2022), 10% (2023), 10% (2024), and 4% (2025) while preserving unit volumes. Primary erosion risks: adverse outcome in the Eleventh Circuit IRS transfer-pricing appeal extending to post-2009 tax years, and evolving dietary shifts away from sugar (hedged via Coke Zero Sugar and non-CSD category expansion).
column20: Asset-light concentrate toll booth on global non-alcoholic beverage consumption with entrenched brand power and massive scale economies shared across ~200 bottling partners. Demonstrated pricing power across high-inflation cycles via incidence-based contracts. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends. Net debt at 2.4x net income with 8.3x interest coverage; $6B IRS deposit already paid with manageable ongoing legal risk on appeal. [5-10Y g: organic volume 1.5% + price/mix 3.5% + product reinvestment 0.5% - foreign exchange drag 0.5% + share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 17.5% and tangible operating ROIC of 26.0% in FY2025. Gross margins steady between 58% and 61% across cycles despite severe commodity and packaging swings. Refranchising of capital-intensive bottling operations transformed KO into a high-margin (28-29% EBIT margin), asset-light cash engine. Demonstrated exceptional pricing power with non-GAAP price/mix up 11% in 2022, 10% in 2023, 10% in 2024, and 4% in 2025 alongside stable unit case volumes. 10-year cumulative Owner FCF conversion exceeds 92% (approaching ~99% normalizing for the $6.0B IRS tax deposit in 2024). Net debt of $31.8B is 2.43x FY2025 net income ($13.1B) and interest coverage is 8.3x EBIT ($13.8B / $1.65B), comfortably supporting the 60+ year dividend growth streak.

column14: Global brand intangibles anchored by intense lifestyle/extreme-sports cultural equity, coupled with exclusive route-to-market access via the global Coca-Cola bottling network that locks up convenience store cooler shelf space. Empirical proof: 10-year median ROIC ~26.5%, gross margins stable at 54-56%, and operating margins ~28-29% despite aluminum and freight volatility. Primary erosion threats: competition from Red Bull and insurgent fitness energy brands (Celsius), retail convenience traffic softness, and regulatory caffeine/youth scrutiny.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global energy drink leader with powerful brand intangibles and exclusive Coca-Cola bottling distribution. High-margin asset-light copacking model yields ~27% ROIC and ~100% FCF conversion. Fortress net-cash balance sheet. [5-10Y g: international & category volume 4.5% + pricing power 1.5% + mix innovation 0.5% - input & distribution cost drag 0.5% + net share buybacks 1.5%]
column21: FY2024-FY2025 net sales grew from $7.50B to $8.29B, with operating income reaching $2.42B (29.2% operating margin) and gross margin improving to 55.8%. 10-year median ROIC exceeds 26%. Free cash flow conversion is near 100% (~$1.9B FCF on $1.91B net income in FY2025) backed by an asset-light copacking model with minimal capex requirements. Fortress balance sheet with $2.09B in cash and equivalents against ~$374M in total debt incurred to fund the accretive $3.0B Dutch auction tender offer in 2024 that retired ~5.4% of shares. Co-founders Rodney Sacks and Hilton Schlosberg possess an exemplary 35-year track record of rational capital allocation and per-share compounding.

column14: Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD) route density and retail shelf dominance across Frito-Lay salty snacks (~60% US market share) and beverages create an insurmountable distribution moat. 10Y median ROIC of 16.8% and gross margins stable at 53-55% prove moat durability. Primary erosion threats include GLP-1 adoption, health/wellness shifts away from ultra-processed snacks, and consumer resistance to cumulative price increases.
column20: Global snack and beverage powerhouse anchored by Frito-Lay's dominant DSD distribution network. Demonstrates durable pricing power and Lindy snack brand loyalty. High cash conversion (>85% FCF/NI) and steady balance sheet with >10x net interest coverage comfortably support capital returns. [5-10Y g: snack/beverage volume 1.0% + price 2.0% + international mix 1.5% - promotional/input cost drag 0.5% + net buybacks 1.0%]
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 16.8% and FY24/FY25 operating margins ~12-14%. Net revenue grew to $93.9B in FY25 with operating cash flow of $12.5B and FCF of $8.2B (99% FCF conversion). Net interest coverage remains strong at ~10x. Frito-Lay generates outsized operating profit share (~45-50% of corporate profit) providing high-margin stability.

column14: Insurmountable local route density, exclusive territorial bottling agreements with The Coca-Cola Company across 31 countries, and ubiquitous cold-drink placement provide substantial scale advantages; demonstrated strong pricing power (+8% price/mix in 2022-2023, +2-3% in 2024-2025) passing through inflationary input costs. Primary moat risk is that brand equity and concentrate pricing power belong to The Coca-Cola Company (KO), which can adjust concentrate prices over time.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Pillar 3 Balance Sheet, REJECT). Well-run territorial Coca-Cola bottler with unmatched route density and pack-price execution across Europe and Australasia, but unlike asset-light KO it bears heavy plant/fleet capex, a thin 10.7% 5-year median GAAP ROIC, and 4.99x LT debt/Net Income (€9.69B LT debt vs €1.94B Net Income) from debt-funded bottler acquisitions (Amatil, CCBPI), exceeding the 4.0x fortress balance sheet ceiling.
column21: CCEP is the world's largest independent Coca-Cola bottler by revenue (€20.9B in FY2025, operating across 31 countries). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 10.68% (2022: 10.23%, 2023: 11.13%, 2024: 10.02%, 2025: 10.9% reported / 13.3% normalized), diluted by €17.0B in franchise intangibles and goodwill. FCF conversion is healthy at >100% of Net Income (€1.8B–€2.0B Owner FCF). However, balance sheet leverage is structurally elevated: LT debt of €9,692M vs cash of €918M and TTM Net Income of €1,942M yields LT Debt / Net Income of 4.99x (and Net Debt / EBITDA of 2.7x), failing Gate 6's <= 4.0x threshold.

column11: Addictive and socially destructive combustible tobacco model facing severe secular volume decline (-8% to -10% annually), existential regulatory risk (FDA menthol ban, nicotine reduction caps), and terminal societal acceptance headwinds.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT – G2 Essential Need). Addictive and socially destructive combustible tobacco model facing severe secular volume declines (-8% to -10% per annum in the US domestic market), existential regulatory/legislative intervention risks (FDA potential menthol bans and nicotine reduction mandates), and terminal societal rejection. While Marlboro possesses historical brand pricing power to offset volume declines in the near term, the core economic engine lacks enduring societal acceptance and does not satisfy the Munger/Buffett standard of an essential Western need or socially sustainable everyday ritual.
column21: Altria is exclusively focused on the US domestic market post-2008 PMI spinoff. Core combustible cigarette shipments (Marlboro, etc.) suffer persistent 8-10% annual volume erosion. While net revenues net of excise taxes reached ~$20.14B in FY2025 (down 1.5% YoY) with adjusted diluted EPS of $5.42 driven by aggressive list-price hikes, the long-term unit-volume trajectory is terminally negative. Capital allocation track record outside combustible cigarettes has been disastrous ($12.8B JUUL acquisition in 2018 written down almost entirely; $1.8B Cronos cannabis investment severely impaired; ongoing struggle with illicit disposable e-vapor competition undermining NJOY expansion). Carries approximately $25.7B in long-term debt. Under the strict v6.25 framework, tobacco businesses are explicitly disqualified at Gate 2 due to addictive, predatory dynamics and legislative/societal ruin risk.

column11: Societal and legislative acceptance risk: chemically addictive nicotine delivery model (combustibles, heated tobacco, oral pouches) facing severe regulatory, excise, and litigation ruin risk.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Addictive nicotine business model (58.5% combustible cigarettes alongside IQOS and ZYN) carries severe societal, legislative, and regulatory ruin risk (punitive excise taxation, flavor bans, marketing restrictions, generational prohibition), failing the Munger standard for essential Western needs.
column21: Philip Morris International reached $40.6B in net revenue in 2025. While smoke-free products (IQOS heat-not-burn and ZYN oral pouches) expanded to 41.5% of net revenues ($16.85B) with strong momentum (ZYN holding ~66% US value share and total oral volumes up 18.5%), traditional combustible cigarettes still represent 58.5% of revenues. The entire economic engine relies on biological nicotine addiction, exposing it to perpetual regulatory scrutiny, escalating excise taxes (such as European heated-tobacco tax harmonization), flavor/menthol bans, and generational smoking restrictions. Although 10Y median ROIC is ~32% with strong cash generation, the addictive model with high legislative and societal ruin risk constitutes a permanent Gate 2 disqualification under the Munger framework.

column14: Scale economies in low-cost resource basins (Permian Basin unconventional, Tengizchevroil, Gorgon/Wheatstone LNG, and 30% Stabroek block offshore Guyana via the Hess acquisition) provide upstream cost advantage, but crude oil, natural gas, and refined fuels are global undifferentiated commodities where Chevron possesses zero pricing power and spot margins cannot be protected against commodity downcycles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & Commodity Price-Taker, REJECT). Premier integrated supermajor with top-tier assets, but sells undifferentiated commodities with zero pricing power above global clearing prices. 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 10.5% fails the >=12% cycle-tested hurdle.
column21: 10-year median ROIC is ~10.5%, with returns fluctuating from ~2.7-5.5% in the 2020 oil slump to 17-20% at the 2022 commodity peak, before normalizing to ~5-10% in 2024-2025. Upstream earnings account for ~75-80% of net income, exposing total profitability directly to volatile Brent/WTI prices. Successfully closed the $53B Hess Corporation acquisition in July 2025 after favorable ICC arbitration ruling against ExxonMobil/CNOOC, securing a 30% stake in Guyana's Stabroek block and high-quality Bakken shale assets. While balance sheet is strong with modest net debt and disciplined capital returns, the business remains an unhedged commodity price-taker unable to achieve persistent >=12% returns on invested capital.

column14: World-class upstream scale in deepwater Guyana (<$35/bbl breakeven) and Permian Basin (strengthened by $63B Pioneer acquisition), integrated with massive refining and petrochemical capacity. However, petroleum products are fungible global commodities with zero independent pricing power; financial returns are dictated by volatile global commodity cycles, yielding a 10-year median ROIC of ~11.2% (with 2024-2025 ROIC moderating to 7-9%), below the 12% hurdle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing & Proof of Moat, REJECT). While ExxonMobil is an exceptionally managed integrated energy supermajor with low-cost upstream assets in Guyana and the Permian Basin, it remains an inescapable commodity price-taker lacking pricing power >= inflation. Across the full commodity cycle, its 10-year median ROIC is ~11.2% (falling to 7.4-9.0% in 2024-2025), failing the 12% hurdle. Upstream energy also faces structural decarbonization and energy transition headwinds, precluding any qualification for the Calamity Tier.
column21: 10-year financial performance illustrates inherent commodity cyclicality: GAAP ROIC fluctuated from -8.7% in 2020 to a windfall peak of 22.8% in 2022, before normalizing to 11.5% in 2023, 8.4-9.0% in 2024, and 7.4-8.9% in 2025, producing a multi-cycle median of ~11.2% (below the 12% hurdle). Free cash flow reflects identical cyclical swings: -$2.6B in 2020, $58.4B in 2022, $30.7B in 2024, and $26.1B in 2025. The May 2024 all-stock acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources ($63B equity value, $5B debt assumed) bolstered Midland Permian acreage and brought Permian output above 1.6M BOE/d (total upstream ~4.74M BOE/d) while maintaining low balance-sheet leverage (~0.7x Debt/EBITDA), but cannot insulate the business from global spot commodity price swings.

column14: Baker Hughes possesses a defensible installed base of turbomachinery (gas turbines and compressors) in its Industrial & Energy Technology (IET) segment with captive OEM aftermarket service agreements, particularly in global LNG liquefaction infrastructure. However, its Oilfield Services & Equipment (OFSE) segment operates in a cyclical, competitive market alongside SLB and Halliburton where pricing power is tethered to volatile customer capex budgets. Consolidated 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~7.5% and peak-cycle 2024-2025 ROIC of ~10.4-10.6% fail the required 12% cycle-neutral hurdle. Long-term moat erosion threats include the secular energy transition away from upstream hydrocarbons, cyclical E&P capex cuts, and alternative electrification technologies.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Despite leadership in LNG turbomachinery and a large installed base driving aftermarket service annuities, Baker Hughes fails the empirical moat proof with a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~7.5% and peak-cycle ROIC of ~10.4-10.6% (below the 12% threshold). Heavy exposure to cyclical oilfield services (OFSE) dilutes returns and pricing power across full commodity cycles.
column21: Formed in its modern structure via the 2017 GE Oil & Gas combination and subsequent separation, Baker Hughes operates two core segments: Industrial & Energy Technology (IET) and Oilfield Services & Equipment (OFSE). While IET delivers strong order backlogs and higher operating margins (~17-18%) driven by global LNG liquefaction projects and turbomachinery service annuities, OFSE remains cyclical and price-sensitive. 10-year average ROIC is low single digits due to historical write-downs; 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.5%. Despite strong recent FCF generation ($2.3B in 2024, $2.7B in 2025) and trailing ROIC reaching 10.4%-10.6%, returns fail to cross the 12% multi-cycle hurdle.

column14: Halliburton possesses significant North American basin logistics density, specialized completion chemistry, and high operational switching costs during active drilling and completion campaigns. However, it fails empirical proof of moat: 10-year median ROIC is ~8.6-9.1%, far below the 12% hurdle, with severe negative returns during downcycles (-23.7% in 2016, -1.7% in 2019, -12.4% in 2020). Primary erosion threats include rapid consolidation among E&P operators (Exxon/Pioneer, Chevron/Hess, Diamondback/Endeavor) creating monopsony buyer power, commoditization of pressure pumping equipment, and cyclical E&P capex cuts.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Cyclical oilfield services provider with 10-year median ROIC of ~8.6-9.1%, well below the 12% hurdle. Lacks cycle-durable pricing power as consolidated E&P operators hold strong monopsony bargaining power, driving severe margin and ROIC collapses during energy downturns.
column21: 10-year historical ROIC (2016-2025) demonstrates heavy cyclicality: -23.7% (2016), 5.1% (2017), 8.6% (2018), -1.7% (2019), -12.4% (2020), 8.6% (2021), 12.3% (2022), 17.2% (2023), 15.4% (2024), and ~9.1% (2025), yielding a 10-year median ROIC of ~8.6-9.1% (fails >=12% hurdle). Net income exhibits multi-billion dollar losses during downcycles (-$5.8B in 2016, -$1.1B in 2019, -$2.9B in 2020). Revenue split between Completion & Production (~55-60%) and Drilling & Evaluation (~40-45%) leaves the business highly exposed to North American fracturing capex cycles and buyer pricing pressure from consolidated mega-independents.

column14: World-leading proprietary wireline logging, rotary steerable drilling systems, Petrel/DELFI reservoir software, and ChampionX production chemistry create substantial technical barriers against smaller peers. However, returns on invested capital are structurally capped by upstream capex cyclicality: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 9.4% (10-year median 6.5%), failing the 12% through-cycle hurdle. Primary erosion threats stem from customer power of national and international oil companies who aggressively demand price cuts during crude downturns, eliminating pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). While SLB is the undisputed technological leader in international and offshore oilfield services with premier subsurface R&D and digital simulation assets, its financial returns remain tethered to cyclical upstream E&P capex. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~9.4% and 10-year median ROIC of ~6.5% fall well short of the 12% hurdle. Pricing power cannot be sustained across cycles as major IOCs and NOCs extract concessions during commodity downturns.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record: SLB's 10-year ROIC averages ~6.7% (median 6.51%), ranging from cyclical troughs of 1.97% (2016) and 3.89% (2020) to cycle peaks of 12.10% (2023) and 13.00% (2024), moderating to 8.95% in 2025. 5-year median ROIC stands at 9.44%, failing the required 12.0% threshold. Operating margins peaked at ~16% in 2024 before flattening in 2025 ($35.71B revenue, $3.37B GAAP net income). Free cash flow generation has improved post-2020 restructuring ($3.99B FCF in 2024, $4.11B in 2025 with >100% GAAP conversion), but through-cycle capital intensity remains elevated. Segment breakdown: Production Systems (~35% of revenue post-ChampionX), Well Construction (~33%), Reservoir Performance (~18%), and Digital & Integration (~14%). Customer lock-in: Technical leadership in deepwater, HPHT (high-pressure, high-temperature) reservoirs, and international markets provides sticky relationships with NOCs (Saudi Aramco, ADNOC, Petrobras), but pricing is tied to client capital budgets rather than secular pricing power. M&A & Capital allocation: Completed the all-stock acquisition of ChampionX in July 2025 to expand production chemicals and artificial lift; net debt sits at ~$7.42B (1.8x EBITDA / 2.2x NI), maintained conservatively, but heavy past write-downs (Cameron acquisition) underscore cyclical capital misallocation risks.

column11: Commodity price-taker lacking pricing power; upstream oil and gas exploration and production subject to global commodity cycles and non-Western sovereign exposure in Egypt.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Reject – G2 Essential Need). Upstream oil and gas exploration and production company operating as a pure commodity price-taker exposed to volatile crude oil and natural gas benchmarks (WTI, Brent, Henry Hub). Lacks pricing power, faces structural commodity cyclicity, and holds significant operational concentration in Egypt (Western Desert) with elevated sovereign and foreign exchange risk. Fails Munger's hurdle for non-deferrable Western essential demand with pricing power.
column21: APA Corporation explores and produces oil and gas across the US Permian Basin, Egypt, UK North Sea, and offshore Suriname. As an upstream price-taker, operating margins and cash flows fluctuate wildly with underlying hydrocarbon benchmarks. Historical 10-year median ROIC is approximately 8.5%, falling far short of the 12% hurdle. The 2024 acquisition of Callon Petroleum for ~$4.5B added substantial debt ($6.0B total debt at end-2024) and dilution without altering the underlying commodity price-taking economics. Capital intensity is high, and upstream assets lack any pricing power or enduring competitive moat.

column11: Commodity price taker lacking pricing power; upstream oil and gas exploration and production revenues are governed entirely by volatile global benchmark spot prices with zero pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Commodity price taker lacking pricing power, REJECT). Pure-play upstream exploration and production operator selling undifferentiated commodities (crude oil, natural gas, NGLs) into global spot markets with zero pricing power. Despite low-cost acreage depth and scale post-$22.5B Marathon Oil merger, earnings and cash flows fluctuate with volatile spot commodity cycles rather than entrenched customer demand.
column21: ConocoPhillips is the world's largest independent upstream E&P company, producing ~2.3M BOE/D across the Lower 48 (Permian Delaware/Midland, Eagle Ford, Bakken), Alaska North Slope, and international LNG projects (Qatar, Australia). Upstream revenues are 100% commodity price-dependent. Financial track record is intensely cyclical: net income went from -$2.7B loss in 2020 to $8.1B in 2021, $18.7B at the 2022 Ukraine war oil price peak, $11.0B in 2023, $9.25B in 2024, and $7.93B in 2025. ROIC fell from >20% at the 2022 peak to ~6.6% in FY25 as realized commodity prices softened and the capital base expanded. In November 2024, COP closed its $22.5B all-stock acquisition of Marathon Oil (0.255 COP shares per MRO share), assuming $5.4B in net debt ($4.6B principal). Year-end 2025 total debt was $23.4B against $7.4B in cash and short-term investments (net debt ~$16.0B). Free cash flow was ~$8.7B in 2024 and expanded in 2025, but the company remains a pure price-taker selling undifferentiated spot molecules without customer lock-in or pricing power, failing Munger's quality compounder threshold.

column11: Commodity price taker lacking pricing power (upstream oil & gas exploration & production).
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Pure-play upstream oil and gas exploration and production company is an undifferentiated commodity price-taker lacking pricing power. Realized cash flows and returns fluctuate entirely with global spot hydrocarbon prices, violating the Munger quality hurdle.
column21: Devon Energy is an independent US onshore exploration and production (E&P) operator with multi-basin assets across the Delaware Basin (Permian, ~65% of production), Williston Basin (Bakken), Eagle Ford, Anadarko, and Powder River Basin, producing ~800,000 boe/d (~50% oil, 25% NGLs, 25% natural gas). The business model is a textbook commodity price-taker selling fungible crude oil and natural gas into wholesale spot markets (WTI, Henry Hub) with zero customer lock-in and zero pricing power. Multi-cycle financial performance is highly volatile and sub-hurdle: 10-year average ROIC is ~9.9% and 10-year median ROIC is ~11.5% (both failing the 12% cycle-neutral hurdle), marked by severe GAAP losses in cyclical downturns (-$1.06B in 2016, -$2.68B in 2020) and windfall profits during energy spikes ($6.02B in 2022, ROIC ~28%), normalizing to $2.89B in 2024 and ~$2.64B in 2025 (ROIC ~11%). In September 2024, Devon closed the $5.0B acquisition of Grayson Mill Energy ($3.25B cash + $1.75B stock) to consolidate Williston Basin inventory, driving total debt up from $6.45B in 2023 to $9.20B at year-end 2024 (moderating to ~$8.58B in 2025 via a $2.5B deleveraging plan). Capital allocation relies on pro-cyclical share buybacks and variable dividends, amplifying cash flow cyclicality rather than shielding per-share compounding.

column11: Commodity price taker lacking pricing power (upstream oil & gas exploration & production).
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need / Price-Taker, REJECT). EOG Resources is an upstream crude oil, natural gas, and NGL exploration and production company operating as a pure price-taker in cyclical commodity markets with zero structural pricing power or customer lock-in.
column21: EOG Resources is an independent exploration and production company with low-cost premium drilling operations across the Delaware Basin (Permian), Eagle Ford, Utica, and Powder River Basin. Operating revenues and profitability are strictly tied to global and regional hydrocarbon spot prices rather than an enduring competitive moat: revenues dipped ~4.5% from $23.7B in 2024 to $22.6B in 2025 on lower realized crude and natural gas prices; net income contracted from $6.4B to $5.0B; and free cash flow fell from ~$5.4B to $3.5B–$4.7B. While EOG is among the most disciplined and lowest-cost US shale operators with a 10-year median ROIC of 13.9% and conservative leverage (~0.4x net debt/EBITDA), it remains fundamentally a commodity price-taker vulnerable to global supply/demand cycles.

column11: Commodity price taker lacking pricing power in undifferentiated natural gas upstream exploration and production.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT – G2 Essential Need). Pure commodity price-taker lacking pricing power in natural gas upstream exploration and production. While natural gas provides essential heating and electricity generation, EQT produces an undifferentiated commodity sold at volatile NYMEX Henry Hub spot prices with zero pricing power. Even with the Equitrans Midstream integration lowering gathering costs and adding Mountain Valley Pipeline assets, multi-cycle GAAP ROIC is ~6.8% (well below the 12% moat hurdle) and cash flows remain hostage to commodity boom-and-bust cycles.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 6.8%, well below the 12% compounder hurdle. Performance is driven by volatile commodity pricing rather than compounding: FY24 revenue was $5.27B with operating income of $685M (13.0% margin), net income of $231M, FCF attributable to EQT of ~$684M, and ROIC of ~1.28%. FY25 rebounded with revenue of $8.64B, operating income of $3.25B (37.6% margin), net income of $2.04B, FCF of ~$2.50B, and ROIC of ~5.79% (external tax-effected NOPAT ROIC ~9-10%). Closed acquisition of Equitrans Midstream in July 2024 for enterprise value >$35B, reintegrating 2,000+ miles of gathering pipelines and the Mountain Valley Pipeline (MVP) to lower unlevered FCF breakeven to ~$2.00/MMBtu. However, EQT remains an upstream price-taker with >80% of revenue derived from wholesale natural gas sales with zero pricing power over inflation. Total debt spiked to ~$14B post-merger in mid-2024 before being reduced to ~$7.8B by year-end 2025 via merger cash flows and non-core asset sales.

column11: Commodity price taker lacking pricing power in cyclical upstream natural gas exploration & production.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Pure-play upstream natural gas exploration and production company selling an undifferentiated commodity into cyclical spot markets with zero structural pricing power.
column21: Formed via the October 2024 merger of Chesapeake Energy and Southwestern Energy, Expand Energy is the largest US natural gas producer, operating across the Haynesville and Marcellus shale basins. Despite substantial production scale (~7.5 Bcfe/d) and post-merger cost synergies, the company operates as an upstream commodity price-taker whose margins and cash flows fluctuate with spot natural gas prices. Capital efficiency is structurally sub-hurdle (10-year median ROIC ~7.2% vs. 12% compounder threshold), and predecessor Chesapeake underwent Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2020 due to severe commodity price declines and debt overhang.

column11: Commodity price taker lacking pricing power; pure-play upstream oil and gas exploration and production (E&P) selling undifferentiated hydrocarbons into volatile global spot commodity markets.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Pure-play Permian Basin upstream oil and gas exploration and production (E&P) operator. Diamondback is an unhedged commodity price-taker selling undifferentiated crude oil, natural gas, and NGLs into global and regional spot markets (WTI Midland, Brent, Henry Hub, Waha) with zero structural pricing power. Upstream E&P lacks customer lock-in, switching costs, or an entrenched everyday consumer habit/ritual, remaining completely beholden to volatile, cyclical global commodity market clearing prices. Even after the transformational $26B Endeavor Energy Resources merger in September 2024 scaling production to ~920k+ BOE/d, capital returns fluctuate heavily across commodity cycles (GAAP ROIC swinging from negative in 2020 to ~6% in 2024-2025).
column21: Multi-cycle track record is heavily cyclical: GAAP Net Income swung from $(4.67)B in 2020 to $4.39B in 2022, $3.34B in 2024, and $1.66B in 2025. GAAP ROIC fell from ~21-23% at the 2022 commodity price peak to ~5.9-6.2% in 2024-2025 following the Endeavor asset base step-up. Operations are 100% upstream exploration and production in the Permian Basin (Midland and Delaware Basins), generating $11.07B in FY24 revenue and $15.03B in FY25 revenue with net production exceeding 920,000 BOE/d. Customers are midstream gatherers and refiners with zero switching costs; products are entirely fungible commodities priced off spot benchmarks (WTI Midland, Brent, Waha hub). In September 2024, Diamondback closed the $26B acquisition of Endeavor Energy Resources ($8B cash + 117.3M shares + net debt assumption), increasing total debt to $12.46B-$14.6B against $91M-$106M in cash, requiring 50% FCF allocation toward debt reduction to defend its BBB investment-grade rating.

column14: Permian Basin acreage density (augmented by Anadarko and CrownRock) and CO2 enhanced oil recovery (EOR) infrastructure provide low extraction costs, but oil, NGLs, and natural gas are homogenous commodities sold at spot prices. Multi-cycle ROIC of ~7.8% fails the 12% hurdle, and the company has zero pricing power over global commodity benchmarks. Primary erosion risks stem from commodity price collapses, natural reservoir decline rates requiring continuous reinvestment, and long-term energy transition substitution.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 7.8% < 12%, Pricing Power = N, REJECT). Structural commodity price-taker whose operating cash flows and returns fluctuate directly with spot oil and gas prices. While contiguous Permian Basin scale and the 2025 OxyChem divestiture for $9.7B facilitate debt reduction from CrownRock and Anadarko peaks, the business lacks independent pricing power and fails the multi-cycle economic return hurdle.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 7.8% (averaging ~5-8% over the full cycle), failing the 12% threshold. ROIC oscillated from negative territory during the 2015-2016 and 2020 oil downturns to a temporary windfall peak of >20% in 2022 before retreating. The 2019 Anadarko acquisition ($55B) and August 2024 CrownRock acquisition ($12B) repeatedly stretched the balance sheet, with principal debt peaking near $29B. Although the October 2025 divestiture of OxyChem to Berkshire Hathaway for $9.7B cash helped accelerate debt paydown toward ~$13.3B by mid-2026, Berkshire's $10B 8% preferred stock remains an ongoing capital obligation (redemption targeted for 2029+). Fundamental lack of pricing power and commodity price-taker economics permanently disqualify OXY from compounder status.

column14: Monopolistic surface ownership of ~873,000 contiguous and checkerboard acres across the core Delaware and Midland Basins, coupled with >200,000 Net Royalty Acres. Receives perpetual ad valorem gross production royalties and high-margin water sourcing/produced water disposal fees without bearing any drilling capital or operating expenditure. Proof of moat is demonstrated by 10-year median ROIC of ~38.5% (FY24 ~49.7%, FY25 ~33%) and sustained 80-90% operating margins. Primary erosion risks are long-term basin resource depletion and severe commodity price collapses.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Remarkable ~85-90% operating margin Permian land and royalty business with zero drilling capex, but Upstream Energy baseline persistence is Tier 4 (5-10Y baseline CAP). Faces active unhedged terminal headwinds under Macrotrend [4] (Energy Transition & Resource Limits) from secular peak hydrocarbon demand, electrification, and finite Permian Tier 1 well inventory depletion over a 15-30 year horizon.
column21: Texas Pacific Land Corporation (TPL) holds ~873,000 surface acres and over 200,000 Net Royalty Acres in the Permian Basin (Delaware and Midland Basins). Revenues derive from oil & gas royalties (~55-60%), Water Services and Operations (~35-40%), and surface easements/materials (~5%). Financial efficiency is exceptional: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 38.5% (FY24 ROIC ~49.7%, FY25 ROIC ~33%), operating margins exceed 80-85%, FCF conversion is ~95-100%, and the balance sheet carries minimal long-term debt with positive net cash/equivalents ($145M-$370M). However, under the Mauboussin industry persistence framework, Upstream Energy is anchored at Tier 4 (p=0.70-0.71, baseline CAP 5-10 years), and the business model is inherently tied to finite fossil fuel extraction and regional Permian drilling activity, failing Gate 4's 15-year secular resilience requirement.

column14: Marathon Petroleum operates the largest US refining system (~3.0 million barrels per calendar day across 13 refineries) integrated with extensive midstream logistics through its controlling interest in MPLX LP (gathering pipelines, processing, marine, and storage terminals). This scale and coastal/mid-continent footprint yield low unit cash operating costs (~$5.20-$5.60/bbl). However, refined products (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel) are standardized, fungible commodities traded on transparent spot benchmarks (NYMEX/Gulf Coast/Chicago/Group 3). MPC possesses zero structural pricing power and cannot unilaterally price above spot crack spreads. Returns on invested capital are volatile and macro-dictated: after a record post-Ukraine refining windfall in 2022-2023 ($14.5B and $9.7B net income), returns normalized rapidly as crack spreads compressed, with FY2025 ROIC dropping to ~9.7% and FY2020 delivering a catastrophic -$9.8B GAAP net loss. Long-term moat erosion risks include structural demand decline from automotive electrification and renewable fuels, heavy decarbonization compliance costs (RINs and LCFS), and zero barrier to customer switching among wholesale fuel distributors.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Marathon Petroleum is the largest US downstream refiner with significant scale advantages and stable midstream fee income via MPLX. However, MPC is fundamentally a price-taker selling fungible commodity fuels whose margins are dictated by volatile global and regional crack spreads rather than proprietary pricing power. Multi-cycle capital efficiency fails the Munger hurdle: FY2020 resulted in a -$9.8B net loss, and as refining margins normalized from the 2022-2023 peak, FY2025 ROIC contracted to ~9.7% (below the 12% cycle-neutral hurdle). Downstream gates 4-6 are strictly nulled per waterfall invariant.
column21: Financial Track Record: Net income attributable to MPC demonstrates extreme cyclicality: $2.64B (2019), -$9.83B (2020 pandemic demand shock and refining asset impairments), $9.74B (2021, aided by the $21B gross / ~$11.6B net cash proceeds from the Speedway retail divestiture), $14.52B (2022 peak post-invasion crack spread windfall), $9.68B (2023), $3.45B (2024), and $4.00B (2025). Revenue tracked $140.4B in 2024 and $132.7B in 2025. ROIC fluctuated from deeply negative in 2020 to >30% during the 2022-2023 refining margin super-cycle, before settling back to ~9.7% in 2025 as crack spreads normalized toward mid-cycle averages ($12.93/bbl R&M margin in Q4 2024). Segment Dynamics: Two primary reporting segments: (1) Refining & Marketing (R&M), which contributes the vast majority of cyclical volatility and throughput (~2.8-2.9M bpd, 92-94% utilization), and (2) Midstream (MPLX LP), which generates stable, fee-based adjusted EBITDA approaching ~$6.5-$7.0B annually, partially cushioning refinery margin swings and funding MPC's standalone dividend/capex. Capital Allocation: Management demonstrated commendable discipline by divesting Speedway to 7-Eleven in 2021 and utilizing proceeds to aggressively repurchase shares (>50% of shares retired between 2021 and 2025), but this financial engineering cannot overcome the underlying commodity price-taking nature of petroleum refining and absence of independent pricing power.

column14: Refining and integrated midstream infrastructure benefit from high replacement costs, unreplicable coastal permits, and complex feedstock integration. However, the economic moat is structurally impaired: products (gasoline, diesel, ethylene) are fungible commodities with zero independent pricing power. Competitors cannot easily build new refineries in the US, but global refining capacity additions, fluctuating crack spreads, and crude slate differentials drive boom-and-bust profitability. Long-term structural erosion stems from transport decarbonization and regulatory costs, exemplified by the accelerated depreciation and closure of the Los Angeles refinery.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). Phillips 66 is a cyclical commodity price-taker across its refining and CPChem petrochemical operations, where margins fluctuate with volatile market crack spreads and chemical supply/demand cycles. The company possesses zero ability to unilaterally price above commodity benchmarks. Full-cycle capital efficiency fails the Munger hurdle, with 10-year average GAAP ROIC hovering around ~5-6% (collapsing to negative during downcycles like 2020), despite temporary windfall spikes in 2022. Activist restructuring by Elliott Management highlights chronic underperformance relative to pure-play peers and heavy capital reinvestment requirements.
column21: 10-year historical GAAP ROIC averages ~5.0%-6.5%, well below the 12% hurdle. Net income swung from -$3.98B in FY2020 to +$11.0B in FY2022 windfall peak, normalizing to $2.12B in FY2024 and $4.40B in FY2025 (heavily boosted by $2.9B in pre-tax asset sale gains and offset by $964M accelerated depreciation on the Los Angeles refinery). Operating cash flow was $4.2B in 2024 and $5.0B in 2025 against high annual capital expenditures ($2.2B-$2.5B). Total debt of ~$19B-$20B against volatile cyclical earnings. Zero pricing power over commodity crack spreads and petrochemical margins.

column14: Unmatched Gulf Coast scale and high Nelson complexity index allow lowest operating costs per barrel among merchant refiners, but Valero is a complete commodity price-taker with zero pricing power over refined petroleum products and crack spreads.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Valero is a best-in-class low-cost Gulf Coast refiner, but operates as a structural commodity price-taker with zero independent pricing power. Profitability and ROIC fluctuate violently with global crack spreads (ROIC dropped to -3% in 2020 and normalized to ~7-10% in 2024 from the 2022 windfall peak), failing Munger's hurdle for enduring moat and pricing power >= inflation.
column21: Valero Energy operates 15 refineries with ~3.2M bpd throughput capacity and Diamond Green Diesel JV. Despite Nelson complexity advantages processing discounted heavy/sour crudes, earnings are governed by external crack spreads rather than pricing power: GAAP ROIC was -2.9% in 2020, 6.3% in 2021, spiked to ~30-40% in 2022 post-Ukraine windfall, and normalized to 7-10% in 2024 as net income fell from $8.8B (2023) to $2.8B (2024). Cash flows cannot be defended via price increases when crack spreads contract.

column14: Kinder Morgan operates North America's largest natural gas transmission network (~83,000 miles of pipelines and ~140 terminals transporting ~40% of US natural gas), with immense right-of-way, regulatory, and capital barriers preventing direct physical replication. However, midstream pipeline economics fail empirical proof of moat: 10-year GAAP ROIC has averaged 4.6% and median ROIC is 5.7% (well below the 12% hurdle), while tangible ROIC peaks under 10% (below 15%). Regulated FERC cost-of-service tariffs and negotiated long-term take-or-pay contracts provide stable fee-based cash flows but strictly cap economic returns on invested capital. Primary erosion risks include long-term energy transition decarbonization, regulatory pipeline opposition, and heavy continuous sustaining capital requirements.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC 5.7% < 12%, REJECT). Irreplaceable interstate pipeline infrastructure, but structurally unable to clear economic return hurdles due to high capital intensity and rate-regulated midstream returns. 10-year GAAP ROIC has consistently hovered between 1.9% and 6.1%, failing the 12% Munger moat proof standard.
column21: Kinder Morgan's 10-year operating history demonstrates persistent sub-hurdle returns on capital: 2016-2025 GAAP ROIC ranged between 1.93% and 6.12% with a 5-year median of 5.67%, and tangible ROIC averaged ~7.5% (peaking at 9.52% in 2025), failing both the GAAP 12% and tangible 15% thresholds. Total invested capital exceeds $61B ($30.8B long-term debt and $31.2B equity as of FY2025) against EBIT of $4.72B and net income of $3.06B. While ~95% of cash flows are fee-based or take-or-pay and FCF conversion is high (1.5x on net income), the asset-heavy nature and FERC tariff regulations cap per-share economic rent generation below compounder standards.

column14: Extensive interstate pipeline network, gathering systems, and fractionation plants represent irreplaceable infrastructure with prohibitive replacement costs. However, pricing is constrained by FERC tariff regulation and pipeline competition, resulting in sub-hurdle capital efficiency (10-year median ROIC of 8.5%, never reaching the 12% threshold).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Despite irreplaceable pipeline and fractionation infrastructure, ONEOK operates with high capital intensity and constrained regulatory/contractual pricing power, generating a multi-cycle median ROIC of only ~8.5% (2020-2025 range 6.3%-10.8%). The structural sub-12% capital efficiency fails the Munger hurdle.
column21: 10-year median ROIC is 8.5% (2020: 6.8%, 2021: 9.8%, 2022: 10.8%, 2023: 9.1%, 2024: ~7.9%, 2025: ~8.1%), failing the 12% Gate 3b hurdle across all cycle points. Recent debt-financed mega-acquisitions (Magellan Midstream for $18.8B in 2023, EnLink and Medallion for $3.3B+ in 2024-2025) expanded total debt to ~$32B against FY25 net income of ~$3.46B (Debt/NI > 9x, Net Debt/EBITDA ~4.6x), diluting returns on capital further.

column14: Targa Resources operates critical gathering and processing assets in the Permian Basin, long-haul NGL pipelines (Grand Prix), and major fractionation/export capacity at Mont Belvieu. While physical rights-of-way and integrated downstream logistics provide substantial barriers to entry, TRGP lacks monopolistic pricing power against major upstream E&P counterparties. Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC averages ~9.1% (2020: -5.9%, 2021: 4.0%, 2022: 11.5%, 2023: 13.8%, 2024: 9.1%, 2025: 10.2%), failing the 12% threshold across the cycle. High ongoing capital intensity and volume sensitivity to upstream drilling activity prevent compounding at super-hurdle rates.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & lacks monopolistic pricing power, REJECT). Targa operates valuable Permian midstream and NGL infrastructure, but its 10-year median ROIC of 9.1% falls well short of the 12% hurdle rate. Heavy ongoing capital expenditure ($2.4B-$3.3B annually), substantial debt load ($16.4B in 2025), and structural dependence on upstream drilling volumes prevent high-return capital compounding.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 9.1% (2020: -5.94%, 2021: ~4%, 2022: ~11.5%, 2023: ~13.8%, 2024: 9.14%, 2025: ~10.2%), failing the 12% cycle hurdle. Operating cash flow grew from $2.3B in 2021 to $3.9B in 2025, but heavy growth capex ramped from $0.5B to $3.3B, compressing GAAP Free Cash Flow to ~$584M by 2025. Long-term debt expanded from $12.1B in 2023 to $16.4B in 2025 (LT debt / net income ~8.5x). Despite ~90% fee-based contracts, volumes and margins remain exposed to upstream E&P drilling cycles.

column14: Transco right-of-way is physically irreplaceable, transporting ~15-20% of US natural gas with new greenfield interstate pipeline construction legally and politically unpermittable in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. However, the business fails the empirical capital efficiency proof: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is only 7.78% (peak 9.95% in 2023, 8.30% in 2025; 10-year range 1.84%–9.95%), well below the 12% hurdle. FERC cost-of-service and negotiated rate regulation structurally cap returns on invested capital while capital intensity remains perpetually high. Key erosion threats include FERC rate case challenges from utilities and long-term state-level building electrification/decarbonization mandates.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 7.78% vs 12% hurdle, REJECT). While the Transco pipeline network represents irreplaceable interstate energy infrastructure, high capital intensity and FERC utility rate regulation structurally constrain capital efficiency below the Munger hurdle across the entire 10-year cycle (GAAP ROIC never exceeded 10.0%, 10Y median 7.78%). Massive capital expenditures ($4.89B TTM in 2025) and heavy leverage ($27.3B debt vs $2.6B net income) permanently depress returns on total invested capital.
column21: 10-year historical GAAP ROIC averaged 5.4% and never reached the 12% threshold: 2016 (2.26%), 2017 (2.60%), 2018 (1.84%), 2019 (3.76%), 2020 (4.75%), 2021 (6.15%), 2022 (7.78%), 2023 (9.95%), 2024 (7.42%), and 2025 (8.30%). Tangible ROIC median is identically 7.78%. Segment revenue is anchored by Transmission & Gulf of Mexico (Transco, Northwest Pipeline) alongside Northeast and Western gathering & processing. While long-term reservation contracts provide volume stability, FERC cost-of-service rate base mechanisms limit economic rent extraction. Capital allocation is burdened by $27.32B in long-term debt against $63M cash, incurring $1.44B in annual interest expense against $4.20B EBIT (interest coverage 2.91x, below the 5.0x safe harbor threshold).

column14: Advisor-client relationships and account transfer friction provide baseline switching costs, but Ameriprise lacks pricing power >= inflation. Structural barriers: Financial planning integration, multi-product distribution (wrap advisory accounts, insurance/annuities), and client inertia/tax transfer friction anchor client assets ($1.69T AUMAA in 2025). Empirical proof: High reported operating ROE (~49-53% ex-AOCI) supported by aggressive share buybacks shrinking equity, but 10-year median ROIC is modest (~14.5%). Primary erosion threats: Persistent passive indexation and fee compression in active asset management (Columbia Threadneedle); intense competition from independent RIAs and discount brokerages capping advisory wrap fees; regulatory scrutiny (SEC Reg BI) and class-action lawsuits on cash-sweep deposit spreads forcing higher client payout yields; and risk of advisor defection with client books.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). Ameriprise benefits from switching costs tied to advisor-client relationships and financial planning lock-in, but structurally lacks pricing power >= inflation across market cycles. Columbia Threadneedle faces secular fee compression and chronic organic active outflows due to low-cost passive ETF alternatives. In Advice & Wealth Management, wrap advisory fee schedules face competitive caps against independent RIAs and discount brokers, while high-margin cash-sweep interest spreads face severe regulatory scrutiny (SEC Reg BI) and class-action litigation forcing higher yields paid to clients. Ameriprise cannot unilaterally raise fee schedules without triggering advisor defection and client asset loss.
column21: Ameriprise reported 2024 GAAP net revenue of $17.26B and GAAP net income of $3.40B, and 2025 GAAP net revenue of $18.48B and GAAP net income of $3.56B ($39.29 adjusted diluted EPS). Total AUMAA reached $1.69T at year-end 2025. While adjusted operating ROE ex-AOCI appears high at ~53%, this is largely driven by persistent share repurchases ($2.8B in 2024, $3.4B in 2025) that heavily reduce the equity base, while 10-year median ROIC sits around ~14.5%. Segment dynamics highlight lack of pricing power: Columbia Threadneedle (~20-25% of revenue) struggles with persistent organic outflows in active equities and industry-wide fee compression. Advice & Wealth Management (~60-65% of revenue) relies on high-touch advisor networks that cannot raise advisory basis-point fee schedules, while sweep cash deposit spreads (a critical source of net interest margin) face ongoing class-action litigation and regulatory pressure under Reg BI regarding uninvested cash yields.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Simple to Understand & Verifiable, REJECT). Following the 2022 merger with Athene, Apollo is an opaque financial conglomerate consolidating over $440B in balance sheet assets, predominantly composed of Athene's retirement annuity liabilities backed by Apollo-originated private credit, direct corporate loans, asset-backed finance (ABF), and structured credit tranches. A substantial portion of the asset portfolio consists of Level 2/3 illiquid instruments valued via internal mark-to-model assumptions rather than observable public prices. Furthermore, Athene heavily utilizes offshore reinsurance treaties in Bermuda and co-investment sidecars (ACRA) to achieve capital relief on complex credit assets, subject to mounting NAIC regulatory scrutiny. Key underlying economic risks—loan-level default probabilities, recovery rates, duration mismatch, and affiliate fee extraction—are fundamentally unobservable and unverifiable from the outside, violating Munger's circle of competence standard.
column21: Consolidated assets expanded to $442B in FY2025 ($363B in FY2024), dominated by Athene's $406B in liabilities. The business combines asset management fee streams with balance-sheet spread earnings. Over 90% of Athene's multi-hundred-billion portfolio is deployed into privately originated fixed income, structured debt, and asset-backed finance manufactured by Apollo, creating a closed-loop vertical integration where Apollo is originator, asset manager, and balance-sheet custodian. Reliance on Level 2/3 matrix-pricing/model valuations and Bermuda reinsurance sidecars (ACRA I & II) obscures true credit risk, loss-given-default, and economic capital adequacy during severe credit market downturns. The NAIC Macroprudential Working Group and Life Actuarial Task Force continue to target private credit opacity, asset adequacy testing, and capital charges on offshore reinsurance structures. Reported ROIC (~13.8%) and GAAP net income are heavily distorted by fair-value accounting adjustments, mark-to-model derivatives, and non-economic spread swings, failing the Munger standard of transparent, externally verifiable financial statements.

column14: Direct-lending origination scale, established sponsor relationships, and long-term locked capital create a structural toll booth on deployed private credit assets. However, empirical moat proof fails with sub-hurdle GAAP ROIC (2-5% vs. 12% hurdle). Moat faces long-term erosion threats from aggressive direct lending expansion by commercial and investment banks, alternative manager copycats compressing spreads, and institutional LP pressure for fee concessions and co-investments.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Despite leading scale in private credit and locked-up fund capital, Ares fails the empirical proof of moat standard with 5-year median GAAP ROIC tracking well below the 12% hurdle (~2-5% across 2021-2025). Furthermore, Ares lacks pricing power >= inflation: asset management fee rates in private debt are subject to institutional fee compression, volume-tier breaks, and zero-fee co-investment demands from large LPs, while underlying par-value debt assets do not appreciate with inflation. Escalating competition from alternative peers and commercial banks partnering in direct lending further erodes loan spreads and fee terms.
column21: Ares Management has scaled AUM from $306B in 2021 to over $622B in 2025, driven by dominant U.S. and European direct lending origination, real estate expansion (GCP International acquisition in 2025), and secondary solutions. Fee-Related Earnings (FRE) grew to $1.77B in 2025. However, reported GAAP ROIC consistently fails the 12% hurdle, averaging ~2-5% over 2021-2025 (2021: ~1.5%, 2022: ~1.0%, 2023: ~2.8%, 2024: ~4.2%, 2025: ~4.5%) due to heavy balance sheet liabilities from consolidated CLOs/funds ($13B-$15B total debt) and significant goodwill/intangibles from acquisitions. Management fee rates in private credit (typically 1.0-1.5% on invested/committed capital) lack upward inflation pass-through, as institutional LPs demand fee breaks and zero-fee co-investment rights on mega-funds. Direct lending spreads have faced compression from bank partnerships and rival mega-funds (Blackstone, Apollo, Blue Owl).

column14: Legacy distribution networks, institutional consultant relationships, and retirement account switching costs provide only weak retention against secular passive indexing. Empirically fails moat proof: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.5% (with FY2023–FY2025 ROIC compressing to 3–6%), far below the 12% hurdle. Complete absence of pricing power as effective fee rates compress under zero-fee passive ETF competition. Moat severely eroded by structural active-to-passive rotation and devastating client outflows (>$120B–$150B) following the Western Asset trade allocation scandal (Ken Leech DOJ/SEC charges and $100M SEC settlement).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & Zero Pricing Power, REJECT). Traditional active asset manager facing secular fee compression, market share loss to low-cost passive ETFs, and chronic institutional net outflows. Capital efficiency is structurally sub-hurdle with a 10-year median ROIC of 8.5% (compressing to 3–6% in FY2023–FY2025 post-Putnam and Legg Mason acquisitions). Severe brand dilution and client redemptions following the Western Asset trade-allocation cherry-picking scandal further impair organic growth.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates structural capital inefficiency and lack of pricing power: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 8.5% fails the 12% hurdle, with FY2023–FY2025 ROIC falling to 3–6%. GAAP operating margins compressed from historical 30%+ levels to ~17% in FY2023 and 9–10% in FY2024–FY2025, burdened by acquisition amortization and integration costs. Long-term debt stands at ~$2.4B–$2.6B from debt-financed acquisitions (Legg Mason, Putnam, Lexington Partners) intended to mask organic outflows in traditional active equity and fixed income. The firm lacks pricing power: adjusted effective fee rates are under secular pressure (~37–38 bps) from passive alternatives (Vanguard, BlackRock). In 2024–2026, subsidiary Western Asset Management suffered catastrophic outflows of $120B–$150B+ and paid a $100M SEC civil penalty after co-CIO Ken Leech was charged with cherry-picking profitable trades, compressing Western Asset AUM to ~$229B and demonstrating extreme key-person and governance risk.

column14: Insurmountable scale economies shared in iShares (over $4T ETF AUM) where massive trading volume drives the tightest secondary bid-ask spreads and lowest total ownership cost, creating a self-reinforcing liquidity flywheel that subscale competitors cannot replicate. Complementary toll booth in Aladdin enterprise software, which manages risk for tens of trillions in global institutional assets with >98% gross contract renewal. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 14.2%, tangible ROIC >100%, steady 35-42% operating margins across market cycles, and record $641B net inflows in 2024. Primary erosion risks include ongoing fee compression in plain-vanilla passive core indexing, index licensing fee inflation, potential integration frictions across massive private market acquisitions (GIP, HPS, Preqin), and political scrutiny around ESG proxy voting.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Unassailable global scale economies shared in asset management ($14.0T AUM) combined with mission-critical Aladdin enterprise software lock-in (>98% retention). Transformative pivot into high-margin private markets (GIP for infrastructure, HPS for private credit, Preqin for data). Structurally insulated from or beneficiary of all 5 macrotrends. Fortress AA- balance sheet with $11.5B cash, minimal net debt of $1.3B, and 11.5x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: market appreciation & organic volume 4.5% + pricing/fee realization 0.0% + private markets & Aladdin mix 3.0% - margin/regulatory drag 0.5% + net repurchases 1.5%]
column21: World's largest asset manager with $14.0T in AUM at FY2025 year-end (up from $11.6T in 2024 and $10.0T in 2023), supported by record organic net inflows of $641B in 2024 and 9% organic base fee growth in 2025. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 14.2% and tangible operating ROIC exceeds 100%, demonstrating structural capital efficiency. FY2025 revenue grew 19% to $24.2B, with technology services (Aladdin, eFront, Preqin) expanding 24% to $1.98B as high-margin recurring SaaS. Moat anchored by iShares scale economies shared (passing low fees to clients while enjoying insurmountable liquidity network effects) and Aladdin's indispensable enterprise risk OS. Capital allocation characterized by visionary counter-cyclical M&A: BGI/iShares in 2009 ($13.5B), GIP in 2024 ($12.5B), Preqin in 2025 ($3.2B cash), and HPS in 2025 ($12B equity), creating a dominant public-plus-private markets powerhouse. Balance sheet is an AA- rated fortress: $11.5B cash vs $12.8B LT debt ($1.3B net debt, repayable in 0.23 years of net income), and EBIT/interest coverage of 11.5x ($7,045M EBIT vs $614M interest). Reported GAAP FCF conversion (58.5%) reflects ASC 810 consolidated fund investments and acquisition closing costs; underlying maintenance capex is negligible ($375M, <7% of net income), supporting consistent dividend compounding ($3.3B TTM) and share repurchases.

column14: World's largest global custodian and collateral manager ($59.3T AUC/A, $2.2T AUM) with deeply entrenched operational switching costs. Institutional clients (asset managers, pensions, sovereign wealth funds, 94% of Fortune 100) embed BNY's custody, middle-office accounting, clearing, and reporting into core daily operations, making custodian migration exceptionally risky, complex, and rare. Empirically demonstrated by 2024-2025 Return on Tangible Common Equity (ROTCE) of 23-26% and ROE of ~14%. Moat erosion threats include fee pressure from passive asset management, institutional deposit cash-sorting in volatile rate environments, and technological disintermediation / direct tokenized settlement.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). While BNY possesses a world-class custody moat (Gate 3a Toll booth / Switching costs, Gate 4 CAP 20) with $59.3T AUC/A and 23-26% ROTCE, it fails Gate 6's strict peace-of-mind fortress balance sheet standard. As a Global Systemically Important Bank (G-SIB) and custody bank, BNY operates a fractional-reserve deposit-taking balance sheet funded by ~$280B+ in institutional deposits and wholesale liabilities. Long-term debt of $31.9B exceeds 4.0x Net Income ($5.55B, LT debt/NI = 5.74x), operating cash flow swings violently with institutional deposit flows, and the institution inherently relies on continuous wholesale market access and central bank liquidity facilities ('the kindness of strangers'). Per the screening methodology, commercial fractional-reserve and custody banks fail Gate 6.
column21:
1. Moat & Market Position: BNY is the #1 global custodian with $59.3T in Assets under Custody and/or Administration (AUC/A) and $2.2T in AUM as of FY2025, servicing 94% of Fortune 100 companies and 96% of the top 100 global banks. Core institutional custody, accounting, and clearing are deeply integrated into client operations, creating prohibitive switching costs.
2. Capital Efficiency & Profitability: FY2025 revenue reached $20.08B with Net Income of $5.55B. ROTCE was 23% in 2024 and 26% in 2025 (ROE ~14%), demonstrating high profitability on tangible capital despite lower asset-turnover GAAP ROIC typical of leveraged financial institutions.
3. Balance Sheet & Gate 6 Failure: FY2025 Long-Term Debt was $31.87B against Net Income of $5.55B (LT Debt / NI = 5.74x, well above the <=4.0x screener threshold). Balance sheet of >$400B in assets is levered against client deposits and repo obligations. Operating cash flows fluctuate drastically due to institutional deposit movements ($96M in 2019, $15.1B in 2022, $687M in 2024, $6.73B in 2025), failing clean multi-year FCF conversion and the 'peace of mind / no kindness of strangers' solvency standard required for Quality compounders.

column14: Global scale leader in alternative asset management ($1.27T total AUM, $922B fee-earning AUM) with unreplicable 40-year performance track record. High switching costs driven by 10+ year closed-end fund lockups, perpetual capital vehicles ($524B AUM), and 85%+ institutional LP re-up rates. Pricing power demonstrated by maintaining premium ~100-150 bps management fees and 15-20% carry across market cycles with zero fee compression. High returns on capital proved by 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 35%+ (never below 17% in a decade). Primary erosion risks include key-man transition risks, retail redemption runs in semi-liquid structures, and growing competition in private credit.
column20: World's premier alternative asset manager with unassailable brand, $920B+ fee-earning AUM, and sticky perpetual/long-dated capital. High pricing power verified by stable fee rates and 35%+ median ROIC. Active beneficiary of AI infrastructure boom (QTS data centers), private credit expansion, and institutional yield demand. Fortress balance sheet with 15x interest coverage and A+ Fitch/S&P rating. [5-10Y g: fee-earning AUM volume 5.5% + asset price appreciation 2.0% + private credit & insurance mix 1.0% - tech & compliance drag 0.5% + buybacks 0.5%]
column21: Total AUM reached $1.27T in FY2025 with $921.7B fee-earning AUM and $523.6B perpetual capital. FY2025 Fee-Related Earnings (FRE) grew to $5.7B ($4.67/share). 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 35.04% and operating ROIC is 40.05%, with FY2025 GAAP ROIC of 35.66%. Free cash flow conversion is exceptional at 114.4% (FY2025 FCF of $4.55B on $3.02B net income). Peak-to-peak earnings compounding confirmed as 2025 Owner EPS ($3.89) eclipsed prior 2019/2022 peaks. Corporate balance sheet maintains an A+ rating with $2.63B in cash, $7.68B in EBIT, and 15.1x interest coverage against $12.58B in long-term fixed-rate senior notes.

column14: QQQ ETF franchise provides a liquidity network effect and brand recognition, but legacy active equity and multi-asset strategies suffer from persistent net outflows and relentless industry fee compression. 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 6.8% (well below the 12% hurdle) and GAAP ROIC plunged negative in 2025 due to a $1.8B intangible impairment. Invesco has zero pricing power to outpace inflation, as passive index competition forces fee yields continually downward.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 6.8% < 12%, zero pricing power, REJECT). While Invesco holds a dominant ETF franchise in the Invesco QQQ Trust with strong liquidity network effects, its broader business is burdened by secular active mutual fund outflows, value-destructive legacy M&A (e.g. OppenheimerFunds write-downs), and relentless industry fee compression. 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 6.8% fails the 12% hurdle, and net management fee yields continue to decline across the cycle.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.8%, failing the 12% hurdle. In 2025, GAAP operating margin fell to -10.9% and net income was severely negative due to a $1.8B non-cash intangible asset impairment (primarily goodwill/intangibles from the OppenheimerFunds acquisition). While Free Cash Flow was positive ($1.12B in 2024 and $1.44B in 2025), total debt remains substantial at ~$9.78B at year-end 2025. Invesco faces structural secular headwinds from passive fee compression and active fund outflows, negating pricing power above inflation.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (gate_1 = N, REJECT). Following the full acquisition and consolidation of Global Atlantic in 2024, KKR transformed from an asset-light alternative manager into a balance-sheet-heavy financial conglomerate with >$410B in assets, >$379B in liabilities, and >$220B in insurance reserves. A substantial portion of Global Atlantic's asset portfolio is deployed into affiliate-originated private credit, asset-based finance, and illiquid Level 3 instruments marked via internal valuation models. This captive insurance structure creates an opaque related-party credit web where true underwriting risk, asset-liability duration matching, and mark-to-market solvency are not verifiable from the outside.
column21: Consolidated balance sheet expanded to $410.1B in assets and $379.2B in liabilities with ~$54.5B in total debt in FY2025 following the 100% buyout of Global Atlantic. Global Atlantic's $220B+ portfolio is heavily invested in private credit, direct middle-market lending, and asset-backed finance originated by KKR's own deal teams. A significant portion of these holdings are categorized as Level 3 assets under ASC 820 with unobservable inputs and internal pricing discretion. Under the Munger framework, opaque long-tail insurance reserves and affiliate-originated credit portfolios fail Gate 1 due to lack of external verifiability and systemic run/liquidity risks.

column14: Massive client switching costs in institutional custody, fund administration, and middle-office processing, combined with multi-generational trust relationships in private wealth management. Proof of moat shown by 19.6% 5-year median ROIC and $5.0B in sticky servicing fees. Primary erosion threats stem from back-office automation by fintech challengers, scale advantages and pricing pressure from larger custody peers (BNY, State Street), and heavy regulatory capital requirements.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). While Northern Trust boasts an enduring, high-trust institutional custody and private wealth franchise with high switching costs (19.6% median ROIC), it operates as a deposit-funded custody bank with $153B+ in assets on $12.7B in equity (>12x balance sheet leverage) and $118B+ in deposits. In accordance with the Munger solvency standard, fractional-reserve and deposit-funded custody balance sheets fail Gate 6 due to inherent duration, interest-rate, and deposit flight vulnerabilities.
column21: FY2025 consolidated revenue of $8.09B with $5.02B in trust and servicing fees ($2.80B Asset Servicing, $2.22B Wealth Management) and $2.41B in net interest income. Total assets of $153.5B supported by $118.7B in deposits against $12.7B in equity, reflecting 12.1x leverage. 10-year median ROIC of 19.57% and owner EPS compounding from $4.51 (2016) to $12.70 (2025). Peak OE EPS was $13.11 in 2024. Despite high returns on tangible capital and deep fiduciary moat, the deposit-funded balance sheet is disqualified under Gate 6 criteria.

column14: Extreme switching costs in institutional custody and fund administration protect an entrenched oligopoly (State Street, BNY Mellon, JPMorgan). Re-platforming custody, accounting systems, and tax reporting entails massive operational risk, keeping client retention above 98%. Anchored by proprietary platforms like Charles River Development (Alpha front-to-back), State Street offsets core custody basis-point fee compression via higher-margin ancillary services (FX trading, securities lending, private market servicing). However, secular fee compression from asset managers remains a persistent margin drag.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). While State Street possesses an enduring institutional moat in custody, fund administration, and ETF management ($53.8T in AUC/A) with high switching costs and sticky client relationships, it operates as a fractional-reserve bank holding company with >13x balance sheet leverage ($366B in assets on $27B equity) funded primarily by ~$245B of institutional deposits.
