However, empirical proof of moat is lacking: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~3.0% and 10-year median ROIC is 7.5%, both failing the 12% hurdle. Primary erosion threats include intense fee pressure upon multi-year contract renewals, bank client consolidation, and competitive incursions from cloud-native core banking challengers (Thought Machine, Mambu, nCino).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Despite high bank switching costs in core banking software (Gate 3a Toll booth), FIS fails to demonstrate economic moat proof with a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~3% and 10-year median ROIC of 7.5%, well below the mandatory 12% hurdle. Massive capital destruction from the $43B Worldpay acquisition in 2019, subsequent $17.6B goodwill impairment in 2022, and discounted 55% carve-out to GTCR at an $18.5B enterprise value in 2024 demonstrate persistent capital misallocation and sub-cost-of-capital returns.
column21: Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC consistently lags the 12% hurdle: FY21 0.67%, FY22 negative due to a $17.6B goodwill impairment, FY23 2.58%, FY24 3.78%, and FY25 ~5.0%, with a 10-year median of 7.5%. Post-Worldpay divestiture in early 2024 (55% stake sold to GTCR for $11.7B net proceeds, retaining 45%), FIS reorganized around Banking Solutions and Capital Markets. While core banking maintains 95%+ client retention due to prohibitive migration friction, pricing power is constrained by bank customer bargaining power and competition from Fiserv and Jack Henry. Historical M&A (SunGard for $9.1B, Worldpay for $43B) severely diluted shareholder returns and bloated invested capital with unamortized intangibles.

column14: High customer switching costs in core banking ledgers (DNA, Premier) where community banks face high operational risk to migrate, combined with an installed merchant POS base via Clover. However, empirical moat proof is lacking: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.2%, failing the 12% hurdle due to the massive capital dilution from the 2019 First Data merger ($22B all-stock plus debt). Pricing power is constrained: bank clients face consolidation and tolerate rather than love legacy platforms, while merchant acquiring faces aggressive competition from modern cloud-native POS and payment facilitators (Toast, Block/Square, Adyen, Stripe).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). While Fiserv benefits from high switching costs in bank core processing and an entrenched merchant acquiring footprint via Clover, it structurally fails the empirical capital efficiency hurdle: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.2% (ranging 3.4% to 8.8%), well below the 12.0% threshold. The 2019 First Data acquisition burdened the balance sheet with $29B+ in debt and over $40B in goodwill/intangibles, permanently diluting return on invested capital. Core banking customers face consolidation and exhibit resistance to price hikes, while merchant acquiring faces intense disintermediation pressure from modern agile platforms like Toast, Block, and Adyen.
column21: 5-year GAAP ROIC (2021-2025) has hovered between 3.4% and 8.8% with a median of ~7.2%, consistently falling short of the required 12.0% hurdle. The 2019 First Data merger left Fiserv with $29.1B in total debt against only ~$800M in cash and ~$3.0B-$3.5B in GAAP net income, creating a debt/net income ratio of ~8.5-9.7x (far exceeding the 4.0x peace-of-mind ceiling). Substantial goodwill and intangibles (> $40B) reflect heavy post-merger invested capital that depresses economic profit spreads near or below WACC (~7.5%). Although Clover generates strong merchant volume and FCF conversion is respectable (~$4B-$5B FCF), persistent low ROIC and competitive pricing headwinds in both merchant solutions and core processing preclude a pass under Gate 3b.

column14: Merchant integrations and ISV partnerships provide localized switching costs, but returns on capital are deeply sub-hurdle (GAAP ROIC 3-5%, 10Y median 8.5%) following debt/goodwill-heavy mega-acquisitions (TSYS). Primary erosion threats include severe commoditisation of merchant acquiring, ongoing market-share loss to API-first unified commerce platforms (Adyen, Stripe) and vertical POS systems (Toast, Clover), and lack of pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power). Legacy merchant acquirer facing severe commoditisation from modern tech platforms (Adyen, Stripe, Toast). Historical capital efficiency fails the Munger hurdle (GAAP ROIC 3-5%, 10-year median 8.5% vs 12% required) burdened by massive goodwill from the $21.5B TSYS mega-merger. Lacks pricing power above inflation as take rates face continuous competitive pressure.
column21: GAAP ROIC has averaged only 3-5% from 2020 to 2025, and 10-year median ROIC is 8.5%, well below the 12% cost of capital hurdle. The $21.5B TSYS acquisition in 2019 saddled the balance sheet with over $25B in goodwill and acquired intangibles, permanently depressing return on invested capital. In core merchant acquiring, Global Payments has suffered continuous market share erosion and pricing pressure from modern unified commerce leaders (Adyen, Stripe) and specialized vertical SaaS providers, eliminating pricing power.

column14: Near-insurmountable switching costs in core banking software (SilverLake, CIF 20/20, Symitar/Episys) serving as the operational central nervous system for ~1,650+ US community banks and credit unions. Core replacements entail 18-24 month operational upheaval and high regulatory risk, producing 98-99% annual client retention with zero voluntary churn. Pricing power demonstrated by multi-year contracts with CPI escalation clauses and high-margin digital module upsells. 10-year GAAP ROIC has consistently ranged between 20% and 26% (median 22.7%), with tangible operating ROIC near 40%. Primary erosion risks are secular community bank M&A consolidation and long-term cloud-native core entrants, offset by expanding account volumes and new credit union core wins.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Quintessential core banking and payment processing toll booth for US regional banks and credit unions with 98-99% retention. Insulated across all 5 macrotrends: charges per transaction/account rather than vulnerable SaaS seats, 100% US domestic focus, asset-light, and virtually debt-free ($40M debt vs $635M EBIT). FCF conversion exceeds 120% of net income with a pristine balance sheet. [5-10Y g: transaction volume 2.5% + digital cross-sell 2.5% + price indexation 1.5% - bank consolidation attrition drag 1.0% + net buybacks 0.5%]
column21: 10-year track record of rock-solid compounding: sales grew from $1.43B (FY16) to $2.54B (FY25), EBIT expanded from $341.7M to $635.0M, and Owner EPS compounded at 7.8% from $3.03 to $6.98 (peak FY25). 10-year GAAP ROIC never fell below 20% (median 22.72%, tangible operating ROIC 39.5%). Owner FCF conversion averaged 121% of GAAP net income over multiple cycles with low capex ($67M capex vs $762M OCF in FY25). Minimal debt ($40M long-term debt vs $503M net income and $12M cash), zero reliance on capital markets, conservative accounting with low SBC (<1.5% of revenue), and disciplined stewardship under David Foss and Greg Adelson.

column14: Global two-sided payment network duopoly (with Visa) operating as an ad valorem toll booth on consumer and commercial spending. Enjoys near-insurmountable switching costs and network effects across billions of cardholders, tens of millions of merchants, and thousands of financial institutions. Pricing power proven by 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 89.4%, tangible ROIC >100%, and operating margins expanding to 57.6%. Inflation is captured automatically via basis-point assessments on nominal transaction value. Primary erosion risks stem from regulatory interventions (Credit Card Competition Act, interchange fee caps) and domestic sovereign A2A payment rails, both mitigated by value-added services, tokenization, and cross-border lock-in.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Elite global payments duopoly operating an inflation-indexed ad valorem toll booth with near-zero capital intensity. Exceptional 5-macrotrend resilience: immune to labor scarcity and energy limits, directly benefits from AI fraud/identity authentication demand, and automatically captures inflation in transaction nominal volume. Balance sheet fortress with net debt repayable in ~0.5 years of FCF and 26x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: global purchase volume 6.0% + cross-border & VAS expansion 3.5% + ad valorem inflation capture 1.5% - regulatory fee drag 1.0% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 10-year track record of superior capital efficiency: FY2025 net revenue $32.8B (+16% YoY), EBIT $18.9B (57.6% operating margin), GAAP ROIC 98.4%, and 5-year median ROIC 89.4%. FCF conversion exceeds 100% (FY2025 Owner FCF of $16.6B vs Net Income of $15.0B; Capex is only $489M or 1.5% of revenue). High-growth Value-Added Services & Solutions grew 23% in FY2025 to $13.3B (over 40% of net revenue), providing massive diversification away from core interchange dispute risks. Balance sheet fortress with $10.6B cash vs $18.3B LT debt (Net Debt/NI 0.51x, EBIT/Interest 26.2x). Capital allocation has retired over 25% of shares outstanding over the last decade while funding disciplined security and analytics acquisitions.

column14: Two-sided network of 400M+ active consumer accounts and ~35M merchants established early checkout ubiquity. However, structural pricing power and moat defensibility have eroded severely. Apple Pay has captured dominant mobile e-commerce share via frictionless native iOS biometric authentication (Face ID), causing PayPal's high-margin branded checkout volume growth to decelerate to 2-4%, trailing e-commerce. Total volume expansion has been driven by unbranded processing (Braintree), a commodity gateway subject to fierce price competition against Adyen and Stripe. As a result, blended take rate has steadily compressed from >2.5% to ~1.67%, and consolidated transaction margins collapsed from >55% to ~45%. PayPal cannot raise prices across the cycle without accelerating customer defection or volume loss to competing digital wallets and acquirers.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). High-margin branded checkout button suffers ongoing market share loss to Apple Pay (native iOS biometric integration) and Shop Pay, decelerating branded volume growth to 2-4% (lagging broader e-commerce). Blended take rate has persistently compressed from >2.5% to ~1.67%, and transaction margin percentage fell from >55% to ~45% due to mix shift into commodity unbranded processing (Braintree). Lacks demonstrable pricing power >= inflation across the cycle without customer defection.
column21: Historical 10-year median ROIC of 14.2% reflects legacy network scale, but economic moat and pricing power have decayed structurally over 2021-2025. Total payment volume (~$1.7-1.8T) has been driven disproportionately by unbranded processing (Braintree), where take rates and margins are thin under price competition with Stripe and Adyen. Core branded checkout (the main profit engine) slowed to 2-4% growth in 2024-2025, ceding share to Apple Pay in mobile commerce (representing ~50% of transactions). Consolidated transaction margin collapsed by ~1,000 bps from peak (>55% to ~45%), and blended take rate fell to ~1.67%. Inability to raise prices without volume defection fails Gate 3b pricing power criteria.

column14: Insurmountable two-sided network effect spanning 4.5B+ cards and 150M+ merchant endpoints via VisaNet. Ad valorem fee structure captures nominal inflation automatically with near-zero marginal processing cost. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 41.6%, tangible ROIC >100%, and operating margins stable at 65-67%. Primary erosion risks include the DOJ civil antitrust debit lawsuit targeting merchant routing agreements and potential US routing legislation (CCCA).
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Quintessential global payments toll booth duopoly with unmatched scale, 66-67% operating margins, and zero credit risk. Ad valorem basis-point fee model provides built-in inflation protection. Fortress balance sheet with $17.2B cash vs $19.6B debt and >40x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: nominal payments volume 5.5% + cross-border travel 1.5% + value-added services (cyber/fraud/advisory) 2.5% + net share buybacks 1.5% - regulatory/interchange litigation drag 1.0%]
column21: Multi-cycle compounding track record: Net revenue expanded from $15.1B in FY2016 to $40.0B in FY2025 (~11.4% CAGR), with operating income rising from $7.9B to $24.0B+ and GAAP net income reaching $20.1B. Five-year median GAAP ROIC is 41.6% (FY25 at 45.0%) and operating ROIC exceeds 100%. Free cash flow conversion is exceptional at 106% of net income (FY25 OCF of $23.1B less $1.5B capex equals $20.9B Owner FCF). Segment drivers: Core consumer payments volume continues steady high-single-digit expansion, cross-border travel volume remains elevated, and Value-Added Services (VAS) grew 24% YoY in FY25 to $10.9B (27% of net revenue), providing high-margin revenue diversification. Balance sheet & capital allocation: Outstanding long-term debt of $19.6B is offset by $17.2B cash and short-term investments (net debt of $2.4B is under 0.15x annual net income); EBIT/interest coverage exceeds 40x. Routine share repurchases ($10B-$15B annually) have retired ~25% of shares since IPO, while dividends have compounded at double digits for 16 consecutive years. Regulatory scrutiny (DOJ civil antitrust debit suit filed 2024, in discovery through 2026-2027; proposed CCCA routing mandates) poses manageable routing/fee concessions but does not impair the core terminal compounding moat.

column14: Square merchant lock-in via integrated POS hardware, payroll, and inventory software, alongside Cash App's 56M+ active P2P network, provides switching barriers and two-sided transaction tolls. However, empirical proof of moat fails decisively: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~3.5% and 10-year median ROIC is 5.2%, far below the 12% threshold. Primary erosion threats include intense competition from vertical POS specialists (Toast, Clover), bank-backed P2P networks (Zelle), payment commoditization by Apple/Google, credit risk in Afterpay BNPL and Cash App Borrow, and past capital misallocation into speculative non-core ventures.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & contested pricing power, REJECT). Block's dual ecosystems (Square and Cash App) exhibit structural switching costs and network effects, but fail empirical proof of moat. 10-year historical median ROIC is 5.2% and 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~3.5%, severely depressed by the dilutive $29B Afterpay acquisition, chronic share-based compensation, and fierce pricing competition in merchant acquiring (Toast, Clover, Shopify) and consumer fintech (Zelle, PayPal, Apple Pay).
column21: Historical Capital Efficiency: Block's 10-year median ROIC stands at 5.2%, with 5-year median GAAP ROIC between 2.0% and 4.4% (2020: ~2.5%, 2021: ~1.5%, 2022: -0.2%, 2023: 1.4%, 2024: 4.4%, 2025: ~7.4%), consistently failing the 12% hurdle. Invested capital ballooned permanently following the $29B all-stock acquisition of Afterpay in 2022, creating massive goodwill and intangible amortization drag. Segment Breakdown: Consolidated FY2024 revenue reached $24.1B ($8.96B gross profit), expanding to $24.2B ($10.4B gross profit) in FY2025. Bitcoin trading represents >40% of top-line revenue but delivers <5% of gross profit due to passthrough economics. Cash App generates ~$5.5B+ gross profit (interchange, instant deposit, Cash App Borrow), while Square delivers ~$4.5B+ gross profit (POS processing, SaaS subscriptions). Pricing Power & Competitive Dynamics: Square take rates face persistent compression as volume shifts to larger SMBs, with aggressive price competition from Clover, Toast, and Shopify. Cash App's monetization relies on instant deposit tolls and subprime consumer lending, constrained by zero-cost bank rails (Zelle, FedNow) and regulatory scrutiny. Balance Sheet & Capital Allocation: Cash and marketable securities of ~$8.5B against long-term debt of ~$5.5B provide adequate liquidity, but shareholder compounding has been heavily diluted by historical SBC exceeding $1.0B annually, speculative ventures (Tidal for $300M, Bitcoin ASIC hardware Proto, Bitkey), and the cyclical credit risks embedded in Afterpay.

column14: Moat source: Deep proprietary biologic patent portfolios, advanced manufacturing know-how, and commercial sales infrastructure in immunology (Skyrizi, Rinvoq) and oncology (Venclexta, Elahere). Proof & Breakdown: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 16.04%, but historical compounding was fundamentally driven by 10-15% annual price hikes on Humira behind 130+ defensive patent thickets. When US exclusivity expired in 2023, pricing power dissolved; Humira revenues collapsed ~50% in 2024 and another 49.5% in 2025 (to $4.54B) under interchangeable biosimilar competition with 50-80% price discounts. Primary erosion threats: Inability to take real price increases above inflation due to mandatory Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) inflation rebates, statutory Medicare price negotiation (Imbruvica selected with a 38% price cut effective 2026), aggressive PBM gross-to-net rebate concessions, and upcoming patent expirations (Venclexta ~2030, Skyrizi/Rinvoq ~2033-2035).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Historical compounding was an artifact of aggressive 10-15% annual price increases on Humira protected by a 130+ patent thicket. The loss of US exclusivity in 2023 caused Humira revenue to collapse ~50% in 2024 and 49.5% in 2025 (to $4.54B) as interchangeable biosimilars took market share at 50-80% discounts. While next-generation immunology assets Skyrizi ($17.56B in 2025) and Rinvoq ($8.30B) have scaled rapidly to offset Humira, AbbVie possesses no structural pricing power >= inflation across the cycle: the Inflation Reduction Act imposes mandatory 100% government rebates on price hikes exceeding CPI-U, Medicare price negotiations imposed a 38% cut on Imbruvica for 2026, and PBM rebate walls force flat-to-declining net realized prices. Furthermore, the business is burdened by $64.5B in long-term debt (15.3x Net Income) from defensive M&A (Allergan, ImmunoGen, Cerevel), negative stockholders' equity (-$3.27B), and finite patent runways on Skyrizi/Rinvoq expiring in 2033-2035.
column21: Financial & Operating Track Record: Total revenue reached $61.16B in FY2025 (+8.6% YoY) as Skyrizi ($17.56B, +50%) and Rinvoq ($8.30B, +39%) offset the collapse of Humira ($4.54B, -49.5%). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 16.04% (FY21: 18.6%, FY22: 20.8%, FY23: 15.5%, FY24: 11.9%, FY25: 16.0%), but tangible ROIC is distorted by -$3.27B in stockholders' equity and $88.3B in goodwill and intangibles. Pricing Power & Patent Vulnerability: Humira demonstrated that AbbVie's pricing power is strictly an artifact of statutory patent exclusivity rather than an enduring economic moat. The IRA legally caps Medicare price hikes at CPI-U and forced a 38% price reduction on Imbruvica taking effect in 2026. Balance Sheet & Capital Allocation: Long-term debt stands at $64.5B against $5.2B cash (Net Debt ~$59.3B). Net Debt to TTM Net Income ($4.23B) is 15.3x, violating the <=4.0x fortress threshold. Negative book equity (-$3.27B) reflects $63B debt-funded Allergan acquisition. Subsequent M&A highlights reinvestment treadmill risk: $8.7B Cerevel acquisition suffered a major Phase 2 clinical failure on lead schizophrenia drug emraclidine in November 2024, resulting in a $3.5B impairment charge in early 2025.

column14: Amgen holds valuable biologic patents and advanced manufacturing know-how, but lacks pricing power >= inflation. Net realized prices have declined annually (-2% in FY24, further drops in FY25) due to biosimilar erosion on legacy biologics (Prolia/Xgeva patent expiration in 2025, Neulasta) and statutory Medicare price negotiation under the Inflation Reduction Act (Enbrel facing >50% price cuts in 2026, Otezla selected in 2025 with a $1.2B impairment). PBM rebates and statutory price caps eliminate positive net pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). Biopharma pioneer possesses deep biologic R&D and manufacturing intangibles, but structurally lacks pricing power >= inflation. Mature blockbuster franchises face continuous biosimilar erosion (Prolia/Xgeva cliff in 2025-2026, Neulasta) and legislative price-setting under the Inflation Reduction Act (Enbrel Medicare cuts >50% in 2026; Otezla selected in 2025 with $1.2B impairment), driving persistent negative net realized price changes (-2% in FY24, down in FY25) despite volume expansion. [5-10Y g: volume expansion/MariTide 4.0% + Horizon rare disease 2.0% - biosimilar erosion & IRA cuts -3.5% - debt paydown drag 1.0% + buybacks 0.5%]
column21: Multi-cycle biopharma financial treadmill: FY24 revenue of $33.4B (+19% YoY driven by Horizon acquisition; base product sales grew 7% on 23% volume growth offset by -2% net price erosion) and FY25 revenue of $36.8B (+10% on 13% volume growth offset by lower net realized prices). GAAP ROIC compressed to 9.7%-12.2% in FY23-FY24 following the $27.8B Horizon acquisition (invested capital expanded over $70B with heavy non-cash amortization) before rebounding to ~14.4% in FY25. Biosimilars continue to erode legacy assets, with Prolia/Xgeva ($4B+ sales) facing immediate loss of exclusivity in 2025-2026 from Sandoz, Samsung Bioepis, and Celltrion. Enbrel was selected in the initial IRA Medicare negotiation round (>50% price reduction from 2026), and Otezla was selected in 2025 triggering a $1.2B non-cash impairment. Total debt of $60.1B at year-end 2024 resulted in debt/EBITDA of ~4.5x and long-term debt/GAAP net income of 7.2x-15x.

column14: Proprietary biologic manufacturing and patent estate in neurology/neurodegenerative diseases fail to protect economic rents once exclusivity lapses. 5-year median GAAP ROIC compressed to ~7.4% (well below the 12% hurdle). The devastating loss of US patent exclusivity on blockbuster Tecfidera (dimethyl fumarate) caused sales to collapse from $4.4B peak to <$1B due to generic entry. Spinraza faces intense competing therapies (Evrysdi, Zolgensma), and Tysabri faces biosimilars. Inability to maintain pricing and margins across patent cycles proves absence of pricing power and structural moat durability.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Biogen's 5-year median GAAP ROIC has collapsed to ~7.4% (FY23 4.9%, FY24 7.4%, FY25 5.6%), trailing far below the 12% hurdle. Peak revenue collapsed from $14.4B in 2019 to ~$9.9B in 2025, and net income dropped >70% from $5.9B to ~$1.3B-$1.6B due to severe generic erosion of Tecfidera and MS franchise pressures. Patent cliffs represent the permanent structural treadmill of biopharma rather than a temporary fixable calamity, and new launches (Leqembi, Skyclarys) carry high co-commercialization and acquisition costs without restoring economic returns.
column21:
Historical Financials & Moat Erosion:
- Capital Efficiency: 10-year average ROIC is 11.2%, and 5-year median GAAP ROIC has degraded to ~7.4% (FY21: 13.2%, FY22: 14.7%, FY23: 4.9%, FY24: 7.4%, FY25: 5.6%), failing the 12% threshold.
- Top-line & Profit Contraction: Total revenue peaked at $14.4B in 2019 and declined by ~31% to $9.68B in 2024 and $9.9B in 2025. GAAP net income fell from $5.9B in 2019 to $1.6B in 2024 and $1.3B in 2025.
- Franchise Patent Cliffs: Tecfidera, which once generated $4.4B (~30% of sales), suffered patent invalidation in 2020 leading to generic competition that decimated sales. Core MS revenue continues secular decline.
- Pipeline & Capital Misallocation: The Aduhelm Alzheimer's saga resulted in commercial failure, regulatory backlash, CMS non-coverage, and full discontinuation/write-downs in 2024. Leqembi (partnered with Eisai) faces complex diagnostic/infusion hurdles and 50/50 profit splits. The $7.3B acquisition of Reata in 2023 for Skyclarys added debt without restoring enterprise ROIC above hurdle.

column14: Protected by proprietary antiviral patent estates (bictegravir, tenofovir alafenamide, lenacapavir) and high clinical switching friction in HIV treatment. However, fails Gate 3b: 5-year median GAAP ROIC (~11.1–11.4%) fails the 12% hurdle due to multi-billion dollar M&A write-downs ($8B+ acquired IPR&D and impairments in 2024 from CymaBay and Immunomedics/Trodelvy). Pricing power is structurally capped by statutory Medicaid/340B rebate formulas and mandatory Medicare IRA price negotiations on high-expenditure drugs.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Despite virology market leadership and robust gross margins (~77–80%), Gilead fails the 12% 5-year median GAAP ROIC hurdle (~11.1–11.4%) due to persistent capital misallocation and acquired IPR&D impairments in oncology M&A ($21B Immunomedics, $4.3B CymaBay). Over 70% of US HIV volume is exposed to government healthcare programs (Medicaid, 340B, Medicare Part D) where statutory price caps and IRA price negotiations eliminate real pricing power above inflation. Extreme concentration in Biktarvy (~$14.3B / ~49% of 2025 revenue) faces generic entry by April 2036.
column21: 1. Financial Track Record: Total revenue of $28.8B in 2024 and $29.4B in 2025. GAAP Net Income was $480M in 2024 (severely depressed by $8B+ in acquired IPR&D and impairments) and rebounded to $8.51B in 2025. GAAP ROIC was 11.2% (2019), 5.9% (2020), 14.7% (2021), 11.1% (2022), 11.4% (2023), 2.9% (2024), and 15.7% (2025). The 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~11.1–11.4%, strictly below the 12% threshold. 2. Segment Breakdown: HIV franchise generated ~$19.6B in 2025, driven by Biktarvy ($14.3B, up 7% YoY), Descovy (~$2.3B), and Genvoya (~$1.7B). Oncology delivered ~$3.3B (Trodelvy ~$1.3B, Yescarta/Tecartus cell therapies ~$2.0B). Liver diseases generated ~$2.8B. 3. Pricing Power & Regulatory Environment: Over 70% of US HIV volume is subject to statutory Medicaid 23.1% rebates, 340B mandatory ceiling prices, and ADAP discounts. The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) imposes inflation penalty rebates and introduces mandatory Medicare Part D price negotiations for top-selling single-source drugs, preventing above-inflation net price realization. 4. M&A & Capital Allocation: Over $30B spent on external oncology acquisitions to replace lost HCV revenues and diversify away from HIV (Immunomedics $21B in 2020, Forty Seven $4.9B in 2020, CymaBay $4.3B in 2024) has resulted in severe clinical trial setbacks (Trodelvy ASCENT-07 endpoint miss), massive goodwill/IPR&D impairments ($8B+ in 2024), and persistent return on capital dilution.

column14: Proprietary patent estate protecting JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib (Jakafi, Opzelura). High gross margins (~88%) and 10-year median ROIC of 12.1% (surging to >30% in FY2025 with $1.29B net income) demonstrate established historical pricing power and capital efficiency. Primary erosion threat is the impending late-2028 patent cliff on Jakafi and high pipeline clinical attrition.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Flagship JAK inhibitor Jakafi generates ~70% of total revenues ($3.62B of $5.14B in FY2025) and faces core patent expiration in late 2028. Biotechnology industry base-rate CAP is 10-15 years, and an unhedged patent cliff on the primary cash generator truncates predictable competitive advantage period to 5 years, well below the 15-year hurdle. Fast-growing Opzelura ($678M in FY2025) and early-stage pipeline are insufficient to offset catastrophic post-2028 generic erosion.
column21: Incyte's 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 12.1% with gross margins consistently between 85-89%. In FY2025, total revenue grew 21% to $5.14B with net product sales of $4.35B and net income of $1.29B (recovering sharply from FY2024's $32.6M net income that was depressed by the $750M Escient upfront IPR&D charge). Operating cash flow reached $1.41B in FY2025 with total cash and marketable securities of $3.6B and negligible debt. However, Jakafi generated $3.62B (70.4% of total revenue) and its primary U.S. patents expire in December 2028. Generic filers (e.g. Hikma settlement) will enter upon patent expiry, precipitating severe generic price and volume erosion. Opzelura reached $678M in FY2025, but non-Jakafi revenues are inadequate to bridge the post-2028 cash flow cliff.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Reject – G1 Understandability). Outside the one-off COVID-19 pandemic windfall (2021–2022), Moderna lacks an established, multi-cycle profitable commercial economic engine. Revenue collapsed by ~90% from a $19.3B peak in FY22 to $1.94B in FY25, generating cumulative net losses exceeding $11B across FY23–FY25 alongside continuous multi-billion cash burn. Its ongoing intrinsic valuation hinges on speculative, binary clinical trial readouts and regulatory clearances across an unproven developmental pipeline, placing it outside the Munger circle of competence.
column21: Multi-cycle financial collapse following the pandemic demand cliff: Revenues plummeted from $18.47B (FY21) and $19.26B (FY22) to $6.85B (FY23), $3.20B (FY24), and $1.94B (FY25). GAAP net losses totaled $(4.71B) in FY23, $(3.56B) in FY24, and $(2.82B) in FY25, with free cash flow of $(4.06B) in FY24 and $(2.07B) in FY25. Despite a seasonal Q3 2026 profit of $162M, full-year operations remain heavily loss-making. To support ongoing R&D cash burn, Moderna issued $2.6B in convertible debt in late 2026. Commercial products are currently limited to Spikevax and mRESVIA in saturated respiratory vaccine markets. The platform has not demonstrated self-sustaining commercial profitability outside government emergency pandemic procurement.

column14: Proprietary VelocImmune mouse genetics platform provides world-class antibody discovery and sustained high ROIC (10Y median ~18.4%), but commercial portfolio suffers from structural patent cliff vulnerability and lack of durable pricing power. Key blockbuster Eylea faces active biosimilar erosion (US franchise net sales fell from $5.97B in FY24 to $4.4B in FY25 despite Eylea HD conversion), and primary US patent on Dupixent expires in late 2027. Statutory IRA Medicare price negotiations, mandatory inflation rebates, and PBM formulary pressure prevent above-inflation pricing.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing, REJECT). While Regeneron is an elite biotechnology innovator powered by its proprietary VelocImmune engine, cash flows are concentrated in two mega-blockbusters subject to inevitable patent expiration: Eylea is actively suffering biosimilar price and volume erosion (US franchise sales down >25% in FY25), and Dupixent faces primary US composition patent expiration in late 2027. Biopharmaceutical commercialization lacks secular pricing power >= inflation due to irreversible patent cliffs, statutory Medicare price negotiation under the IRA, and PBM rebate pressure.
column21: Multi-cycle capital efficiency has been strong with a 10-year median ROIC of ~18.4% and substantial free cash flow ($3.66B in FY24, ~$4.1B in FY25; ~26% FCF margin). Balance sheet is a fortress with $18.8B+ in cash and marketable securities against $2.71B in total debt. However, FY25 revenue was flat at $14.3B (+1% YoY) as U.S. Eylea franchise sales contracted sharply from $5.97B in FY24 to $4.4B in FY25 due to biosimilar aflibercept launches (Pavblu, Yesafili), despite Eylea HD growth to $1.6B. Dupixent global sales ($17.8B in FY25 via Sanofi partnership) face US composition-of-matter patent expiration in October 2027 and EU expiration in 2029. Patent expiration permanently impairs unit drug economics and eliminates above-inflation pricing power, failing Gate 3b.

column14: Unassailable global monopoly in cystic fibrosis (CF) transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators (Trikafta/Kaftrio, Alyftrek). Decades of structural biology and medicinal chemistry patents protect the franchise through 2037 (Trikafta) and 2039+ (vanzacaftor triple). Inelastic pricing power demonstrated by universal Western reimbursement at ~$300k+/patient/year with zero clinical churn. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 59.6% and operating ROIC of 90.5% provide empirical proof of moat. Primary long-term erosion risk is eventual 2037+ patent expirations and nascent genetic curative therapies.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Unrivaled biopharmaceutical monopoly in cystic fibrosis with patent protection extending into late 2030s, complemented by pipeline expansion into non-opioid pain (Suzetrigine) and gene-edited cell therapies (Casgevy). Debt-free fortress balance sheet with >$5B in cash and marketable securities and 50%+ normalized ROIC. [5-10Y g: CF global patient penetration 3.0% + Alyftrek vanzacaftor upgrade 2.0% + Suzetrigine pain launch 2.5% - R&D reinvestment drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 10-year financial record demonstrates extraordinary compounding: revenue expanded from $1.7B in 2016 to $12.0B in 2025, with operating EBIT rising from $10M to $4.17B. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 59.64% with tangible ROIC of 90.48%. FCF conversion exceeds 80% over multi-year cycles (2025 FCF of $3.19B vs Net Income of $3.95B; 2024 dip was driven solely by a one-off non-deductible $4.4B AIPR&D accounting charge for the Alpine Immune Sciences acquisition). Peak Owner EPS reached a new high of $15.32 in FY2025. Balance sheet carries zero long-term funded debt ($0.0M) and over $5.08B in cash and marketable securities. Commercial CFTR treatments face zero direct competition across ~90% of addressable CF patients globally.

column14: RNAi platform pioneer with proprietary GalNAc-siRNA delivery conjugates and dominant global patent estate across rare genetic diseases (hATTR, AHP, PH1) and cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM). Commercial pricing power is extraordinary ($300k-$500k/patient/yr) with gross margins >85%. FY2025 HELIOS-B expansion validated platform economics as revenues surged 81% to $3.71B and GAAP net income turned positive to $313.7M. Moat erosion threats include patent cliffs in the 2030s (~2035) and competing oral/gene-editing modalities.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Alnylam's RNAi platform achieved commercial profitability in FY2025 following the landmark HELIOS-B ATTR-CM expansion, biotechnology has an empirical base-rate persistence of only 10-15 years (Tier 3). Crucially, the franchise faces an active terminal disruption headwind from one-time curative in vivo CRISPR gene editing (Intellia/Regeneron NTLA-2001 Phase 3 MAGNITUDE trial) which permanently eliminates hepatic TTR production, threatening to render chronic lifelong quarterly RNAi injections obsolete. Compounding patent expirations in ~2035 and oral small-molecule competition (BridgeBio Attruby) cap CAP at 5 years (< 15 hurdle).
column21: Over 2016-2024, Alnylam posted continuous GAAP net losses (peaking at -$1,131M in FY2022 and -$278M in FY2024) with negative 5-year median GAAP ROIC (-65.9% to -100%) due to massive clinical development expenses. In FY2025, commercial uptake of Amvuttra (vutrisiran) following the HELIOS-B Phase 3 trial and FDA approval for ATTR-CM drove an 81% surge in net product revenue to $2.99B and total revenue to $3.71B, delivering its first annual GAAP net income of $313.7M and operating profit (EBIT) of $501.6M. Cash stood at $1,657.2M against ~$1.0B in convertible debt. Extreme orphan drug pricing power ($300k-$500k/patient/year) yields gross margins >85%. However, structural biotechnology runway is tightly constrained: primary composition of matter patents expire around 2035, oral competitors like BridgeBio's acoramidis are expanding, and one-time in vivo CRISPR gene editing therapies (NTLA-2001) threaten to permanently displace chronic quarterly RNAi maintenance therapy.

column14: Oligopolistic distribution scale alongside McKesson and Cencora, handling ~25% of US pharmaceutical volume. However, CAH is a pure pass-through logistics intermediary with razor-thin operating margins (~1.0%) and zero unconstrained pricing power over either upstream branded drug manufacturers (who set WAC prices) or consolidated downstream PBMs/health systems. Demonstrated by the 2024 loss of the OptumRx contract (16% of sales, ~$33B) during competitive RFP rebidding. Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC is sub-hurdle and severely impaired by $6B+ in opioid litigation liabilities, with persistent negative book equity (-$2.9B in FY2025).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). Thin-margin (~1% operating margin) wholesale drug distributor operating as a pass-through intermediary between pharma manufacturers and consolidated PBMs/retailers. Possesses zero unconstrained pricing power; demonstrated by customer churn when OptumRx (16% of sales) defected to McKesson in 2024. Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC is severely impaired by $6B+ opioid litigation liabilities and negative book equity (-$2.9B in FY2025), failing the Munger capital-efficiency standard.
column21: CAH operates in a tight oligopoly alongside McKesson and Cencora (controlling 90%+ of US prescription drug distribution) with FY2025 revenue of $254.2B, but operating margins remain microscopic at 1.03% ($2,613M EBIT) and gross margins are ~3.2%. Upstream branded drug prices are fixed by manufacturers, while downstream PBMs and retail pharmacy chains exert severe pricing pressure; in FY2024, CAH lost its contract with OptumRx (~$33B / 16% of revenue) to McKesson during renewal bidding. Historical GAAP ROIC has been deeply negative in crisis years (FY2019: -46.8%, FY2021: -31.4%) driven by $6B+ in opioid litigation liabilities, and book equity remains negative (-$2,883M in FY2025) with negative tangible equity of -$16.5B against $7.0B in long-term debt. Even with OptiFreight logistics and specialty distribution growth, CAH is structurally a low-margin commodity logistics provider lacking pricing power >= inflation.

column14: Rational 90%+ US drug distribution oligopoly protected by irreplaceable physical cold-chain logistics, regulatory licenses, and deep workflow integration with health systems and community oncology. Fee-for-service contracts and specialty distribution protect real gross profit, sustaining multi-cycle GAAP ROIC well above 50%.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Indispensable US pharmaceutical distribution oligopolist handling ~one-third of domestic prescription volume with leading oncology and specialty franchises. Formidable moat rooted in physical cold-chain logistics, deep provider integration, and high switching costs. Resilient across all 5 macrotrends with demographic aging as a durable volume tailwind. Exceptional FCF conversion (>150%) and conservative net debt (<2.1x net income). [5-10Y g: rx/specialty volume 4.5% + specialty mix/acquisitions 1.5% - wholesale contract repricing drag 0.5% + share repurchases 2.5%]
column21: FY2025 revenue reached $321.3B with EBIT of $2.63B and Owner FCF of $3.06B, delivering FCF conversion of 167.5% of net income. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 97.0% (operating ROIC >100%) due to rapid working capital turns and fee-for-service / specialty contracts. Oligopolistic market structure (>90% controlled by Cencora, McKesson, and Cardinal Health) prevents price wars. High-margin specialty leadership reinforced by Retina Consultants of America ($4.4B cash outlay) and OneOncology integration. Balance sheet carries $4.36B cash against $7.54B debt, yielding net debt of $3.19B (~1.0x Owner FCF), with the core Walgreens prime vendor agreement secured through 2029.

column14: Henry Schein benefits from switching costs in its proprietary practice management software (Dentrix, Dentrix Ascend) and significant scale in dental/medical distribution logistics. However, its economic moat has been structurally eroded by rapid consolidation of dental practices into corporate Dental Support Organizations (DSOs) wielding intense pricing leverage, alongside transparent online e-commerce competition and peer rivalry (Patterson, Benco). Operating margins have collapsed from ~7.2% in FY2019 to ~4.95% in FY2025. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 9.78%, well below the 12% hurdle, with FY2023-FY2025 hovering at 8.9%-9.8% even after full cyber incident normalization, proving lack of real pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 9.78% < 12%, lack of pricing power >= inflation, REJECT). While Henry Schein maintains established scale in dental distribution and practice software (Dentrix), structural consolidation of solo dentists into corporate Dental Support Organizations (DSOs) has shifted purchasing leverage upstream, compressing GAAP operating margins from ~7.2% (2019) to ~4.95% (2025). The sub-10% GAAP ROIC persists beyond the temporary late-2023 cyberattack, driven by $4B+ of debt-funded M&A that diluted capital returns ($5.2B goodwill/intangibles vs. $3.2B equity, $2.3B debt). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS has stagnated below 2019/2021 levels ($4.68 in FY2025 vs. $5.38 in FY2019), failing the Munger moat and pricing power standard.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates structural capital efficiency erosion: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 9.78%, failing the 12% threshold (FY2021: 17.14%, FY2022: 13.43%, FY2023: 9.78%, FY2024: 8.86%, FY2025: 9.50%). Operating margins compressed from 7.19% in FY2019 and 6.87% in FY2021 to 4.98% in FY2023, 4.90% in FY2024, and 4.95% in FY2025 on $13.18B revenue. Although the October 2023 BlackCat cyberattack caused operational disruption, operations normalized in 2024-2025 with $20M insurance recovery in Q1 2025, yet normalized ROIC remains under 10%. Balance sheet has deteriorated from serial M&A: LT debt expanded from $822M in 2021 to $2,310M in FY2025 (LT debt / Net Income of 5.8x; interest expense rose from $27M to $150M, lowering interest coverage to 4.35x), with $5,231M in goodwill and intangibles on $3,245M equity. Peak owner EPS has failed to compound ($4.68 in FY2025 vs. $5.38 in FY2019). Activist pressure from Ananym Capital and a $250M white-knight injection from KKR underscore ongoing structural governance and margin challenges under DSO buyer concentration.

column14: Co-leads the indispensable 90%+ US pharmaceutical distribution oligopoly (~33% share) alongside Cencora and Cardinal Health, augmented by The US Oncology Network (2,600+ providers). Operating model functions as a vital toll booth with fee-for-service contracts and proprietary workflow integration (iKnowMed EHR) creating high switching costs. Empirical proof: Operating ROIC sustainably >50-100% on negative operating working capital, EBIT doubled from $2.49B (FY19) to $6.21B (FY25), and operating margins expanded despite massive throughput. Primary erosion threats: Regulatory scrutiny over oncology practice consolidation, PBM contract disputes, and biosimilar margin compression.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Essential co-leader of the US drug distribution oligopoly and dominant community oncology platform. Insulated from AI disruption and demographic aging acts as a powerful secular volume tailwind. Exemplary capital allocation under CEO Brian Tyler: pruned lower-margin European operations, settled opioid litigation, and retired ~50% of outstanding shares since FY16. Outstanding cash conversion (FCF/NI >130% 5Y average) and pristine balance sheet with 25x interest coverage and net debt of just 0.54x net income; negative book equity is purely an artifact of FCF-funded share buybacks and non-cash litigation charges. [5-10Y g: US pharma/specialty volume 4.0% + oncology/biopharma mix 2.0% + manufacturer fee price 1.0% - regulatory/biosimilar margin drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 3.0%]
column21: FY16-FY25 revenue expanded from $198.5B to $403.4B with FY25 EBIT reaching $6.21B and Net Income of $4.76B. Exceptional cash generation with FY25 Owner FCF of $5.47B (FCF conversion 115% in FY25, 5Y average >130%) on minimal capex requirements ($436M, ~0.1% of sales). Diluted share count reduced from ~230M in FY16 to ~116M in FY25, propelling Owner EPS from $25.00 (FY16 peak) and $8.04 (FY19) to $40.73 in FY25 (10Y CAGR 10.3%, 5Y CAGR >25%). Balance sheet is exceptionally robust with $3.98B cash against $6.53B total debt, yielding net debt of $2.55B (0.54x Net Income) and EBIT/interest coverage of 25.1x ($6.21B EBIT vs $247M interest expense). Nationwide opioid settlement is fully accrued with structured payout obligations easily absorbed by annual operating cash flows exceeding $6B.

column14: Abbott's economic moat rests on high customer switching barriers and consumable toll-booth dynamics across Medical Devices and Diagnostics. FreeStyle Libre commands >50% global CGM patient volume with >8 million active users purchasing recurring bi-weekly sensor replacements at >70% gross margins. In Diagnostics, closed-loop Alinity/Architect analyzers lock hospital laboratories into proprietary multi-year reagent consumable contracts. Structural heart franchises (MitraClip, TriClip, Navitor) benefit from extensive clinician procedural training and high switching costs. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 12.8%, tangible operating ROIC >25-50%, gross margins consistently 55-57%, and FCF conversion of 80.6%. Primary erosion risks include competitive encroachment from Dexcom in CGM, GLP-1 therapy penetration moderating intensive diabetes therapies, and preterm infant formula product liability claims.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global diversified medtech and healthcare leader anchored by the FreeStyle Libre CGM franchise, structural heart devices, closed-loop diagnostic lab analyzers, and leading pediatric/adult nutrition brands. Highly insulated from AI disruption and a prime secular beneficiary of global demographic aging. Fortress balance sheet with net debt of just $1.4B (0.2x net income) and 16.3x interest coverage; $670M NEC infant formula settlement is comfortably absorbed by normal cash flow. [5-10Y g: FreeStyle Libre & medtech device volume 5.5% + diagnostic & nutrition pricing 1.5% + emerging markets pharma mix 1.0% - margin/litigation drag 0.5% + share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: Abbott generates >$44B in diversified revenue across Medical Devices ($17B+, led by $7.6B Libre CGM and structural heart), Diagnostics ($9B+ core lab/point-of-care), Nutrition ($8B+ Similac/Ensure), and Established Pharmaceuticals ($5B+ branded generics). Capital efficiency is verified by a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 12.8% and tangible operating ROIC of 53.3%. Free cash flow conversion averages 80.6% ($6.7B FCF in FY2025 on $6.5B Net Income). De-leveraging discipline is exemplary: debt reduced from $27.2B post-St. Jude in 2017 to $9.9B in FY2025, offset by $8.5B in cash (net debt $1.4B vs. $8.1B EBIT; interest coverage 16.3x). 52 consecutive years of dividend increases (Dividend King). Post-COVID testing normalization is complete, with organic core device and diagnostic volumes resuming high-single-digit peak-to-peak earnings expansion.

column14: Infusion pump installed bases (Spectrum, Novum IQ) provide modest switching costs via proprietary tubing sets and drug libraries, but the moat is structurally weak. Large-volume IV solutions, basic hospital consumables, and generic injectables are commoditized price-taker categories sold under multi-year fixed-price GPO contracts (Vizient, Premier). 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.5%, well below the 12% hurdle. Massive value destruction from the $12.4B debt-financed Hillrom acquisition ($3B+ goodwill impairment) and persistent FDA recalls confirm lack of pricing power and moat erosion against Becton Dickinson and ICU Medical.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & No Pricing Power, REJECT). 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~6.5% falls far short of the 12% hurdle. Infusion pump switching costs are overwhelmed by commoditized IV solutions and hospital consumables sold under fixed-price GPO contracts that lack inflation pass-through power. Value-destructive capital allocation in the $12.4B debt-funded Hillrom acquisition and subsequent $3B+ impairment cement sub-hurdle returns.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 6.5%. ROIC collapsed across 2020-2025 (2020: 9.0%, 2021: 3.5%, 2022: -8.5%, 2023: 2.3%, 2024: ~0.0%, 2025: -1.4%) driven by persistent margin compression from plastic/resin/freight inflation, FDA infusion pump recalls (Spectrum/Novum IQ), and a $3.1B goodwill impairment on Hillrom. Management acquired Hillrom in late 2021 for $12.4B enterprise value funded with >$11B of debt at cyclical peak, triggering severe leverage that forced the divestiture of its Kidney Care unit (Vantive) to Carlyle in January 2025 for $3.8B ($3.3B net cash) to pay down debt. Fragile supply chain highlighted by Hurricane Helene flooding its Marion, NC plant in late 2024, halting 60% of US IV fluid production.

column14: BDX possesses extensive manufacturing scale in high-volume clinical consumables (syringes, needles, vacutainers, IV catheters) and installed infusion pump hardware. However, it fails proof of moat: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 5.45% (10-year range 2.0%-7.7%), well below the 12% hurdle. Dilutive mega-acquisitions (CareFusion $12.2B, C.R. Bard $24B, and Edwards Lifesciences Critical Care $4.2B) loaded the balance sheet with $36.0B in goodwill and intangibles on $25.4B of equity (negative tangible equity of -$10.6B). Pricing power is heavily constrained by hospital Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs like Vizient, Premier) running competitive tenders on commoditized consumables. Moreover, chronic Alaris pump quality issues (2020-2023 FDA shipping hold, 2025 legacy bezel recall, 2026 Class I infusion set recall) have triggered pricing concessions and customer friction.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 5.45%, REJECT). Serial debt-funded mega-acquisitions (CareFusion, Bard, Edwards Critical Care) permanently burdened the capital base with $36B of goodwill and intangibles, suppressing GAAP ROIC to 2.0%-5.6% for eight consecutive years. Hospital GPO tender procurement caps pricing power on basic consumables, while multi-year Alaris infusion system Class I recalls erode commercial contracting leverage.
column21: 10-year financial history demonstrates chronic sub-hurdle returns on capital: GAAP ROIC was 7.71% in 2016, 7.06% in 2017, 4.24% in 2018, 3.59% in 2019, 2.02% in 2020, 5.56% in 2021, 5.46% in 2022, 5.03% in 2023, 5.02% in 2024, and 5.45% in 2025 (5-year median 5.45%, never exceeding 6% post-2017). As of FY2025, Goodwill and Intangibles stand at $36,001M against Total Equity of $25,390M, resulting in negative tangible equity of -$10,611M. Long-term debt of $17,621M represents 10.5x net income ($1,678M), exacerbated by $3.2B of new debt taken in 2024 to fund the $4.2B Edwards Lifesciences Critical Care acquisition. While FCF conversion is healthy (133% in FY2025) and operating cash flow reached $3,430M, the capital-diluted balance sheet and hospital GPO tender resistance prevent compounding at attractive economic rates.

column14: High physician switching barriers and clinical procedural lock-in across catheter labs and operating rooms. Interventional cardiologists and electrophysiologists train extensively on Boston Scientific's proprietary hardware consoles and delivery platforms (Farapulse PFA generator, Watchman TruSpeed/FLX Pro LAAC delivery systems, SpyGlass DS direct visualization endoscopy). Once integrated into hospital workflows, treatment protocols, and inventory supply chains, switching to alternative platforms incurs severe capital re-equipment hurdles, clinical retraining, and staff re-credentialing. Proof of moat is reflected in 28.2% 5-year median operating (tangible) ROIC (reaching 42.1% in FY2025) and stable ~70% gross margins. Primary erosion threats stem from fast-follower PFA launches by Medtronic (PulseSelect/Affera), Abbott (Volt), and J&J (Varipulse), as well as clinical shifts in concomitant procedure scheduling.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global cardiovascular and interventional medtech leader anchored by Farapulse PFA, Watchman LAAC, and single-use endoscopy. Procedural switching costs and clinical training create durable lock-in, driving ~70% gross margins and >28% operating ROIC. Structural beneficiary of demographic aging with resilient 113% FCF conversion and 10.4x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: procedure volume growth 5.5% + premium innovation mix/price 1.5% + Axonics/tuck-in expansion 1.0% - PFA competition/pricing drag 0.5% + operating leverage/buybacks 0.5%]
column21: Multi-cycle track record of durable growth and operating leverage: Net sales expanded from $9,076M in FY2016 to $20,074M in FY2025 (~9.2% CAGR), with FY2025 organic growth reaching ~15.8% powered by Farapulse PFA scaling to over $1B in its first commercial year. GAAP EBIT expanded from $447M in 2016 to $3,613M in 2025, lifting operating margins from ~5% to 18.0% GAAP and operating (tangible) ROIC to 42.1% in FY2025 (5-year median 28.2%). Gross margins remain consistently defended at ~70.5%. Cash generation is exceptional, with Owner FCF conversion averaging well above 100% of GAAP Net Income (FY2025 Owner FCF of $3,359M on $2,892M NI = 116%; TTM conversion 113.2%). Balance sheet remains sound: Net debt of $9.17B against TTM NI of $2.89B equates to 3.17 years of earnings (<= 4.0x threshold), and EBIT/Interest coverage is 10.35x ($3,613M / $349M). S&P affirms A- investment grade rating. Tuck-in capital allocation demonstrated by successful Axonics integration ($3.7B, closed Nov 2024) in sacral neuromodulation. Normalization of growth to 5-6% in 2026 reflects competitive PFA entrants (MDT, ABT) and transient operational disruption from a late-August 2026 cyber incident, but the core procedural lock-in remains structurally intact.

column14: Proprietary enzymatic sensor chemistry, micro-filament wire technology, FDA iCGM clearance, and tight automated insulin delivery (AID) pump integration (Tandem, Insulet) provide a defensible technological barrier. However, the moat is severely undermined by head-to-head competition with Abbott Laboratories (FreeStyle Libre), persistent 5-8%/year per-patient net ASP deflation from PBM retail pharmacy rebate concessions, and margin dilution from lower-priced over-the-counter lines (Stelo).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). Single-product continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) specialist operates in an intense duopoly against Abbott Laboratories (FreeStyle Libre). Dexcom lacks pricing power >= inflation: realized revenue per patient faces persistent structural annual ASP deflation driven by retail pharmacy channel rebate concessions, aggressive Abbott price competition, and lower-priced OTC expansion (Stelo). Volume growth cannot mask the structural absence of pricing power required by Munger's standard.
column21: Revenue grew from $1.93B in FY2020 to $4.03B in FY2024 and $4.66B in FY2025 driven by unit volume expansion, but GAAP gross margins compressed from ~68% in 2021 to 60.1% in 2025 due to manufacturing transition costs and pharmacy channel mix shift. Realized per-patient revenue has fallen from >$3,500/yr in legacy DME channels to <$2,000/yr in retail pharmacy and ~$1,000/yr for Stelo OTC. In Q2 2024, unexpected rebate concessions to secure pharmacy formulary placement and DME market share losses forced a major full-year guidance cut, triggering a >40% stock plunge. Dexcom cannot raise prices at or above inflation without immediately hemorrhaging market share to Abbott Libre.

column14: ~78% gross margins and ~28% EBIT margins sustained across cycles via RESILIA tissue durability premium pricing, decade-long PARTNER clinical trial moats, and interventional cardiologist switching costs. Primary threat is Medtronic/Boston Scientific competition in mature TAVR and hospital DRG reimbursement pressure.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global category king in transcatheter heart valve therapies with >60% global TAVR share and pioneer status in tricuspid/mitral transcatheter replacement (EVOQUE, PASCAL). Divestiture of Critical Care to BDX for $4.2B cash sharpened pure-play focus on structural heart. Insulated from macro disruptions with massive demographic aging tailwind. Pristine balance sheet with $2.3B+ net cash and 62x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: TAVR procedure volume 5.5% + TMTT portfolio expansion 2.5% + RESILIA pricing/mix 0.5% - clinical trial R&D drag 0.5% + share buybacks 1.0%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 19.8% and tangible operating ROIC of 27.1%. FY2025 net sales reached $6.07B (+11.5% YoY) with gross margins sustained at 78-79%. Cash conversion normalized post-divestiture with FY2025 Owner FCF of $1.28B converting at 119% of GAAP net income ($1.07B). Net cash of $2.34B ($2.94B cash vs. $598M debt) with 62x interest coverage ($1,264M EBIT / $20.4M interest). TAVR retains ~75% US and >60% global market share supported by PARTNER 1-3 and EARLY TAVR trials; TMTT segment grew >40% in 2024-2025 propelled by FDA approval of Evoque and Pascal Precision.

column14: Massive global installed base of over 4 million medical imaging, ultrasound, and patient care systems creates high switching costs in service contracts and clinical workflow integrations. However, 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 11.5% (failing the >=12% hurdle), and post-spin 2023-2025 ROIC hovers between 7.5% and 10.5%. Core imaging operating margins (~10-13%) structurally lag Siemens Healthineers (>21%), reflecting lower pricing power against hospital GPOs and fixed-price contract inflation risk.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 11.5% < 12%, REJECT). While GE HealthCare maintains an indispensable global installed base of >4M diagnostic systems and sticky recurring service revenue, its 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 11.5% (and 2023-2025 ROIC of 7.5-10.5%) fails the 12% Munger capital hurdle. Core imaging EBIT margins (~10-13%) structurally lag Siemens Healthineers (>21%), and hospital GPO bargaining power plus fixed-price equipment backlogs restrict pricing power relative to inflation.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 11.5%, with post-spin 2023-2025 GAAP Net Income of $1,614M, $2,050M, and $2,154M delivering GAAP ROIC between 7.5% and 10.5%, below the 12% hurdle. Total adjusted EBIT margins sit at 15.3-16.3%, with core Imaging operating profitability lagging Siemens Healthineers' Imaging margin (>21-25%). The business carries approximately $10.0B-$10.5B in total debt and legacy liabilities from its 2023 GE spin-off, resulting in Long-Term Debt / Net Income of ~4.6-4.9x. While recurring service and consumable contracts generate steady cash flow, hospital capital equipment spending is subjected to aggressive GPO procurement and fixed-price backlog commitments, leaving insufficient pricing power to earn super-normal returns on invested capital.

column14: Closed-loop proprietary consumables, clinic workflow integration, and integrated reference lab software create 97%+ customer retention. 10-year GAAP ROIC consistently 53-97% (5-yr median 61.2%) with EBIT margins >31%. Consistent 4-5% net annual price increases executed with negligible churn in a cash-pay market. Key risk is corporate vet clinic consolidation.
column20: Dominant global veterinary diagnostics leader with a captive installed base of point-of-care analyzers generating ~80% recurring consumable and reference lab revenues. Unassailable switching costs backed by 97%+ customer retention and consistent 4-5% net annual price realization in a cash-pay animal health market free from reimbursement caps. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends with labor-saving clinical automation. Fortress balance sheet with net debt under 0.2x Net Income and 35x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: vet diagnostic testing volume 4.5% + net pricing 3.5% + menu innovation/inVue mix 1.5% - margin drags 0.0% + share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 61.2% and operating ROIC of 89.1%. Revenue grew from $1.78B (2016) to $4.30B (2025) with EBIT margins expanding from 19.7% to 31.6%. Free cash flow conversion consistently exceeds 82% of net income ($997M Owner FCF in FY2025 vs $125M capex). Global installed base of premium chemistry and hematology instruments drives recurring diagnostic consumables, rapid assays, and cloud software (VetConnect PLUS) with >97% customer retention. Pricing power proven by 4-5% annual price increases with near-zero churn. Net debt of $195M is repayable in ~2 months of Owner FCF, with EBIT interest coverage of 35x. Diluted share count systematically reduced via disciplined FCF buybacks.

column14: Insurmountable surgeon cognitive training lock-in originating in medical residencies and fellowships, reinforced by 4,000+ patents and tens of millions of historical procedures. High-margin razor-and-blade toll booth extracts ~$1,860+ in proprietary instruments per procedure with 83-85% recurring revenue. 10Y median ROIC of 16.5% and 68% gross margin confirm strong pricing power. Primary erosion risks (Medtronic Hugo, J&J Ottava, hospital capex budgets) are mitigated by unmatched clinical data, switching friction, and the da Vinci 5 technology leap.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global robotic-assisted surgery monopoly with an insurmountable ecosystem moat built on residency surgeon training, 4,000+ patents, and an 83-85% recurring revenue razor-and-blade model (~$1,860+ per procedure in proprietary instruments). Multi-year da Vinci 5 supercycle driving system placements, utilization, and Force Feedback adoption. Pristine balance sheet with zero debt and >$8B in total cash and investments. [5-10Y g: procedure volume 10.5% + da Vinci 5/Force Feedback price 1.5% + Ion/SP mix 1.0% - international expansion SG&A drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: 10-year GAAP ROIC median of 16.5% (Operating ROIC 17.1%) maintained consistently above 12% across economic cycles and pandemic elective surgery disruptions. Gross margins steady at 66-70% and GAAP operating margins >28%. 10-year cumulative operating cash flow of $17.3B converts to $12.5B in free cash flow (83.7% multi-year FCF/Net Income conversion), with 2022-2024 capex bubble ($1.1B/yr) normalizing to $540M in 2025 as major Sunnyvale/Mexicali DV5 manufacturing facilities reached completion. Razor-and-blade model generates >83% recurring revenue from single-use EndoWrist/Force Feedback instruments and annual service contracts. Gary Guthart's engineering-focused stewardship has compounded Owner EPS at 16.0% CAGR (2016-2025: $2.19 to $8.08) while maintaining zero long-term debt and accumulating >$8B in cash and investments.

column14: Moat derives from high surgeon switching costs, deep clinical training familiarity, extensive IP portfolios, and rigorous FDA PMA regulatory hurdles in cardiac rhythm management, spine, and neuromodulation. However, quantitative proof of moat is lacking: 5-year median GAAP ROIC has hovered in the 5-7% range (10-year median 9.2%), deeply diluted by $41B+ in unamortized goodwill from the 2015 Covidien acquisition. Gross and operating margins compressed under post-2021 inflation (operating margin fell from 21%+ to ~17-19%) due to an inability to pass cost increases through hospital GPO contracts. Primary ongoing erosion threats include persistent 1-3% annual ASP deflation imposed by hospital GPOs and government reimbursement authorities, intensifying competition from focused peers (Boston Scientific, Abbott, Stryker), and product quality/FDA recall setbacks.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Bureaucratized medtech conglomerate burdened by the $42.9B Covidien acquisition, carrying over $41B in goodwill that structurally caps multi-cycle GAAP ROIC at 5-7%, far below the 12% threshold. Hospital GPO purchasing power and national healthcare reimbursement limits impose persistent 1-3% net price deflation, leaving Medtronic with negative real pricing power and stagnant 10-year real per-share earnings.
column21: Medtronic (MDT) generated $32.4B revenue in FY24 and $33.5B in FY25 across Cardiovascular, Medical Surgical, Neuroscience, and Diabetes. Despite leading market shares in cardiac rhythm management and spine devices, GAAP ROIC has hovered at 5.0%-7.1% over the past 5 years (FY23: ~5.5%, FY24: ~5.1%, FY25: ~6.2%; 10-year median 9.2%), severely diluted by $41.7B in goodwill from the 2015 Covidien acquisition (over 45% of total assets). GAAP operating margins fell from 21%+ pre-2020 to 17.1% in FY24 and 19.5% in FY25 under cost inflation, demonstrating inability to pass cost increases through hospital GPO fixed-price contracts. While FCF remains solid ($5.2B in FY24 and FY25) and debt is manageable ($25B long-term debt against $4.7B net income), the business structurally fails Gate 3b capital efficiency and pricing power hurdles without any temporary fixable calamity.

column14: Consumable 72-hour tubeless insulin pod model distributed via retail pharmacy channels; patients lock into automated algorithms and continuous CGM integration. Moat proved by 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 16.55% (rising to 21.0% in 2025) and stable gross margins near 68%. Primary erosion threats include patent expirations, commoditization of patch hardware (CAFC overturned EOFlow trade secret injunction in 2026), and low switching costs compared to durable medical equipment.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Insulet's Omnipod 5 currently dominates the tubeless insulin pump segment and expanded into Type 2 diabetes in late 2024, the business faces severe 10-15+ year runway constraints. Over a 15-year horizon, mechanical insulin delivery faces existential technological substitution from biological cures (e.g. Vertex VX-880/VX-264 stem cell-derived islet therapies achieving insulin independence) and incretin/GLP-1 multi-agonists reducing insulin dependency in T2D. Furthermore, patch pump hardware faces accelerating commoditization following core patent expirations, the 2026 CAFC reversal of Insulet's trade secret injunction against EOFlow, and competing offerings from Tandem (Mobi/Sigi) and Medtronic. Because Omnipod is dispensed on a 30-day pharmacy model without 4-year DME lock-in, patient switching friction is low.
column21: Historical financials show long gestation before profitability: GAAP ROIC was negative to sub-5% from 2016 to 2022, only expanding to 16.56% (2023), 16.55% (2024), and 21.00% (2025) as Omnipod 5 scaled. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 16.55% and tangible ROIC median is 18.43%. Free cash flow conversion is structurally constrained (5-year fcf_conv = 0.6447, below 80%) due to heavy continuous capex required for automated pod assembly lines ($191.6M TTM capex, $200M Malaysia plant opened in 2024) to produce disposable 3-day pods. Balance sheet carries $930.8M LT debt vs $716.1M cash (net debt $214.7M) with interest coverage of ~8.0x. Single-product concentration (>95% Omnipod) leaves the company highly exposed to long-term MedTech/biologic substitution.

column14: Dominant global sleep apnea toll booth (~70% global share, >90% US share post-Philips recall) protected by AirView (>28M connected devices) and Brightree SaaS deeply embedded in HME clinical and billing workflows. Razor-and-blade model locks in high-margin recurring mask and accessory resupply. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 22.9% (27.4% in FY25) and gross margins expanding to 59.4% prove formidable pricing power well above medical inflation.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Undisputed global leader in sleep-disordered breathing with ~70% global share and razor-and-blade consumable resupply lock-in. Real-world 2025-2026 data shows GLP-1 therapies act as a diagnostic funnel (+11% CPAP initiation) rather than a replacement, with sleep medicine adopting multimodal standards. Balance sheet fortress with >$1.07B net cash and 88.8% FCF conversion. [5-10Y g: patient diagnosis & device/mask volume 5.5% + price/product mix 1.5% + software/reinvestment 0.5% - competitive/freight drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 22.91% expanding to 27.39% in FY2025 ($1.89B EBIT on $5.65B revenue); tangible ROIC of 50-74%. GAAP gross margins expanded 270 bps to 59.4% (60.0% non-GAAP). Multi-year Owner FCF conversion of 88.8% ($1.55B Owner FCF vs $156M capex in FY25). Pristine balance sheet with $1.47B cash against $399M LT debt (net cash $1.07B; zero net interest expense). 9-year Owner EPS CAGR of 18.1% ($2.75 in FY16 to $10.74 in FY25) with zero cycle dips. Real-world IQVIA/claims studies of >2.5M patients confirm GLP-1 users have 10.8 percentage point higher CPAP initiation and superior resupply adherence, invalidating terminal obsolescence thesis.

column14: High switching costs in newborn screening diagnostics (>60% global market share) and proprietary life science antibodies/reagents (BioLegend) embedded in clinical and lab protocols. However, the business structurally fails proof of moat: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.5%, and FY23-FY25 GAAP ROIC languishes at 3.6%-4.5% due to an insurmountable ~$6.6B goodwill/intangibles load from the peak-bubble $5.25B BioLegend acquisition in 2021. Primary erosion threats include China Volume-Based Procurement (VBP) mandatory price cuts and persistent biopharma R&D spending headwinds preventing pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Revvity possesses entrenched niche franchises in newborn screening and BioLegend research reagents, but structurally fails the Munger quality hurdle with a 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 8.5% and FY23–25 ROIC of only 3.6%–4.5%. The $5.25B acquisition of BioLegend at the 2021 valuation peak saddled the balance sheet with >$6.5B in goodwill, permanently suppressing returns on capital. Furthermore, government-mandated price cuts under China Volume-Based Procurement (forcing the divestiture of China immunodiagnostics) and biopharma destocking reflect an inability to consistently pass through price increases above inflation across the cycle.
column21: 10-year historical median ROIC is 8.5%, well below the 12% threshold. Post-divestiture/rebranding revenue was $2.755B in FY24 and $2.856B in FY25. FY25 GAAP Diluted EPS was $2.07 ($2.20 in FY24), yielding net income of ~$250M-$260M against invested capital of ~$9.7B ($7.3B equity + $3.4B debt - $1.0B cash), resulting in GAAP ROIC of ~3.6%-4.5%. In FY25, RVTY recognized a $700.7M goodwill impairment charge across EMEA, China, and Latin America units, leaving $6.61B in goodwill on the balance sheet. China VBP price compression and biopharma budgetary pressures have constrained top-line growth and margin expansion.

column14: High regulatory switching costs on FDA-validated device contract sterilization (AST) and closed-loop hospital sterile processing consumables enable consistent 2-3%+ annual price increases across cycles. Tangible ROIC >25-32% proves moat despite non-cash goodwill/PPA amortization.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global infection-prevention and contract device sterilization duopoly/toll booth with ~80% recurring revenue across hospital consumables, AST contract processing, and service agreements. High regulatory switching costs (FDA-validated sterilization protocols) and closed-loop hospital SPD workflows protect durable pricing power (2-3% annual price increases). Tangible ROIC >25-32% demonstrates true underlying capital efficiency masked at GAAP level by Cantel PPA amortization. Balance sheet de-levered to 1.5x Net Debt/Owner FCF and 18x interest coverage post-HuFriedy dental divestiture. [5-10Y g: surgical & AST procedural volume 4.0% + pricing power 2.5% + high-margin AST/bioprocessing mix 1.0% - EPA regulatory/labor cost drag 0.5% + capital return & bolt-ons 1.5%]
column21: 10-year tangible ROIC averaged 25-45% (FY2025 tangible ROIC 32.1%, operating ROIC 24.5%; GAAP ROIC of 7-10% suppressed by Cantel Medical non-cash PPA amortization). Multi-year Owner FCF conversion exceeds 135% (FY2025 Owner FCF $910.7M vs GAAP NI $782.3M, OCF $1,341.4M). Core segments: Healthcare (infection prevention capital equipment, SPD chemistries, endoscopy maintenance), Applied Sterilization Technologies (AST contract radiation/EO sterilization toll booth, >$1B revenue, >$500M operating profit), and Life Sciences (biopharma contamination control). Successfully completed $787.5M divestiture of non-core dental segment (HuFriedyGroup) to Peak Rock Capital in 2024, deploying proceeds to de-lever balance sheet from $3.1B to $1.8B LT debt. Net Debt/Owner FCF stands at 1.51x and EBIT interest coverage is 18.2x ($1,101.8M EBIT vs $60.7M interest). Peak Owner EPS compounded at 13.9% CAGR from $1.45 (FY2016) to $9.12 (FY2025).

column14: Closed-loop Mako robotic surgery ecosystem ($1M+ capital install) creates insurmountable switching costs for orthopedic surgeons and hospitals, locking in exclusive pull-through of Stryker joint implants with >95% retention. In MedSurg, proprietary razor-and-blade consumables (Neptune fluid waste cartridges, Sage hygiene, 1788 camera systems) provide recurring high-margin cash flows. Strong pricing power demonstrated by +1.0-1.5% positive net price realization across inflationary cycles. Erosion threats include competing robotic platforms (Zimmer ROSA, J&J Velys) and potential hospital capital spending deceleration.
column20: Best-in-class medtech compounder dominating orthopedic robotics and specialized hospital equipment. High switching costs anchored by the closed-loop Mako robotic ecosystem (>1.5M procedures, >95% pull-through implant retention) and indispensable MedSurg consumable franchises (Neptune, Sage, 1788 visualization). Multi-decade tailwinds from demographic aging and hospital automation insulate against macro risks. Robust balance sheet with net debt amortizable in <3.5 years of Owner Earnings and 8.0x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: procedure & robotic volume 6.0% + pricing & premium mix 1.5% + tuck-in reinvestment 1.5% + net buybacks 0.5%]
column21: 10-year financial operating history demonstrates exceptional compounding: revenue expanded from $11.3B in FY2016 to $25.1B in FY2025 (11.2% CAGR), driven by organic growth >10% and high-synergy tuck-in acquisitions (Wright Medical, Vocera, Inari Medical). Tangible/Operating ROIC consistently exceeds 35-50% (FY2025: 40.8%), while reported GAAP ROIC is 11.3% due to $25B in accumulated acquisition goodwill and intangibles. Free cash flow conversion is superior at 106.6% of GAAP Net Income over 5 years (FY2025 Owner FCF of $4.04B vs NI of $3.25B), reflecting light capex requirements (~3% of sales). Positive pricing realization (+1.0-1.5%) achieved counter to industry deflationary trends due to differentiated robotic clinical outcomes and proprietary consumables. Solid balance sheet: Net Debt of $10.85B is 2.68x Owner FCF and 3.34x Net Income, supported by $4.01B cash and strong EBIT interest coverage of 8.05x ($4.89B EBIT vs $607M interest).

column14: Orthopedic surgeons face high switching costs due to familiarity with proprietary instrumentation, kinematics, and ROSA surgical robotics. However, structural pricing power is absent: hospital GPOs, Medicare DRG bundles, and international tenders (China VBP) inflict chronic -1% to -2% annual net price deflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & negative pricing power, REJECT). While knee and hip implants benefit from surgeon switching costs, Zimmer Biomet structurally lacks pricing power, enduring -1% to -2% annual realized price deflation from hospital GPOs and government tenders (China VBP). 10-year median ROIC of ~7.5% falls well below the 12% Munger compounder threshold due to goodwill bloat from the Biomet merger and subsequent M&A.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.5% (FY23 4.5%, FY24 4.4%, FY25 ~3.5%), far below the 12% hurdle. High gross margins (69-71%) are offset by SG&A/R&D and amortization of intangibles. The 2015 Biomet merger saddled the balance sheet with over $8B in goodwill and intangibles. Net realized pricing is consistently negative (-1% to -2% per year) across reconstructive hips and knees, offsetting procedure volume gains. Total debt stands at ~$7.5B ($6.9B long-term), while competitive pressure from Stryker's Mako robotics platform continues to challenge ROSA.

column14: Dominant acute-care hospital networks and ambulatory surgery centers with 30-50% bed share in high-growth Sunbelt MSAs create irreplaceable physical healthcare infrastructure with Certificate of Need and capital barriers. Empirical proof shown by 10-year median ROIC of 24.9% and industry-leading ~19-20% EBITDA margins. Local market density enables mid-single-digit (4-5%) annual commercial rate increases that offset wage inflation, though government payer rate pressures (Medicare/Medicaid) present ongoing margin constraints.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Premier US hospital operator with unmatched Sunbelt density and Frist family stewardship, but capital structure is burdened by $41.6B in long-term debt (6.13x LT debt/net income vs 4.0x ceiling) and negative equity (-$6.0B) resulting from multi-year debt-funded share repurchases. [5-10Y g: organic admissions 2.5% + commercial pricing/acuity mix 2.5% + margin 0.0% + net buybacks 2.5%]
column21: SEC EDGAR data confirms 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 24.9% (20.6% in FY2016 to 27.9% in FY2025) and FCF conversion of 107% in FY2025 ($8.7B Owner FCF vs $6.8B NI). However, long-term debt stands at $41,603M against $1,040M cash (Net Debt $40.6B) and FY2025 net income of $6,784M, yielding a 6.13x LT debt / NI ratio (far exceeding the 4.0x maximum). Stockholders' equity is -$6,027M due to aggressive debt-funded buybacks over the decade, triggering the disqualifying financial engineering red flag. Operating interest coverage has averaged 4.0x-5.4x across the cycle, falling short of the >5.0x through-the-cycle peace-of-mind fortress standard.

column14: Physical footprint of over 330 inpatient behavioral health facilities and acute care hospitals is protected by state Certificate-of-Need (CON) regulations, specialized psychiatric licensing, and high replacement capital costs. However, proof of moat fails: 10-year median ROIC is ~10.5% (below the 12% threshold), and pricing power is severely constrained by Medicare/Medicaid reimbursement schedules and managed care contracts that cannot outrun structural clinical labor and nurse wage inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). While Universal Health Services possesses an irreplaceable inpatient behavioral and acute hospital physical footprint protected by Certificate of Need (CON) laws, its 10-year median ROIC of ~10.5% fails the 12% hurdle. UHS lacks structural pricing power above inflation due to heavy dependence on fixed, lagged government reimbursement (Medicare/Medicaid) and commercial managed care contracts, leaving margins vulnerable to structural clinician and nurse wage inflation.
column21:
Universal Health Services operates acute care hospitals and behavioral health centers across the US and UK.
Multi-Cycle Capital Efficiency: 10-year median ROIC is ~10.5% (source: 10-K filings, v1 workbook), with troughs of ~7.1-7.4% during pandemic/labor surges and recoveries to ~10.4-11.5% in 2024-2025, consistently below the 12% Munger compounder hurdle.
Pricing Power & Payor Mix: Over 50% of patient days/revenues are derived from government programs (Medicare and Medicaid) with legislated, lagged fee updates that fail to cover real-time nurse wage inflation and agency staffing costs.
Capital Intensity: Heavy recurring maintenance capital expenditures ($800M-$1B annually) and long-term debt of ~$4.5B-$5.0B (~4.5x net income) constrain free cash flow conversion and shareholder returns.
Regulatory Scrutiny: Subject to recurring federal regulatory scrutiny and False Claims Act settlements (e.g., $122M DOJ settlement in 2020 regarding behavioral health admissions).
