[5-10Y g: commercial aero build volume 5.0% + spares pricing power 2.5% + IGT and defense mix 1.5% - raw material lag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: Operating performance transformed post-Arconic spin under CEO John Plant: operating margin expanded from 12.3% in 2021 to 24.8% in 2025, with FY2025 revenue reaching $8.25B and operating income reaching $2.05B. GAAP ROIC expanded from 8.7% (2021 trough) to 22.7% (2025), while tangible ROIC reached 57.8%. Multi-year Owner FCF conversion is 91.8% ($1.53B Owner FCF in FY2025 vs $1.51B Net Income). Balance sheet strengthened substantially: gross debt lowered from $4.23B (2021) to $2.86B (2025) against $742M cash, leaving net debt at $2.12B (1.4x NI, 1.0x EBITDA) and interest coverage >9.4x. Holds sole-source or primary-source positions on CFM LEAP, Pratt & Whitney GTF, GE9X, and F-35 airframe/engine platforms.

column14: Sole-source classified defense electronics, certified tactical radio installed base (Falcon IV, SINCGARS), and domestic duopoly in solid rocket motors (Aerojet Rocketdyne) create insurmountable switching barriers. While 5-year GAAP ROIC (5-7%) is depressed by heavy merger goodwill, underlying tangible operating ROIC exceeds 20% on hard capital.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Balance Sheet). Long-term debt of ~$11.1B against net income of ~$1.5B results in LT Debt / NI of ~7.2x (substantially exceeding the <=4.0x ceiling), while EBIT/interest coverage of ~4.1x falls short of the >5.0x fortress threshold following debt-funded acquisitions of Aerojet Rocketdyne and Link 16. Tangible equity remains negative.
column21: L3Harris operates across four core defense segments: Communication Systems, Integrated Mission Systems, Space & Airborne Systems, and Aerojet Rocketdyne. Free cash flow conversion is strong ($2.68B FCF in FY25 vs ~$1.5B net income), supported by LHX NeXt operational efficiencies. However, the balance sheet was substantially leveraged to fund the $4.7B cash acquisition of Aerojet Rocketdyne in 2023, expanding total debt to over $11B against $19.3B equity and $20.3B goodwill (resulting in negative tangible net worth). With interest expense at ~$550M-$600M and EBIT at ~$2.3B-$2.5B, interest coverage is ~4.1x (below the 5.0x minimum requirement), failing Gate 6.

column14: Irreplaceable sovereign defense industrial infrastructure. Sole-source provider of the 5th-generation stealth fighter (F-35) with 3,000+ planned lifetime airframes across 19 partner nations, PAC-3 missile defense, THAAD, HIMARS, and Aegis naval combat systems. High barriers created by classified security clearances, specialized tooling, and FAR cost-plus/statutory procurement frameworks. Moat proven by 10-year median ROIC of 18.2% and gross margin stability around 12–13%. Primary erosion risks stem from Pentagon fixed-price developmental contract write-downs and customer monopsony margin caps.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT). World's premier defense prime contractor passes Gates 1–5 on sovereign defense necessity and an unassailable $160B+ backlog, but fails Gate 6 on balance sheet quality and earnings durability. Negative tangible equity (-$6.8B) resulting from decades of debt-funded share buybacks, elevated total debt ($21.7B) exceeding 4.0x normalized earnings, recurring multi-hundred-million fixed-price developmental contract write-downs, and working-capital delivery freezes (e.g. F-35 TR-3 milestone withholdings) violate Munger's peace-of-mind and peak-to-peak compounding standards. [5-10Y g: missiles/fire control volume 4.0% + F-35 sustainment 2.0% + contract indexation 1.0% + buyback 1.0% - fixed-price developmental drag 1.5%]
column21: Lockheed Martin is the world's largest defense contractor ($75.0B FY25 revenue, 72% US Government / DoD). Segment breakdown: Aeronautics ~$28.5B (F-35, C-130), Missiles and Fire Control ~$12.5B (PAC-3, HIMARS, Javelin), Rotary & Mission Systems ~$17.5B (Sikorsky, Aegis), Space ~$13.0B. 10-year median ROIC is 18.2% with multi-year FCF conversion averaging >100% ($6.9B FCF vs $5.0B Net Income in FY25; $18.4B 3-year cumulative FCF vs $17.3B Net Income). However, capital structure displays severe financial engineering: $21.7B in total debt against $6.7B in stockholders' equity, yielding -$6.8B in negative tangible equity due to aggressive debt-funded share repurchases. Total debt to FY25 net income stands at 4.33x (exceeding the 4.0x peace-of-mind threshold). Earnings power has degraded from a 2023 peak EPS of $27.55 to $22.31 in 2024 and $21.49 in 2025 due to classified fixed-price development program losses and F-35 TR-3 software delivery pauses, failing Gate 6.

column14: Irreplaceable classified defense infrastructure (Air Force Plant 42, solid rocket motor test ranges) and sole-source stealth/nuclear triad franchises (B-21 Raider, Sentinel ICBM). Demonstrates contractual cost-plus recovery on mature programs with historical ROIC averaging ~11-14%, though fixed-price development contracts exposed the company to temporary inflationary margin compression.
column19: Broken metric: Gate 6 fails on multi-year Owner FCF conversion (~56-65% 5-year average vs >=80% hurdle) and peak-to-peak earnings power due to a $1.56B pre-tax charge on B-21 Raider Low-Rate Initial Production (LRIP) fixed-price lots and Section 174 mandatory R&D tax amortization drag. Moat proof: Indispensable, sole-source prime contractor anchoring the US nuclear triad (B-21 stealth bomber, Sentinel ICBM) with record $95.7B backlog (1.10 book-to-bill); 2025 FCF rebounded +26% to $3.3B as cash conversion recovered toward 80%. Fix catalyst: B-21 transition from loss-making LRIP to profitable full-rate production, DoD policy pivot away from fixed-price development bids, and Section 174 tax normalization; Kill-switch: Additional multi-billion-dollar fixed-price overrun charges on B-21 production lots or Sentinel program cancellation / re-competition following Nunn-McCurdy restructuring.
column20: Strategic aerospace and defense prime contractor anchoring the US nuclear triad with irreplaceable classified manufacturing infrastructure and sovereign sole-source franchises. Temporary fixed-price B-21 contract losses and Section 174 tax drag depressed 5-year FCF conversion to ~60%, but 2025 FCF rebounded to $3.3B with record $95.7B backlog. Balance sheet is secure with net debt/NI at ~2.5x and 7.3x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: B-21 stealth bomber ramp 3.0% + space/missile defense volume 2.5% + pricing/escalation 1.5% - fixed-price drag/overruns 1.0% + share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: Northrop Grumman is the prime contractor for two of the three legs of the modernized US nuclear triad: the B-21 Raider strategic stealth bomber and the LGM-35A Sentinel ICBM. 2025 sales reached $42.0B with a record $95.7B backlog (book-to-bill 1.10). In 2023, management absorbed a $1.56B pre-tax charge on the fixed-price B-21 Low-Rate Initial Production (LRIP) phase due to post-pandemic inflation. In 2024, Sentinel triggered a Nunn-McCurdy breach due to complex ground infrastructure scope changes, but was certified by the DoD as vital to national security. Operating performance rebounded in 2024-2025, with Net Income reaching $4.18B and Free Cash Flow surging to $3.30B in 2025 (+26% YoY). Long-term debt is managed at ~$14.5B against $4.4B in cash (net debt/NI ~2.5x), with EBIT interest coverage exceeding 7x. Management under Kathy Warden has established strict bidding discipline, refusing fixed-price development contracts to protect return on capital.

column14: Dual commercial and defense moat: Collins Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney hold irreplaceable sole-source positions across commercial airframes (Airbus A320neo, Boeing 787, A220) and military platforms (F-35 F135, F-15/F-16 engines), generating high-margin aftermarket spares and MRO cash flows across 30+ year fleet lifespans where FAA regulatory certification and extreme switching costs eliminate substitution risk. Raytheon holds entrenched technological franchises in missile defense (Patriot, NASAMS), precision strike (Tomahawk, AMRAAM), and naval radar (SPY-6) backed by classified IP and sovereign procurement integration. Gross margins remain stable at 18-20% through cycles. Primary erosion risks stem from fixed-price defense contract cost overruns and engine performance issues, but high switching barriers and multi-year order backlogs protect economics.
column19: Broken metric: Gate 6 fails due to balance sheet leverage (gross long-term debt of $37.7B vs 2025 net income of $7.11B yields ~5.3x leverage, exceeding the <=4.0x threshold; net debt ~$31.7B is ~4.5x) and multi-billion-dollar cumulative cash compensation drain to airline customers resulting from the Pratt & Whitney GTF powder metal recall (~$1B cash outflow in 2024 and ~$1B in 2025). Intact moat proof: Structural competitive position is completely unimpaired; Pratt & Whitney retains its ~50% duopoly share on the Airbus A320neo family with an 8-year backlog, Collins Aerospace maintains sole-source content across major civil and military programs, and Raytheon's defense backlog sits at an all-time high ($200B+ total company backlog). Fix catalyst & kill-switch: Peak inspection shop visits and aircraft-on-ground disruptions passed in 2024-2025; shop turnaround times are compressing and cash compensation outflows step down in 2026-2027 as free cash flow expands toward $8.5B+, enabling rapid debt paydown ($3.4B retired in 2025). Kill-switch triggers if powder metal cracking recurs in post-2021 engine builds, if airlines cancel A320neo GTF orders for CFM LEAP in volume, or if the FAA mandates an uncontained fleet-wide redesign.
column20: Aerospace and defense titan qualifying under Calamity pass. Collins Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney possess irreplaceable commercial aerospace infrastructure with 30-year aftermarket spare parts pricing power, while Raytheon is a core beneficiary of multi-decade Western geopolitical rearmament across NATO. Passes Gates 1-5; fails Gate 6 due to post-merger debt leverage (debt/NI ~5.3x) and temporary GTF powder metal recall compensation cash drains. Underlying moats and $200B+ backlog remain fully intact as FCF rebounds toward $8.5B+ in 2026. [5-10Y g: commercial aero aftermarket volume 4.0% + defense procurement volume 2.5% + pricing power 1.5% - GTF inspection compensation drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: Revenues rose from $67.1B (2022) to $68.9B (2023), $74.5B (2024), and ~$80.5B (2025), driven by commercial aerospace recovery and surging defense demand. Operating margins recovered to 10-12% post the 2023 GTF operating charge ($3.0B pre-tax). FCF conversion is robust: FY2024 FCF was $4.5B on $4.8B net income (94%), FY2025 FCF reached $7.9B on $7.1B net income (111%), and FY2026 FCF guidance is $8.25B-$8.75B. Operating ROIC on tangible capital exceeds 15%, though GAAP ROIC (~6-8%) remains accounting-depressed by $53.3B in merger goodwill from the 2020 UTC/Raytheon combination. Total debt stood at $37.7B at year-end 2025 (down from $41.1B in 2024) against $6.0B+ cash, yielding interest coverage of ~6.0x. Order backlog reached record levels exceeding $200B ($130B+ commercial, $70B+ defense), demonstrating enduring customer lock-in across commercial and government clients.

column14: Extreme regulatory switching costs and sole-source toll booth moat. Approximately 90% of revenue is derived from proprietary products, with ~80% from sole-source positions engineered onto FAA/military aircraft type certificates. Recertification via FAA Parts Manufacturer Approval (PMA) is economically irrational for competitors given low component dollar value relative to certification costs and safety liabilities. Demonstrates legendary pricing power with consistent 5-8%+ annual price increases across cycles with negligible customer volume churn, supporting a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 16.6% (FY2025: 23.0%) and operating ROIC >100%. Key erosion risks include airline PMA consortia and heightened DoD procurement scrutiny.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Outstanding proprietary aerospace aftermarket toll-booth monopoly with ~90% proprietary parts and >80% FCF conversion, but fundamentally rejected under Munger's peace-of-mind fortress balance sheet standard. Total debt of $29.3B ($26.5B net debt) against FY2025 net income of $2,074M results in a net debt to owner earnings ratio of 12.8x (far exceeding the <=4.0x ceiling) and Net Debt/EBITDA of ~6.0x. FY2025 interest coverage of 2.65x (EBIT $4,165M / Net Interest $1,572M) is well below the >5.0x hurdle. Intentional PE-style financial engineering (debt-funded special dividends) has driven stockholders' equity to -$9.7B, leaving the business permanently dependent on the continuous 'kindness of strangers' in debt capital markets. [5-10Y g: commercial flight hours 4.0% + proprietary aftermarket pricing 4.0% + bolt-on M&A 2.5% - interest drag 0.5%]
column21: Multi-decade operating history establishing sole-source positions on commercial (Boeing, Airbus) and defense platforms. FY2025 revenue reached $8,831M with EBIT of $4,165M (47.2% EBIT margin). GAAP ROIC has averaged 16.6% over 5 years (FY2025: 23.0%), with tangible operating ROIC >100%. Free cash flow conversion is consistently high (FY2024: $1,692M FCF / $1,714M NI = 98.7%; FY2025: $1,664M FCF / $2,074M NI = 80.2%). However, balance sheet leverage is structurally excessive: FY2025 long-term debt of $29,291M against cash of $2,808M (net debt $26,483M). Net interest expense of $1,572M results in EBIT interest coverage of only 2.65x (spec threshold >5.0x). Net debt to net income is 12.8x (threshold <=4.0x) and net debt to EBITDA is ~6.0x. Stockholders' equity is -$9,686M due to repeated debt-financed special cash dividends.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket capital purchases (business jets, specialized vehicles) deferrable in recessions.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Textron is heavily exposed to cyclical and discretionary big-ticket corporate and consumer purchases through its Textron Aviation segment (Cessna Citation business jets, Beechcraft turboprops) and Industrial segment (E-Z-GO golf carts, specialized commercial vehicles). In economic contractions and recessions, corporate jet purchases and fleet expansions are easily deferred or cancelled. Textron lacks the non-discretionary essentiality or entrenched daily habit required of a compounding franchise, as further evidenced by sub-hurdle multi-cycle ROIC of 5-8%.
column21: Textron Inc. operates four primary segments: Textron Aviation (~40% of FY2025 revenue at $5.96B), Bell (~29% at $4.28B), Industrial (~22% at $3.21B), and Textron Systems (~8% at $1.25B). Business jets (Cessna Citation) and specialized vehicles represent classic big-ticket, deferrable cyclical capital purchases rather than essential functional necessities or high-frequency everyday habits. Historical capital efficiency demonstrates persistent vulnerability to cyclicality: GAAP/operating ROIC was 4.4% in 2020, 6.4% in 2021, 6.4% in 2022, 7.6% in 2023, 5.7% in 2024, and 6.4% in 2025 (10-year median ROIC ~9.5%), consistently failing the 12% compounder hurdle across all cycle stages.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Understandability: Reject Standard a). Pre-profit, capital-intensive space launch and satellite systems business model lacking an established economic engine or multi-cycle profitable operating track record. The company remains deeply unprofitable (net losses of -$190.2M in FY2024 and -$198.2M in FY2025) with accelerating negative free cash flow (-$116.0M in FY2024, -$321.8M in FY2025) to fund massive capex and R&D for the unproven Neutron medium-lift rocket program. Long-term commercial unit economics are highly speculative and face severe competitive pressure from SpaceX.
column21: Multi-cycle track record: Completed de-SPAC in August 2021 and has never generated positive GAAP operating profit, net income, or free cash flow in any fiscal year. FY2024 revenue of $436.2M (+78% YoY) resulted in an operating loss of -$181.7M, net loss of -$190.2M, and negative FCF of -$116.0M. FY2025 revenue reached $601.8M (+38% YoY), yet net losses remained heavy at -$198.2M and negative FCF expanded to -$321.8M due to capital expenditure scaling for Neutron launch infrastructure and Archimedes engine development. Segment breakdown: Space Systems represents ~70% of revenue (satellite buses, separation systems, solar power, reaction wheels) and Launch Services represents ~30% (Electron small rocket). Small dedicated launch offers limited pricing power and operating leverage. Capital structure: Persistently reliant on external capital market funding ('kindness of strangers'), including $355M of convertible debt due 2029 and ongoing equity dilution. Consistently negative ROIC and absence of proven cash-generative economic engine trigger immediate Gate 1 rejection.

column14: Dominant dealer network density (over 2,000 North American locations providing mission-critical 2-hour parts and maintenance dispatch during narrow harvest windows) paired with proprietary John Deere Operations Center precision ag telemetry and connected machinery ecosystem creates massive farmer switching costs. Empirically demonstrated by 10-year median ROIC of ~17% and sustained 3-5% annual pricing realization over equipment cost inflation. Primary erosion threats include right-to-repair legislative mandates, prolonged crop price slumps squeezing farm capex, and competitive entry in autonomy/electrification.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Despite Deere's unrivaled agricultural moat, mission-critical precision ag technology, and strong operational ROIC (~17%), its capital structure is heavily leveraged by its captive finance subsidiary, John Deere Capital Corporation. Total consolidated enterprise debt stands at ~$63.9B ($43.5B long-term, $13.8B short-term) against cash of $8.3B, yielding net debt of ~$55.6B. Net debt to FY25 net income ($5.03B) is 11.1x (and 5.5x even against peak FY23 net income of $10.17B), far exceeding the 4.0-year limit. Crucially, the captive finance model's structural reliance on rolling over billions in short-term commercial paper to fund dealer wholesale floorplans and customer retail notes violates Munger's peace-of-mind balance sheet standard (freedom from the 'kindness of strangers').
column21: Deere & Company generates strong multi-cycle operating returns with 10-year median ROIC of 16.8% and operating margins remaining in the mid-to-high teens across cycles (FY23 revenue $61.3B, net income $10.17B; FY24 revenue $51.7B, net income $7.10B; FY25 revenue $45.7B, net income $5.03B). Revenue is split across Production & Precision Ag (~$17.3B in FY25), Small Ag & Turf (~$10.2B), Construction & Forestry (~$11.4B), and Financial Services. High switching barriers stem from its exclusive dealer network (>2,000 North American locations) and digital ecosystem (300M+ engaged acres on Operations Center). However, consolidated debt is ~$63.9B ($43.5B long-term, $13.8B short-term borrowings including commercial paper), while stockholders' equity is $26.0B and cash is $8.3B. Equipment Operations alone carries $8.8B long-term debt against $6.3B cash, but parent equity fully underpins John Deere Capital Corporation ($34.8B long-term debt). Consolidated Net Debt / Net Income of ~11.1x in FY25 (5.5x at FY23 peak) and ongoing reliance on commercial paper funding fail Gate 6 Pillar 3.

column14: Freight brokerage is a highly fragmented commodity intermediary business with over 15,000 active brokers. Shippers utilize multi-broker routing guides with near-zero switching costs, and carriers multi-home across digital load boards. CHRW possesses no defensible structural moat barriers. Proof of moat fails: gross margins and operating profits are dictated by cyclical spreads between shipper contract rates and spot carrier purchase costs, resulting in extreme cyclicality (operating income dropped 66% from $1.26B in 2022 to $427M in 2023) and zero independent pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing, REJECT). Asset-light third-party freight brokerage operating in a fragmented, highly competitive market with no customer switching costs. Shippers tender loads via automated routing guides to whichever broker or asset carrier offers the lowest rate, while truck drivers multi-home across competing load boards. CHRW is a commodity spread price-taker lacking structural pricing power, evidenced by a 65% net income collapse during the 2022-2023 freight downcycle.
column21: North American Surface Transportation (NAST) generates ~65-70% of gross profits, with Global Forwarding contributing ~20-25%. Financial performance is acutely cyclical: revenues fell from $24.70B in 2022 to $17.60B in 2023, while net income dropped from $940.5M (EPS $7.40) to $325.1M (EPS $2.72) before partially recovering to $465.7M in 2024 and $587.1M in 2025. Total debt was reduced from $1.4B in 2024 to $1.1B in 2025 against $161M cash (net debt ~$939M). While asset-light logistics yields solid optical returns on tangible capital in cycle upswings, CHRW has zero structural pricing power or customer lock-in to protect margins against cyclical freight spot rate movements.

column14: Global toll booth and high switching costs in cross-border air/ocean freight forwarding and customs brokerage. Intermediates cargo capacity between shippers and carriers across 100+ countries, maintaining net revenue margins across freight cycles. Customs clearance involves deep enterprise ERP integrations and regulatory compliance with near-zero customer churn. High ROIC (>60-70% 10-year median) proves strong moat; primary risks are carrier disintermediation and geopolitical trade contractions.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Premier non-asset-based global freight forwarder and customs broker with an entrenched toll-booth moat, zero debt, >70% operating ROIC, and legendary decentralized profit-sharing culture. Insulated from energy transition and benefits from supply chain complexity. [5-10Y g: global trade volume 2.5% + customs brokerage share 1.5% + net revenue yield management 1.0% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 79.1% and operating ROIC of 79.7%, driven by an asset-light model with capex under 0.5% of revenues. FCF conversion averages 101.6% of Net Income. Balance sheet carries zero long-term debt and $1.31B in cash. Normalized Owner EPS has compounded from $3.51 in 2018 to $5.97 in 2025, demonstrating secular peak-to-peak earnings growth through freight cycles.

column14: Global express hub-and-spoke air network (Memphis World Hub, 680+ aircraft) and sorting infrastructure are virtually impossible to replicate from scratch, but fails empirical proof of moat. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.5% (10-year avg ~9.5%), persistently below the 12% quality hurdle across all cycle stages. Pricing power is constrained by UPS, Amazon logistics insourcing/expansion, regional parcel carriers, and belly-cargo substitution; lost the major USPS air cargo contract to UPS in 2024.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). While FedEx operates an irreplaceable global air express and ground logistics network, heavy capital intensity ($4B-$6B+ annual capex for aircraft, hubs, and vehicle fleet) and competitive pressure from UPS and Amazon keep operating margins at 5.5-7.0% and multi-cycle ROIC at 7-8%, well below the 12% threshold.
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 7.5% (FY20 4.3%, FY21 10.2%, FY22 8.5%, FY23 7.4%, FY24 7.5%, FY25 ~7.0%), consistently failing the 12% hurdle even during peak pandemic package volume surges. Operating margins oscillate between 5.5% and 7.0%. Ongoing capital intensity ($4.1B capex in FY25, $5.2B in FY24) dampens returns on capital. Pricing power is limited against UPS and Amazon, underscored by the loss of the foundational USPS domestic air cargo contract in 2024.

column14: UPS operates massive physical route density and integrated hub-and-spoke sortation networks with enterprise B2B pickup lock-in. However, the moat suffers severe structural erosion: it lacks pricing power above inflation without shedding customer volume and market share. The 2023 Teamsters labor contract created a structural cost disadvantage against non-union rivals, while Amazon Logistics successfully insourced and disintermediated delivery, stripping away high-density volume. Shippers actively divert volume to FedEx, USPS, and regional carriers upon aggressive price hikes.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing & Proof of Moat, REJECT). UPS operates an indispensable physical parcel network, but it lacks genuine pricing power above inflation without shedding customer volume and market share. The landmark 2023 Teamsters labor agreement significantly escalated union wage and benefit costs, causing margin compression that could not be passed through to price-sensitive customers. Furthermore, Amazon Logistics has permanently disintermediated UPS's former largest customer (shedding over 50% of Amazon volume), while commercial shippers diverted volume to FedEx and regional carriers, depressing operating margins (~8%) and dropping normalized ROIC toward ~11-13% with sub-hurdle incremental ROIIC.
column21: Historical ROIC was elevated during the 2020-2022 pandemic e-commerce boom (peak ROIC 25-30%), but normalized post-pandemic ROIC deteriorated to 16.8% (2023), 13.7% (2024), and 11.4-12.9% (2025). Operating margins fell from 13.0% (2021) and 13.8% (2022) to 7.4% (2023) and ~8% (2024-2025) following the 2023 Teamsters wage contract (~$170k full-time driver comp). Total U.S. package volume declined as shippers diverted 1.2-1.5M packages/day during negotiations and Amazon insourced logistics. Amazon volume fell from >11% of revenue and 20-25% of volume toward <5%, requiring UPS to close dozens of sortation centers and cut headcounts under 'Fit to Serve'. Annual capex of $4.0-5.0B in automation generates defensive, sub-hurdle incremental returns.

column14: Entrenched architectural specification lock-in via certified hardware consultants embedding Schlage, Von Duprin, and LCN into Division 8/28 building schedules. Extreme switching costs from institutional master-key systems and strict life-safety fire/ADA compliance codes where liability prevents substitution. Empirical proof: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 23.9% (operating tangible ROIC ~97%), stable ~42-44% gross margins, and consistent pricing realization exceeding inflation. Primary erosion threat is electronic access control disintermediation, though Allegion effectively embeds EAC into its mechanical door footprints.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global leader in commercial, institutional, and residential security hardware and access solutions. Wide moat anchored by architectural specification dominance (Schlage, Von Duprin, LCN) and high-switching-cost master key installed bases. Insulated from AI disruption with tailwinds from electronic access integration. Strong cash conversion (~92% FCF/NI) and conservative balance sheet (~1.5x net debt/EBITDA, 8.5x interest coverage). [5-10Y g: institutional volume 2.0% + pricing power 2.5% + electronic access mix & bolt-ons 2.5% - integration/R&D drag 0.5% + net buybacks 1.5%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 23.9% and tangible operating ROIC of 96.7%. 10-year FCF conversion averages ~98% of net income with capex under 2.5% of sales. Americas segment generates ~80%+ of revenue and >27% operating margins driven by non-residential institutional retrofit and replacement cycles. Pristine balance sheet with net debt to EBITDA of ~1.5x and EBIT/Interest coverage of 8.5x.

column14: North American water heating duopoly (~35-37% residential share, >50% commercial share) protected by contractor-specified wholesale distribution (800+ independent supply houses) and professional plumber brand loyalty for same-day emergency replacements. Empirical proof includes a 10-year average GAAP ROIC above 20% (5Y median 21.2%, FY24-25 ~25-27%) and gross margin defense around 38-40% despite volatile steel and freight inflation. Key erosion threats include long-term disintermediation via retail big-box channels (Lowe's), Chinese domestic market price competition, and technological substitution during the transition to heat pumps.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Dominant North American water heater duopoly (~35-37% residential, >50% commercial share; 21.2% 5Y median ROIC) faces terminal runway constraints capped at 10 years due to active 5-macrotrend headwinds: [3] Geopolitical & China real estate secular contraction (~20% sales headwind from China property slump and aggressive domestic brand competition), and [4] Energy Transition disruption from DOE 2029 efficiency mandates requiring heat pump water heaters, which threatens legacy atmospheric tank economics and invites scaled HVAC conglomerate competition.
column21: Empirical financial track record shows strong historical capital efficiency: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 21.2% (FY24 ~25%, FY25 ~26%), operating margins of 17-19%, and robust free cash flow conversion (>90-100% of net income; FY24 FCF $474M, FY25 FCF $546M). Balance sheet is pristine with total debt of ~$193M offset by cash and marketable securities (~$193M-$276M) and negligible net debt. Revenue breakdown: North America (~75-80% of sales, ~85% of EBIT) and Rest of World (~20-25% of sales, primarily China). While the North American wholesale plumbing channel creates an entrenched emergency replacement moat for legacy tanks, organic volume has stagnated (net sales flat at $3.85B in 2023, $3.82B in 2024, and $3.83B in 2025). The business faces secular growth caps and terminal disruption from the multi-year collapse of China's property market and the impending 2029 DOE regulatory shift toward heat pump water heating.

column14: Carrier possesses brand recognition, a vast installed base, and entrenched dealer/distributor relationships in residential and commercial HVAC. However, it fails Gate 3b proof of moat: 5-year median GAAP ROIC has languished in the 6-8% range (2021: ~11%, 2022: ~8%, 2023: ~8%, 2024: ~6%, 2025: ~6-7%), well below the 12% hurdle. Carrier lacks the direct sales/service lock-in of Trane Technologies, relying heavily on two-step wholesale distribution where independent contractors face low barriers to switching between Carrier, Lennox, Trane, and Daikin. The €12B acquisition of Viessmann Climate Solutions at the peak of European heat pump subsidies in 2024 permanently diluted capital efficiency with >$10B of goodwill and intangibles, followed by severe residential volume contractions in Europe and North America.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & Inadequate Pricing Power, REJECT). While Carrier has a leading global footprint in HVAC equipment, its multi-cycle capital efficiency fails the Munger quality hurdle with a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~7% (peaking around 11% in 2021 and dipping to 5.6-7.1% in 2024-2025). The business relies on two-step wholesale distribution in residential HVAC, exposing it to distributor destocking, cyclical construction downturns, and direct competition from Daikin, Trane, and Lennox. Capital allocation was severely set back by the €12B peak-multiple acquisition of Viessmann in 2024, burdening the balance sheet and diluting returns right before a sharp European heat pump downturn.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record shows GAAP ROIC consistently below hurdle: 2021 ~10.8-11.2%, 2022 ~8.3%, 2023 ~7.9%, 2024 ~5.6-6.8%, and 2025 ~5.8-7.1%, yielding a 5-year median of ~7.5% vs. the 12% requirement. GAAP operating margins have hovered around 8-11% (2021: 11.6%, 2023: 10.6%, 2024: 10.1%, 2025: ~8.3-10.0%), trailing direct peer Trane Technologies (17-19% operating margins, 20-25% ROIC). Carrier underwent a massive portfolio overhaul, divesting Fire & Security and Commercial Refrigeration to fund the €12B ($14.2B) acquisition of Viessmann Climate Solutions in early 2024. Despite applying ~$6B of divestiture proceeds to debt reduction, gross debt remains ~$12.3B with post-deal leverage near 2.8x-3.0x EBITDA. Viessmann suffered from post-acquisition residential volume contractions (-30% to -40% in European heat pumps in 2024-2025 following German subsidy revisions and gas price normalizations). Carrier lacks the direct sales branch model and high-margin recurring service attach rates of Trane, relying instead on two-step distribution through independent distributors (e.g., Watsco) and dealers.

column14: High switching costs in proprietary building management systems (Metasys) and installed-base services, alongside York industrial chillers for mission-critical data center cooling; supported by tangible operating ROIC > 20% and demonstrated pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Leading commercial HVAC and building automation provider fails Munger peace-of-mind balance sheet standards due to elevated leverage (long-term debt of $8.6B vs. FY25 net income of $1.7B, yielding LT debt / NI of ~5.1x vs. <=4.0x hurdle), persistent multi-year restructuring and separation expenses, negative tangible equity, and capital allocation prioritizing a $5.0B accelerated share repurchase over debt reduction. [5-10Y g: data center/commercial HVAC 4% + building services 3% + price 1% - restructuring drag -1%]
column21: Following the August 2025 close of the $8.1B sale ($5.0B net cash proceeds) of its Residential & Light Commercial HVAC unit to Bosch, Johnson Controls operates as a pure-play commercial building solutions provider with ~$23B in continuing revenue and solid operating margins (10-14%). However, 10-year GAAP ROIC has averaged 7-10% (median 9.2%) weighed down by $17B+ of goodwill and intangibles dating from the 2016 Tyco merger. Reported cash conversion has been repeatedly depressed by restructuring and separation costs. Balance sheet remains overleveraged with total debt of $9.9B ($8.6B long-term debt) against FY25 net income of $1.7B (LT debt / NI ~5.1x, exceeding the <=4.0x maximum). Management directed the $5.0B net proceeds from the Bosch sale into an accelerated share repurchase rather than deleveraging, failing Gate 6.

column14: Direct-to-dealer (D2D) distribution model bypasses independent two-step wholesalers for ~75% of sales, embedding high switching costs via Lennox Premier Dealer certification, proprietary diagnostic tools, warranty handling, and co-op marketing. 10-year median ROIC is ~28% with operating margins near 17-18%. Primary erosion threat is private equity contractor consolidation demanding multi-brand wholesale sourcing.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Lennox achieves high returns on capital via its proprietary direct-to-dealer network, structural runway is limited. Capital Goods base-rate persistence is Tier 3 (10-15Y). The rapid private equity consolidation of independent residential HVAC contractors directly threatens Lennox's captive dealer moat by shifting procurement to multi-brand wholesale distributors (Watsco, Ferguson). Exiting Europe leaves Lennox >90% dependent on mature North American residential replacement cycles, with high-ticket consumer financing vulnerable to structural interest rates.
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 28.5% with operating margins of 17-18% and FCF of $640M-$785M. Revenue splits ~65% Home Comfort Solutions (Residential) and ~35% Building Climate Solutions (Commercial); ~75% replacement / 25% new construction. However, Lennox is pure-play North American without global scale, competing against Daikin, Carrier, and Trane. Private equity rollups of local HVAC dealers aggregate buying power away from proprietary direct-to-dealer networks.

column11: Discretionary and deferrable home improvement products (architectural paint and decorative plumbing fixtures) tied to cyclical housing turnover and discretionary remodel spending.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Decorative architectural coatings (Behr paint, Kilz primers) and decorative plumbing fixtures (Delta, Hansgrohe, Brizo) represent deferrable home improvement and remodeling purchases rather than non-displaceable daily essentials or high-frequency Lindy habits. Demand is heavily cyclical and tied to existing home sales turnover and discretionary consumer remodel spending, leading to volume contractions during housing market lulls. Extreme customer concentration with The Home Depot (representing ~38% of consolidated net sales) further compounds commercial vulnerability.
column21: Masco operates across two segments: Plumbing Products (~66% of sales; Delta, Brizo, Hansgrohe) and Decorative Architectural Products (~34% of sales; Behr, Kilz). Net sales declined from $7,971M in 2023 to $7,828M in 2024 (-2%) and $7,562M in 2025 (-3%) due to depressed existing home sales and deferred DIY paint projects. While operating margins (17.4% in 2024, 16.5% in 2025) and ROIC (>30%) are healthy due to disciplined cost management and asset-light assembly, ~38% of consolidated sales are concentrated at a single customer (The Home Depot), which holds retail exclusivity for Behr. The business is fundamentally tethered to cyclical and deferrable residential remodel cycles.

column14: Massive proprietary installed base in commercial HVAC, mission-critical Tracer building automation controls, and company-owned direct technician service network create high customer switching costs. Empirically proven by 5-year median ROIC of ~18.5% (ROIC >20% in 2024-2025), robust gross margins, and consistent positive pricing realization (+3-5% annually) driving operating margins from 14% to >18%. Primary erosion threats include low-end residential HVAC commoditization and competition from Asian OEMs in ductless split systems.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global leader in commercial HVAC and climate solutions with powerful switching costs anchored by installed base and direct service network. Active beneficiary of AI data center thermal cooling demand and secular building decarbonization/energy efficiency. Clean balance sheet with net debt/NI ~1.2x and interest coverage ~17.5x. [5-10Y g: commercial & data center volume 3.5% + equipment pricing 2.0% + services & controls mix 2.0% - regulatory refrigerant/tariff drag 0.5% + share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 10-year median ROIC ~18.5% with 2024-2025 ROIC >20%. FY2024 revenue $19.8B (+12%), FCF $2.8B (109% conversion); FY2025 revenue $21.3B (+7.5%), operating income $3.97B, net income $2.94B, FCF conversion 98%. Total debt of $4.6B (net debt ~$3.5B) against $2.94B net income yields net debt/NI of 1.19x and interest coverage of 17.5x. Pure-play climate leader benefiting from mission-critical commercial HVAC, data center cooling, and transport refrigeration (Thermo King).

column14: North American LTL network density across ~370 service centers and linehaul lanes creates scale economies shared. Proof of moat shown by 3-year median GAAP ROIC of 45.8% (FY23: 69.9%, FY24: 45.8%, FY25: 12.9%) and annual 4.9-5.9% General Rate Increases (GRIs). Primary erosion threats include low-cost non-union competitors (ODFL, Saia), shipper TMS spot-bidding, and cyclical freight downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). North American LTL network density (~370 terminals) provides operational scale economies shared and historical median GAAP ROIC of 45.8%. However, the business faces active, unhedged terminal headwinds across three macrotrends: chronic commercial driver shortages and labor cost inflation (Macrotrend 2), capital-intensive diesel fleet decarbonization and zero-emission mandates (Macrotrend 4), and high capital intensity compounded by $4.26B in carveout debt (Macrotrend 5). Capped at CAP = 10 by the Rule of Secular Resilience, failing the 15-year hurdle.
column21: FedEx Freight (NYSE: FDXF) was spun off from FedEx Corp in June 2026 as an independent publicly traded company. Operates North America's largest LTL network with $8.8B-$9.4B in annual revenue across ~370 service centers. 3-year median GAAP ROIC of 45.8% (FY23: 69.9%, FY24: 45.8%, FY25: 12.9%) and tangible ROIC median >60% demonstrate historical network moat, maintained through disciplined 4.9-5.9% annual General Rate Increases (GRIs). However, FY25 EBIT declined 62% to $540M and OCF fell to $167M (Owner FCF -$225M) amidst freight cyclicality. The business faces structural terminal labor constraints (truck driver scarcity), mandatory diesel fleet transition capex under EPA/CARB rules, and a heavy post-spin debt burden ($4.26B LT debt vs $655M TTM net income, with -$497M negative equity resulting from a pre-spin debt dividend to parent FedEx). Under the 5-Macrotrend framework, persistent labor and energy transition headwinds cap CAP at 10 years, failing Gate 4.

column14: Scale economies shared in North American domestic intermodal (>100k containers) and private fleet replacement (DCS). However, JBHT lacks independent pricing power; intermodal must maintain a discount to highway trucking, making JBHT a price-taker during freight downturns when overcapacity triggers aggressive spot discounting.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). North American intermodal and dedicated transportation leader with scale economies shared, but lacks invariant pricing power across the cycle. Intermodal rates must price at a discount to over-the-road trucking; during freight recessions and capacity gluts, JBHT becomes a cyclical price-taker, causing severe margin compression (operating margin fell from 9.4% in 2022 to 6.9% in 2024) and dragging trough ROIC below the 12% hurdle (11.2% in 2024).
column21: 10-year median ROIC is ~13.8%, but cyclical: 21.6% in 2022 (freight peak), 14.6% in 2023, 11.2% in 2024 (below 12% hurdle), and 12.4% in 2025. Operating margins compressed from 9.4% in 2022 to 6.9% in 2024. Intermodal (JBI, ~47% of revenue) and Dedicated (DCS, ~32% of revenue) provide operating scale and multi-year contract stability, but brokerage (ICS) and truckload (JBT) are exposed to brutal spot rate competition. CapEx cycles for container and tractor fleet replacement create lumpy FCF (-$118M in 2023, +$618M in 2024, +$948M in 2025). Net debt of ~$1.0B is manageable (EBIT interest coverage >10x), but structural inability to price above inflation in freight downcycles fails Gate 3b.

column14: Self-reinforcing network density and irreplaceable physical terminal footprint (250+ owned/zoned cross-dock service centers) create massive scale economies shared. Unmatched service execution (99% on-time delivery, 0.1% cargo claims ratio vs industry average 1.5%) drives durable pricing power (revenue per cwt up 4-6% p.a. across all freight cycles). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 32.7% (24.4% in 2025 trough) with best-in-class operating ratio (70-75% vs 85-95% for peers). Erosion threats from freight recessions or price wars are blunted by ODFL's premium service brand and low-cost non-union structure.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. The undisputed premier less-than-truckload (LTL) motor carrier in North America with an unreplicable nationwide terminal network, 99% on-time delivery, industry-leading operating ratio, net-cash balance sheet, and proven pricing power above inflation across freight cycles. Beneficiary of supply chain reshoring and insulated from AI disruption. [5-10Y g: LTL tonnage market share gains 3.0% + revenue per cwt pricing 3.5% + terminal density reinvestment 1.0% - cyclical/cost drag 0.5% + share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 10-year track record of industry-leading capital efficiency: 10-year GAAP and Tangible ROIC averaged >27% (peak 40.1% in 2022, trough 24.4% in 2025). Operating ratio consistently outperforms unionized and non-union peers by 800-1500 bps (75.2% in FY2025, improving to 71.5% in Q3 2026). Pristine balance sheet with essentially zero debt ($20M total debt vs $120M cash) and negligible interest expense. Outstanding capital allocation discipline demonstrated by walking away from overpriced Yellow terminal bidding in 2023, preserving balance sheet strength while continuing counter-cyclical network capex and share repurchases. Owner FCF conversion consistently near or above 100% of Net Income.

column14: (1) What prevents competitors from arbitraging away returns: EMCOR possesses specialized engineering know-how, BIM prefabrication capabilities, deep relationships with general contractors and facility owners, and the largest aggregate pool of scarce skilled craft labor (union electrical and mechanical trades) in North America. (2) Empirical proof of moat: While 5-year median ROIC is high (~19.5% historical median, spiking to >40-50% in 2024-2025 during the AI data center buildout), this capital efficiency is mathematically driven by an asset-light working capital model rather than pricing power. Historically (2014-2020), operating margins hovered tightly in the 4.0% to 5.8% range, reflecting competitive bidding. (3) Primary erosion threats: Customer project deferrals in non-residential construction, cyclical capex normalization among hyperscalers and semiconductor manufacturers, wage inflation/craft labor shortages eroding fixed-price margins, and competition from national and regional specialty contractors (e.g., Comfort Systems, Quanta, local union shops).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). EMCOR is an exceptionally well-run specialty electrical and mechanical contractor currently enjoying peak-cycle earnings and record margins (~10%) from hyperscale AI data centers and reshoring mega-projects. However, specialty contracting lacks a structural, cycle-neutral economic moat. Work is won via competitive bidding or negotiated GMP/cost-plus contracts where bargaining power remains with facility owners and general contractors. Outside of cyclical supply crunches for skilled trades, operating margins historically average 4-6%, proving that pricing power cannot be sustained above inflation across the full business cycle without volume loss or competitive substitution.
column21: Multi-Cycle Financial Track Record: Revenues grew from $6.7B in FY15 to $14.6B in FY24 and over $15B in FY25. Consolidated operating margins averaged 4.0%-5.8% from 2014-2020 before expanding to 9.2% in FY24 and 10.1% in FY25, propelled by the unprecedented surge in hyperscale data center, semiconductor fab, and industrial cleanroom construction. GAAP ROIC expanded from historical averages of 15-20% (10Y median 19.5%) to 52.6% in 2024 and 41.8% in 2025; however, this high ROIC is primarily an artifact of an asset-light balance sheet with negative invested capital in certain operating units (funded by billings in excess of costs). Segment Breakdown: U.S. Electrical Construction (~35-40% of revenue, leading margins >12%), U.S. Mechanical Construction (~35-40%), U.S. Building Services (~20-25%), and Industrial Services. Divested lower-margin UK operations in 2024. Pricing Power & Customer Lock-in: Contracts are project-based (fixed-price lump sum, GMP, time & materials, cost-plus); building owners and general contractors routinely solicit competing bids from regional and national MEP peers (e.g. Comfort Systems USA, Quanta, Cupertino Electric). FCF & Balance Sheet: FCF generation is stellar (>100% net income conversion, ~$1.3B FCF in 2024, ~$1.2B in 2025), and the balance sheet is pristine with >$1.1B in cash and virtually zero funded long-term debt, providing exceptional downside protection. Nevertheless, contracting remains an inherently cyclical, project-dependent industry without an unassailable pricing moat across full macroeconomic cycles.

column14: Specialized off-site modular MEP fabrication capacity, proprietary BIM modeling, and scarce skilled trades labor pool provide project execution differentiation in high-density data centers. However, the business is fundamentally a mechanical and electrical subcontractor operating under competitive bid and fixed-price contracts without customer switching costs, locking-in contracts, or pricing power through full construction cycles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). While Comfort Systems USA possesses specialized mission-critical HVAC, piping, and modular prefabrication engineering know-how for hyperscale data centers and advanced manufacturing, contracting is inherently a project-based, competitively bid business. The company generates the majority of revenues from fixed-price contracts and lacks unilateral pricing power across the full business cycle, as demonstrated by operating losses and low single-digit margins (0-3%) during construction downcycles (2010-2014). Recent record margins and ROIC reflect acute cyclical labor scarcity and an AI data center infrastructure boom rather than an unassailable structural economic moat.
column21: Long-term financial history reveals significant cyclicality: operating margins were -3.4% in 2011 and averaged 3-6% from 2012-2019 before surging to 10-12%+ during the post-2022 AI data center hyper-cycle (net income expanded from $323M in FY23 to $522M in FY24 and $1.02B in FY25 on $9.10B revenue, with backlog reaching $11.9B). While 10Y median ROIC stands at 24.2% and balance sheet is conservative ($62M LT debt in 2024), contracting revenues are primarily fixed-price without inflation-linked escalators or structural customer switching lock-in. Customers (hyperscalers, general contractors) face zero disincentive to rebid future phases across competing MEP contractors (EMCOR, Limbach, Cupertino Electric) once cyclical labor scarcity eases.

column14: Specialized engineering talent, complex infrastructure consulting, and long-standing client relationships, but lack of pricing power in competitive bidding and human-capital intensity limit returns. Erosion threats include procurement price pressure, commoditization of routine design work by AI/BIM automation, and wage inflation for technical talent.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%). Jacobs Solutions operates as a premier global provider of engineering, design, and consulting services for critical infrastructure and water, but historical 10-year median ROIC of ~10.8% falls short of the 12% hurdle. Engineering consulting suffers from competitive procurement pressures, heavy reliance on billable professional hours, and goodwill from serial M&A (e.g. CH2M Hill, PA Consulting), preventing sustained super-normal returns on capital.
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 10.8% (FY2022 ~9.2%, FY2023 ~9.8%, FY2024 ~8.1-10.0%, FY2025 ~11.6%), consistently below the 12% threshold across the cycle. Despite successfully spinning off lower-margin government services (CMS and Cyber & Intelligence merged into Amentum in Sept 2024) to streamline into higher-value infrastructure, consulting margins remain capped by competitive bidding and professional staff costs. Operating margins hover in the 8-11% range, and heavy goodwill from past acquisitions dilutes reported invested capital returns.

column14: Largest specialized lineman and craft labor workforce in North America with proprietary Northwest Lineman College training pipeline, but returns are constrained by competitive bidding, low-margin project execution (GAAP operating margin ~4.5-5.5%), and utility rate-case cost discipline. Primary erosion risks include labor wage inflation, fixed-price project cost overruns, and utility customer insourcing.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Specialty utility infrastructure contractor operating at thin GAAP operating margins (4.5–5.5%) with a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~7.5–8.5%, falling well short of the mandatory 12% capital efficiency threshold. Despite secular tailwinds from grid modernization and renewable/data center interconnections, Quanta remains a project contractor lacking the pricing power and structural economic moat required to generate excess economic rents across the cycle.
column21: Quanta Services operates as a specialty engineering and construction contractor for electric power, renewables, and underground infrastructure. While revenue has compounded strongly due to electric grid hardening, energy transition, and large acquisitions (Blattner in 2021 for $2.7B, Cupertino Electric in 2024 for $2.7B), profitability is structurally constrained by the economics of construction contracting. Over 2020-2024, GAAP operating margins ranged from 4.1% to 5.2% and GAAP ROIC averaged ~7.5%–8.5% (2020: ~7.0%, 2021: ~6.4%, 2022: ~6.9%, 2023: ~8.3%, 2024: ~8.8%), never approaching the 12% hurdle. Serial large-scale M&A has bloated invested capital with substantial goodwill and intangible assets ($5B+), keeping ROIC low even during peak utility capex cycles. Regulated utility clients enforce rigorous cost oversight and competitive bidding, preventing Quanta from exercising genuine inflation-plus pricing power.

column14: Operates premier, unreplicable toll road concessions over scarce rights of way (Toronto 407 ETR, Texas Managed Lanes LBJ/NTE/I-66/I-77) that provide real-time dynamic congestion pricing and contractual toll escalation outpacing inflation. Competitors cannot replicate these urban transit corridors due to land scarcity, environmental permitting, and massive capital barriers. Primary erosion threats include finite concession duration, political/regulatory pushback on dynamic toll rates, and execution cost overruns in construction.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Ferrovial controls world-class irreplaceable infrastructure concessions (Toronto 407 ETR, Texas Managed Lanes LBJ/NTE/I-66/I-77) with proven dynamic congestion pricing, its competitive advantage period is fundamentally truncated. As a hybrid civil engineering and concession group with ~80% of revenue derived from construction contracting, its Mauboussin persistence base rate is Tier 4 (CAP 5–10 years). Severe secular headwinds on Macrotrend 2 (manual civil construction labor scarcity and wage inflation) and Macrotrend 5 (cost of capital and refinancing friction on €9.4B of debt), combined with contractually finite concession lifespans and political risk around dynamic toll caps, prevent a 15+ year runway.
column21: FY2025 revenue reached €9,627M (+8.6% LfL), with Construction generating €7,653M (79.5% of total) at a thin 3.9% adjusted EBIT margin. Toll Roads (Cintra) drove group profitability with adjusted EBITDA of ~€1,000M+ supported by strong traffic on Texas Managed Lanes (NTE, LBJ) and distributions from 407 ETR (equity accounted). Balance sheet carries €9,356M in long-term debt (€5,114M net debt) against €1,508M EBIT, resulting in €438M annual interest expense. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 9.86% (tangible ROIC ~10.6-11.2%), distorted by heavy capital expenditure, project-level financing, and lower-margin civil contracting. Concession portfolios carry finite contract horizons (LBJ/NTE to 2061, I-77 to 2069, JFK NTO to 2060).

column14: Unrivaled global dealer network (150+ independent dealers, ~2,700 locations) and massive installed base create insurmountable barriers in machine uptime, 24-hour parts distribution, and secondary market resale value. Proven by 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 20.7%, operating ROIC of 24.0%, and sustained positive pricing realization through the 2021-2024 inflationary surge. Primary erosion threats include low-cost Asian competitors expanding in emerging markets and alternative powertrain technology transitions.
column20: Dominant global heavy equipment and power systems franchise protected by an irreplicable 100-year dealer distribution and service network. Highly resilient across macrotrends as a key provider of autonomous mining technology, data center backup power generation, and equipment for infrastructure reshoring and mineral extraction. ME&T manufacturing operations operate in a net cash position with consolidated net debt repayable in 2.3 years and 98% multi-year FCF conversion. [5-10Y g: machine volume 2.5% + pricing power 2.0% + services/parts mix 1.5% - cyclical margin normalization 0.5% + net share buybacks 2.5%]
column21: 10-year track record demonstrating multi-cycle resilience and O&E execution. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 20.68% and Operating ROIC of 23.95%. Multi-year Owner FCF conversion of 97.97% ($9.24B FCF on $8.88B net income in FY2025). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS compounded from $13.42 in 2019 to $22.39 in 2024. Industrial ME&T balance sheet holds net cash ($9.98B cash vs ~$8.6B debt), with consolidated debt backed by Cat Financial receivables. Growing aftermarket parts and services revenues ($22B+) provide strong cycle damping.

column14: Extensive global distribution and service network provides replacement parts and maintenance lock-in, but captive truck OEMs (Daimler Truck, PACCAR, Volvo) have developed their own proprietary powertrains (Detroit Diesel, PACCAR MX, Volvo D13) and actively limit Cummins' pricing power. Historical ROIC is cyclical (5.2% in FY2023 post-$2.04B emissions settlement; FY2024 boosted by Atmus divestiture), while operating margins remain modest at 8-11%. Terminal decarbonization headwinds threaten the diesel core, while Accelera clean tech remains deeply unprofitable with $458M in 2025 impairments.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Truck OEMs (Daimler, PACCAR, Volvo) have vertically integrated captive engines, stripping Cummins of independent pricing power. Modest operating margins (8-11%) and severe Clean Air Act emissions penalties ($2.04B in 2023) demonstrate lack of an unassailable moat. Secular decarbonization creates terminal risk for the diesel core, while Accelera remains loss-making with $458M in 2025 write-downs.
column21: 10-year median ROIC is ~15.2%, but multi-cycle returns are volatile. FY2023 GAAP ROIC plunged to 5.2% due to a $2.04B pre-tax regulatory settlement for emissions defeat devices ($1.675B cash civil penalty paid in FY2024, crashing FCF to $279M on $3.95B net income). Operating margins average 8-11% with gross margins at 24-25%, reflecting intense OEM bargaining power and cyclical capital goods dynamics. Accelera clean tech revenue of $460M (~1.4% of total sales) recorded $458M of impairment/restructuring charges in FY2025. Total debt stood at $7.55B as of year-end 2025.

column14: Barriers to Entry: PACCAR's premium Kenworth, Peterbilt, and DAF nameplates command industry-leading residual values, driver preference, and dealer loyalty, backed by an extensive network of 2,200+ global dealer locations and global distribution scale in PACCAR Parts. Proof of Moat: 86 consecutive years of net profitability through severe economic and freight recessions; 10-year median ROIC of ~18.5%, with cycle peaks reaching 18.8% in 2023 and 15.7% in 2024. Primary Erosion Threats: The whole-truck manufacturing segment (~70% of revenue) is inherently tied to cyclical freight carrier capex; in downcycles, carriers defer fleet renewal and OEMs must discount build slots or offer subsidized financing. Long-term capital demands are further elevated by decarbonization mandates (BEV/hydrogen powertrains and battery joint ventures like Amplify Cell Technologies), risking powertrain commoditization.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing & Proof of Moat, REJECT). While PACCAR is an exceptionally managed commercial vehicle manufacturer with premier brands (Kenworth, Peterbilt, DAF) and 86 consecutive years of net profitability, its core whole-truck operations (~70% of revenue) sell into a deeply cyclical freight transport market. PACCAR lacks unconstrained pricing power >= inflation across the full cycle; during freight recessions (as evidenced in 2024-2025 where truck revenues fell 22% and ROIC compressed to ~9.1-9.5%), OEMs must grant price concessions and incentives to maintain build schedules, failing the Munger standard for cycle-resilient pricing power.
column21: Multi-Cycle Track Record: 86 consecutive years of net profitability. 10-year median ROIC is ~18.5%, but fluctuates with freight cycles (ROIC ~11-12% in 2020, 18.8% in 2023, 15.7% in 2024, and ~9.1-9.5% in 2025). Consolidated revenues were $33.66B in 2024 and $28.44B in 2025 (-15.5%), with Truck net sales declining 22% from $24.84B to $19.37B on 144,200 deliveries. Segment Breakdown: Truck (~68% of 2025 revenues); PACCAR Parts (~24% of revenues, growing from $6.67B in 2024 to $6.87B in 2025 as a high-margin aftermarket stabilizer); PACCAR Financial Services (~8% of revenues, $2.21B in 2025 with $15.64B in portfolio debt). Capital Allocation: Zero manufacturing debt, fortress manufacturing balance sheet, consistent ~50% net income dividend payout via regular and special dividends, and $1.17B in 2025 R&D/capex. Despite operational excellence, cyclical truck discounting during freight downturns precludes structural pricing power >= inflation across the cycle.

column14: Installed base of ~23,000 locomotives provides captive aftermarket parts and services. However, returns on invested capital are structurally sub-hurdle (5-year median GAAP ROIC of 7.23%, with every year since the 2019 GE Transportation merger below 10%) due to $14B of merger goodwill/intangibles and immense countervailing buyer power from consolidated Class I freight railroads operating under Precision Scheduled Railroading.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 7.2% < 12%, REJECT). While Wabtec holds an entrenched North American locomotive installed base supporting recurring aftermarket service, its GAAP ROIC is structurally depressed (5-year median 7.23%, failing the 12% hurdle every year over the past 9 years). Concentrated Class I freight railroad buyers exert strong procurement leverage and maintain long asset lifecycles, constraining autonomous pricing power and returns on capital.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record reflects 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 7.23% (2021: 4.96%, 2022: 5.60%, 2023: 7.23%, 2024: 9.36%, 2025: 9.69%), failing the 12% hurdle. The 2019 GE Transportation acquisition brought $14.05B of goodwill and intangibles onto the balance sheet against $11.14B in equity. column14: Unassailable two-sided network effect and regulatory switching costs as the SEC-mandated proxy clearinghouse handling >80% of US beneficial share votes. 17.1% 5-year median GAAP ROIC, >100% tangible ROIC, and 98%+ client revenue retention. Primary erosion risks (SEC fee schedule changes, broker consolidation, blockchain disintermediation) remain well-hedged by ongoing digital automation.

column21: 10-year GAAP ROIC compounded from 13.9% to 19.2% (5-year median 17.1%), with tangible operating ROIC >100%. column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 22.6% and operating ROIC of 25.0%. Owner FCF conversion averages 93.4% ($1.3B-$1.5B+ annual owner FCF). Revenue compounded from $1.45B in FY2017 to $4.65B in FY2025, with Net Income expanding from $394M to $1.55B. Balance sheet is an unassailable fortress with $0 funded debt and $1.9B+ in cash. Multi-year service agreements with automatic price escalation clauses and customized garment branding/RFID tracking generate substantial customer switching friction. Moat proven by 27% 5-year median GAAP ROIC, ~78% operating tangible ROIC, and steady gross margin expansion past 50%. Primary erosion risks include sharp cyclical employment drawdowns reducing client headcount and potential antitrust headwinds on large-scale M&A.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Dominant North American uniform and facility services route monopoly with unmatched route density, pricing power, and elite owner-operator execution. column21: 10-year GAAP ROIC expanded from 13.5% in FY2016 to 31.7% in FY2025 (median 27.0%); operating tangible ROIC exceeds 75%. Continuous peak-to-peak EPS compounding through COVID disruptions (Owner EPS compounded from $1.12 in FY2016 to $5.21 in FY2025 at ~16% CAGR). Proven pricing power with gross margin expanding from ~44% to >50%.

column14: Government IT services and systems integration lack a structural economic moat. While security clearances and customer intimacy offer mild incumbency advantages, federal procurement rules (FAR, CAS), DCAA audits, and mandatory contract recompetes every 3 to 7 years invite intense price-based bidding from capable peers (General Dynamics IT, Booz Allen, CACI, SAIC). Multi-cycle median GAAP ROIC (~8-11%) falls short of the 12% threshold, and pricing power above wage inflation is structurally constrained by government cost-plus fee caps and LPTA/best-value competition.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (3a = None, 3b = N, REJECT). Defense and civil government IT contractor operates in a competitive procurement framework governed by the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR). Mandatory periodic recompetes, statutory fee caps on cost-plus work, and wage inflation exposure on fixed-price contracts preclude durable pricing power above inflation. Multi-cycle median GAAP ROIC historically sits around 8-11%, failing the 12% capital efficiency hurdle.
column21: 10-year historical GAAP ROIC has averaged ~8-11% (FY16 4.3%, FY17 5.7%, FY18 7.7%, FY19 9.9%, FY20 7.7%, FY21 8.3%, FY22 7.8%, FY23 3.5%, recovering to ~13.8% in FY24 and ~15.5% in FY25), with 5-year median ROIC below 12%. Substantially all revenues derive from US government prime and subcontracts (DoD, Intelligence Community, FAA, VA, DHS) subject to budgetary sequestration, continuing resolutions, and open competition mandates under the Competition in Contracting Act.

column14: High customer switching costs and prohibitive qualification/recertification barriers (FAA, FDA, ISO) across aerospace, medtech, and laboratory testing lock in customers, enabling steady 2-3% pricing power above inflation with zero churn. 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 14.1% and operating margins expanding from 20.6% in 2016 to 25.8% in 2025 confirm moat durability against customer consolidation or industrial cyclicality.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Premier niche instrumentation and precision electromechanical compounder with unassailable switching costs across aerospace, medtech, and automation. High pricing power demonstrated by consistent 2-3% annual price increases with zero churn. Highly resilient across all 5 macrotrends with negligible capex needs (<2% of sales) and fortress balance sheet (interest coverage >23x, net debt/EBITDA <0.8x). column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 14.1% and operating ROIC >200% on tangible capital. Unbroken 10-year Owner EPS CAGR of 10.96% ($2.69 in 2016 to $7.67 in 2025) demonstrating pristine peak-to-peak compounding through the 2020 pandemic. FCF conversion averages 107.6% of net income with capex under 1.8% of sales ($130M on $7.4B revenue). Segment revenue split: Electronic Instruments Group (~70% of sales) and Electromechanical Group (~30% of sales). Highly disciplined M&A playbook proven by rapid deleveraging following the $1.9B Paragon Medical acquisition in late 2023, reducing net debt from $2.9B to under $1.7B in 2024 and net debt to 0.42x annual net income by 2025. Interest coverage stands at a fortress 23.5x ($1,910M EBIT vs $81M interest expense).

column14: Proprietary solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) stack intellectual property (400+ patents) and long-term on-site service/maintenance contracts create switching costs, but economic returns are structurally depressed by high stack refurbishment/replacement expenses and competitive displacement risks from gas turbines, reciprocating engines, and grid interconnections.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). While Bloom Energy captures strong 'speed-to-power' tailwinds from AI data centres and C&I customers facing multi-year grid interconnect queues, it fails to demonstrate empirical moat proof or economic profitability. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~2.1% (far below the 12% hurdle), burdened by cumulative net losses since inception (accumulated deficit of ~$3.99B through FY2025), high periodic stack replacement costs, and chronic reliance on convertible debt offerings and equity dilution.
column21: 10-year and 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~2.1%, failing the 12% capital efficiency hurdle. Despite top-line revenue scaling from $1.20B (FY22) to $1.33B (FY23), $1.47B (FY24), and $2.02B (FY25), Bloom continues to generate GAAP net losses (-$88.4M in FY25), with GAAP operating margins remaining in low single digits (1.5% in FY24, 3.6% in FY25). Accumulated deficit stood at $3.99B at the end of FY25. Capital structure features heavy use of convertible senior notes (e.g., 2.5% Green Notes due 2025, 3.0% Green Notes due 2029) and repeated debt-for-equity exchanges to manage debt maturities and liquidity.

column14: Core moat is rooted in a massive global installed base of distributed control systems (DeltaV, Ovation) and mission-critical measurement instrumentation (Rosemount, Micro Motion, Fisher valves) embedded in continuous process facilities (chemical, refining, power, life sciences). Switching costs are near-prohibitive due to severe operational disruption risk, 24/7 continuous process downtime costs, and strict regulatory requalification burdens. Historical 10-year median ROIC of 14.2% and gross margins >42-45% demonstrate pricing power, but returns on total invested capital have been diluted by heavy acquisition goodwill (AspenTech, NI). Erosion threats include open process automation (OPAF) standards and IT/OT convergence.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Emerson commands an entrenched installed base in process automation (DeltaV, Fisher, Rosemount), it operates in Tier 3 Capital Goods (baseline CAP 10-15 years) and faces severe structural headwinds under the 5-Macrotrend framework. A significant portion of its process automation revenue remains anchored to fossil fuel refining, chemicals, and hydrocarbon infrastructure facing long-term energy transition headwinds (Macrotrend 4). Simultaneously, the ongoing transition toward open-architecture, software-defined automation (Macrotrend 1) challenges proprietary hardware lock-in, forcing multi-billion dollar defensive M&A (AspenTech, National Instruments) at full valuations that introduce substantial cyclicality, goodwill dilution, and integration complexity. Net CAP is capped at 5 years, failing the 15-year threshold.
column21: Fiscal 2024-2025 revenue reached $17.5B-$18.0B with segment EBITA margins expanding to 26-27.6% and FCF of $2.9B-$3.2B. However, consolidated ROIC has been suppressed into the 7-8% range following aggressive portfolio reshuffling ($8.2B acquisition of National Instruments and $7.2B full buyout of AspenTech funded by the sale of Copeland/Climate Technologies). While the legacy process installed base provides resilient recurring aftermarket maintenance, test & measurement and discrete automation face high cyclical volatility. Heavy exposure to energy and chemical capex cycles coupled with high purchase-price goodwill impairs long-term compounding predictability, limiting CAP to <15 years.

column14: Engineering specification approvals in commercial/industrial electrical blueprints, UL/NEMA safety certifications, deep electrical distributor network integration (Graybar, WESCO), and substantial switching costs once equipment is embedded in facility electrical architecture. Proven by 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 15.8%, segment operating margins expanding to 24.5% in 2025, and sustained positive price realization. Primary erosion threats stem from well-capitalized global peers (Schneider Electric, ABB, Siemens) sharing distributor channels and capacity additions.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Eaton is a leading electrical equipment provider currently benefiting from the data center power surge, Capital Goods is structurally anchored to Tier 3 persistence (10-15Y baseline) where excess returns face rapid competitive fade (f=0.21-0.25) from global peers (Schneider, ABB, Siemens) expanding manufacturing capacity. Additionally, Eaton carries an unhedged terminal headwind in its legacy Vehicle segment (~$2.5B sales, 9% of total) producing ICE truck transmissions and valvetrains facing secular phase-out from fleet decarbonization, reducing CAP below the 15-year hurdle.
column21: Multi-Cycle Financial Track Record: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 15.8% (recovering from 5.2% in 2020 to 13.8% in 2024 and ~12-15% in 2025). Net income expanded from $1.41B in 2020 to $3.79B in 2024 and $4.09B in 2025. Segment operating margins expanded from ~16-17% in the 2010s to a record 24.0% in 2024 and 24.5% in 2025. Free cash flow reached $3.5B in 2024 and $3.6B in 2025, converting ~88% of GAAP net income. Segment Breakdown (FY2025): Electrical Americas $13.28B (48.4% of sales, record margin driven by data center and utility megaprojects), Electrical Global $6.82B (24.8%), Aerospace $4.25B (15.5%), Vehicle $2.51B (9.1%), and eMobility $0.60B (2.2%). Total net sales reached $27.45B (+10% YoY). Moat & Pricing Power: Engineering specification approvals in architectural blueprints, UL/NEMA safety codes, distributor shelf lock-in with Graybar and WESCO, and installed-base switching costs. Demonstrated pricing power with 3-5%+ annual price realization across 2022-2025 offsetting material inflation. Capital Allocation & Balance Sheet: Long-term debt stood at $9.89B at FY2025 year-end against $4.09B net income (~2.4x net debt/NI) and interest coverage of 21.6x. Disciplined pruning of lower-return assets (divested Hydraulics for $3.3B in 2021) and bolt-on acquisitions (Fibrebond, Ultra PCS). Runway Failure: Capital goods competitive dynamics, multi-brand distributor presence, and secular phase-out of the $2.5B ICE vehicle segment cap longevity below the 15-year CAP threshold.

column14: Dominant North American factory automation franchise (~40-50% domestic PLC share) powered by Allen-Bradley/ControlLogix installed base and deep engineering switching costs; plant engineers are trained on Studio 5000 and factory rewiring incurs catastrophic downtime risk. Empirical proof: 10-year median ROIC ~16% and ~40% gross margins. Primary erosion threats: open industrial automation standards (OPAF, IEC 61499), software-defined virtual PLCs running on commodity IPCs, and Siemens' global scale advantage.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Rockwell holds an entrenched installed base in North American factory automation via Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, its terminal runway is capped by structural shifts toward Software-Defined Automation (SDA), virtualized PLCs (vPLCs), and Open Process Automation (OPAF) standards that decouple control software from proprietary hardware backplanes. Combined with high cyclicality in discrete manufacturing capex (FY24 sales down 9%, net income down 37% from FY23 peak) and fierce global competition from Siemens outside North America, ROK fails the 15-year secular resilience threshold.
column21: Rockwell Automation generates ~$8.3B in revenue across Intelligent Devices (~45%), Software & Control (~30%), and Lifecycle Services (~25%). Historical ROIC is solid (FY24 GAAP ROIC 15.2%, FY25 14.6%, 10-year median 16.2%), supported by high switching costs in operational technology (OT) control layers and an exclusive North American distributor network (Wesco, etc.). However, earnings power is deeply cyclical: GAAP net income dropped from $1,387M in FY23 to $953M in FY24 (-31%) and $869M in FY25 (-37% from peak) due to customer inventory destocking and slower capex in automotive, semiconductor, and battery markets. More critically, the long-term durability of its proprietary hardware architecture faces structural headwinds from IT/OT convergence, software-defined control (vPLCs), open standards (OPAF), and PC-based automation (Beckhoff, Siemens). Long-term debt of $2.6B and total debt of $3.2B against cash of ~$0.5B; interest coverage remains healthy (>8x), but the business model fails the 15-year unhedged disruption runway standard of Gate 4.

column14: High switching costs and severe operational risk of data center downtime (critical power and thermal infrastructure integrated into hyperscaler facility blueprints, supported by a 3,500+ technician global service network). Proof of moat: 5-year median ROIC ~14.2%, scaling to >25% in FY2024-FY2025 with adjusted operating margins expanding above 20% and adjusted FCF reaching ~$1.9B. Primary erosion threats: Hyperscaler standard-setting via Open Compute Project (OCP) modular architectures designed to eliminate vendor lock-in, intense competition from integrated electrical conglomerates (Schneider Electric, Eaton) possessing in-house switchgear and circuit breaker supply chains, and rapid hardware transition cycles in direct-to-chip liquid cooling.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Vertiv is a key beneficiary of current hyperscaler AI data center buildouts providing critical thermal and power infrastructure, it is a cyclical capital goods hardware manufacturer (Tier 3 persistence, baseline CAP 10-15 years). The business faces rapid technology cycle risks in liquid cooling architectures, intense competition from full-suite electrical giants (Schneider Electric, Eaton) that possess in-house switchgear/breakers, and commoditization pressure from hyperscale tech giants actively championing Open Compute Project (OCP) standardized modular designs to avoid proprietary lock-in. Hardware sales are transactional capex purchases subject to severe cyclical digestion following AI infrastructure waves, limiting confident moat duration to 5 years.
column21: Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE: VRT) specializes in critical digital infrastructure, generating ~80% of revenue from data center power and thermal management. Net sales surged 28% in FY25 to $10.23B with adjusted operating margins expanding to 20.4% and adjusted FCF reaching ~$1.9B, driven by high rack-density AI cooling demand (liquid cooling CDUs, Liebert precision chillers). ROIC rebounded from single digits in FY21-FY22 to ~28% in FY25, and net leverage declined to ~0.5x EBITDA. However, Vertiv's track record reveals pronounced cyclicality and operational vulnerability: in 2021-2022, operating income collapsed due to fixed-price customer contracts and lack of component pricing power amid supply chain disruption. Unlike diversified electrical peers (Schneider Electric, Eaton), Vertiv lacks internal manufacturing of low-voltage electrical switchgear and circuit breakers. Furthermore, customer concentration among a handful of hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Google, AWS) creates long-term structural vulnerability, as hyperscalers leverage Open Compute Project (OCP) standards and Asian ODM partnerships to disintermediate proprietary thermal/power hardware.

column14: Extreme local route density, 120-year Lindy brand equity (Orkin), and commercial compliance lock-in create insurmountable barriers to entry. Pest eradication is a non-discretionary sanitation necessity representing a negligible budget expense, enabling consistent 3-4%+ annual pricing realization with minimal churn. 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 35.3% and tangible ROIC >100% confirm moat endurance. Primary erosion risks: technician labor wage inflation, digital customer acquisition cost inflation, and tuck-in M&A integration friction.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global leader in route-based pest and termite control (Orkin, Fox, HomeTeam) operating an asset-light recurring subscription engine with 80%+ contract revenue. Unassailable local route density and 120-year Lindy brand equity deliver consistent 3-4% pricing power above inflation and 35%+ GAAP ROIC. Structurally insulated from all 5 macrotrends as physical pest eradication cannot be automated by AI and benefits from warming climate trends. Pristine balance sheet with net debt under 0.8x Net Income and 25x+ interest coverage. [5-10Y g: organic customer volume 4.0% + pricing realization 3.5% + tuck-in M&A 2.0% - technician wage/marketing drag 0.5% + share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: Empirical track record: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 35.3% and tangible Operating ROIC >100%.
