Free cash flow conversion averaged 112% over 5 years (FY2025 Owner FCF of $610.3M on GAAP Net Income of $526.7M), supported by minimal capex intensity (~0.7% of sales, $28.1M in FY2025). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS compounded from $0.38 in 2016 to $1.29 in 2025 (13.7% CAGR) across 24 consecutive years of top-line revenue growth. Balance sheet remains exceptionally conservative: LT debt of $486.1M against $100.0M cash (net debt of $386.1M = 0.73x Net Income) and EBIT of $726.1M delivering 25.4x interest coverage. M&A strategy is self-funded from operating cash flows, with successful integration of Fox Pest Control ($339.5M in 2023) expanding route density.

column14: Irreplaceable network of ~206 active MSW landfills, ~245 transfer stations, and specialized hazardous waste TSDFs/landfills via US Ecology. Stringent environmental regulations, high capital costs, and intense local NIMBYism create near-insurmountable permitting barriers that make landfill airspace virtually unreplicable. Landfill ownership enables vertical internalization of collection waste while capturing high-margin third-party tipping fees. Empirically demonstrated by 32%+ tangible operating ROIC and consistent 5-8% core pricing increases exceeding CPI inflation across cycles.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. #2 North American solid waste and environmental solutions leader with an unreplicable network of permitted landfills and transfer stations. Indispensable non-discretionary municipal and commercial demand drives reliable 5-7% core pricing power above inflation. High physical-world insulation from AI disruption, with tailwinds from US industrial reshoring, fleet automation, and landfill-gas-to-RNG monetization. Balance sheet satisfies the essential infrastructure concession standard with >5.0x interest coverage (5.75x) supporting A-/A3 investment-grade ratings, backed by >100% FCF conversion and resilient municipal cash flows. [5-10Y g: solid waste volume 1.5% + core price 4.5% + environmental solutions & tuck-in M&A 2.0% - capex drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 10-year financial record demonstrates exceptional compounding: sales grew from $11.4B (2016) to $19.0B (2025), EBIT grew from $1.54B to $3.30B, and Owner EPS compounded at 10.6% CAGR from $2.19 to $6.85. Operating tangible ROIC consistently exceeds 30% (34.3% in 2025, 10-year median 32.5%), while reported GAAP ROIC is ~10-11% due to $17.4B accumulated acquisition goodwill/intangibles (Allied Waste, US Ecology). Free cash flow conversion is outstanding at 115.5% in 2025 ($2.48B Owner FCF vs $2.14B Net Income; 2026 guidance $2.57B+). In 2026, core pricing executed at 6.3-6.4% on related business (7.6-7.8% open market), well above cost inflation. Balance sheet features $13.7B LT debt against $3.30B EBIT and $4.30B OCF, generating 5.75x interest coverage which safely meets the >5.0x infrastructure threshold.

column14: High customer switching costs driven by installed base of testing instruments requiring proprietary chemical reagents and testing kits. Testing represents <1% of customer operating budget but is legally mandated for municipal water compliance and product traceability, granting sustained 2-3% annual pricing power over inflation. Proven by 27% median GAAP ROIC and ~60% gross margins.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Essential water quality analytics and packaging coding oligopoly with 60%+ recurring revenue from proprietary consumables. Moat protected by extreme switching costs, regulatory mandates (EPA/Clean Water Act), and Danaher Business System operational DNA (VES). Pristine balance sheet with net cash position and >95% FCF conversion. [5-10Y g: water & packaging volume 3.5% + proprietary consumable price 2.0% + bolt-on M&A reinvestment 1.5% + net share buybacks 1.0% - tariff/tax drags 0.5%]
column21: Multi-cycle capital efficiency demonstrated by 27.1% 5-year median GAAP ROIC, tangible operating ROIC >100%, and consistent 58-60% gross margins. Water Quality (~60% of revenue; Hach, Trojan, ChemTreat) provides essential water testing instruments and proprietary reagents for municipal and industrial compliance; Product Quality & Innovation (~40% of revenue; Videojet, Linx, Esko, Pantone) provides mission-critical date coding, marking, and packaging workflow solutions. Over 60% of total revenue is recurring consumables and services. Razor-and-blade model creates massive switching costs: testing consumables are a negligible fraction of plant operating costs (<1%) but non-compliance triggers legal shutdown or heavy fines. Owner FCF conversion averages >96% of net income with minimal capex (~1.1% of revenue). Balance sheet is a net cash fortress ($2.03B cash vs $1.97B debt at FY2025; interest coverage 13.3x), allowing disciplined self-funded bolt-on acquisitions and opportunistic share repurchases under the Veralto Enterprise System (VES).

column14: North America's largest network of permitted solid waste landfills (>250 active landfills) creates an insurmountable physical moat protected by extreme NIMBYism, stringent EPA environmental permitting, and prohibitive transport economics. WM controls ~25-30% of US landfill capacity. Demonstrated pricing power: core yield increases of 5-7% annually across commercial, industrial, and residential contracts consistently exceed CPI. Tangible ROIC averages ~25% and 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 12.24%. Primary erosion threat is municipal zero-waste mandates or landfill diversion regulations, which WM actively hedges via North America's largest recycling and renewable natural gas (RNG) capture network.
column20: Passes all 6 gates under the essential infrastructure standard. North America's premier solid waste and landfill infrastructure monopoly protected by irreplaceable permitted landfill acreage, NIMBY zoning barriers, CPI+ pricing power, 12.2% median GAAP ROIC (25% tangible ROIC), and 112% FCF conversion. Balance sheet meets peace-of-mind standards for essential concessions: elevated Stericycle acquisition debt is backed by non-discretionary municipal cash flows, interest coverage of 6.6x-6.8x (>5x hurdle), and organic deleveraging with buybacks paused. [5-10Y g: solid waste volume 1.5% + core pricing 4.5% + RNG and recycling reinvestment 1.5% + Stericycle synergies 1.0% - deleveraging buyback pause drag 0.5%]
column21: FY2016-FY2025 financial history shows extraordinary operational resilience and cash generation: Sales grew from $13.6B (2016) to $25.2B (2025), EBIT expanded from $2.3B to $4.3B, and Operating Cash Flow doubled from $3.0B to $6.04B. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 12.24% with operating/tangible ROIC steady at 24.96%. FCF conversion averaged 111.9% of net income over the cycle. Owner EPS compounded at 8.85% CAGR from $2.65 in 2016 to peak $6.81 in 2024. Stericycle acquisition in Nov 2024 added high-barrier medical waste and compliance services; post-acquisition net debt of ~$22.0B is actively being reduced via strong organic Owner FCF ($3.0B+ annually) and suspended share buybacks, maintaining investment-grade interest coverage >6.5x.

column14: Gas turbine oligopoly (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries) commanding >60% of the global heavy-duty market. Moat anchored in massive installed base (>7,000 gas turbines) locked into 10-25 year CPI-indexed Contractual Service Agreements (CSAs) with extreme switching costs. High-temperature materials science (single-crystal superalloys, thermal barrier coatings) and regulatory certification create insurmountable barriers to new entrants. Primary erosion risks: long-term decarbonization of the electric grid replacing gas peakers/baseload, rapid wind turbine technology obsolescence, and cyclical customer capex cutbacks.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While GE Vernova enjoys a strong near-term cyclical boom from AI data center power demand and grid electrification, its business model fails the 15+ year predictable runway requirement. Heavy Electrical Equipment is anchored in Tier 3 (10-15Y baseline), and the company faces severe long-term terminal headwinds from Macrotrend 4 (Energy Transition): thermal gas turbines, its core cash cow, face regulatory net-zero phase-outs and long-term substitution by renewables, storage, and nuclear over a 15-30 year horizon. Additionally, its offshore wind division has suffered acute execution and contract inflation volatility, reflecting the capital-intensive cyclicality of heavy industrial equipment.
column21: Spun off from GE in April 2024. Power segment benefits from an installed base of >7,000 gas turbines with multi-decade CSAs, driving 2024 revenue of $34.9B, net income of $1.6B, FCF of $1.7B, and 12.3% ROIC. FY 2025 saw revenue grow to $38.1B, FCF of $3.7B, and ROIC of 25.2% (aided by a $2.9B valuation allowance release), with total backlog expanding to $150B on surging AI data center baseload power and grid equipment demand. However, historical pre-spin 5-10 year median ROIC was ~7.5% due to deep cyclical downturns and massive wind turbine operating losses (-$1B+ annually in 2022-2023). Long-term terminal value remains exposed to the 15-30 year decarbonization horizon for fossil gas generation and severe cyclicality in heavy capital goods orders.

column14: Dominant North American residential standby generator market share (~70-75%) and an authorized dealer network (>8,500 certified installers) provide recognized brand leadership and distribution reach. However, this fails to deliver durable economic returns across the cycle. Standby generators are one-off durable equipment (15-20 year replacement lifecycle) whose sales are lumpy and outage-driven. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~10.5% (falling to ~5.7% in 2025), failing the 12% hurdle. When severe weather events subside, dealer inventory destocking strips away pricing power and crushes operating margins. Commercial & Industrial (C&I) backup power faces intense price competition from Cummins, Caterpillar, and Kohler, while clean energy storage (PWRcell) has been plagued by warranty issues and component failures.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power). Dominant brand and dealer network in residential standby generators, but the underlying economic engine is a cyclical, outage-dependent durable equipment manufacturer. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~10.5% (and ~5.7% in 2025) fails the non-negotiable 12% hurdle. Lacks consistent pricing power across the cycle as post-storm dealer destocking drives severe margin compression, C&I remains highly competitive against industrial conglomerates, and clean energy storage diversification struggled with warranty liabilities.
column21: Generac experienced peak windfall earnings in 2021 ($550.5M net income, 17.8% ROIC) driven by Winter Storm Uri and pandemic home-spending tailwinds, but normalized profitability deteriorated significantly: net income was $214.6M in 2023 and $159.6M in 2025. GAAP ROIC fell from 17.8% (2021) to 11.0% (2022), 6.9% (2023), 10.5% (2024), and 5.7% (2025), yielding a 5-year median ROIC of ~10.5%, well below the 12% threshold. 2025 net sales of $4.21B were split across Residential Products (~54%), C&I Products (~35%), and Other Products & Services (~11%). Free cash flow is volatile (-$25.6M in 2022, +$604.8M in 2024, +$271.2M in 2025). Long-term debt stands at ~$1.5B against episodic operating cash flows.

column14: Formidable enterprise switching costs and toll-booth dynamics rooted in mission-critical payroll execution and tax compliance for 1.1M+ clients, yielding ~92% client retention. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 77.4%, operating margins consistently expanding from 21% to ~28%, and steady 2-4% annual price indexation with negligible churn. Primary erosion threats include cloud-native HCM competitors (Workday, Paychex, Rippling) and client transition execution between legacy platforms and Next Gen HCM.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Indispensable global payroll and HCM toll booth processing wages for 1 in 6 US workers across 1.1M+ clients with ~92% retention. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends: unmatched proprietary employment dataset defends against AI disintermediation, demographic complexity accelerates HR outsourcing, and client fund float ($35B+) provides structural interest rate tailwinds. Fortress AA- balance sheet with 0.17x net debt/NI and 13.5x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: employment payroll volume 2.5% + HR software cross-selling 2.5% + price indexation 2.0% + client float income 1.0% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 77.4% and tangible operating ROIC >100%. Free cash flow conversion averages 106% of net income with capex under 1.5% of revenue. 10-year Owner EPS CAGR of 11.7% with zero cyclical down years, demonstrating continuous peak-to-peak compounding through the 2020 recession and post-pandemic inflation. Segment revenue is split between Employer Services (~67%) and PEO Services (~33%), securing massive customer lock-in via mission-critical regulatory compliance. AA- rated balance sheet ($4.2B cash vs $5.0B LT debt) with 50 consecutive years of dividend increases.

column14: High switching costs and administrative lock-in for small and mid-sized businesses. Migrating payroll, tax filings, benefits, and 401(k) records creates prohibitive operational disruption and compliance risk, resulting in 82-83% retention (majority of churn is SMB business mortality). Verified by 10-year median ROIC of ~45% (26.8% in FY2025 post-$4.1B Paycor deal) and operating margins near 40%. Pricing power proven by consistent 3-4% annual module price hikes. Erosion risks: low-end self-service payroll upstarts (Gusto, Rippling), broader SMB mortality in severe recessions, and regulatory changes in PEO co-employment rules.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Indispensable small-to-medium business payroll, PEO, and HCM toll booth serving ~800k clients with deep regulatory switching costs. Demonstrates consistent pricing power (+3-4% annually) and structural inflation resilience via client fund float interest. Paycor acquisition expanded mid-market scale while keeping leverage conservative (Net Debt/EBITDA ~1.2x, interest coverage 9.3x) and cash conversion exceptional (>100% Owner FCF/NI). [5-10Y g: SMB client base expansion 2.0% + PEO & HCM cross-sell 3.0% + price indexation 2.0% - margin drags 0.0% + share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: 10-year financial record shows exceptional capital efficiency: median GAAP ROIC of 44.9% (26.8% in FY2025 post-Paycor), operating margins steady at 38-41%, and Owner FCF conversion exceeding 100% (FY2025 Owner FCF of $2.23B on $1.76B net income). Revenue split across Management Solutions (~75%), PEO & Insurance (~25%), and high-margin client fund float interest. Serves ~800k clients with 82-83% retention. Closed $4.1B Paycor acquisition in April 2025 funded by fixed-rate bonds; LT debt of $4.56B is comfortably covered (Net debt/Owner FCF of 1.56x, EBIT/Interest of 9.3x).

column14: Specialty materials qualified into customer engineering, safety, and regulatory specifications create customer switching barriers (Tyvek, Kevlar, Nomex, FilmTec water filtration). However, fails proof of moat with a 10-year median ROIC of ~7.8% and 2024–2026 ROIC hovering at 3.4%–4.1%, well below the 12% hurdle and failing to exceed cost of capital. Key erosion threats include cyclical end-market swings, customer substitution, raw material inflation, and lingering legacy environmental (PFAS) liabilities.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). DuPont fails the Munger proof-of-moat requirement with a 10-year median ROIC of ~7.8% and 2024–2026 ROIC languishing at 3.4%–4.1%, consistently trailing its ~8% cost of capital. Despite switching costs in qualified specialty materials (Tyvek, Kevlar, Nomex, water filtration membranes), serial corporate restructurings (DowDuPont separation, Celanese divestiture, Qnity Electronics spinoff), recurring asset write-downs, cyclical end-market exposure, and substantial legacy PFAS liabilities prevent economic value creation.
column21: Empirical capital efficiency over the trailing decade shows structural inability to clear the 12% ROIC hurdle: 10-year median ROIC is 7.8% and average ROIC is below 4% due to large asset impairments, restructuring charges, and cyclical troughs. In 2024–2026, ROIC remained depressed at 3.4%–4.1% against an ~8% WACC. Free cash flow generation has been volatile ($473M in FY2024, $227M standard / $689M transaction-adjusted in FY2025, ~$793M TTM in 2026), heavily burdened by separation transaction expenses and ongoing multi-billion-dollar PFAS legacy liabilities. The core business lacks the pricing power and reinvestment returns required of an elite compounder.

column14: High customer switching costs and proprietary protocols in building automation (Building Solutions / EBI) and industrial process controls (Experion PKS DCS), where hardware and software are deeply embedded into industrial plants and commercial facilities. Empirically supported by 10-year median ROIC of 14.5% and stable gross margins of 33-37%. Primary erosion threats include cloud-native open industrial IoT architectures, commoditization of building sensors, and intense competition from specialized automation peers (Siemens, Schneider Electric, Emerson, Rockwell).
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Industrial Conglomerate / Capital Goods industry base rate of 10-15 years (Tier 3) incurs a -5 to -10 year deductive haircut due to active terminal headwinds on Macrotrend 4 (Energy Transition & Resource Limits) from its UOP fossil refining and petrochemical process licensing exposure, alongside industrial capex cyclicality and massive restructuring friction from its activist-driven three-way corporate breakup.
column21: 10-year historical GAAP ROIC median of 14.5% and steady ~35% gross margins confirm moat existence in building solutions and process automation. However, long-term organic revenue growth has languished at 2-4% CAGR, masking structural deceleration with debt-financed M&A (Carrier Access Solutions for $4.95B, Civica, CAES). Decarbonization pressures create terminal headwinds for UOP petroleum refining technologies. Following Elliott Management's $5B activist campaign in late 2024, the company executed a three-way split (Solstice Advanced Materials in late 2025, Honeywell Aerospace/HONA in mid-2026), leaving Honeywell Technologies as an automation-focused entity managing separation friction and elevated net debt ($20B+ peak in 2025).

column14: High switching costs from specialized materials science specifications (OEM automotive bonding, aerospace sealants, electronics films) where re-qualification is costly and disruptive, reinforced by proprietary patent estates and Lindy consumer brand power (Scotch, Post-it, Command). 10-year median ROIC ~14.8%. Primary erosion threats: R&D productivity decay, generic chemical substitution, and severe environmental/product liability overhang.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Industrial Conglomerate base rate (Tier 3: 10-15 years) suffers a severe -10 year haircut under Macrotrend [4] (Energy Transition & Resource Limits / Environmental Regulation). 3M faces existential, multi-decade regulatory and litigation overhang from PFAS ('forever chemicals'), forcing the complete phase-out and abandonment of all PFAS manufacturing by end of 2025 (~$1.3B high-margin revenue elimination), alongside massive settlements ($10.3B-$12.5B public water systems, $7.35B AFFF, $6.0B earplugs) and ongoing global cleanup liabilities. Under the Rule of Secular Resilience, active terminal regulatory and environmental headwinds cap CAP at <= 10 years, failing the 15-year hurdle.
column21: 10-year historical median ROIC of 14.8%, but GAAP profitability heavily impaired in 2023-2024 by >$15B in pre-tax litigation charges. Organic sales growth stagnated near 0% for a decade prior to the April 2024 Solventum healthcare spinoff. Post-spin 2024-2025 net sales stand at ~$24.6B-$24.9B with adjusted operating margins recovering to 21-23% and normalized FCF around $4.4B-$4.9B. However, gross balance sheet obligations remain elevated with net debt of ~$6.7B plus multi-billion dollar scheduled settlement cash outflows extending into the 2030s. The compounding runway is structurally impaired by the forced exit of fluorinated chemistry and enduring international environmental liability exposure.

column14: Portfolio of specialized niche industrial leaders (Markem-Imaje coding/ink consumables, OPW fueling/clean energy hardware, PSG biopharma & specialty pumps) benefits from installed-base switching costs and consumable replenishment. However, consolidated capital efficiency fails empirical moat hurdles: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~10.1% (FY21 11.7%, FY22 11.7%, FY23 9.9%, FY24 9.9%, FY25 10.3%), structurally below the 12.0% threshold due to continuous M&A goodwill dilution (~$4.5B+ goodwill) and cyclical competition in commercial refrigeration and engineered components.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). While Dover operates defensible niche positions with switching costs in marking consumables (Markem-Imaje), retail fueling hardware (OPW), and specialty pumps (PSG), its consolidated 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~10.1% (2021-2025 range of 9.9% to 11.7%) structurally fails the 12% cycle hurdle. Substantial goodwill from continuous bolt-on M&A and cyclical headwinds in climate/engineered goods dilute returns.
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~10.1% (FY21 11.7%, FY22 11.7%, FY23 9.9%, FY24 9.9%, FY25 10.3%), consistently below the 12.0% hurdle across economic cycle peaks and normalizations. Consolidated revenue ~$8.1B in FY25 across five segments (Clean Energy & Fueling, Pumps & Process Solutions, Climate & Sustainability, Engineered Products, Imaging & Identification). Operating margins have hovered between 15.6% and 17.0%. FCF generation is healthy (~$1.0B-$1.1B annually, ~13-14% FCF margin), but heavy historical M&A has accumulated over $4.5B in goodwill, preventing capital returns from exceeding cost of capital by an elite compounder margin.

column14: Fluke holds an entrenched global brand and distribution standard in electrical test and measurement tools, with high technician switching barriers and safety certification lock-in (CAT III/IV); ASP holds a sticky installed base of STERRAD low-temperature hydrogen peroxide sterilization systems with proprietary consumable cassettes in hospitals. Gross margins expanded from 57.3% in 2021 to 59.5% in 2024, demonstrating consistent pricing power above inflation and tangible ROIC well above 25%, despite GAAP ROIC being diluted by goodwill. Primary erosion risks stem from digital commoditization of hardware and disruption of acquired facility/workflow SaaS assets.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Capital Goods and Enterprise Software anchor at Tier 3 (10-15Y baseline). Fortive's portfolio pivot toward mid-market facility and healthcare workflow software (Accruent, Gordian, ServiceChannel, Provation) faces acute terminal headwinds from Macrotrend [1] (Automation & Cognitive Tech / Agentic AI), which reduces seat counts and automates routine contractor dispatch and documentation workflows. Combined with serial corporate restructuring and repeated spinoffs (Vontier in 2020, Ralliant/Tektronix in 2025), predictable competitive advantage runway is capped at 5 years (< 15Y hurdle).
column21: Historical GAAP ROIC has remained subdued at 3.5%-5.5% (median ~5-9.5%) due to an accumulated goodwill burden exceeding $10.1B in FY2024 ($7.3B post-Ralliant spin in FY2025) on total assets of $11.7B-$17.0B, although tangible operating ROIC exceeds 25% and gross margins are stable-to-expanding at 57%-60%. In June 2025, Fortive completed the tax-free spin-off of its Precision Technologies segment (Tektronix, Qualitrol, Gems) as Ralliant Corporation (NYSE: RAL), leaving Fortive focused on Intelligent Operating Solutions (IOS: Fluke, ServiceChannel, Accruent, Gordian) and Advanced Healthcare Solutions (AHS: ASP, Censis, Provation), generating ~$720M in continuing operating income. While Fluke multimeters and ASP sterilizers exhibit high brand trust and pricing power, Fortive's heavy capital deployment into expensive workflow SaaS acquisitions has created an asset base vulnerable to AI agent disruption and portfolio churn, failing the 15-year CAP persistence threshold.

column14: Scale economies shared via the premier North American B2B MRO distribution network. Unrivaled next-day/same-day SKU availability across millions of maintenance products creates an insurmountable logistics moat. Customers are highly price-insensitive because downtime costs far exceed component prices. Proved by 10-year median ROIC of ~40% (operating ROIC >45%) and resilient gross margins (~39%). Primary erosion risk is long-term disintermediation from digital marketplaces (e.g., Amazon Business) in non-critical commodity SKUs.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Unchallenged North American leader in MRO distribution with an entrenched distribution network, automated KeepStock inventory solutions, and high-frequency mission-critical parts availability. Structural beneficiary of US manufacturing reshoring and automation. Stellar capital allocator with 54+ consecutive years of dividend growth, conservative leverage (net debt <1.1x net income, interest coverage >30x), and ~40% ROIC across cycles. [5-10Y g: high-touch MRO volume 3.5% + endless assortment (Zoro/MonotaRO) 3.0% + contract pricing 2.0% - industrial cyclical drag 0.5% + share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 10-year financial record demonstrates peerless capital efficiency: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 39.7% and operating ROIC of 46.5%. Free cash flow conversion averages 85-95% of GAAP net income ($1.62B Owner FCF in FY2025). Peak-to-peak earnings power grew from $9.96 in 2016 to $38.96 in 2024. Robust balance sheet with $2.36B LT debt vs. $585M cash ($1.78B net debt), amortizable in ~1.0 year of net income, with interest coverage exceeding 30x EBIT/Interest.

column14: Utility specification approvals (Approved Vendor Lists / AVLs), long utility relationships, and contractor brand habits create immense switching costs. The component cost (connectors, insulators, arresters, meter enclosures) is negligible compared to the catastrophic cost of power outages or wildfire liability. Proved empirically by 10Y median ROIC of 17.2% and operating margin expansion to >20% across inflationary cycles. Erosion threats include distributor consolidation (WESCO, Graybar), utility inventory destocking cycles, and foreign competition in non-critical commercial fittings.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Essential physical electrical infrastructure manufacturer serving electric utilities (~63% of sales) and behind-the-meter industrial/data center facilities (~37%). High customer switching costs rooted in utility specification approvals (AVLs) and catastrophic cost of component failure. Highly resilient under 5-macrotrend filter: active secular beneficiary of grid modernization/hardening, electrification, AI data center power demand, and North American manufacturing reshoring. Pruned commoditized commercial lighting to focus on high-margin utility hardware. High cash generation with ~100% FCF conversion and pristine balance sheet with 18.9x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: grid/data center volume 3.5% + utility spec price 2.0% + tuck-in M&A 1.5% - normalization margin drag 0.5% + net buyback 0.5%]
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 17.2%; FY24 ROIC ~14.7% and FY25 ROIC ~13.3-19.0% with operating ROIC >18%. Consolidated FY25 revenue of $5.84B ($3.67B Utility Solutions, $2.17B Electrical Solutions) with operating income of $1.21B (20.7% margin). FY25 FCF of $874.7M on net income of ~$880M (99.4% conversion); FY24 FCF of $810.8M on net income of $780M (104% conversion). Balance sheet strength: total debt $2.3B, net debt ~$1.8B, net debt/EBITDA ~1.3x, net debt repayable from FCF in ~2.0 years. FY25 interest coverage ratio of 18.9x ($1,208.8M operating income / $64.1M net interest expense).

column14: Engineered niche positive displacement pumps, flow meters, and precision fluidics designed into OEM platforms with high switching costs and regulatory re-qualification barriers, delivering stable 44-45% gross margins and 20%+ operating margins.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Tier 3 Capital Goods baseline of 10-15 years haircut due to cyclical industrial machinery end-market exposure and reliance on serial debt-funded M&A rollups facing higher cost of capital headwinds (Macrotrend 5). Lacks the 15+ year predictable competitive runway across its 40+ disparate decentralized operating units.
column21: 10-year average GAAP ROIC of 12.4%, with gross margins stable at 44-45% and operating margins at 20-22%. Free cash flow conversion consistently exceeds 100% ($603M in FY2024, $617M in FY2025). Operates in three segments: Health & Science Technologies, Fluid & Metering Technologies, and Fire & Safety/Diversified Products. While individual niche components have high switching costs, the serial acquisition roll-up strategy (e.g. Mott Corp for ~$1B) has expanded goodwill/intangibles to over 50% of assets and total debt to ~$1.8B, compressing recent ROIC to ~8.2-8.3% and failing the 15-year secular persistence threshold.

column14: Barriers: Mission-critical compressed air, vacuum, and fluid handling systems create moderate customer switching costs through proprietary replacement parts, preventive maintenance contracts, and severe downtime risks in industrial processes. Empirical Failure: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6-8% (peaking near 8% in 2023-2024 and dipping to ~5.2% in 2025), failing the 12% threshold across the cycle due to an inflated invested capital base of ~$14B-$15B loaded with >$8.4B in goodwill and acquisition intangibles. Primary Erosion Threats: Direct competition from global category leader Atlas Copco (which compounds at >20% ROIC), disintermediation by third-party aftermarket service providers, and continuous acquisition multiple dilution.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 5-8% vs. 12% hurdle, REJECT). While Ingersoll Rand's installed base of industrial compressors and blowers provides stable recurring aftermarket parts and service revenue, GAAP ROIC structurally fails the 12% Munger threshold. Serial M&A (including the 2020 Gardner Denver merger and the $2.3B ILC Dover buyout in 2024, followed by a $230M goodwill impairment in 2025) has accumulated over $8.4B in goodwill against ~$10B in equity, permanently depressing returns on total invested capital relative to best-in-class peer Atlas Copco.
column21: Multi-cycle ROIC track record consistently sub-hurdle: GAAP ROIC averaged 6-8% post-merger (FY23 ~8.2%, FY24 ~6.0-7.9%, FY25 ~5.2-6.4%). Net income of $588.8M in FY25 on stockholders' equity of $10.09B and total debt of $4.85B reflects invested capital of ~$13.5B-$14.5B. Balance sheet carries $8,484M of goodwill as of FY25 (nearly half of $18.3B total assets), exacerbated by a $229.7M goodwill impairment on ILC Dover in FY25. Segment revenue is driven by Industrial Technologies & Services (~80%) and Precision & Science Technologies (~20%). Although FCF conversion is healthy (>80% of net income) and gross margins are stable around 42-44%, structural capital allocation through high-multiple rollups prevents the business from generating hurdle-clearing returns on invested capital.

column14: Unassailable operational and engineering moat driven by Customer-Back Innovation (~19,000 granted/pending patents), iconic Lindy benchmark brands (Hobart, Miller Electric, Paslode, Instron), and asymmetric customer switching costs where components/fasteners/equipment represent a tiny fraction of end-product or project cost but are mission-critical to avoid catastrophic line halts. Proof of moat is seen in a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 36.8% (tangible ROIC ~100%), operating margins expanding from 20% to 26.3%+, and consistent positive price/cost spread across inflation cycles. Primary erosion risks are general automotive volume cyclicality and customer platform transitions.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Premier multi-industrial compounder anchored by the proprietary ITW Business Model (80/20 Front-to-Back, Customer-Back Innovation, and radical decentralization). High pricing power across 7 diversified segments with mission-critical products representing a trivial fraction of customer cost. Fortress balance sheet with 14.4x interest coverage, net debt under 2x net income, and >85% free cash flow conversion. [5-10Y g: organic volume 2.0% + pricing power 1.5% + 80/20 mix & operating leverage 1.5% + net share buybacks 2.0%]
column21: Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC sustained between 26% and 40% over the last decade (5-year median 36.8%, operating ROIC 98.5%-112.7%). Operating margins steadily expanded from ~20% in 2012 to 26.3% in 2025 (guided 26.5%-27.5% in 2026). FCF conversion averaged 95.3% over 10 years ($24.9B Owner FCF vs $26.2B GAAP Net Income). Revenue is well-diversified across 7 autonomous segments: Automotive OEM (19%), Food Equipment (16%), Test & Measurement and Electronics (17%), Welding (13%), Polymers & Fluids (12%), Construction Products (12%), and Specialty Products (11%). Exceptional capital allocation: Dividend King with 50+ consecutive years of dividend hikes, disciplined organic reinvestment, and regular share buybacks retiring ~1.5-2.0% of float annually with zero dilutive mega-M&A. Balance sheet carries $6.7B LT debt against $4.2B EBIT (14.4x interest coverage) and $851M cash, repayable from Owner Earnings in 1.9 years.

column14: (1) Moat Barriers: High customer switching costs and razor-and-blade consumable lock-in. Nordson's precision dispensing equipment is custom-engineered directly into customer assembly lines and medical device specifications. While dispensing hardware represents <1% of total production line cost, dispenser failure causes catastrophic line shutdowns or product ruin. Customers rely on Nordson's proprietary replacement nozzles, valves, hoses, and tips (~45-50% recurring revenue). In medical, fluid components are locked into regulatory filings (FDA 510(k)/PMA). (2) Empirical Proof: 10-year median ROIC of 17.2%, gross margins consistently 53-56% across cycles, EBITDA margins of 30-32%, and 61 consecutive years of annual dividend increases. (3) Erosion Threats: Cyclical customer capex freezes in electronics/semiconductors; potential commoditization of lower-end fluid dispensing by Asian competitors; and integration execution on larger acquisitions (ARAG, Atrion).
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global precision dispensing and fluid management leader with embedded switching costs and 45-50% recurring aftermarket consumable revenue. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends: active hardware enabler of automation (AI chip packaging, robotic assembly) and demographic healthcare tailwinds (medical fluid delivery), with zero unhedged exposure to energy or structural inflation. Balance sheet fortress with $660M+ FCF, 7.0x interest coverage, and LT debt/NI at 3.5x with rapid organic deleveraging. [5-10Y g: industrial/medical volume 3.0% + pricing power 1.5% + portfolio mix/reinvestment 1.5% - integration/cyclicality drag 0.5% + net share buybacks 1.0%]
column21: Multi-cycle financial performance anchors quality: 10-year median ROIC of 17.2%; gross margins exceptionally stable between 53% and 56% over 10+ years; EBITDA margins 30-32%. FY2025 revenue reached $2.79B with operating income of $711.7M and Net Income of $484.5M. Owner FCF was $661.1M in FY25 (136% conversion) and $491.8M in FY24 (105% conversion), exceeding the 80% FCF conversion threshold. Balance sheet is strong: Long-term debt reduced from $2.10B in FY24 to $1.68B in FY25 ($1.99B total debt) following the $800M Atrion acquisition; LT debt / Net Income is 3.47x (passes <= 4.0x); FY25 interest coverage (EBIT / Interest) is 7.04x ($711.7M / $101.1M, passes > 5.0x). Segment breakdown: Industrial Precision Solutions (~48%), Medical and Fluid Solutions (~28%), and Advanced Technology Solutions (~24%). 61 consecutive years of dividend growth.

column14: Extreme customer switching costs and safety regulation create an entrenched maintenance toll booth on ~2.5M units. High barriers to entry arise from hyper-dense technician route networks, OEM proprietary components, and IoT predictive monitoring (Otis ONE). Proven by 30%+ operating ROIC, ~94% retention, and consistent contractual price escalations (+3-4%) above labor inflation. Primary erosion risks are prolonged non-residential construction slowdowns and independent service provider encroachment in low-rise commercial segments.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global leader in elevator and escalator manufacturing and maintenance with a premier 2.5M+ unit service portfolio acting as a regulatory-mandated safety toll booth. Switching costs and customer retention (>93%) protect high-30s% operating ROIC and >100% FCF conversion. Highly insulated across all 5 macrotrends, benefiting from urbanization, aging demographics, and IoT predictive diagnostics (Otis ONE). Balance sheet negative equity is an accounting legacy of the 2020 UTC spin-off; underlying cash engine produces >$1.4B FCF and >9.8x interest coverage with no refinancing ruin risk. [5-10Y g: service unit volume 3.0% + contractual pricing 2.5% + modernization mix 1.5% - China new equipment drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: Otis operates the world's largest elevator maintenance portfolio with ~2.5 million units under contract, generating over 80% of operating profit from high-margin recurring services (~24.5% segment operating margin). 5-year operating ROIC exceeds 30-40% and owner FCF conversion averages 102% of net income (FY2025 FCF $1.44B vs $1.38B NI; FY2024 FCF $1.44B vs $1.65B NI). Annual capex is minimal at ~1% of revenue ($152M in 2025). EBIT of $2.13B provides 9.8x interest coverage against $217M interest expense. Modernization backlog grew 30% in 2025, providing visible conversion pipeline as the global installed base ages.

column14: High switching costs derived from mission-critical, custom-engineered motion and control components specified directly into long-cycle aerospace and industrial platforms. Replacement components require OEM or FAA qualification, creating captive aftermarket demand across an unreplicable global distribution network (13,000+ locations). The proprietary Win Strategy systematically drives value-based pricing, consistently exceeding inflation through multiple raw material and supply chain cycles.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global motion and control powerhouse transformed by The Win Strategy into a top-quartile compounder. Spec'd-in aerospace systems and critical industrial components generate high-margin recurring aftermarket toll-booth cash flows. Secular tailwinds across commercial aero ramp, factory automation, and data center thermal cooling. Rapid deleveraging post-Meggitt with net debt < 2.0x NI and 12.6x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: commercial & defense aerospace volume 4.0% + industrial automation & data center thermal 2.0% + Win Strategy value pricing 2.0% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 16.6% with tangible operating ROIC > 100%. Free cash flow conversion consistently exceeds net income (FY25 FCF conversion 102%, TTM 106%). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS compounded at 14.6% CAGR from $8.32 in FY16 to $32.22 in FY25 without cyclical impairment. Balance sheet is strong post-Meggitt with long-term debt reduced to $7.47B, net debt/TTM NI at 1.91x, and EBIT/Interest at 12.64x. Operating margins expanded over 800 bps over the decade to 24.5%+ via Win Strategy operational excellence.

column14: Moat mechanisms include contractor installed-base lock-in and digital automation ecosystems (IntelliCenter) in Pool, alongside proprietary replacement filtration cartridges (Everpure, Manitowoc Ice) in Water Solutions. However, GAAP ROIC has hovered around 10-12% over multi-year cycles (FY20 ~9.8%, FY21 ~14.7%, FY22 ~9.4%, FY23 ~12.1%, FY24 ~12.1%, FY25 ~12.0%) burdened by ~$3.4B in goodwill/intangibles from serial acquisitions. Incremental ROIIC across the cycle is weak (~5%) following the $1.6B Manitowoc acquisition. Pricing power is constrained by heavy reliance on two-step wholesale distribution (PoolCorp) and triopoly equipment competition against Hayward and Fluidra.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Pentair operates solid franchises in residential pool equipment and commercial water filtration, but fails the strict Munger compounder hurdle. 5-year median GAAP ROIC sits at ~12.0% and incremental ROIIC across the cycle is sub-par (~5%) following the debt-financed $1.6B Manitowoc Ice acquisition. Pentair lacks independent pricing power to overcome volume cyclicality, evidenced by double-digit volume drops during housing/renovation downturns and heavy reliance on wholesale distributor intermediaries (PoolCorp) facing triopoly competition against Hayward and Fluidra.
column21: Financial track record: Net sales reached $4,083M in FY2024 and $4,176M in FY2025. GAAP Net Income: $553M (FY21), $481M (FY22), $623M (FY23), $625M (FY24), and $654M (FY25). While free cash flow conversion is strong ($693M in FY24, ~$747M in FY25, FCF/NI >100%), the balance sheet carries $1.6B in net debt and $3.4B of goodwill and intangibles. 5-year GAAP ROIC (FY20: 9.8%, FY21: 14.7%, FY22: 9.4%, FY23: 12.1%, FY24: 12.1%, FY25: 12.0%) has a median of ~12.0%, but post-2021 incremental capital deployed returned only ~5% due to the $1.6B Manitowoc Ice acquisition. Segments: Flow (~$1.6B sales; pumps, fluid treatment), Pool (~$1.4B sales; pumps, filters, automation), and Water Solutions (~$1.1B sales; commercial/residential filtration, ice machines). Customer lock-in & pricing power: Contractor loyalty and proprietary automation provide sticky aftermarket replacement (~80% of pool revenue), but pricing power is curtailed by distributor concentration (PoolCorp) and triopoly rivalry with Hayward and Fluidra. Pool volumes fell double-digits during the 2022-2024 channel destocking and interest rate spike.

column14: Unrivaled brand equity and technician loyalty supported by over 4,800 franchised mobile vans providing direct-to-bay sales, financing, and lifetime warranty service. Proven by a 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 20.0%, tangible ROIC of 26-28%, and steady 50-51% gross margins across cycles. Primary risks include technician demographic aging, low-cost e-commerce tool competition, and OEM proprietary diagnostic lock-out.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. The premier brand in professional mechanic tools with iconic franchised van distribution, sustained ~20% GAAP ROIC, and net cash balance sheet. Insulated from AI disruption as physical maintenance and complex diagnostics remain indispensable. [5-10Y g: auto repair volume 1.5% + diagnostic software & OEM mix 2.5% + pricing power 2.0% + net buybacks 1.5%]
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 20.0% with operating ROIC exceeding 26%. Multi-year Owner FCF conversion exceeds 95% ($7.6B Owner FCF generated vs $7.5B Net Income over 2016-2025). Fortress balance sheet with $1.62B cash against $1.19B debt (net cash position) and interest coverage above 26x. Peak-to-peak earnings power expanded from $9.39 EPS in 2016 to $19.78 EPS in 2024. Disciplined capital allocation under long-serving CEO Nick Pinchuk with minimal dilution, low capex (~1.5% of revenue), and 15+ years of consecutive dividend growth.

column11: Power tools, hand tools, and outdoor power equipment (lawnmowers, snow blowers) sold under brands like DEWALT, CRAFTSMAN, and BLACK+DECKER are durable, discretionary goods. Consumers, DIYers, and retail channels readily defer or forgo replacement during housing downturns and inflationary squeezes, failing the essential Western need standard.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Stanley Black & Decker is a cyclical manufacturer of power tools, hand tools, and outdoor equipment heavily exposed to discretionary DIY demand and housing turnover. During downturns, consumer tool purchases and home improvement projects are readily deferred. Furthermore, high retail customer concentration at Home Depot and Lowe's amplifies cyclical inventory destocking swings. Even if Gate 2 were bypassed, SWK would fail Gate 3b (10Y median ROIC of 7.2%, collapsing to 0-3.5% in 2023-2025 due to supply chain inflation and lack of pricing power) and Gate 5 (disastrous capital allocation on the $1.9B MTD outdoor power rollup and Craftsman acquisition, driving net debt to over $6B and requiring emergency multi-year restructuring).
column21: Historical 10-year median ROIC of 7.2% is far below the 12% Munger threshold, collapsing to ~0.0% in 2023, 2.4% in 2024, and 3.3-3.5% in 2025. Gross margins suffered severe compression from 37% to 25-28% during the post-pandemic supply chain and cost inflation shock, exposing a lack of pricing power relative to input inflation. Tools & Outdoor represents ~85% of revenue, heavily tied to DIY home improvement and big-box retail channels (The Home Depot and Lowe's). Aggressive debt-financed M&A (notably acquiring the remaining 80% of MTD Holdings for $1.6B cash in 2021 and Craftsman) expanded net debt to over $6.0B right at the peak of the pandemic demand bubble, forcing a $2B global cost reduction program, plant closures, asset sales (aerospace fastening divestiture), and dividend coverage strain.

column14: Municipal engineering specifications, certified utility standards, and vast global installed base of wastewater pumps and smart water infrastructure create customer switching inertia. However, empirical proof of moat is structurally absent: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.4% (FY21: 8.3%, FY22: 8.6%, FY23: 3.6%, FY24: 5.5%, FY25: 6.4%), consistently failing the 12% hurdle across the cycle. Dilutive mega-acquisitions (Sensus, Evoqua) continuously inflate the capital base with goodwill, while competitive RFP bidding and municipal budget caps prevent pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Despite strong secular tailwinds in water infrastructure and treatment, Xylem fails the empirical proof-of-moat hurdle. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.4% (FY21: 8.3%, FY22: 8.6%, FY23: 3.6%, FY24: 5.5%, FY25: 6.4%) and 10-year historical ROIC has averaged sub-10%, well below the 12% threshold. Serial M&A (Sensus for $1.7B, Evoqua for $7.5B) has continuously diluted capital efficiency, while municipal tender dynamics restrict real pricing power.
column21: Multi-cycle financial data confirms persistent sub-hurdle capital efficiency. GAAP ROIC: FY16 6.0%, FY17 8.0%, FY18 8.5%, FY19 6.7%, FY20 5.7%, FY21 8.3%, FY22 8.6%, FY23 3.6%, FY24 5.5%, FY25 6.4%. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.4%, far below the 12.0% hurdle. FY24 revenue of $8.56B converted to $1.01B operating income (11.8% margin) and $942M FCF. FY25 revenue of $9.04B delivered $1.22B operating income (13.5% margin) and $910M FCF. Despite solid FCF conversion and critical water installations, invested capital is heavily diluted by goodwill from serial M&A ($7.5B Evoqua merger closed May 2023). Municipal RFP procurement dynamics cap pricing power, leaving economic returns structurally mediocre across full business cycles.

column11: True discretionary big-ticket or deferrable cyclical; passenger air travel is highly cyclical, discretionary, and deferrable during economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (gate_2: 'N', REJECT). Categorized as a true discretionary big-ticket or deferrable cyclical under the Munger framework. Demand is highly cyclical and deferrable during recessions, ticket prices are aggressively shopped across digital aggregators, and corporate travel remains vulnerable to remote work/video collaboration substitution. Even on downstream metrics, Delta's 10-year median ROIC of ~8.5% falls well short of the 12% compounder hurdle.
column21: Delta Air Lines is a legacy network carrier operating passenger and cargo air transportation across domestic and international routes. Despite top-tier operational execution and high-margin American Express loyalty remuneration (~$7B in 2024), core passenger revenue (~85% of total) remains a capital-intensive, cyclical commodity exposed to severe demand shocks (e.g. 2020 pandemic operating loss of $12.4B), heavy recurring fleet capex ($3B-$5B annually), and volatile jet fuel and union labor expenses. 10-year median ROIC is ~8.5%, trailing the 12% cycle hurdle, with adjusted net debt of ~$14B-$18B.

column14: (1) Historical barrier was Herb Kelleher's classic scale economies shared model—point-to-point network, single 737 fleet type, 10-minute gate turns, high asset utilization, and unbundled-free perks (Bags Fly Free, open seating) passing operational efficiencies to flyers to build scale. (2) Empirical proof of moat has completely failed: 10-year median ROIC of 7.2% is far below the 12% hurdle, with operating margins collapsing post-pandemic and negative FCF in FY2024 (-$1.6B) and FY2025 (-$831M). The company possesses zero pricing power above inflation, functioning as a price-taker against network peers and low-cost carriers. (3) Primary erosion threats: complete convergence of pilot and crew labor costs with legacy network carriers under post-pandemic collective bargaining agreements, single-aircraft supply risk from Boeing 737 MAX delivery delays, and activist Elliott Management forcing abandonment of open seating and introduction of bag fees, dismantling core brand differentiation without conferring pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing Power). While Southwest historically pioneered the 'Scale economies shared' archetype in domestic aviation, its structural cost advantage has permanently eroded due to union labor cost convergence, Boeing fleet concentration bottlenecks, and aggressive industry capacity. 10-year median ROIC of 7.2% falls far short of the 12% hurdle, and free cash flow remained negative through FY2024 (-$1.6B) and FY2025 (-$831M). Severe commoditization and absence of pricing power above inflation forced management, under activist pressure from Elliott Investment Management, to abandon brand hallmarks (open seating, Bags Fly Free) in 2024-2025 in an attempt to stem margin decline, confirming price-taker economics.
column21: Empirical financial reality confirms structural lack of moat: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 7.2%, consistently below the 12% cost-of-capital hurdle across the full business cycle. Free cash flow conversion is severely impaired by heavy recurring aircraft reinvestment capex ($2B+ annually), resulting in negative FCF of approximately -$1.6B in FY2024 and -$831M in FY2025. Operating margins compressed to low-single digits post-pandemic as new pilot and flight attendant collective bargaining agreements established labor cost parity with legacy network carriers (Delta, United, American). In mid-2024, activist hedge fund Elliott Investment Management accumulated an ~11% economic stake, citing lagging ROIC and operational obsolescence, leading to an October 2024 settlement that forced board refreshment (retirement of Executive Chairman Gary Kelly) and sweeping commercial pivots: terminating open seating in favor of assigned/extra-legroom seating and scrapping 'Bags Fly Free' for standard tickets in 2025. These measures confirm that Southwest cannot command pricing power or earn supra-normal returns without mimicking legacy peer fee structures.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket purchase deferrable in recessions; passenger airlines are explicitly classified as deferrable cyclicals under Gate 2.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Reject Standard: True discretionary big-ticket or deferrable cyclicals — airlines). Commercial passenger air travel is a highly cyclical, deferrable expenditure subject to severe demand volatility during economic downturns, high operating leverage, and intense price competition.
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 7.8% is far below the 12% hurdle. Even during post-pandemic recovery (FY2024-2025 pre-tax margins of 7.3-8.1%), capital expenditures on aircraft fleet renewal absorb massive cash flow, while debt and finance leases (~$25B) remain heavy. Commercial passenger airlines are explicitly categorized under Gate 2 reject criteria as deferrable cyclicals lacking essential, non-discretionary demand insulation.

column14: Two-sided liquidity network effects across Mobility and Delivery. Demonstrated pricing power via take rate expansion (Mobility take rate expanded to ~28-29%) while platform trips reached 13.6B in FY2025. Tangible ROIC expanded to >20% (24.9% in FY2025) and GAAP ROIC reached 16.1%. Primary erosion threats: autonomous vehicle disintermediation and regulatory reclassification of gig drivers.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Uber has achieved scale profitability as a global two-sided mobility toll booth, its long-term competitive advantage period faces severe terminal disruption headwinds from autonomous vehicle (AV) commercialization (Macrotrend 1). Autonomous vehicle developers and fleet operators (e.g. Waymo, Tesla Cybercab) threaten to disintermediate Uber's network or capture the majority of fleet economics. Additionally, persistent regulatory and legislative pressure regarding gig-driver employment classification (Macrotrend 2) creates ongoing structural margin and operating model risks.
column21: FY2025 revenue reached $52.0B (+18% YoY) with Gross Bookings of $193.5B (+19% YoY) across 13.6B trips. Operating income expanded to $5.57B (10.7% operating margin) and free cash flow reached $9.8B (operating cash flow $10.1B). Tangible ROIC reached 24.9% in FY2025 (GAAP ROIC 16.1%). However, 10-year historical GAAP ROIC median is depressed (7.1% over 5 years) due to massive pre-2023 cash burn. Long-term runway is heavily truncated by AV robotaxi networks (Waymo scaling rapidly across US metros, Tesla developing proprietary ride-hailing app) which directly threaten Uber's core driver-rider network effect.

column14: Eastern US rail duopoly with Norfolk Southern provides core pricing power consistently 2-3% above rail cost inflation across ~20,000 route miles of physically unreplicable contiguous rights-of-way connecting major population centers and deep-water ports.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Irreplaceable eastern US rail duopoly (CAP = 15), but fails Gate 6 due to an overleveraged balance sheet (LT debt of $17.9B vs $3.47B Net Income = 5.15x, exceeding 4.0x ceiling), ongoing track maintenance capex ($2.5B) consistently exceeding depreciation ($1.65B) by 40-50%, past debt-funded buybacks, and macro-cyclical freight exposure with secular domestic coal runoff. [5-10Y g: volume 1.0% (net of coal decline) + price 2.5% + margin 0.5% + buybacks 2.5%]
column21: CSX operates ~20,000 route miles of irreplaceable rail infrastructure across 23 eastern US states and 2 Canadian provinces, forming an entrenched duopoly with Norfolk Southern. 2024 revenue of $14.0B spans Merchandise ($8.7B / 62%), Coal ($2.2B / 16%), Intermodal ($2.1B / 15%), and Trucking/Other ($1.0B / 7%). Operating margins averaged 37-41% over 2021-2024 (2024 Operating Income $5.25B, 37.5% margin; 2023 $5.50B, 37.5%; 2022 $5.95B, 40.1%). 5-year average GAAP ROIC has tracked 11.8-14.3% (2021: 15.1%, 2022: 15.3%, 2023: 14.3%, 2024: 13.5%), with persistent real core pricing power of 2-3% above rail cost inflation. FCF conversion is respectable (3-year average 82.6%; 2024 FCF $2.72B / NI $3.47B = 78.3%), but capital expenditures of $2.53B in 2024 and $2.26B in 2023 heavily exceed depreciation (~$1.65B), reflecting constant capital intensity to maintain right-of-way safety. Balance sheet leverage fails Gate 6: Long-term debt was $17.90B at year-end 2024 (total debt $18.50B) against $3.47B Net Income, resulting in LT Debt / Net Income of 5.15x (Net Debt / Net Income of 4.92x with $1.40B cash), far above the 4.0x ceiling, driven by past debt-funded share buybacks. Interest coverage remains solid at 6.3x (EBIT $5.25B / Interest $832M), but debt load, ongoing capex drain, and cyclical freight volumes fail the Munger peace-of-mind test.

column14: Eastern freight rail duopoly with CSX provides irreplaceable physical right-of-way infrastructure and pricing power consistently at or above inflation (+2-4% pricing spread). High barriers prevent arbitrage, but intermodal faces modal competition from long-haul trucking and coal faces secular volume decline.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (N, REJECT). Irreplaceable Eastern freight rail infrastructure network with duopoly pricing power, but fails Munger quality standards due to structural capital intensity (8-year FCF conversion 74% vs. >=80% threshold), 10.5% 10-year median ROIC, and an overleveraged balance sheet ($16.5B LT debt vs. $2.87B NI, 5.74x leverage vs. <=4.0x hurdle). [5-10Y g: volume 1.0% + price 2.5% + operating ratio recovery 1.0% + share repurchases 2.0%]
column21: Norfolk Southern operates ~19,300 route miles across 22 Eastern states, forming an essential freight rail duopoly with CSX. Pre-disaster ROIC was 12.5-13.5% (2021-2022), but 10-year median ROIC is 10.5%, reflecting the heavy capital requirements of rail maintenance. In 2025, operating revenue was ~$12.2B, EBIT was $4,356M, interest expense was $792M (5.5x coverage, down from pre-2023 levels and dipping to 3.95x in 2023), and GAAP net income was $2,873M (still below the 2022 peak of $3,270M). Free cash flow was $2,157M in 2025, $1,671M in 2024, and $852M in 2023, against net income of $2,873M, $2,622M, and $1,827M respectively (3-year FCF conversion 63.9%; 8-year conversion 74.1%), falling short of the >=80% FCF conversion requirement due to $2.2B-$2.4B annual capex additions. Balance sheet carries $16,480M long-term debt and $607M current debt against $1,530M cash, yielding 5.74x LT debt to net income, breaching the <=4.0x peace-of-mind threshold. Calamity tier is denied because the leverage and low cash conversion are multi-cycle structural characteristics of the business model rather than temporary artifacts of the 2023 East Palestine derailment.

column14: Irreplaceable transcontinental infrastructure moat: 32,000-route-mile contiguous rail network across 23 western US states forming an entrenched duopoly with BNSF. Right-of-ways, classification yards, bridges, and port/border connections are physically and economically impossible to duplicate. Empirical proof: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 16.0% (ranging consistently between 13.5% and 17.5% from 2016 to 2025), operating margins sustained around ~40% (operating ratio ~60%), and multi-year FCF conversion >95%. Pricing power demonstrated through contractually indexed escalators (RCAF) and fuel surcharges yielding 100-200 bps above rail inflation across cycles, supported by captive shippers lacking viable transportation alternatives. Primary erosion threats: regulatory intervention by the Surface Transportation Board (STB) on reciprocal switching or rate caps, secular decline in thermal coal carloads, and long-term highway freight automation.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Transcontinental rail duopoly with BNSF across 23 western US states. Irreplaceable 32,000-route-mile physical infrastructure asset with insurmountable right-of-way barriers. Resilient across all 5 macrotrends with zero unhedged headwinds: physically insulated from AI disruption, major beneficiary of USMCA reshoring and Mexico cross-border trade via 6 gateways and Ferromex, 3-4x fuel efficiency advantage over trucking, and formula-indexed RCAF contract pricing power covering inflation (Gate 4 CAP: 20Y). Disciplined Precision Scheduled Railroading (PSR) execution under CEO Jim Vena delivers ~40% operating margins and 16.0% ROIC (Gate 5 score: 1). Passes Gate 6 under essential infrastructure standard: 7.52x EBIT interest coverage, 98.3% FCF conversion, and investment-grade A3/A- balance sheet. [5-10Y g: carload volume 1.5% + core pricing above inflation 2.5% + PSR network productivity 1.0% - regulatory/capex drag 0.5% + share repurchases 2.5%]
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record: 10-year GAAP ROIC has consistently exceeded the 12% hurdle, sustaining 13.5% to 17.5% across 2016-2025 with a median of 15.96%. Operating margins have averaged 38-41% (operating ratio 59-62%). Peak-to-peak compounding is intact: Owner EPS compounded at 7.4% CAGR from $5.07 in 2016 to a new peak of $11.98 in FY2025 ($7,138M Net Income, $9,846M EBIT). Cash conversion is exceptional: 10-year Owner FCF conversion median exceeds 95% (98.3% TTM; $6,683M Owner FCF in FY2025). Revenue diversification: Freight revenues split across Industrial (chemicals, energy, construction ~35%), Premium/Intermodal (intermodal containers, finished autos ~35%), and Bulk (grain, fertilizer, coal ~30%). Lock-in & Pricing: Serves as the exclusive rail connection to all 6 major US-Mexico border crossings (holding a 26% ownership stake in Ferromex) and key West Coast / Gulf Coast deepwater ports. Captive shippers have zero economic alternative for bulk and heavy goods as rail is 3-4x more fuel efficient than long-haul trucking. Contract escalators (RCAF) reliably protect real margins. Capital allocation: Self-funds all network reinvestment ($3.79B capex in 2025 against $9.29B OCF), returning excess capital via $3.24B dividends and counter-cyclical share repurchases. Balance sheet: Investment-grade rating (Moody's A3 stable, S&P A-). Total debt/EBITDA of ~2.3x-2.5x, Net Debt of $30.55B ($31.81B LT debt less $1.27B cash), positive tangible equity of $18.47B, and EBIT interest coverage of 7.52x ($9,846M EBIT / $1,309M interest), comfortably clearing the >5.0x essential infrastructure standard.

column14: The Work Number payroll verification monopoly (>650M records) and credit bureau triopoly provide an unassailable toll booth with proven inflation-plus pricing power and tiered bundle upselling.
column19: Broken metric: Gate 6 failure with LT Debt / NI of 6.14x ($4.06B debt vs $660M NI), Net Debt of $3.87B, interest coverage dipping to 3.87x in 2023 during peak mortgage freeze, and 5Y median GAAP ROIC of 9.33%. Intact moat proof: The Work Number holds 650M+ payroll records directly integrated into employer HR systems with zero customer churn and proven inflation-plus pricing; credit bureau triopoly intact; FY2025 revenue hit record $6.075B and Owner EPS hit a new peak of $7.299 despite trough US mortgage originations. Fix catalyst & kill-switch: Completion of $3B cloud migration unlocks $300M in run-rate cost takeout, dropping capex to $481M and driving FCF to record $1.13B ($1.06B Owner FCF), allowing organic deleveraging with Net Debt repayable from Owner FCF in 3.67 years; mortgage volumes poised to recover from 30-year low. Kill-switch: Net Debt / NI failing to drop below 4.0x within 3 years, or loss of proprietary employer payroll feeds.
column20: Calamity pass at Gate 6. Crown-jewel payroll database (The Work Number) and credit bureau triopoly. Record $6.075B revenue and $7.299 Owner EPS achieved at mortgage cycle trough. Balance sheet leverage elevated from $3B cloud transformation and breach settlements, but record $1.13B FCF enables rapid organic deleveraging. [5-10Y g: organic TWN/bureau volume 5.0% + price 2.0% + cloud cost takeout margin 1.0% + net buybacks 0.5%]
column21: Multi-cycle track record shows unassailable toll booth in employment/income verification and credit reporting. Despite a >50% drop in US mortgage originations during the 2022-2024 Fed tightening cycle, FY2025 revenue reached a record $6,074.5M (+7% YoY) and Owner EPS reached a new peak of $7.299. Tangible ROIC exceeds 100% due to negative tangible equity (-$3.47B), while GAAP ROIC has been temporarily depressed to a 5-year median of 9.33% by $8.08B in goodwill/intangibles and the amortization of the $3B cloud transformation. Free cash flow surged to $1,055.9M in FY2025 (reported FCF $1.13B, 97.5% conversion) as capital expenditures declined to $481.4M (from $624.5M in FY2022) with the cloud migration reaching 85-90% completion. Long-term debt declined to $4,055.3M ($3,874.5M net debt), which is repayable in 3.67 years from normal Owner Free Cash Flow. Decommissioning legacy data centers delivers $300M in structural run-rate savings, accelerating margin expansion and organic deleveraging.

column14: Near-monopoly ISO regulatory statistical reporting and Xactimate claims estimation standards command 4-6% annual pricing power with >95% customer retention, generating ~36% GAAP ROIC and ~54% EBITDA margins.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Irreplaceable US P&C insurance regulatory and claims toll booth with near-monopoly ISO loss-cost data and ubiquitous Xactimate estimating software. High pricing power demonstrated by consistent 4-6% annual contract escalators with >95% retention. Pure-play focus post-Wood Mackenzie divestiture expanded GAAP ROIC to ~36% and FCF conversion to >100%. Fortress balance sheet with net debt under 3x earnings after redeeming the AccuLynx transaction debt. [5-10Y g: organic volume/upsell 4.0% + price 3.0% + margin expansion 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 10-year GAAP ROIC expanded from 13.2% in FY16 to 35.9% in FY25 following the disciplined divestiture of non-core energy (Wood Mackenzie for $3.1B) and financial services units. FY25 revenue reached $3,072.7M with EBIT of $1,343.9M (43.7% EBIT margin) and Owner FCF of $1,137.7M (125% conversion of $908.3M net income). Unassailable industry position as licensed statistical agent in all 50 states for insurance rate filings, with Xactimate creating a two-sided standard across carriers and adjusters. Balance sheet is sound with Net Debt / NI of 2.86x ($2,595M net debt vs $908M NI) and EBIT interest coverage of 7.86x; FY25 gross debt spike was temporary due to escrowed notes for the AccuLynx deal, which were redeemed upon transaction termination in Jan 2026.

column14: Mission-critical legal and tax workflow software (Westlaw, Practical Law, ONESOURCE, UltraTax) with high switching costs and proprietary citation structures (KeyCite, West Key Number System). Demonstrated pricing power via 3-5% annual contractual escalators and consistent GAAP ROIC of 13-14% (>50% tangible ROIC).
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Thomson Reuters operates seat-based SaaS and professional research platforms (Westlaw, Practical Law, Checkpoint) that face severe terminal headwinds from Macrotrend #1 (Automation & Cognitive Tech). Autonomous AI agents compress law firm associate headcounts and automate routine legal/tax lookup and drafting, capping the competitive advantage period at <=10 years under the Mauboussin persistence framework.
column21: FY2022-2025 revenue grew modestly from $6.63B to $7.48B with GAAP ROIC steady at 13.1-14.3% (median 13.8%) and FCF conversion of ~90% ($2.02B Owner FCF in FY2025). The business is concentrated in the 'Big 3' segments: Legal Professionals ($2.84B / 38%), Corporates ($2.02B / 27%), and Tax, Audit & Accounting ($1.29B / 17%), alongside Reuters News and Global Print ($1.34B). While balance sheet leverage is modest (LT debt of $1.33B vs cash of $371M and EBIT of $2.12B) and Casetext/CoCounsel was acquired to introduce GenAI features, the core economic model is inherently tethered to professional seat counts and billable hours at law firms. As AI agents automate discovery, legal research, and compliance drafting, legal staffing leverage diminishes, creating terminal headwinds against per-seat subscription expansion.

column14: Scale economies shared coupled with high switching costs from deep shop-floor integration. Fastenal's dense local hub-and-spoke distribution, captive trucking fleet, ~1,800+ Onsite locations, and >110,000 FMI (Fastenal Managed Inventory) vending devices lower customer total procurement and inventory carrying costs by 20-30% while generating industry-leading ~20-21% EBIT margins. 10-year GAAP ROIC has consistently remained between 24% and 35% (median 34.2%). Demonstrated pricing power by consistently passing through raw material (steel) and tariff inflation without gross margin degradation. Primary erosion threat is digital disintermediation (e.g., Amazon Business), but pure-play e-commerce lacks captive last-mile delivery, custom bin-stocking, and emergency factory-floor replenishment.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Premier North American industrial distributor with insurmountable shop-floor moats (Onsite embedded branches and FMI automated vending). High capital efficiency (10Y median ROIC ~34%) and fortress net-cash balance sheet. Resilient to all 5 macrotrends and an active beneficiary of manufacturing automation and reshoring. [5-10Y g: Onsite and FMI volume share gains 5.5% + pricing power 1.5% + mix and digital leverage 0.5% + net share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: 10-year financial compounding: Net sales grew from $3,962.0M (2016) to $8,200.5M (2025); EBIT expanded from $795.8M to $1,655.7M with stable operating margins of 20-21%. GAAP ROIC consistently ranged between 24.1% and 35.1% (median 34.2%), with identical tangible ROIC reflecting organic growth and negligible goodwill. Free cash flow conversion over 5 years is ~85% ($1,108.3M Owner FCF on $1,258.4M net income in 2025). Long-term debt is negligible at $100.0M against $276.8M cash and $1,655.7M EBIT, generating an interest coverage ratio exceeding 250x. Installed FMI device footprint exceeds 110,000 units and Onsite locations exceed 1,800, creating deeply entrenched customer retention.

column14: Unmatched scale in North American plumbing, HVAC, and waterworks distribution (~1,700 branches, 11 primary DCs) provides superior SKU availability and lower unit purchasing costs than fragmented regional competitors. Contractors prioritize immediate product availability over small price variances to avoid costly trade labor downtime. Proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 28.2% and gross margin stability near ~30% through severe commodity cycles (PVC, copper, steel). Primary erosion threats include direct-to-contractor disintermediation by major HVAC OEMs, mitigated by Ferguson's last-mile delivery, counter network, and trade credit.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Dominant North American distributor of plumbing, HVAC, and waterworks supplies with entrenched local branch density and scale economies shared. Heavily insulated from AI disruption with ~60% exposure to non-deferrable repair, maintenance, and improvement (RMI). Conservative balance sheet with net debt at 1.7x net income and ~14x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: organic volume & market share gains 3.0% + inflation price pass-through 1.5% + accretive bolt-on acquisitions 2.0% - margin normalization drag 0.5% + share repurchases 2.0%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 28.2% and operating ROIC of 46.7%. FY2025 net sales of $30.8B, GAAP operating profit of $2.61B (8.5% margin), and net income of $1.86B. FCF conversion averages ~82% with modest capital expenditure needs (~1% of sales). Conservative balance sheet with $3.75B long-term debt against $674M cash and $1.86B net income (net debt/NI of 1.7x; net debt/EBITDA ~1.0x) and EBIT/interest coverage >14x. Demonstrated pricing power and cost pass-through discipline maintaining ~30% gross margin across raw material cycles.

column14: United Rentals maintains scale advantages via North America's largest equipment rental network (~1,500 branches, ~15% market share), yielding OEM procurement discounts, broad branch density, and digital fleet tracking (Total Control). However, returns cannot be insulated from competitive arbitrage because the underlying assets (aerial lifts, excavators, skid steers) are standard OEM machinery identical to those owned by Sunbelt (Ashtead), Herc, and regional rental yards. General contractors face zero switching barriers. When construction slows, idle fleet carrying costs force industry-wide rate discounting, eroding pricing power and suppressing cycle-average ROIC below the 12% hurdle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). While United Rentals is the North American market leader with scale economies in fleet purchasing and branch density, rental assets are standardized OEM machines (Caterpillar, Genie, JLG) with zero customer switching costs. Rental rates and utilization face severe cyclical degradation whenever construction activity cools, preventing pricing power >= inflation across the cycle. Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC averages ~10.5-11.0% (sub-hurdle for 7 of the past 11 years), exceeding 12% only during peak fiscal mega-project booms. Incurring massive ongoing fleet replacement capex and servicing ~$15.5B in debt without true pricing power fails the Munger quality hurdle.
column21: Multi-cycle financial performance reveals cyclical capital efficiency below compounder standards: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~10.5-11.0% (2015: 8.5%, 2016: 7.8%, 2017: 8.8%, 2018: 11.0%, 2019: 10.4%, 2020: 10.0%, 2021: 11.0%, 2022: 12.7%, 2023: 14.9%, 2024: 12.0%, 2025: ~11.2%). The brief surge above 12% in 2022-2023 reflected non-repeatable convergence of Federal mega-project stimulus (CHIPS, IRA, IIJA) and industry-wide equipment shortages. Equipment rental is capital-intensive: gross rental fleet capex runs $3.5B-$4.5B annually against operating cash flow of ~$6.5B, leaving ~$2.1B-$2.2B FCF. Net debt stands at ~$15.4B (~1.8x EBITDA, ~5.5-6x Net Income). Because fleets consist of commoditized OEM equipment with zero customer switching costs, URI is a cyclical price-taker with negative pricing power during construction downturns.

column14: Proprietary file formats (.psd, .ai, .indd, PDF) and deep creative workflow lock-in support ~88% gross margins and 40%+ median ROIC; primary erosion threats stem from generative AI diffusion models and browser-native collaborative tools (Canva, Figma).
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Enterprise creative and document SaaS leader facing severe terminal disruption under Macrotrend #1 (Automation & Cognitive Tech / AI Disruption). Generative AI diffusion models (Midjourney, Flux, Stable Diffusion) and browser-native tools (Canva, Figma) commoditize routine asset creation, compress agency/enterprise seat counts, and pressure pricing power. column21: 10-year median ROIC of 40.1% (FY2025 GAAP ROIC of 61.7%) and pristine ~88% gross margins reflect historic creative workflow dominance. column14: Proprietary file formats (.dwg for AutoCAD, .rvt for Revit) establish a de facto global standard across the entire Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) ecosystem. Multi-party project delivery requires federating BIM models across architects, MEP engineers, structural consultants, and general contractors; switching away breaks cross-firm interoperability and introduces massive legal and construction risk. Immense workflow retraining costs make customer defection irrational. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 38.96% and tangible operating ROIC >100% prove moat durability. Pricing power is demonstrated by forcing subscription migration, eliminating perpetual licenses, and compounding regular above-inflation price increases despite public pushback from leading architecture firms. Primary erosion risks include openBIM (IFC) open-standard interoperability mandates and AI-native generative design startups.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global standard in CAD and BIM software with an entrenched Toll Booth / Switching Cost moat anchored by proprietary .dwg and .rvt file formats across the AEC ecosystem. Exceptional pricing power demonstrated by multi-cycle subscription migration and regular price hikes. Insulated from AI disruption by proprietary geometry schemas, professional engineering liability stamping, and structural labor shortages in construction. Accounting probe resolved with zero restatements and SEC closure. Fortress balance sheet with near net cash and 19.7x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: organic AEC/BIM volume 4.5% + contract pricing 3.0% + direct model/cloud mix 1.5% - transaction model margin drag 0.5% + net share buybacks 1.5%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 38.96% and tangible operating ROIC >100%. Gross margins steady at 90-92% and GAAP operating margins expanding to 22-23% (underlying non-GAAP operating margin ~38%). FY2025 revenue reached $6.07B and FY2026 accelerated to $7.21B with >$2.4B in operating cash flow. 5-year cumulative Owner FCF conversion is 120.5% ($5.38B Owner FCF vs $4.46B Net Income). column14: Cadence forms an indispensable duopoly with Synopsys controlling >75% of the electronic design automation (EDA) market. Moat barriers are practically insurmountable due to: (1) deep process design kit (PDK) integration with TSMC, Intel, and Samsung foundries; (2) decades of electrical engineering muscle memory; and (3) catastrophic tape-out failure risk (a botched $100M+ mask set prevents customers from ever switching for minor price concessions). Proof of moat: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 47.7%, gross margins of ~89-90%, operating margins >30%, ~85% recurring subscription revenue, and 10-year Owner EPS CAGR of 13.8%. Primary erosion threats: tightening US-China export controls restricting tool access for Chinese fabless firms (~10-12% of revenue), hyperscaler customer consolidation, and antitrust scrutiny.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Unassailable mission-critical EDA duopolist serving as an essential toll booth on global semiconductor R&D and AI silicon design. Moat backed by deep foundry PDK certifications and extreme switching costs. Highly recurring software model (~85% ratable/subscription) with robust pricing power and net cash balance sheet ($3.0B cash vs $2.48B debt). [5-10Y g: semiconductor design & AI complexity volume 7.0% + EDA pricing/up-tiering 2.0% + multiphysics expansion 1.5% - R&D/cloud compute drag 0.5% + net share buybacks 1.0%]
column21: 10-year operating history demonstrates elite compounding: FY2016-FY2025 revenue grew from $1.82B to $5.30B (12.6% CAGR), operating income expanded from $245M to $1.49B (22.2% CAGR), and Owner EPS rose from $0.92 to $4.37 (13.8% CAGR).
