column21: FY2025 net sales reached EUR 32.67B with net income of EUR 9.61B and FCF of EUR 11.03B (115% conversion). 4-year cumulative FCF of EUR 33.9B on EUR 30.6B net income yields 110.6% multi-year cash conversion. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 98.6% with operating ROIC >100%. Gross margins expanded above 51% (guided to 54-56% for FY2026). Cash and equivalents of EUR 12.92B against EUR 2.71B long-term debt yields a fortress net cash position of EUR 10.21B with EBIT interest coverage of 97.4x. Peak-to-peak earnings power expanded from EUR 14.13 in FY2022 to EUR 24.71 in FY2025.

column14: Board-level spec-in lock-in across >75,000 SKUs and >125,000 diversified customers. Analog ICs represent a negligible fraction (<1-2%) of customer system BoM but are catastrophic to system failure, creating insurmountable switching costs and multi-million-dollar redesign/recertification hurdles. Gross margins are structurally sustained at 65-70% (adjusted ~68-70%) and trough adjusted operating margins remain >40%. Operating/tangible ROIC exceeds 60-190%+, while GAAP ROIC is optically deflated by non-cash merger amortization from Linear Tech and Maxim. Primary long-term erosion risks include customer in-house ASIC design at high volumes, low-end Asian analog commoditization, and cyclical inventory corrections.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global high-performance analog and mixed-signal duopolist (ADI + Linear + Maxim) with mission-critical board-level spec-in lock-in across industrial, automotive, and communications infrastructure. Structurally insulated from or actively benefiting from all 5 macrotrends via factory automation, EV battery management systems, AI data center power stages, and a resilient hybrid manufacturing model. Highly cash-generative with 138% multi-year FCF conversion and net debt repayable in ~1.4 years of Owner FCF. [5-10Y g: industrial/auto/datacenter volume 4.5% + pricing/mix 1.5% + operating leverage 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates exceptional compounding: sales grew from $3.4B in FY16 to $11.0B in FY25, with peak Owner EPS advancing from $5.47 (FY18) to $8.59 (FY23) and trough EPS holding at $6.03 (FY24). Gross margins consistently range between 65% and 70%. Multi-year Owner FCF conversion is 138% of GAAP Net Income ($3.96B FCF in FY25 vs $2.27B NI), reflecting heavy non-cash intangible amortization ($2.0B D&A) from the Linear Technology and Maxim Integrated acquisitions. Operating/tangible ROIC consistently exceeds 60% (192% in FY23, 63% in FY25). Segment breakdown (FY25): Industrial 45%, Automotive 30%, Communications/Datacenter 13%, Consumer 13%. Balance sheet is solid with $2.5B cash against $8.1B long-term debt; net debt of $5.6B is covered by ~1.4 years of Owner FCF, and EBIT/interest coverage stands at 9.2x.

column14: x86 duopoly cross-license with Intel and proprietary chiplet/FPGA IP prevent commodity entry. However, 5-year median GAAP ROIC (~3.2%-5.4%) is severely sub-hurdle (<12%) due to $49B Xilinx acquisition dilution/amortization, and AMD operates as a price-taking challenger to Intel in CPUs and Nvidia in GPUs without autonomous pricing power over inflation. Primary erosion threats include Nvidia's CUDA software lock-in, hyperscaler custom in-house ASICs, and ARM architecture expansion in client/server.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~3.2%-5.4% is severely sub-hurdle (<12.0%) following the $49B Xilinx acquisition asset base inflation and non-cash intangible amortization. As a fabless challenger to Intel in CPUs and Nvidia in GPUs, AMD lacks cycle-wide pricing power over inflation, relying on discounting and price/performance trade-offs rather than autonomous price-setting power. Calamity Tier is inapplicable as Anchor Gate 4 fails (CAP <= 10 due to 100% single-source leading-edge foundry reliance on TSMC in Taiwan and rising ARM/hyperscaler custom ASIC substitution).
column21: Fabless semiconductor designer with four core reporting segments: Data Center (EPYC server CPUs, Instinct AI accelerators, Pensando DPUs), Client (Ryzen PC processors), Gaming (Radeon GPUs, semi-custom console SoCs), and Embedded (Xilinx FPGAs/adaptive SoCs). While Lisa Su engineered an impressive turnaround from 2015-2016 operating losses via Zen microarchitecture execution, AMD's financial compounding record fails the Munger standard. The $49B all-stock acquisition of Xilinx in February 2022 added ~$49B in goodwill and acquired intangibles, expanding the invested capital base and triggering billions in annual non-cash intangible amortization. As a result, GAAP ROIC collapsed from >40% in FY2021 to 1.5% in FY2022, 0.6% in FY2023, 2.4% in FY2024, and ~4.8% in FY2025, yielding a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~3.2%-5.4%, well below the 12% hurdle. 10-year median ROIC sits at ~11.5%. Competitive dynamics further confirm lack of autonomous pricing power: AMD is a price-taking challenger to Intel in CPUs (historically relying on discounting to capture server share) and a distant challenger in AI/datacenter GPUs where Nvidia maintains >85% market share and ~75% gross margins protected by the CUDA proprietary software ecosystem. Instinct accelerators must be discounted against Nvidia Hopper/Blackwell to incentivize adoption. Furthermore, hyperscalers (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Microsoft Maia, Meta MTIA) are actively developing proprietary internal silicon, capping merchant pricing power. Structurally, AMD is 100% reliant on TSMC in Taiwan for leading-edge foundry fabrication (N5/N4/N3), presenting an unhedged geopolitical single-point-of-failure headwind under Macrotrend 3 (CAP <= 10). Balance sheet is conservatively financed with net cash (~$6.8B cash vs ~$2.5B debt), but sub-hurdle capital efficiency and challenger pricing dynamics eliminate AMD from compounder status.

column14: Extreme switching costs and toll-booth positioning across custom AI accelerators (XPUs/ASICs co-designed with hyperscalers like Google and Meta), data center Ethernet switching silicon (dominant Tomahawk and Jericho families with >70% merchant share), and mission-critical enterprise private cloud infrastructure (VMware Cloud Foundation). Switching costs proven by successful transition of VMware to full-stack subscription bundles with effective 2-5x price increases while maintaining core enterprise retention, and non-GAAP gross margins exceeding 75% with consolidated adjusted EBITDA margins >60%. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 16.0% (depressed temporarily in FY24 by the $86B VMware transaction, rebounding to 16.0% in FY25) alongside astronomical tangible operating ROIC (>100%) due to fabless asset-light production. Primary erosion threats include hyperscaler in-sourcing of custom silicon design, open-source Ethernet consortium shifts, customer resistance/attrition from aggressive VMware pricing, and TSMC foundry concentration.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Premier hybrid infrastructure titan combining an unassailable custom AI ASIC/accelerator and Ethernet networking franchise with high-cash-flow VMware private cloud software. Demonstrates immense pricing power through VMware subscription bundling and standard-setting networking silicon margins. Fabless capital-light profile produces >$26B in annual FCF with leverage rapidly deleveraging (net debt / FCF < 1.7x; interest coverage ~8x). [5-10Y g: custom AI ASIC & networking volume 6.0% + VMware enterprise software 2.5% + pricing/mix 1.5% - customer concentration drag 0.5% + net debt paydown & share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: Broadcom delivers exceptional capital efficiency and cash generation. FY2025 revenue reached $63.9B (+24% YoY), driven by $20B in AI semiconductor revenue (+65% YoY across Google TPU/Meta custom XPUs and Tomahawk 5/6 networking) and $27.0B in Infrastructure Software (+26% YoY). 5-year median GAAP ROIC stands at 16.0%, while tangible operating ROIC exceeds 100% due to Broadcom's fabless manufacturing model (FY25 capex of just $623M on $63.9B revenue). Multi-year Owner FCF conversion is 122% of GAAP Net Income ($26.9B FCF vs. $23.1B NI in FY25). Balance sheet health is robust post-VMware: Long-Term Debt was reduced to $62.0B against $16.2B cash (Net Debt $45.8B, repayable in ~1.7 years of FCF; LT debt / NI is 2.68x, well below the 4.0x ceiling). FY25 EBIT of $25.5B covers interest expense of $3.21B by 7.94x. Owner EPS set a new all-time peak of $6.42 in FY2025, up from $4.07 in FY2023 and $2.74 in FY2022 (27.1% OE EPS CAGR), confirming peak-to-peak compounding.

column14: First Solar's proprietary thin-film Cadmium Telluride (CdTe) semiconductor technology and US domestic manufacturing presence provide specialized IP and domestic content bonus eligibility under the IRA. However, empirical proof of moat is absent: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.2% (sub-hurdle < 12%), and cumulative multi-year free cash flow has been negative due to ongoing heavy fab capex ($1.39B in 2023, $1.53B in 2024). Recent operating income ($1.39B in 2024) is heavily subsidized by $857M of Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credits. Primary erosion threats include severe global crystalline silicon (c-Si) manufacturing overcapacity in China and Southeast Asia, continuous module price deflation, policy risk regarding IRA subsidies and import tariffs, and zero customer switching costs among utility developers shopping on levelized $/W.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 8.2% median < 12%, REJECT). Thin-film CdTe technology provides differentiated US manufacturing IP, but solar modules remain a commoditized hardware product where utility buyers procure strictly on levelized cost of energy ($/W). 10-year median ROIC of 8.2% fails the 12% hurdle rate. Recent profitability is heavily dependent on US policy subsidies (monetizing $857M of Section 45X tax credits in 2024 against $1.39B operating income). Lacks pricing power >= inflation against fierce global crystalline silicon overcapacity.
column21: 10-year median ROIC is 8.2% (well below the 12% hurdle rate). Historical returns across cycles: 2020 ROIC 4.9% (gross margin 25.1%), 2021 ROIC 8.4% (net income $468.7M, OCF $237.6M, capex $540.3M -> FCF -$302.7M), 2022 ROIC -0.5% (net loss -$44.2M, gross margin 2.7%), 2023 ROIC 10.4% (net income $830.8M, OCF $602.3M, capex $1,386.8M -> FCF -$784.5M), 2024 ROIC 12.8% (net income $1,292.0M, OCF $1,218.0M, capex $1,526.1M -> FCF -$308.1M). Recent earnings are artificially supported by IRA Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Tax Credits ($857M generated/sold in 2024, providing ~$819M in cash proceeds and driving over 60% of $1.394B operating income). Capital intensity is high with continuous multi-billion dollar fab expansions (Ohio, Alabama, Louisiana) absorbing cash flow, resulting in negative cumulative FCF over 2021-2024. Solar module pricing is dictated by global c-Si supply-demand dynamics and Chinese overcapacity, eliminating pricing power above inflation.

column14: Historically defended by massive leading-edge semiconductor fab capital requirements and ubiquitous x86 software ecosystem lock-in. However, empirical proof of moat has completely unraveled: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 4.8% (against the 12% threshold) and GAAP net margins/ROIC turned severely negative in FY2024-2025. Gross margins dropped from >60% to the 35-40% range. Primary erosion threats include permanent manufacturing process leadership loss to TSMC, persistent market share losses in data center CPUs to AMD, secular shift of hyperscaler capex toward Nvidia GPUs and custom AI ASICs, and growing customer adoption of ARM-based architectures.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power). 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 4.8% fails the 12% hurdle by a wide margin, with catastrophic net losses in FY2024 (-$18.8B) and FY2025 (-$0.3B). Historical pricing power and gross margins have eroded due to AMD's competitive surge in server/PC CPUs, Nvidia's dominance of data center AI compute spend, and staggering operating losses in Intel Foundry (~$13B in 2024). Moat is structurally broken rather than facing a temporary fixable calamity.
column21: Multi-cycle ROIC has collapsed to a 5-year median of 4.8%, with FY2024 GAAP net loss of $(18.8)B (operating loss of $(11.7)B) and FY2025 net loss of $(267)M (operating loss of $(2.2)B). Intel Foundry incurred ~$13B in operating losses in 2024 and remained heavily unprofitable in 2025 due to low external customer adoption and high EUV depreciation. Free cash flow was deeply negative (~-$10B+ across 2023-2025), forcing complete dividend suspension, major layoffs, asset divestitures (Altera stake sale), and government/external capital injections. Gross margins fell from historical 60%+ levels to ~35-40% under sustained pricing pressure from AMD and product substitution toward Nvidia accelerators.

column14: Embedded microcontroller (PIC, AVR) and analog/mixed-signal sockets historically created switching costs via customer firmware lock-in and development ecosystems (MPLAB). However, Microchip fails empirical proof of moat: 10-year GAAP ROIC fell below 12% in 6 of the last 10 fiscal years (FY2018 6.3%, FY2019 3.7%, FY2020 5.9%, FY2024 2.0%, FY2025 3.5%), and incremental ROIIC since the 2018 Microsemi acquisition is negative as EBIT fell from $714M in FY2018 to $490M in FY2025 on expanded capital. Furthermore, pricing power failed the cycle test: aggressive price hikes and coercive non-cancellable Preferred Supply Program (PSP) contracts during the 2021-2022 chip shortage caused severe customer backlash, inventory digestion, and a ~45% top-line collapse ($8.44B to $4.40B). Primary erosion threats include customer migration toward standard ARM Cortex-M cores and open RISC-V architectures, along with aggressive Chinese domestic MCU substitution.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). While Microchip benefits from embedded switching costs in microcontroller sockets (Gate 3a: Toll booth / Switching costs), it fails empirical proof of moat and through-the-cycle pricing power. GAAP ROIC fell below 12% in 6 of the past 10 fiscal years (2.0% in FY2024, 3.5% in FY2025), and post-Microsemi incremental ROIIC is negative. Microchip's aggressive COVID-era Preferred Supply Program (PSP)—forcing 12-18 month non-cancellable orders and steep price increases—alienated customers, drove socket redesigns toward ARM/RISC-V alternatives, and led to a catastrophic 48% revenue crash ($8.44B to $4.40B) and factory underutilization. Further burdened by $5.5B in debt (6.6x normal owner earnings, interest coverage only 2.2x), MCHP fails the Munger standard of enduring, cycle-tested capital compounding.
column21: Multi-cycle capital efficiency: GAAP ROIC collapsed from cycle peak of 19.5% in FY2022 to 2.0% in FY2024 and 3.5% in FY2025. Over the full 10-year period (FY2016-FY2025), GAAP ROIC breached 12% in only 4 years (FY2017: 15.7%, FY2021: 12.4%, FY2022: 19.5%, FY2023: 18.3%), with sub-hurdle returns throughout FY2018-FY2020 (3.7%-6.3%). Revenue & earnings volatility: Revenues peaked at $8,438.7M in FY2022 before collapsing to $4,401.6M in FY2024 and $4,713.1M in FY2025. Operating income (EBIT) plummeted from $3,116.0M in FY2022 to $296.3M in FY2024 and $490.1M in FY2025. Pricing power & customer lock-in: Microchip historically relied on proprietary architectures (PIC, AVR) and development tools (MPLAB). However, its coercive Preferred Supply Program (PSP) during the pandemic supply crunch locked clients into rigid non-cancellable terms. Once shortages eased, customers aggressively drew down stockpiles, cancelled follow-on orders, and accelerated second-sourcing to standard ARM-based MCUs (STM32, NXP) and RISC-V, demonstrating lack of durable pricing power independent of shortage windfalls. Debt & Balance sheet: In 2018, Microchip acquired Microsemi for $10.1B, expanding long-term debt to nearly $9B. Long-term debt remains excessive at $5,496.4M against cash of $240.3M (net debt ~$5,256M). With TTM EBIT of $490.1M and interest expense of $221.3M, interest coverage stands at a precarious 2.21x (well below the >5.0x safety threshold). TTM dividend payments of $984.0M vastly exceeded GAAP net income ($230M) and free cash flow ($615.6M), consuming liquidity while leverage remains high (Net debt / TTM NI > 22x, Net debt / normal OE ~6.6x).

column14: Proprietary BCD (Bipolar-CMOS-DMOS) process technology integrates power, analog, and digital control on a single monolithic die, delivering superior power density and thermal efficiency. Sticky design-in switching costs in cloud computing, enterprise data, and automotive applications require extensive customer board re-spins and thermal re-qualification to displace. Moat proven by 5-year median ROIC >21% and gross margins >55%. Primary erosion threats include scale analog IDMs (Texas Instruments, Infineon, Renesas, ADI) deploying captive 300mm fabs, alongside aggressive multi-sourcing by tier-1 hyperscalers.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Tier 3 semiconductor baseline (10-15Y) receives haircut due to severe unhedged Macrotrend [3] exposure: 100% fabless wafer fabrication concentrated in Taiwan/Asian foundries, alongside >85% Asia ship-to revenue (>50% mainland China). Furthermore, rapid 2-3 year hardware architectural cycles and hyperscaler multi-sourcing (e.g. Nvidia Blackwell power allocation shifts to Renesas and Infineon) limit competitive advantage longevity well below the 15-year threshold.
column21: Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR) exhibits strong financial metrics with FY2024 revenue of $2.21B (+26% to $2.79B in FY2025) and ROIC consistently between 21% and 34%, with zero long-term debt and >$1B in cash. However, as a fabless power IC vendor, MPWR lacks captive wafer fabrication and relies heavily on external foundries (TSMC and Asian partners). Greater China accounts for 50-55% of ship-to revenues and Asia overall represents >85%. In enterprise data and AI accelerators, hyperscalers aggressively multi-source power delivery (demonstrated by Nvidia allocating Blackwell VRM/PMIC sockets across MPWR, Renesas, and Infineon), exposing MPWR to socket displacement across 2-3 year product cycles and capping CAP at 5 years.

column14: High customer switching costs in custom silicon ASIC co-design (e.g. AWS Trainium/Inferentia) and proprietary SerDes/optical DSP IP create project lock-in across product cycles. However, the moat fails empirical verification: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 6.5% and the company posted consecutive GAAP net losses from FY2021 through FY2025. Primary erosion threats include extreme hyperscaler customer concentration, monopsonistic pricing pressure depressing custom silicon gross margins, potential insourcing of chip design by cloud titans, and intense merchant competition from Broadcom and Nvidia.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Structural failure of empirical moat test: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.5% (sub-12% hurdle) with consecutive GAAP net losses from FY2021 through FY2025. Heavily dilutive serial M&A (Cavium, Inphi, Innovium) burdened the balance sheet with goodwill and amortization, while massive annual stock-based compensation dilutes owners. Hyperscaler monopsony power in custom ASICs depresses margins and eliminates pricing power >= inflation.
column21: Multi-cycle financial performance demonstrates chronic inability to meet the 12% GAAP ROIC standard. Reported GAAP net income was negative across FY2021 (-$277M), FY2022 (-$421M), FY2023 (-$164M), FY2024 (-$933M), and FY2025 (-$885M), yielding a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of approximately -2% and a 10-year median ROIC of 6.5%. While non-GAAP numbers look rosier, the divergence is driven by hundreds of millions in annual stock-based compensation ($600M-$800M+/yr) and heavy amortization of intangibles from serial M&A ($6B Cavium, $10B Inphi). In custom silicon (ASICs), Marvell is highly dependent on a handful of hyperscalers (Amazon AWS, Microsoft, Google), who dictate terms, compress gross margins (custom ASIC gross margins typically 35-45% vs 60%+ corporate average), and can dual-source or insource design, eliminating pricing power.

column14: High capital intensity ($10B+ per fab shell) and leading-edge semiconductor physics (EUV, 1-gamma DRAM, G9 NAND, HBM3E/HBM4 packaging) restrict leading DRAM manufacturing to a 3-player oligopoly (Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix). However, memory bits are standardized JEDEC commodities lacking switching costs, leaving Micron as a price-taker subject to severe boom-bust cycles. Gross margins swing from negative (-8% in FY23) to peak (~40% in FY25). Primary erosion threats include cyclical overcapacity additions, aggressive capital expenditure by Korean peers, Chinese state-subsidized competition (CXMT, YMTC), and geopolitical restrictions in China.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & Commodity Price-Taker, REJECT). Micron participates in a 3-player DRAM and 5-player NAND oligopoly, but memory products remain standardized JEDEC commodities with zero customer switching costs. Micron lacks pricing power across the cycle, with average selling prices dictated by spot/contract market supply gluts and shortages. 10-year median ROIC is sub-hurdle at ~8.2%, swinging from deeply negative (-12.1% in FY23) to cyclical peaks (+14.5% in FY25). Massive ongoing capital expenditure requirements ($13.8B in FY25) to maintain node transitions (1-beta/1-gamma DRAM, high-layer 3D NAND, HBM3E/HBM4 packaging) structurally depress multi-cycle free cash flow conversion.
column21: Empirical financial record confirms chronic cyclicality and commodity price-taking behavior: (1) ROIC: 10-year median ROIC is ~8.2%, below the 12% Munger hurdle. ROIC collapsed to -12.1% in FY23 (industry trough) and 1.6% in FY24, rebounding to 14.5% in FY25 during the AI/HBM upcycle. (2) Revenue & Net Income: Revenue plunged from $30.8B in FY22 to $15.5B in FY23 with a net loss of -$5.83B, recovering to $25.1B in FY24 (net income $778M) and $37.38B in FY25 (GAAP net income $8.54B). (3) Free Cash Flow & Capex: Highly capital-intensive manufacturing treadmill. FY23 FCF burned -$6.12B, FY24 FCF was $121M, and in FY25, despite $8.54B net income, capex expanded to $13.80B, yielding only ~$1.67B in FCF (<20% conversion). (4) Pricing Power: No structural pricing power above inflation; ASPs fluctuate with spot memory market balances. High customer concentration among hyperscalers and PC/mobile OEMs who aggressively negotiate memory prices.

column14: Full-stack proprietary CUDA developer ecosystem (4.5M+ developers, 18+ years of code library lock-in) coupled with NVLink high-bandwidth interconnects and system-level architectures (DGX, NVL72) create an unassailable switching-cost moat on accelerated computing. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 80.0% and gross margins reaching ~75% across successive GPU generations (A100 to H100 to Blackwell). Primary erosion threats: Hyperscaler in-house ASIC deployments (Google TPU, AWS Trainium, Meta MTIA) for mature inference workloads, open-source software layer maturation (PyTorch 2.0 / Triton decoupling from CUDA), and extreme customer concentration.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet, REJECT). While NVIDIA possesses an extraordinary founder-led accelerated computing franchise with an unassailable CUDA moat (Gate 3b Y, Gate 4 CAP 15, Gate 5 score 2), it fails Gate 6 due to: (1) Multi-year Owner FCF conversion of 76.8% (fcf_conv = 0.768 < 0.80 standard) driven by massive working-capital absorption during exponential hardware ramps, and (2) Severe cyclicality and extreme customer concentration (four hyperscalers generate 61% of FY2026 revenue) at peak ~60% operating margins; merchant GPU earnings historically fell 65% during the 2022 inventory digestion cycle, failing the repeatable non-windfall earnings power standard. [5-10Y g: AI compute/networking volume 9.0% + software/platform mix 2.0% - margin normalization 1.0% - SBC dilution 0.5% + net buyback 2.5%]
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record shows exceptional peak returns but high cyclical amplitude: GAAP ROIC collapsed to 10.4% in FY2022 before surging to 80.0% (FY2023), 114.5% (FY2024), and 94.9% (FY2025). Revenue grew from $27.0B (FY2022) to $215.9B (FY2026) with EBIT margins reaching ~60.4% ($130.4B EBIT). However, cumulative 5-year Owner FCF of $181.9B on Net Income of $236.8B yields a multi-year FCF conversion of 76.8% (below the 80% hurdle), weighed down by working capital and supply chain commitments. In FY2026, top 4 hyperscaler customers accounted for 61% of total revenue (22%, 15%, 13%, and 11%), exposing earnings to violent contraction upon any moderation in cloud AI infrastructure capex. Balance sheet itself is sound ($10.6B cash vs $7.5B debt; interest coverage >500x), but earnings repeatability fails Pillar 1 and cash conversion fails Pillar 2.

column14: AEC-Q100 and ISO 26262 ASIL-D functional safety qualifications create multi-year (3-5 year) automotive platform design cycles and 7-10+ year production lock-in, where Tier-1 suppliers and OEMs cannot switch microcontroller or vehicle networking silicon without costly recertification. Proof of moat is demonstrated by a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 18.1% (tangible ROIC >40%) and resilient ~57-58% gross margins sustained through the 2024-2025 auto inventory downcycle. Primary erosion threats include the architectural transition toward centralized zonal compute (which consolidates discrete ECUs) and aggressive state-subsidized Chinese domestic auto-chip substitution.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Automotive semiconductor leader with entrenched switching costs in microcontrollers and radar, but faces active terminal headwinds under the 5-Macrotrend framework. Specifically, Macrotrend 3 (geopolitical realignment and aggressive Chinese domestic auto-chip substitution targeting its ~17% direct China revenue and broad APAC auto supply chain) along with OEM architectural migration to centralized zonal compute compresses socket counts. Under Mauboussin Tier 3 semiconductor persistence (baseline 10-15Y), these structural headwinds cap CAP at 10 years.
column21: 10-year financials show steady compounding: FY2025 revenue was $12.27B, with GAAP operating income of $3.05B (24.8% operating margin). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 18.1%, with tangible ROIC averaging >50% post-2020. Free cash flow conversion is robust at 85.6% ($1.96B Owner FCF vs $2.02B net income in FY2025). Segment revenue (FY2025): Automotive $7.12B (58.0%), Industrial & IoT ~$2.2B (~18%), Mobile ~$1.5B (~12%), Communication Infrastructure & Other ~$1.5B (~12%). Direct China revenue is ~$2.04B (~17%), with higher indirect exposure via assembly in China. Balance sheet shows $10.97B debt and $3.27B cash (net debt $7.7B), with interest coverage of 6.5x. Gate 4 failure is driven by Mauboussin Tier 3 semiconductor baseline (10-15Y) subject to a -5Y haircut under Macrotrend 3: geopolitical supply chain reshoring and state-mandated Chinese domestic automotive chip localization (e.g. MIIT 20-25%+ domestic sourcing mandate targeting foreign MCUs and analog ICs), alongside OEM transition to centralized zonal architectures.

column14: Automotive and industrial qualification cycles (AEC-Q100, functional safety) create meaningful design-in switching costs across multi-year vehicle platforms. However, power semiconductors lack pricing power >= inflation, facing mandatory annual OEM price-downs and aggressive price deflation in Silicon Carbide (SiC) from surging Chinese capacity. Primary erosion threats: state-subsidized Chinese SiC wafer/module competition, cyclical auto/industrial demand swings, and commoditization of power discretes.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). While onsemi benefits from sticky automotive design-in qualification cycles, it lacks pricing power >= inflation across the cycle. Auto and industrial OEMs continuously extract annual price-downs, and aggressive capacity expansion by Chinese SiC competitors has led to sharp wafer/device price deflation, forcing onsemi to curtail capex and fab expansions. Multi-cycle returns on capital remain volatile with GAAP operating margins plunging to ~1.4% in the 2025 cyclical trough.
column21: Fiscal 2025 revenue fell 15.3% YoY to $6.0B (from $7.08B in 2024 and $8.25B in 2023 peak) due to broad automotive and industrial inventory destocking. GAAP operating margin compressed from ~25% in 2024 to 1.4% in 2025 ($84M operating income) under fab underutilization and manufacturing realignment charges. Trailing ROIC dropped to single digits (~8.9%). Despite solid FCF ($1.4B in 2025 via capex pacing and working capital release) and conservative balance sheet management, power discretes and SiC suffer structural price deflation and commoditization risks from low-cost Chinese competitors, failing the Munger standard for pricing power.

column14: Qualcomm maintains an extraordinary wireless R&D patent estate (3G/4G/5G SEPs) and leading Snapdragon mobile SoC/modem-RF design capabilities. However, pricing power is structurally constrained: QTL patent licensing royalties are legally capped per handset under global antitrust settlements (China NDRC, Korea KFTC, Apple settlements) and FRAND commitments, preventing pricing expansion with inflation. Concurrently, QCT (~85% of revenue) faces structural customer disintermediation as its top modem customer, Apple, deploys in-house 5G modem silicon starting 2025-2026, while Android OEMs continuously dual-source with MediaTek to cap chip ASPs.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While Qualcomm possesses an elite wireless R&D patent portfolio and market-leading Snapdragon mobile processors, it lacks unconstrained pricing power >= inflation. Licensing royalties (QTL) are legally capped on a per-handset basis following global antitrust settlements and FRAND commitments, precluding inflation-linked royalty expansion. In chipsets (QCT), Qualcomm faces structural disintermediation as Apple transitions to proprietary in-house modems, while Android smartphone OEMs exert aggressive pricing resistance and dual-source with MediaTek.
column21:
Financial Track Record: FY2024 revenue of $38.96B (up 9% YoY) and GAAP net income of $10.14B; FY2025 revenue reached $44.28B with non-GAAP net income of $13.30B (GAAP net income $5.54B affected by tax/legal charges) and FCF of ~$12.82B (~29% FCF margin). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~26.5%, demonstrating superior historical capital efficiency.
Segment Breakdown: QCT generates ~85% of total revenue across Handsets, Automotive, and IoT; QTL generates ~15% of revenue but a disproportionate share of operating profits with >70% operating margins.
Pricing Power & Customer Concentration: Apple historically contributed 10-15%+ of revenue; Apple began deploying its own in-house 5G cellular modem in 2025-2026, permanently phasing out external modem purchases from Qualcomm. Licensing royalties are legally constrained: China NDRC settlement caps royalty base at 65% of device price with absolute per-handset caps ($400 wholesale ceiling); similar FRAND commitments constrain European and US royalties. In mobile silicon, MediaTek provides an aggressive competitive alternative in sub-flagship tiers, capping QCT ASP expansion.
Geopolitical & Supply Chain Exposure: Over 45% of total revenues are billed to Chinese smartphone OEMs (Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, Honor) or devices assembled in China, and Qualcomm is 100% fabless, relying critically on TSMC (Taiwan) and Samsung for cutting-edge wafer fabrication.
Capital Allocation & Balance Sheet: Healthy net leverage with cash and marketable securities exceeding $13B against ~$15B long-term debt; consistent share repurchases and growing dividends, but unable to escape structural customer disintermediation and antitrust royalty ceilings.

column14: Proprietary patent estates in BAW/SAW filters and RF front-end module integration provide entry barriers against commodity assemblers, but fail to confer an economic moat against monopsonistic customer power. With Apple representing ~67-69% of net revenue, Skyworks is subjected to continuous contractual price-downs and socket dual-sourcing (e.g. Apple dual-sourcing key sockets to Broadcom and Murata in 2025, stripping 20-25% of iPhone content). Multi-year ROIC collapsed to ~6.9% in FY24 and ~5.8-7.2% in FY25, breaching the 12% hurdle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat Proof & Pricing Power, REJECT). Extreme customer concentration with Apple (~67-69% of net revenue) leaves Skyworks with zero pricing power against a monopsonistic buyer. Dual-sourcing of key iPhone RF sockets to Broadcom and Murata stripped 20-25% of content in 2025 device cycles, and multi-year ROIC collapsed to 5.8-7.2% in FY24-FY25, failing the mandatory 12% hurdle.
column21: Revenue contracted from $5.49B in FY22 to $4.77B in FY23, $4.18B in FY24, and $4.09B in FY25 as mobile handset cycles cooled and content share eroded. Over 67% of net sales are concentrated in Apple (~85% of which is iPhone-related), leaving Skyworks vulnerable to socket loss and annual ASP price concessions. In early 2025, Apple dual-sourced major low-band and RF filtering sockets to Broadcom and Murata for the iPhone 17 cycle, resulting in an estimated 20-25% content reduction. ROIC contracted sharply from historical 10-year medians (~14.2%) to 6.9% in FY24 and 5.8-7.2% in FY25, failing the Gate 3b hurdle. While free cash flow conversion remains healthy ($1.67B FCF in FY24, $1.11B in FY25) and the balance sheet carries modest net cash ($1.3B cash vs $1.0B term debt), strong cash generation cannot offset the absence of customer pricing power and structural moat erosion.

column14: Extreme design-in switching costs across 80,000+ catalog analog and embedded processing components sold to 100,000+ industrial and automotive customers. Pennies-per-part chips spec'd into mission-critical circuit boards create 10-15+ year sticky lifecycles where redesign costs dwarf component savings. Empirically demonstrated by 10-year GAAP ROIC averaging >35% (troughing at ~19-20% during cyclical downturns) and consistent ~60%+ through-cycle gross margins, further reinforced by a structural ~40% unpackaged die cost advantage from internal 300mm wafer fabrication.
column19: 1. Broken metric: Actual cash FCF conversion collapsed to ~30-40% of net income in 2023-2025 due to a massive $4.5B-$5.0B/year capex surge for 300mm fab construction (Sherman TX, Lehi UT) during an industrial/auto cyclical destocking, requiring ~$7B of debt issuance to sustain the $5B annual dividend. 2. Intact moat proof: Moat remains impregnable with 80,000+ catalog parts, 60%+ gross margins, and trough GAAP ROIC of ~19-20%; internal 300mm manufacturing widens the cost moat by 40% vs 200mm peers and guarantees US supply chain resilience. 3. Catalyst & kill-switch: Capex peaked in 2024-2025 and steps down to $2.0B-$3.0B in 2026 under dynamic capacity management agreed post-Elliott activist engagement, backed by $1.6B in CHIPS Act direct grants; FCF inflects sharply back to $6B-$8B+, restoring organic dividend coverage and rapid balance sheet deleveraging without dilution. Kill-switch: Capex persisting >$4B beyond 2026 without FCF recovery or net debt exceeding 4.0x net income.
column20: Calamity pass (temporary Gate 6 capex depression). Dominant catalog analog leader with unassailable design-in switching costs across 80,000+ products and 100,000+ customers. Capex peaked at ~$4.5B-$5.0B/year for 300mm fabs, depressing actual FCF conversion to ~30-40% and temporarily inflating debt to fund the dividend; capex step-down to $2.0B-$3.0B in 2026-2027 and CHIPS Act funding unlock a sharp multi-billion dollar FCF recovery and rapid deleveraging. [5-10Y g: analog/embedded unit volume 4.5% + price 0.5% + 300mm cost/FCF recovery 1.5% + net share repurchases 1.0%]
column21: 10-year track record proves exceptional capital efficiency: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 29.0% (peaking at 55.2% in 2021 and troughing at 18.8% in 2024 and 19.9% in 2025) and tangible ROIC consistently above 22%. Gross margins remained 60-68% through the cyclical downturn. Revenue comprises Analog (~75-80%) and Embedded Processing (~15-20%) across industrial, automotive, and personal electronics, with zero customer concentration (<10%). Operating margins sustained at 35-50%. Capex elevated to $4.55B-$5.07B/yr in 2023-2025 to build 300mm fabs, causing FCF to dip and debt to rise to $13.5B (net debt $10.3B, 2.7x NI, interest coverage >12x). Management constructively engaged with Elliott Management in 2024 to moderate 2026 capex to $2.0B-$3.0B, securing an inflection to $6B+ FCF.

column14: Early design-in switching costs and COSMOS software telemetry create stickiness during active cloud server deployment cycles, but returns face severe long-term arbitrage from well-capitalized merchant competitors (Broadcom, Marvell) and hyperscaler internal ASIC initiatives. No multi-cycle ROIC track record (GAAP net loss of -$83.4M in FY2024 following March 2024 IPO; founded 2017), while extreme customer concentration (>70% from a single hyperscaler) eliminates structural pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While Astera Labs has established leadership in high-speed PCIe/CXL retimers and smart fabric switches for AI clusters, it lacks a multi-cycle track record of capital efficiency (GAAP net loss of -$83.4M in FY2024 following its March 2024 IPO). With over 70% of revenue concentrated in a single hyperscaler (and ~86% across the top three), the company is subject to monopsonistic customer leverage, standard merchant semiconductor ASP deflation, and fierce competition from Broadcom and Marvell, precluding demonstrated pricing power >= inflation across a full economic cycle.
column21: Astera Labs was founded in 2017 and completed its IPO in March 2024. FY2024 revenue was $396.0M with a GAAP net loss of -$83.4M and negative GAAP ROIC. While revenue expanded to $853.0M in FY2025 and surged in FY2026 driven by AI data center capex cycles, it lacks a 5-10 year multi-cycle record of GAAP ROIC >= 12%. SEC Form 10-K filings reveal extreme customer concentration: a single major hyperscaler (Amazon/AWS) accounts for >70% of total revenue, and the top three customers account for ~86%. Astera competes directly against Broadcom and Marvell in high-speed connectivity silicon, leaving it vulnerable to architectural platform redesigns, hyperscaler internal silicon initiatives, and structural merchant semiconductor price deflation.

column14: Extreme ecosystem switching costs across billions of devices with 30+ years of software optimization. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 16.16% and gross margins exceed 95%. Pricing power demonstrated by migration to Armv9 and Compute Subsystems (CSS) doubling per-chip royalties, though customer friction (Qualcomm litigation) and RISC-V consortiums represent emerging long-term erosion risks.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet: fcf_conv = 18.6% vs 80% hurdle). Ubiquitous CPU architecture toll booth with dominant mobile/edge compute share and pristine zero-debt balance sheet, but chronic post-IPO stock-based compensation (~$1B/year against ~$900M Net Income) severely impairs free cash flow conversion to owners. [5-10Y g: chip unit volume 3.0% + v9/CSS royalty rate & licensing mix 8.0% + margin 2.0% - SBC dilution 2.0%]
column21: Arm holds an unassailable toll booth on global computing architectures, powering >99% of smartphones and rapidly gaining share in cloud hyperscalers (AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt) due to superior performance-per-watt. Gross margins consistently exceed 95%, and 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 16.16% (tangible ROIC >20%). Armv9 and Compute Subsystems (CSS) transition roughly doubles royalty rates per chip. The balance sheet is a pristine fortress with zero long-term debt and $2,751M in cash. However, Gate 6 fails decisively on Pillar 2 (Free Cash Flow Conversion): reported 5-year Owner FCF conversion is only 18.6% (fcf_conv = 0.186 vs. >= 0.80 hurdle). Over FY23-FY25, stock-based compensation totaled $2,909M ($1,037M in FY23, $820M in FY24, $1,052M in FY25), averaging nearly $1B annually and exceeding total GAAP net income ($3,075M 5-year cumulative NI vs. $572M Owner FCF). Because this massive equity dilution is an ongoing structural compensation model rather than an isolated temporary calamity, Arm fails Gate 6.

column14: Single-agent Falcon platform with kernel telemetry and threat graph exhibits high switching costs, but fails proof of moat: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is negative (-2.0% to 0.0%) and GAAP operating income was negative in 9 of the last 10 fiscal years due to immense stock-based compensation ($1.10B in FY25, ~23% of revenue). Pricing power was also impaired post-July 2024 outage by commercial discounting and customer commitment packages.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Enterprise endpoint security leader fails empirical proof of moat: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is negative (-2.0% to 0.0%) and GAAP EBIT has been negative in 9 of the last 10 fiscal years (-$293.3M in FY25) due to massive stock-based compensation dilution ($1,096.7M in FY25). Pricing power was additionally compromised by post-July 2024 outage customer commitment packages and discounting concessions. Even if evaluated at Gate 4, runway CAP would be capped at 5 years (<15Y threshold) due to rapid cybersecurity obsolescence, Microsoft Defender E5 bundling, and platform architecture shifts out of Windows kernel space. Calamity Tier is denied as negative GAAP ROIC predates the outage and Gate 4 fails anchor standards.
column21: Financial Track Record (FY2017–FY2025): Revenue expanded from $118.8M (FY17) to $4,812.0M (FY25), but cumulative GAAP net income and operating income remain negative across its public history. GAAP EBIT was -$142.5M (FY21), -$190.1M (FY22), -$19.1M (FY23), -$116.4M (FY24), and -$293.3M (FY25). Reported 'free cash flow' of $1.07B in FY25 is an artifact of adding back $1,096.7M in stock-based compensation (SBC), which constitutes a real operating expense diluting common equity. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is negative, failing the mandatory 12% hurdle (and tangible ROIC is negative, failing 15%). Following the catastrophic July 19, 2024 Falcon sensor update outage (crashing 8.5M Windows machines), CRWD issued extensive 'Customer Commitment Packages' involving contract discounting, flexible terms, and complimentary modules ($60M+ in concessions and direct expenses), demonstrating pricing concessions to prevent customer defection. Balance sheet holds $5.23B cash against $745.5M debt, but capital allocation is heavily diluted by ongoing SBC issuance.

column14: High switching costs across 700k+ enterprise firewall/SD-WAN installations running FortiOS, combined with proprietary FortiASIC silicon delivering 5-10x price-performance and power efficiency advantages over x86 peers. Gross margins consistently 79-81% (services >85%) and multi-year ROIC well above 40%. Primary erosion threats are cloud-native SASE substitution and recurring zero-day vulnerability disclosures.
column20: Founder-led network security and Unified SASE market leader with proprietary FortiASIC cost advantages and >$1.9B net cash. High enterprise switching costs across branch/cloud firewalls support >80% gross margins and pricing power. [5-10Y g: secure networking & SASE volume 8.0% + subscription pricing 1.5% + mix expansion 1.0% - D&A/capex drag 0.5% + net share buybacks 1.5%]
column21: Fortinet has demonstrated elite compounding over 15+ public operating years, scaling revenue from $1.28B (2016) to $6.80B (2025) with operating margins expanding to 30.7%. Proprietary custom ASIC silicon provides enduring price/performance moat and 55% global firewall unit share. Structural negative working capital and upfront deferred revenue billings yield multi-year Owner FCF conversion of 115-132% ($2.16B FCF vs $1.85B NI in FY2025). Founder Ken Xie holds substantial insider equity (~16%); fortress balance sheet holds $2.50B cash against $497M debt ($2.0B net cash, interest coverage >100x).

column11: Non-essential and easily forgone consumer software; native OS security (Microsoft Defender, Apple XProtect) and statutory free credit freezes render third-party consumer security and identity suites non-essential.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Consumer cyber safety and identity protection products (Norton, Avast, LifeLock, AVG) are discretionary, non-essential, and easily forgone. Modern operating systems provide robust native protection (Microsoft Defender, Apple XProtect) at zero incremental cost, rendering third-party antivirus obsolete for mainstream consumers. Customer retention is heavily reliant on auto-renewal inertia and dark-pattern billing rather than essential utility.
column21: Gen Digital generated FY2025 revenue of $3.94B and GAAP net income of $643M across Consumer Security (~65%) and Identity & Information Protection (~35%). While operating cash flow reaches ~$1.2B, customer acquisition relies heavily on OEM trial bundles and auto-renewal inertia subject to FTC and global regulatory scrutiny over negative-option billing. Built-in OS security solutions (Windows Defender, Apple security) provide free, highly effective protection, making third-party suites discretionary and easily forgone. Furthermore, the company carries $8.35B in debt following the debt-funded Avast merger (net debt/net income ~12.5x), resulting in negative tangible equity.

column14: Extreme enterprise switching costs and network effects across M365, Azure, Windows, and enterprise identity (Active Directory) create deep workflow lock-in that competitors cannot replicate without massive switching friction. Empirically proven by 10-year median GAAP ROIC >34%, operating margins expanding from ~30% to >46%, and recurring 9-15% M365 E3/E5 pricing increases with virtually zero enterprise churn. Primary erosion threats: open-source AI tooling bypassing proprietary enterprise software layers, escalating AI datacenter capex driving heavy D&A margin drag, and antitrust/bundling scrutiny.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Indispensable enterprise software monopoly and cloud infrastructure oligopolist with insurmountable switching costs across Office 365, Azure, Windows, and Active Directory. Empirically verified pricing power with negligible customer churn. Pristine AAA-rated fortress balance sheet with net debt repayable in under two months of earnings and >50x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: enterprise cloud/AI volume 8.0% + enterprise seat price/mix 2.5% - GPU capex depreciation drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: Multi-cycle 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 34.7% and operating ROIC >45%. Owner FCF conversion exceeds 95% of GAAP net income ($131.5B FCF on $133.7B NI). Operating margins expanded from 30.1% in FY2016 to 46.8% in FY2025. Long-term debt of $31.1B against $20.9B cash leaves net debt of $10.1B, which is 0.08x TTM net income. Interest coverage is 50.9x with AAA credit rating.

column14: Mission-critical enterprise workflow system of record with 98%+ renewal rates, extreme customer switching costs across IT service management (ITSM) and enterprise operations, and demonstrated pricing power yielding 15%+ median ROIC.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Enterprise workflow SaaS model remains fundamentally monetized via fulfiller seat licenses across ITSM, CSM, and HRSD. Under Macrotrend #1 (Automation & Cognitive Tech / AI Disruption), autonomous agentic AI systems that resolve IT incidents, service requests, and customer queries directly exert severe deflationary pressure on corporate IT support headcount, capping long-term seat expansion. Compute cost inflation from generative AI inferencing adds gross margin headwinds. Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.
column21: ServiceNow demonstrates exceptional historic financial performance: FY2025 revenue reached $13.28B (+21% YoY) with 98%+ gross renewal rate, GAAP ROIC of 17.05% (5-year median 15.2%), tangible ROIC of 27.22%, and FCF conversion of 137% ($2.75B Owner FCF). However, despite the launch of Now Assist and AI tier restructuring (Foundation, Advanced, Prime), the economic core remains tied to enterprise fulfiller seat licenses. Autonomous agentic AI resolution of corporate helpdesk tickets introduces structural deflation to customer IT/support headcount growth, limiting predictable secular runway below the 15-year hurdle required by Mauboussin persistence standards.

column14: High enterprise switching costs across Strata (network firewalls), Prisma (cloud security), Cortex (SOC), and Idira (CyberArk identity). Ripping out architectural security plumbing entails high operational and downtime risk. Gross margins sustained at ~74-75%.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Systems software baseline in Tier 3 (10-15Y) subject to severe terminal obsolescence haircuts. Cybersecurity is an unrelenting Red Queen's race characterized by rapid 3-5 year technology shifts and displacement risk. Defending its platform requires continuous, highly dilutive mega-M&A (e.g. $25B CyberArk acquisition in 2026, $3B Chronosphere) rather than self-sustaining organic expansion. Faces intense competition from Microsoft Security's native $30B+ ecosystem and AI-native disruption.
column21: Revenue expanded from $1.76B in FY2017 to $11.48B in FY2026. GAAP operating profitability was negative through FY2022 due to heavy stock-based compensation ($1.08B in FY2024, $1.30B in FY2025, $1.77B in FY2026). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 13.8%, but GAAP ROIC fell to 3.6% in FY2026 after the $25B CyberArk acquisition expanded invested capital to $27.5B. While enterprise switching costs are real, high competitive fade rates, hyperscaler bundling (Microsoft E5), and dependence on serial M&A limit predictable moat longevity below the 15-year threshold.

column14: Twilio benefits from developer habituation, rich API documentation, and pre-built global telecom carrier integrations. However, core CPaaS (SMS and voice) is a commoditized pass-through utility subject to carrier A2P 10DLC surcharges that compress gross margins (~50-52%). Low switching costs for large enterprise accounts, multi-vendor routing by customers, and lack of pricing power above inflation prevent economic rents. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~5.2%, failing the 12% threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Developer-friendly CPaaS API layer lacks pricing power above inflation and faces structural commoditization in core SMS messaging. 5-year median GAAP ROIC (~5.2%) fails the 12% capital efficiency hurdle. Downstream gates strictly nulled under waterfall.
column21: Twilio generated $4.46B in revenue in 2024 with a GAAP operating loss of $(54)M (-1.2% GAAP operating margin) and GAAP net loss of $(109.4)M. FY2025 revenue reached $5.07B with modest GAAP operating income of $157.8M (~3.1% margin). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~5.2% (and historically negative), well below the 12% hurdle. Gross margins remain capped in the 50-54% range due to network carrier pass-through fees. While FCF improved via cost cuts and SBC moderation, Twilio operates as an aggregator of commoditized carrier messaging where enterprises multi-home, negating pricing power above inflation.

column14: CDW leverages scale economies shared across procurement and distribution, aggregating >100,000 SKUs from 1,000+ technology OEMs (Cisco, Apple, Microsoft, Dell, Lenovo) to serve >250,000 enterprise and public sector customers. However, it operates as a pass-through intermediary with thin gross margins (~21.7%-21.9%) and low operating margins (~6.4%-6.8%). It completely lacks independent pricing power >= inflation, as standardized hardware and software licenses are easily price-shopped across rival VARs (TD SYNNEX, Insight, SHI) or procured direct from OEMs and hyperscaler cloud marketplaces.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). CDW operates as an IT solutions provider and value-added reseller (VAR) connecting technology OEMs with corporate and public sector clients. While it achieves scale economies in procurement and efficient working-capital turnover (supporting a 10Y median ROIC of ~16%), it completely lacks independent pricing power >= inflation. Gross margins (~21.8%) and operating margins (~6.5%) reflect pass-through distribution economics dependent on OEM vendor rebates and competitive RFP bidding. Customers can easily switch to rival VARs (TD SYNNEX, Insight, SHI) or procure directly from OEMs and hyperscaler cloud marketplaces, leaving CDW without an enduring economic moat under Munger's criteria.
column21: Multi-cycle financials: Net sales were $23.7B in FY22, $21.4B in FY23, $21.0B in FY24, and $22.4B in FY25. GAAP operating margins remained compressed at 6.8% (FY23), 6.8% (FY24), and 6.4% (FY25), with net income of $1,104M, $1,078M, and $1,067M respectively. Gross margins hover at 21.7%-21.9%. While working-capital velocity supports a 10-year median ROIC of ~16.2%, CDW operates as a price-taking middleman with no structural ability to raise prices above inflation without volume attrition. Disintermediation from direct OEM sales forces (Dell, Apple) and hyperscaler cloud marketplaces (AWS, Azure) poses an ongoing secular headwind. Total debt stood at ~$5.6B at year-end FY25.

column14: Massive iOS ecosystem lock-in (iCloud, iMessage, cross-device continuity, Apple Watch, and Apple Pay) creates insurmountable consumer switching costs proved by >90% iPhone retention and multi-decade median ROIC of 76.9%. Pricing power proven by higher ASPs via Pro/Pro Max mix shift and recurring Services expansion (26%+ of total revenue at ~74% gross margins). Primary erosion risks include antitrust scrutiny on App Store take-rates (EU DMA) and potential renegotiation or capping of Google search revenue-share (TAC).
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global consumer hardware and services ecosystem hegemon with >2.2B active installed devices and >90% iPhone customer retention. Pricing power demonstrated by Pro-tier mix escalation and high-margin Services growth (>$109B). Pristine balance sheet with LT debt / NI of 0.70x and >$100B in annual operating cash flow. Disruption runway set at CAP 15Y after a -5Y haircut for TSMC Taiwan foundry concentration and China assembly exposure, actively mitigated by diversification into India and TSMC Arizona. [5-10Y g: device & services volume 3.5% + ASP & pricing 1.0% + services mix 1.5% - regulatory TAC/DMA margin drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 2.5%]
column21: 10-year GAAP ROIC median of 76.9% (reaching 98.1% in FY2025). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS compounded from $2.08 in FY2016 to $7.47 in FY2025 (16.4% CAGR). FCF conversion exceeds 92% across cycles. Gross margins expanded from 38% to >46% as high-margin Services reached $109.2B in FY2025. Long-term debt of $78.3B against EBIT of $133.1B and Net Income of $112.0B (debt/NI = 0.70x). More than $700B returned through disciplined share repurchases over the last decade, reducing share count by over 35%.

column14: Dell benefits from global supply chain scale, enterprise sales distribution, and fleet financing (DFS), but lacks a defensible economic moat. Operating margins are structurally low (5.6-6.1% in CSG; 11.7-12.8% in ISG; ~6.5-7.2% overall). Gross margins have compressed from ~24% to 20-22% with AI server expansion, demonstrating that Dell acts as an OEM system integrator unable to capture pricing power above inflation or markup high-cost Nvidia GPUs against competitors like Lenovo, HPE, Supermicro, and ODMs.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Dell operates as an x86 hardware assembler and OEM system integrator across commoditized PCs (CSG) and enterprise servers (ISG). While direct enterprise sales relationships and fleet deployment tools provide modest customer retention, Dell possesses zero pricing power above inflation. Consolidated operating margins remain thin at 6.5–7.2%, and booming AI server volumes dilute gross margins toward 20–22% because upstream semiconductor hegemons (Nvidia) extract the economic surplus while downstream enterprise clients face low switching costs to competing hardware vendors.
column21: FY25 revenue was $95.6B with GAAP operating income of $6.24B (6.5% margin), comprising CSG at $48.4B (6.1% operating margin) and ISG at $43.6B (12.8% operating margin, including $9.29B AI servers). FY26 revenue reached $113.5B (+19% YoY) with GAAP operating income of $8.15B (7.2% margin), driven by ISG surging 40% to $60.8B (11.7% operating margin; $24.7B AI servers shipped, $43B+ backlog) while CSG delivered $51.0B (5.6% operating margin). Despite surging AI server demand, corporate gross margins compressed to ~20-22% due to high-cost GPU pass-throughs. Total debt stood at ~$31.5B in FY26 against ~$11.5B in cash/investments (with significant non-recourse DFS financing debt). Negative tangible equity and thin mid-single-digit operating margins reflect a commoditized hardware assembler lacking pricing power.

column14: Enterprise switching costs in installed base, mission-critical infrastructure integration, GreenLake hybrid cloud contracts, and Aruba/Juniper networking portfolios provide customer retention, but fail to generate economic rents. 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 7.5%, and FY24–FY26 ROIC remains depressed at ~0–8%, far below the 12% hurdle. Severe commoditization in x86 servers and storage, intense pricing pressure from Dell, Lenovo, and white-box ODMs, public cloud disintermediation, and inability to pass through component price swings prevent pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & zero pricing power above inflation, REJECT). While HPE maintains entrenched enterprise relationships and switching costs in networking (Aruba, Juniper) and hybrid cloud (GreenLake), its core compute and storage businesses are commoditized enterprise IT hardware. 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 7.5% and FY24–FY26 ROIC of ~0–8% consistently trail the 12% cost-of-capital hurdle. Intense competition from Dell, Lenovo, and white-box ODMs prevents real pricing power above component inflation.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 7.5% (well below the 12% minimum threshold). FY24 GAAP operating margin of ~6.8% and ROIC ~5.0%; FY25 GAAP ROIC fell to ~0–3% amidst Juniper integration and compute margin pressure; FY26 estimates project ROIC recovering only to ~4–8%. Free cash flow conversion is volatile ($1.5B FCF in FY24, ~$1.0B GAAP FCF in FY25 on $30B–$34B revenue), burdened by heavy capex, capitalized software, and working capital cycles. Total debt expanded significantly to >$18B following the $14B Juniper Networks acquisition. In core server/compute and storage segments, HPE is an architectural price-taker against Dell, Lenovo, and hyperscale ODMs, lacking the pricing power and structural capital efficiency required of a world-class compounder.

column14: Printer installed base and cartridge DRM firmware controls historically operated as a razor-and-blade toll booth, while Personal Systems (~68% of sales) is a commoditized hardware assembler. The moat is severely eroding: secular decline in printed pages (-3% to -5% p.a.) driven by paperless workflows eliminates consumable volume, while PC margins remain structurally capped at 5-7% with zero pricing power against Lenovo and Dell. Repeated firmware lockouts have accelerated customer churn to refillable tank systems.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). HP operates a commoditized PC assembly business (~68% of revenue) with thin operating margins (5.7-7.1%) and zero pricing power against Lenovo and Dell, paired with a mature printing segment (~32% of revenue) in irreversible secular decline due to paperless digital workflows. HP lacks the ability to raise prices at or above inflation without accelerating customer volume attrition; attempts to protect printer supplies margins via aggressive firmware DRM lockouts have sparked regulatory fines, consumer backlash, and defection to third-party tank systems. Stagnant multi-year top line and low operating margins fail the Munger compounder hurdle.
column21: FY2024 revenue of $53.6B and FY2025 revenue of $55.3B remain below FY2018 ($58.8B) and the pandemic peak FY2022 ($63.0B), reflecting stagnant-to-negative real revenue over the cycle. Operating margins compressed from 9.1% in FY2021 to 7.1% in FY2024 and 5.7% in FY2025 due to component cost inflation and persistent decline in high-margin printing supplies (Q4 FY2025 print revenue down 4% y/y). FCF of $2.9B-$3.3B is largely consumed by dividends and share buybacks that previously pushed stockholders' equity into negative territory (-$1.32B in FY2024, -$346M in FY2025) with ~$6.0B-$6.5B net debt. Dynamic Security DRM firmware updates sparked litigation and consumer defection to continuous tank alternatives, disproving enduring pricing power.

column14: NetApp's ONTAP storage operating system creates sticky customer lock-in and high switching costs across enterprise data architectures, sustaining ~70% gross margins in all-flash systems. However, the business suffers from structural hardware deflation ($/GB) and intense competitive pressure from Pure Storage, Dell EMC, and cloud-native hyperscalers, preventing pricing power >= inflation across the cycle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While NetApp benefits from sticky switching costs around its proprietary ONTAP storage OS and maintains ~70% gross margins in all-flash arrays, it lacks pricing power >= inflation across the cycle. Enterprise data storage is subject to chronic capacity-unit deflation ($/GB) and fierce multi-vendor RFP procurement battles against Dell EMC, Pure Storage, and public cloud native storage (AWS, Azure). Despite massive exponential growth in enterprise data volumes over the past decade, NetApp's revenue stagnated from $6.12B in FY15 to $6.57B in FY25 (~0.7% CAGR), severely lagging cumulative US inflation and proving that price increases cannot be pushed through without volume or market share losses.
column21: Financial Track Record: Over FY2015–FY2025, NetApp's annual revenue rose from $6,123M to $6,572M (a 10-year cumulative gain of only 7.3%, or ~0.7% CAGR), severely trailing cumulative US CPI inflation (~30%) despite exponential enterprise data growth. While gross margins expanded to ~70% (FY23: 66.2%, FY24: 70.7%, FY25: 70.2%) due to a shift toward high-margin all-flash arrays (AFF) and cloud storage services, top-line dollar expansion has remained virtually flat. Capital Efficiency & Cash Conversion: Net income hovered between $580M (FY15) and $1,186M (FY25). Reported GAAP ROIC appears elevated (>50%) primarily due to extensive share repurchases reducing stockholders' equity to ~$1.0B–$1.5B against total debt of ~$2.5B–$3.0B and cash of ~$3.0B. Annual Free Cash Flow runs consistently at $1.4B–$1.5B (clean conversion >100% of GAAP net income). Competitive Dynamics & Pricing Power: Storage hardware procurement is inherently deflationary per capacity unit. In enterprise storage RFPs, NetApp faces relentless competitive price pressure from Dell Technologies (which cross-subsidizes via server bundles) and Pure Storage (taking share with proprietary DirectFlash architecture). Concurrently, enterprise workloads continue migrating toward hyperscaler cloud-native tiers (AWS S3, Azure Blob). Consequently, NetApp cannot consistently raise prices at or above inflation without inducing customer defections, failing the Gate 3b hurdle.

column14: Direct-to-Flash modules (DFM) and proprietary Purity operating environment create switching costs and high enterprise customer retention via the Evergreen subscription model. However, enterprise storage is structurally exposed to competitive RFP commoditization from giants (Dell, NetApp, HPE), persistent NAND flash cost deflation, and hyperscaler custom architectures, preventing sustained pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & Lack of Above-Inflation Pricing Power, REJECT). Enterprise flash storage vendor benefits from switching costs via its proprietary Purity OS and Evergreen subscription upgrade model. However, structural industry economics prevent compounding at scale: 5-year median GAAP ROIC hovers around 3-6% (well below the 12% hurdle), burdened by heavy R&D requirements and massive stock-based compensation ($421M in FY25 vs $107M GAAP net income). Enterprise storage remains subject to fierce RFP discounting against Dell, NetApp, and HPE, preventing independent above-inflation pricing power.
column21: Pure Storage (PSTG / Everpure) FY25 revenue reached $3.17B with GAAP operating income of $85.3M (2.7% margin) and GAAP net income of $106.7M. Reported free cash flow of $526M is heavily distorted by $421.3M in stock-based compensation expense (diluting owner cash generation). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~3-6% (v1 workbook estimate 8.5%), failing the 12% minimum hurdle. While gross margins remain solid at ~70-72% and net cash stands over $1.8B, high competitive intensity in enterprise storage hardware and structural SBC drag prevent superior multi-cycle capital compounding.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Reject Standard b: Not Verifiable from Outside). External verifiability of financial statements is fatally compromised by opaque accounting practices, recurring reporting crises, and extensive circular related-party transactions with brother-owned suppliers (Ablecom and Compuware). Auditor Ernst & Young abruptly resigned in October 2024 stating it was unwilling to be associated with management's financial statements and could no longer rely on management's representations. Although replacement auditor BDO filed delayed FY24 reports in early 2025, it maintained an adverse opinion on internal controls over financial reporting amid ongoing DOJ and SEC inquiries. Recidivist governance issues (following a 2018 Nasdaq delisting and 2020 SEC settlement) place SMCI squarely outside the circle of competence for an enduring compounder.
column21: Super Micro Computer (SMCI) designs and manufactures high-performance server and storage solutions, benefiting from the generative AI hardware buildout. Despite rapid top-line growth ($7.1B in FY23 to $14.99B in FY24 and ~$22.0B in FY25), capital efficiency and cash generation are erratic. Gross margin fell sharply from 18.0% in FY23 to 13.8% in FY24 and 11.1% in FY25 due to fierce pricing competition against Dell, HPE, and Taiwanese ODMs (Foxconn, Quanta, Wiwynn). Operating margin dropped to ~5.7% in FY25. Working capital swings and inventory build for AI servers produced negative Free Cash Flow of -$2.6B in FY24 on ~$1.2B reported Net Income. Crucially, external financial verifiability failed in October 2024 when auditor Ernst & Young resigned over integrity, governance, and internal control concerns. While BDO issued a clean opinion on belated FY24 statements in February 2025, it issued an adverse opinion on internal controls over financial reporting. Substantial related-party dealings with family entities (Ablecom and Compuware) and active DOJ/SEC investigations confirm persistent accounting opacity.

column14: NAND flash memory operates as a highly cyclical commodity market subject to severe boom-and-bust supply/demand imbalances. While SanDisk shares fab scale with Kioxia in the Flash Ventures JV and possesses proprietary BiCS technology and enterprise SSD qualification relationships, it possesses zero structural pricing power across the cycle. Through-cycle capital efficiency fails the Munger hurdle (historical median ROIC of 8.5% vs. 12% threshold; FY2025 operating margin was -18.7%). Primary erosion threats include global memory oversupply, aggressive capacity additions from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, technological obsolescence from rapid layer-stacking transitions, and state-subsidized competition.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 8.5% < 12%, REJECT). Pure-play NAND flash memory producer lacks structural pricing power across the business cycle. Despite short-term AI-driven cyclical margin surges in FY2026, SanDisk is a price-taker subject to recurring boom-bust memory downcycles (exemplified by -18.7% operating margins in FY2025). Long-term median ROIC of 8.5% fails the 12% hurdle rate, and continuous multi-billion dollar fab capex is required merely to maintain market share against Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.
column21: Spun off from Western Digital in February 2025 as an independent NAND flash memory company (NASDAQ: SNDK) sharing manufacturing JVs with Kioxia. Financial track record exhibits extreme cyclicality: FY2025 operating margins collapsed to -18.7% amid an industry-wide NAND downturn before rebounding to 61.2% in FY2026 on tight supply and AI enterprise SSD demand. 10-year median ROIC is 8.5%, substantially below the 12% hurdle. Flash memory prices experience long-term secular bit price deflation, meaning high-margin periods represent unrepeatable cyclical peak profits rather than structural economic moats. Massive capital reinvestment and wafer fab equipment spending required to scale BiCS 3D NAND layers prevent consistent economic value creation over full cycles.

column14: Duopoly with Western Digital in high-capacity 3.5" HDDs backed by proprietary Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording (HAMR/Mozaic) head and media technology. However, moat fails the economic test: 10-year median ROIC of 11.2% falls short of the 12% threshold, gross margins swing wildly from 18% in troughs to 45%+ at cyclical peaks, and structural $/TB storage deflation combined with concentrated hyperscaler purchasing power prevents consistent inflation-plus pricing.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing & Proof of Moat, REJECT). While Seagate and Western Digital form a tight duopoly in mass-capacity HDDs with proprietary HAMR/Mozaic engineering know-how (Gate 3a), the business suffers from severe cyclical earnings volatility, structural $/TB price deflation, and extreme customer concentration among cloud hyperscalers who extract price concessions. 10-year median ROIC is 11.2%, failing the 12% hurdle. In downcycles, operating margins swing negative and equity was wiped into negative territory (-$1.5B in FY2024), demonstrating an absence of inflation-plus pricing power.
column21: Multi-cycle financial track record shows extreme cyclicality and sub-hurdle capital efficiency. 10-year median ROIC is 11.2% (below the 12% Munger threshold). In the FY2022–FY2024 downcycle, revenues fell ~44%, gross margin plunged to 18.3% in FY2023, operating margin turned negative, and net loss reached -$529M, pushing stockholders' equity to -$1.5B in FY2024 with ~$5.4B in debt. While AI mass-storage demand and tight supply discipline generated a strong cyclical rebound in FY2025–FY2026, storage hardware faces permanent price-per-terabyte deflation and monopsonistic pressure from cloud hyperscalers (Microsoft, AWS, Google, Meta). Long-term substitution risk from declining QLC NAND flash costs further limits durable pricing power.

column14: Proprietary areal-density engineering (ePMR, UltraSMR) establishes a global duopoly with Seagate in nearline HDDs, but chronic $/TB price deflation, severe cyclical demand whip-saws, and hyperscaler procurement power preclude through-cycle pricing power and suppress historical returns.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Pure-play HDD manufacturer post-SanDisk spin. Despite nearline HDD duopoly with Seagate, 10-year median ROIC of ~6.8% is far below the 12% hurdle. Relentless $/TB price deflation and deep cyclical downturns (negative ROIC of -2.1% and -$1.2B FCF in FY23) demonstrate lack of through-cycle pricing power.
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 5.7%-6.8% severely trails the 12% threshold, oscillating between cyclical peaks (>20% in FY25-FY26 AI storage buildout) and severe troughs (-2.1% in FY23). Free cash flow exhibits extreme volatility (-$1.2B in FY23). Spin-off of SanDisk flash business completed in February 2025 leaves WDC focused on HDDs. Concentrated hyperscaler customer base (cloud titans) commands intense bargaining power, capturing technological productivity gains via continuous $/TB deflation.

column14: Dow possesses scale economies and low-cost feedstock integration via world-scale ethylene and polyethylene crackers on the US Gulf Coast and Western Canada. However, empirical capital efficiency confirms lack of an economic moat: 10-year median ROIC is only ~7.2% (falling to 6% in 2023-2024 and -1% in 2025). The company is an undifferentiated commodity price-taker whose margins fluctuate with global supply-demand swings and energy spreads, leaving it vulnerable to persistent Chinese capacity overbuild and European structural energy disadvantages.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 7.2% 10Y median vs 12% hurdle, REJECT). Dow is a cyclical commodity chemical producer selling undifferentiated polyethylene, ethylene oxide/glycol, and basic chemical intermediates. Despite world-scale US Gulf Coast integrated assets, it operates as a pure global price-taker subject to volatile feedstock spreads and Chinese overcapacity gluts. It cannot reliably price above inflation or generate double-digit returns on capital across the cycle (2023-2024 ROC 6%, 2025 ROC -1%, with 2025 FCF of -$1.42B).
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 7.2% fails the 12% hurdle. GAAP Net Income was $660M in 2023, $1,201M in 2024, and collapsed to a net loss of $(2,444)M in 2025. Free cash flow swung from $2,808M in 2023 to $(37)M in 2024 and $(1,417)M in 2025 due to heavy capital expenditures ($2.5B-$2.9B annually, including the Path2Zero net-zero project). Total long-term debt of $17.8B against $3.8B in cash leaves net debt at ~$14.0B. Operating segments: Packaging & Specialty Plastics (~50% of sales), Industrial Intermediates & Infrastructure (~25%), Performance Materials & Coatings (~25%). Bulk commodity products lack switching costs and price at global spot parity.

column14: Prohibitive permitting barriers, strict zoning restrictions, and steep weight-to-value transport economics create 20-30 mile local quarry monopolies. Proven by 14.3% 5-year median GAAP ROIC, 22.9% tangible ROIC, and 12 consecutive years of EBITDA margin expansion through high cost-inflation cycles.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Premier vertically integrated aggregates, cement, and infrastructure solutions leader in North America and Europe. Moat underpinned by irreplaceable permitted quarry reserves with 20-30 mile haul-radius local monopolies and consistent compounding pricing power above inflation. Structurally insulated from AI disruption and well-positioned to benefit from US infrastructure (IIJA), manufacturing onshoring, and grid buildouts. Strong balance sheet with Net Debt / NI at 3.3x and 6.7x interest coverage supporting disciplined bolt-on M&A. [5-10Y g: organic volume 1.5% + pricing above inflation 2.5% + solution mix / bolt-on reinvestment 2.0% - energy/capex drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 14.3% and operating/tangible ROIC of 22.9%. Multi-year Owner FCF conversion of 83.6% ($14.1B cumulative FCF on $16.9B net income). EBIT compounded from $3.3B in 2021 to $5.4B in 2025 with Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding to 20.5%. Owner EPS reached a new cycle peak of $5.54 in 2025 (13.5% CAGR). Rational capital allocation under Albert Manifold: disciplined portfolio pruning of lower-return assets (European distribution, BuildingEnvelope) reinvested into high-return aggregate footprints (e.g. $2.1B Martin Marietta South Texas acquisition) alongside primary NYSE listing migration and S&P 500 entry. Balance sheet carries $4.1B cash with Net Debt / NI of 3.3x and 6.7x interest coverage.

column14: Local haul-radius quarry monopolies (low value-to-weight ratio limits truck transport to ~25-50 miles) and stringent local permitting barriers create an irreplaceable infrastructure moat. Pricing power has been demonstrated across three decades with uninterrupted positive annual aggregates pricing gains, including +10% in FY2024 ($21.80/ton) and +7% in FY2025 ($23.30/ton).
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Peace-of-Mind Balance Sheet & Real Cash Conversion). Irreplaceable US Sunbelt quarry franchise with unassailable pricing power, but fails Gate 6 on excessive leverage (4.66x debt/NI at $5.29B debt vs $1.14B net income), heavy maintenance/growth capex absorption (multi-year FCF conversion 68.7% vs 80% hurdle), and sub-hurdle 8.4% 10-year median GAAP ROIC diluted by serial debt-funded acquisitions.
column21: Martin Marietta Materials (MLM) operates irreplaceable aggregates quarries across high-growth Sunbelt and non-residential hubs. While local haul-radius protection enables steady pricing power (aggregates ASP up 10% in FY2024 to $21.80/ton and up 6.9% in FY2025 to $23.30/ton), the business model fails Gate 6 criteria: (1) 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.41% (ranging from 7.9% to 10.1%, with FY2024's 15.4% distorted by a one-off divestiture gain of $2.1B South Texas cement assets to CRH); (2) Multi-year Free Cash Flow conversion is 68.69%, falling well short of the 80% hurdle due to intensive quarry stripping, equipment overhaul, and fleet replacement capex ($807M capex vs $637M D&A in FY2025); (3) Long-term debt stands at $5,293M against $1,137M net income and $67M cash, yielding a Net Debt / Net Income ratio of 4.60x (and Debt / NI of 4.66x), exceeding the <= 4.0x ceiling. Capital allocation under CEO Ward Nye has successfully shifted the portfolio toward pure-play aggregates, but ongoing debt-funded M&A keeps leverage structurally elevated.

column14: Captive local quarry natural monopolies protected by insurmountable zoning regulations, environmental permitting barriers, and high bulk trucking costs (~25-mile economic radius). Proof of moat verified by steady expansion in cash gross profit per ton ($11.33/ton in 2025, +6.8% YoY) and 17.7% tangible operating ROIC through construction cycles. Primary erosion risks include long-term reserve depletion near core metros, shifts in urban development corridors, and severe rail/transport freight cost inflation.
column20: Premier North American aggregates infrastructure franchise. Irreplaceable local quarry network with exceptional pricing power through the cycle. Beneficiary of US reshoring, data center buildout, and federal infrastructure spending with zero AI displacement risk. Strong balance sheet with leverage at 2.0x EBITDA and 6.8x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: aggregates volume 1.5% + price 4.5% + unit margin expansion 1.0% + buybacks/bolt-ons 1.0%]
column21: Aggregates represent essential civil infrastructure inputs with captive local distribution dynamics. Operating tangible ROIC consistently 17-22% over the past decade (17.7% in FY2025; GAAP ROIC ~10% burdened by acquisition goodwill). Peak-to-peak compounding intact with Owner EPS compounding at 13.2% CAGR from $3.09 (FY2016) to a record $8.65 (FY2025). 5-year FCF conversion averages 89.4% ($1,072M FCF on $1,077M NI in FY2025). Demonstrated uninterrupted pricing power with 2025 cash gross profit per ton up +6.8% to $11.33 and ASP up +4.3% to $21.98. Balance sheet disciplined with net debt of $4.18B (3.88x NI, 2.0x EBITDA), interest coverage of 6.76x, and BBB+ investment grade credit rating.

column14: Tier-1 long-life permitted orebodies (Grasberg, Morenci), but pure price-taker in global commodity markets with 10-year median ROIC of 10.2% (< 12%).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT).
