column21: Federal Realty Investment Trust (FRT) owns ~102 properties comprising over 26 million square feet of retail and mixed-use real estate in affluent coastal metropolitan submarkets (D.C., Boston, Silicon Valley, Southern California). Financial track record demonstrates structural capital intensity: 10-year GAAP ROIC ranges from 3.0% to 5.5% (median ~5.5%), well below the 12% hurdle. 2024-2025 net income of $286M-$402M and operating cash flow of $575M-$622M support ~2.3x-3.5x interest coverage against $4.8B-$5.0B in total debt. Despite an admirable 55+ year dividend growth streak, capital efficiency is bounded by commercial real estate cap rates rather than compounding economic rents.

column14: Scarce entitled infill locations and local municipal zoning restrict new open-air retail development, but Kimco lacks pricing power above inflation and fails the proof-of-moat capital return test. 5-year median ROIC is ~2.2%, well below the 12% threshold, with contractual 1.5-3.0% rent escalators constrained by tenant occupancy costs.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 2.2%, REJECT). While Kimco owns high-quality grocery-anchored shopping centers on scarce infill suburban land, retail real estate generates structurally sub-hurdle returns on capital (5Y median ROIC ~2.2% vs. 12% threshold). Contractual lease escalators are modest and pricing power is constrained by tenant retail economics, failing Charlie Munger's proof-of-moat standard.
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~2.2% (FY20: 1.94%, FY21: 1.54%, FY22: 2.12%, FY23: 2.42%, FY24: 2.12%, FY25: 2.60%), with 10-year median ROIC of 4.8%, far below the 12% minimum hurdle. Total debt stands at ~$8.86B against FY25 net income of $592.8M and FFO of ~$1.2B, reflecting real estate leverage required to support low asset yields. Significant acquisitive expansion (RPT Realty $2.0B all-stock acquisition in 2024, Weingarten in 2021) expands gross leasable area across Coastal/Sunbelt hubs but fails to overcome structural real estate capital intensity and thin tenant spread economics.

column14: Realty Income commands massive physical scale (>15,400 commercial properties) and an investment-grade balance sheet (A3/A-) that lowers borrowing costs relative to smaller net-lease competitors. However, empirical capital efficiency fails the Munger hurdle: 10-year median ROIC is 5.2%, and 2023-2025 ROIC hovered between 3.0% and 3.5%, far below the 12% standard. Contractual net-lease escalators (1.0-2.0% annual bumps or capped CPI) fail to provide real pricing power above inflation during inflationary spikes. Primary erosion threats include higher cost of capital compressing acquisition spreads, tenant credit distress in retail/pharmacy, and reliance on continuous external capital issuance.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). While Realty Income possesses a massive, diversified net-lease portfolio (>15,400 properties) with high occupancy (98%+), it fails the empirical hurdle of capital compounding. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 5.2% (recent 2023-2025 ROIC averaging 3.0-3.5%), far below the 12% Munger standard. Triple-net commercial leases feature fixed 1-2% annual rent escalators or capped CPI bumps that provide insufficient pricing power against high inflation. Growth is structurally dependent on continuous external debt and equity financing to acquire properties at thin spreads (150-170 bps over cost of capital), rather than internal compounding.
column21: 10-year median ROIC of 5.2%; 2023 ROIC 3.1%, 2024 ROIC 3.3%, 2025 ROIC ~3.4-3.5%. Portfolio comprises 15,400+ commercial properties primarily leased to defensive retailers (grocery, convenience, dollar stores, quick-service dining). While occupancy remains high (~98.6%) and tenant diversification is robust, net lease economics inherently generate low single-digit returns on total invested capital. Initial acquisition cash yields of ~7.3% in FY2025 against debt-to-EBITDA of ~5.4x leave thin economic profit margins. Contractual escalators lag inflationary surges, failing Gate 3b.

column14: Entitled infill grocery-anchored shopping centers in high-density suburban markets are protected by municipal zoning barriers and land scarcity. However, capital efficiency is structurally capped by commercial property cap rates (5-7%), resulting in a 10-year median GAAP ROIC of only 5.1%, well below the 12% threshold. Pricing power is limited to contractual 2-3% lease bumps and cyclical re-leasing spreads, with ongoing tenant disintermediation risks from e-commerce.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 5.1% < 12%, REJECT). Established grocery-anchored suburban shopping center REIT with high-quality infill real estate in affluent suburban trade areas. While municipal zoning restrictions and physical site scarcity provide localized barriers to entry, commercial real estate asset yields of 5-7% structurally prevent the business from achieving the required 12% multi-cycle GAAP ROIC hurdle. Pricing power is constrained by retail tenant lease negotiation dynamics and long-term secular competition from digital commerce.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 5.1% (FY2024-2025 ROIC ~4.7-5.0%), failing the >=12% proof-of-moat hurdle. Portfolio comprises ~480 shopping centers (>80% grocery-anchored by dominant operators like Publix, Kroger, Whole Foods, Albertsons) across high-income suburban US markets. Leased occupancy remains high at ~96.5% with same-property NOI growth of ~3-5% post-pandemic, but contractual rent escalators average 2-3% annually. Total consolidated debt of ~$5.0B with net debt-to-EBITDAre of ~5.1x and fixed-charge coverage of ~4.1-4.3x reflect disciplined investment-grade REIT leverage, but sub-hurdle asset-level returns on capital permanently disqualify the business under Munger compounding standards.

column14: SPG holds premier Class-A malls, The Mills, and Premium Outlets occupying scarce, highly entitled infill real estate in affluent US metros where physical replication is practically impossible. However, the business structurally fails empirical moat return hurdles: 10-year and 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 5.8%-7.5% (well below the 12% Munger threshold). Primary erosion threats stem from secular e-commerce substitution, tenant apparel bankruptcies, co-tenancy lease protections, and the ongoing capital reinvestment required to redevelop vacant anchor department stores into mixed-use spaces.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC 5.8%-7.5% < 12%, REJECT). Premier retail REIT owning top-tier Class-A malls and Premium Outlets on irreplaceable infill locations, but capital-intensive commercial real estate structure yields structural multi-cycle GAAP ROIC well below the 12% threshold. E-commerce secular substitution and retailer negotiating leverage constrain through-cycle pricing power above inflation.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.5%, with FY23-FY25 annual ROIC ranging between 5.8% and 7.4%, failing the Gate 3b >= 12% hurdle. While Simon achieves high domestic property occupancy (~96%) and positive leasing spreads, operating income before other items has remained flat-to-modest ($1.46B in 2024 vs $1.52B in 2023) on an invested capital base over $30B. Net debt to EBITDA stands at ~5.2x with >$25B in debt, reflecting a leveraged real estate model that fails the Munger hurdle for high-return compounding.

column11: Non-essential / easily forgone product or service. Self-storage is an optional convenience used during moves or clutter accumulation rather than an essential necessity or everyday habit.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need & Entrenched Habits, REJECT). Self-storage is an optional, deferrable service tied to moving activity and clutter storage rather than an essential functional need or daily habit. Easily forgone or vacated during economic tightening.
column21: Extra Space Storage operates >3,700 locations following the $14B Life Storage merger. Self-storage demand is discretionary and non-essential, subject to housing turnover cycles and high customer churn. Capital efficiency is structurally sub-hurdle (5Y median GAAP ROIC of 5-7% vs 12% requirement), and debt load is heavy ($11B+ debt vs ~$800M net income).

column11: Non-essential, deferrable overflow storage service; discretionary consumer spending vulnerable to moves, decluttering, and economic belt-tightening.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Public Storage provides self-storage rentals, which represent a discretionary and deferrable convenience rather than an essential functional necessity or entrenched everyday habit. Units store non-essential household overflow and clutter, making contracts easily cancellable during economic strain or housing freezes. Furthermore, capital-intensive real estate asset intensity results in multi-year ROIC of ~7-8%, failing quality compounding hurdles.
column21: Public Storage (PSA) operates ~3,000 self-storage properties across the US with ~218M sq ft. While PSA achieves high property-level NOI margins (>77%) and maintains an A-rated balance sheet, self-storage fails Munger essentiality. Storage space is a deferrable consumer discretionary expense driven by temporary moves and excess clutter. During 2023-2025 post-pandemic normalization and sluggish housing turnover, pricing power on new move-ins contracted. Structurally, capital-intensive real estate ownership caps 10-year median ROIC at ~8.2% (2024-2025 ROIC ~7.2%), far below the >=12% compounding hurdle.

column14: Operating density across dispersed homes provides localized maintenance efficiencies, but fails to generate economic returns above capital cost. 5-year median ROIC of ~4.5-4.8% is far below the 12% hurdle. Extreme competition from millions of mom-and-pop landlords and apartments caps pricing power, while the FTC's 2024 $48M deceptive junk-fee settlement highlights regulatory resistance to fee-based extraction.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 4.8%, REJECT). Single-family rental REIT model is asset-heavy with structural ROIC of ~4.5-4.8%, far below the 12% threshold. Local market operating density cannot overcome high tenant substitution from fragmented mom-and-pop rentals, while the 2024 FTC deceptive pricing/junk-fee settlement underscores severe regulatory friction on institutional landlord fee practices.
column21: 5-year median ROIC is 4.8% (4.2%-4.7% in FY2024-2025), well below the 12% hurdle. Total debt stands at ~$8.0-8.5B with Debt/EBITDA of ~5.8-6.1x. In September 2024, the FTC finalized a $48M settlement against Invitation Homes for deceptive undisclosed junk fees (mandatory smart home/utility fees) and unfair eviction/deposit withholding practices, demonstrating that pricing power is constrained and subject to intense federal and local regulatory backlash.

column14: Contractually locked ~3% fixed annual rent escalators in the US, local CPI-linked pricing internationally, and +6-10% rental renewal spreads at CoreSite data centers protect real pricing power against inflation. High tenant switching costs and strict zoning/siting barriers prevent tower replication, driving multi-tenant colocation tangible ROIC consistently between 20% and 48%.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT – Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Premier US and international communications tower portfolio and CoreSite interconnection hubs backed by long-term non-cancellable tenant leases. However, the business model carries $33.8B of long-term debt (12.9x net debt/net income) and an interest coverage ratio of only 3.56x EBIT/Interest, failing the >5.0x infrastructure threshold. Distributing $3.18B in dividends annually (>100% of GAAP Net Income), AMT structurally relies on uninterrupted access to debt capital markets to refinance regular multi-billion dollar debt maturities, failing Munger's peace-of-mind fortress balance sheet standard.
column21: FY2025 revenue reached $10.64B with EBIT of $4.85B and GAAP Net Income of $2.63B. Free cash flow conversion is strong at 140.5% (Owner FCF of $3.61B vs $2.63B NI), supported by low maintenance capex and high operating cash flow ($5.46B). Tangible ROIC has consistently remained between 20% and 48% (48.7% in FY2025), confirming strong pricing power and colocation operating leverage on established tower assets. Following the strategic divestiture of the distressed India operations to Brookfield in 2024, management has focused on developed markets (US and Europe) and CoreSite data center expansions (underwriting at mid-teens stabilized yields). However, the balance sheet carries $33.83B in long-term debt against $1.47B in cash. Interest expense of $1.36B results in an EBIT interest coverage of only 3.56x, well below the >5.0x minimum required for essential infrastructure, while Net Debt / Net Income sits at 12.3x (and LT Debt / Net Income at 12.9x), far exceeding the 4.0x ceiling. Because REIT tax qualification mandates paying out >=90% of taxable income (TTM dividends of $3.18B exceed GAAP Net Income), AMT cannot organically deleverage from retained earnings and remains permanently dependent on debt capital market refinancing.

column14: US macro tower network embeds non-cancellable 5-15 year master leases with ~3% annual contractual escalators and ~90% incremental colocation margins. However, overall corporate capital efficiency was diluted to sub-6% ROIC by a disastrous $19B+ fiber and small-cell rollup.
column20: Fails Gate 5 (Score = 0, REJECT). While pure-play US macro towers are irreplaceable physical infrastructure with contractual ~3% escalators, executive leadership pursued a decade-long value-destructive M&A rollup in fiber/small cells ($19B+ spent at sub-hurdle returns). This empire-building resulted in ballooning debt (~$22B+), severe shareholder dilution, an activist proxy battle, three CEO changes in two years, an $8.5B fiber asset fire-sale at a steep realized loss, and a ~32% dividend cut. Flunks Munger/Thorndike capital allocation standard.
column21: Historical 10-year GAAP ROIC averaged just 5.9%, far below the 12% hurdle, driven by capital-intensive fiber rollups. Total debt peaked above $22B with interest coverage of ~2.5x-3.0x, far below the 5.0x fortress threshold. Following intense activist pressure from Elliott Management, former CEO Jay Brown departed in Jan 2024; Crown Castle agreed in 2024-2025 to sell its fiber and small cell business for $8.5B to Zayo/EQT to pay down >$7B of debt, and slashed the dividend by ~32% from $6.26 to $4.25 per share.

column14: Zoning restrictions, high capital costs, and local permitting make macro cell towers virtually irreplaceable physical infrastructure. Long-term leases (5-15 years) feature contractual ~3% annual escalators in the US and CPI/inflation-indexed escalators in international markets (Brazil), sustaining ~80% tower cash flow margins and 12-18% GAAP ROIC (19-32% tangible ROIC). Pricing power is proved by contract renewal terms and minimal competitive tenant churn, with churn driven almost entirely by carrier consolidation (Sprint/T-Mobile and Dish/EchoStar) rather than pricing pressure.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). While SBA operates an irreplaceable tower portfolio with ~80% gross margins, its balance sheet fails Munger's solvency standard: long-term debt of $11.0B represents 10.4x TTM net income ($1,053.6M), interest coverage is critically low at ~2.87x EBIT/interest ($1,342.8M EBIT vs ~$468M interest expense), and cumulative debt-funded buybacks have produced -$4.85B in negative stockholders' equity. The company relies continuously on the 'kindness of strangers' to refinance tower ABS and senior notes in debt capital markets at higher interest rates.
column21: Multi-cycle operational strength with 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 12.2% (tangible ROIC 19-32%) and robust Owner FCF conversion (>100% of NI). However, balance sheet leverage is structural and severe: long-term debt stands at $10,964.5M against cash of $264.6M (net debt ~$10.7B, or ~6.4x annualized EBITDA). Interest expense climbed to ~$468M in FY2025, depressing interest coverage to 2.87x, well below the 5.0x infrastructure threshold. Negative stockholders' equity (-$4,853.5M in FY2025) reflects multi-year debt-funded repurchases. Ongoing capital market dependency is demonstrated by large continuous refinancings ($3.5B senior notes and $2.0B term loan in 2026 to retire maturing debt). Carrier consolidation headwinds (Sprint churn of $50M+/yr tapering by 2027 and Dish/EchoStar bad debt/churn) add revenue friction amidst rising refinancing costs.

column14: While Weyerhaeuser controls ~10.5 million acres of irreplaceable, low-cost commercial timberland across North America, its economic engine is tied to commodity wood products (lumber, OSB) and sawlogs. 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.2%, failing the 12% hurdle. The company is a price-taker on spot commodity lumber markets with zero structural pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 6.2% < 12%, REJECT). Weyerhaeuser is the largest private timberland owner in North America, but its earnings are dominated by commodity lumber, OSB, and logs. It operates as an unhedged price-taker tied to cyclical residential construction starts and spot lumber benchmarks, lacking pricing power or hurdle-rate multi-cycle capital returns.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 6.2% (peaked at 16.3% in 2021 during the historic pandemic lumber squeeze, then collapsed to ~3.0-4.2% in 2024 and ~3.1-4.9% in 2025). Net income plunged from $2.61B in 2021 to $396M in 2024 and $324M in 2025 on revenue of $6.91B. Lumber and OSB realizations are dictated by spot market indices (Random Lengths) and housing starts, confirming zero pricing power over inflation across the full business cycle.

column14: Exclusive state-granted franchise service territories across 11 states and ownership of the nation's largest electric transmission network (~40,000 miles of transmission lines, including ~90% of US 765-kV lines) create an insurmountable physical and regulatory barrier to entry. Proof of moat is demonstrated by formulaic cost-of-service rate-base recovery and authorized ROEs of 9.25%-10.50% set by state PUCs and FERC, granting reliable nominal pass-through of fuel and capital costs. Primary erosion risks stem from regulatory lag, state commission rate pushback amidst escalating retail bills, and rising capital costs.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet; g6_default=N). While AEP possesses an unreplicable transmission network and state-regulated franchise monopoly (Gates 1-5 pass), its structural business model fails Munger's peace-of-mind balance sheet standard. Capped at a 6-7% regulated ROIC, AEP requires massive, continuous capital spending ($100B 5-year capex plan for 2027-2031) that vastly exceeds operating cash flow, resulting in perpetual negative free cash flow after total capex. Balance sheet carries $44.1B+ in long-term debt (total debt reaching $54.4B in 2026), representing ~11.9x TTM net income (far exceeding the <=4.0x ceiling) and weak interest coverage of 2.62x (below the >5.0x threshold). The company is structurally reliant on the perpetual 'kindness of strangers' via continuous debt and equity market issuance.
column21: Empirical 10-year financials verify the structural utility profile: 10-year GAAP ROIC has remained tightly range-bound between 2.6% and 7.3% (5-year median 6.26%), constrained by regulated rate base mechanics. In FY2025, AEP generated $3,696M in net income and $6,944M in operating cash flow against reported capex of $3,453M (with expanded multi-year capital plans ramping to $100B across 2027-2031, or ~$20B/year). Total debt escalated from $17.4B in 2016 to $44.1B in FY2025 and $54.4B by Q3 2026. Financial leverage is acute: LT Debt / Net Income sits at 11.94x (violating the <=4.0x threshold), while EBIT of $5,319M vs interest expense of $2,026M yields an interest coverage ratio of just 2.62x (well below the >5.0x hurdle). Cash balance stands at only $197M. Perpetual reliance on external capital markets to refinance debt maturities and fund grid expansion fails Gate 6.

column14: Largest US commercial nuclear fleet (~21 GW across 21 reactors) representing physically unreplicable generation assets due to extreme construction capital costs ($30B+) and decadal NRC licensing lead times. Protected by IRA Section 45U Nuclear PTC inflation-indexed floor ($43.75/MWh) and demonstrated pricing power via long-term hyperscaler PPAs (20-year Microsoft PPA for Crane Clean Energy Center). Key erosion threats include FERC transmission/colocation tariff disputes, wholesale power market design changes, and post-2032 PTC policy expiration risk.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet, REJECT). Constellation operates the nation's premier carbon-free nuclear fleet with unreplicable baseload generation assets benefiting from structural AI data center power demand and the IRA Section 45U PTC floor. However, it fails Munger's cash conversion and fortress balance sheet test: multi-year Owner FCF is deeply negative (-$20B+ cumulative over 2020-2025, fcf_conv = -258%) due to heavy nuclear maintenance/refueling capex ($2.95B in 2025) and collateral margin volatility. Furthermore, the $26.6B EV acquisition of Calpine re-introduces substantial debt leverage and commodity gas exposure, failing the peace-of-mind solvency standard.
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 6.31% (2020: 1.2%, 2021: -1.8%, 2022: 2.6%, 2023: 6.3%, 2024: 20.3%, 2025: 11.5%). Owner FCF conversion is severely negative (-258% multi-year), with negative FCF in 5 of 6 years (-$1.19B in 2020, -$2.71B in 2021, -$4.16B in 2022, -$7.90B in 2023, -$5.36B in 2024, +$1.25B in 2025 against $2.32B Net Income). Generates ~21 GW of carbon-free nuclear power at >94% capacity factors. Secured 20-year PPA with Microsoft for 835 MW Crane restart. Capital structure burdened by $16.4B equity / $26.6B EV acquisition of Calpine closed in early 2026.

column14: Exclusive state-granted franchise monopoly over transmission and distribution grids across the Carolinas, Florida, and Midwest. The physical grid infrastructure is legally and economically impossible to replicate, providing complete territory lock-in with regulated cost-of-service rate-setting and fuel pass-through mechanisms.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (g6_default N, REJECT). Regulated electric utility operating under state-capped returns on equity (5.4% 5-year median GAAP ROIC). Continuous multi-billion capital expenditure plan ($14.0B capex in FY2025, $103B 5-year plan) exceeds operating cash flow, resulting in negative organic free cash flow and persistent equity dilution. Balance sheet is heavily levered with $80.1B in long-term debt against $4.97B net income (16.1x debt-to-earnings), and interest coverage is weak at 2.37x (far below the >5.0x fortress threshold). Structurally reliant on continuous capital market debt and equity issuances to fund ongoing operations.
column21: Duke Energy Corporation operates regulated electric and natural gas utilities across 6 states (Carolinas, Florida, Indiana, Ohio, Kentucky) serving 8.4M electric and 1.7M gas customers. Multi-year financial track record demonstrates the structural limits of regulated utilities: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 5.44% (FY2025: 5.94%, FY2024: 5.68%, FY2023: 5.44%, FY2022: 4.97%), with tangible ROIC averaging 6.0-7.0%. FY2025 reported revenue of $31,741M, EBIT of $8,626M, interest expense of $3,634M, and net income of $4,968M. Interest coverage (EBIT/Interest) is 2.37x, well below the 5.0x peace-of-mind hurdle. Long-term debt stood at $80,108M at year-end 2025 ($87.2B total debt including current maturities, plus $2.6B commercial paper), against total cash of $245M. Long-term debt to net income is 16.1x. Operating cash flow of $12,330M was outpaced by $14,024M in capex, creating negative free cash flow before financing, with management budgeting an expanded $103B 5-year capital plan requiring continual external debt and equity financing.

column14: Exclusive state-granted franchise territory and CPUC rate-base regulation grant Southern California Edison a statutory monopoly over regional power transmission and distribution.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Traditional regulated electric utility is anchored to Tier 4 baseline persistence (CAP 5-10Y). California inverse condemnation doctrine and escalating catastrophic wildfire liabilities (e.g., 2025 Eaton Fire losses, AB 1054 fund depletion risk) combined with massive grid-hardening capex requirements prevent secular compounding.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 5.6% reflects capped regulatory returns on invested capital. Realized earnings remain severely volatile due to multi-billion-dollar wildfire liabilities (2017-2018 Thomas/Woolsey fires and 2025 Eaton Fire). Long-term debt exceeds $36B against $17.6B equity, requiring continuous debt issuance to fund $6.5B+ annual capex.

column14: Exclusive state-granted franchise territory for electric and gas distribution in CT, MA, and NH creates an insurmountable geographic barrier and captive customer base. Tariffs are set via cost-of-service rate-base regulation with formulaic cost recovery. However, allowed returns are capped by state utility commissions and FERC, exposing the firm to regulatory lag and disallowances.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Traditional regulated utility anchor falls in Mauboussin Tier 4 baseline persistence (5-10 years). Faces severe unhedged terminal macrotrend headwinds: Energy Transition capital misallocation (over $2.5B cumulative impairments and exit costs on offshore wind joint ventures) and Structural Cost of Capital/Inflation headwinds where massive ongoing capex ($4B+/year) and heavy debt load ($30B+) collide with hostile regulatory rate-setting in Connecticut (PURA).
column21: Eversource operates regulated electric, natural gas, and water utilities across Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire serving ~4.4M customers. While possessing an exclusive territorial distribution monopoly, its 10-year median ROIC is just ~4.9%, structurally limited by utility rate-base regulation and heavy debt. Annual capex ($4.48B in 2024, $4.16B in 2025) perpetually exceeds operating cash flow, resulting in negative free cash flow (-$45M in 2025) and continuous debt dilution (total debt reached $30.28B by year-end 2025 against recurring earnings of ~$1.7B). Its foray into offshore wind ended in a disastrous divestiture to GIP with $1.95B in 2023 impairments, $524M in 2024 closing losses, and continued contingent liability drag in 2025-2026. Coupled with an adversarial regulatory climate at Connecticut PURA, Eversource lacks secular compounding resilience and fails the 15-year CAP threshold.

column14: State-granted exclusive retail electric franchise monopolies across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas prevent duplicate grid infrastructure. Rate-base formula rate plans (FRPs) pass through fuel and capital costs with authorized ROEs of ~10.5-11.0%. Primary erosion risks stem from regulatory lag, severe Gulf Coast hurricane storm restoration costs, and rising cost of capital.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Inherently capital-intensive regulated electric utility failing Munger cash generation and balance sheet endurance standards: massive debt load of $27.9B against $1.77B net income (15.7x leverage vs <=4.0x threshold), thin interest coverage of 2.40x (threshold >5.0x), negative free cash flow (-$2.53B in 2025 due to $7.68B capex vs $5.15B OCF), and ongoing reliance on debt issuance and structured equity dilution to finance rate base growth.
column21: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 4.98%, structurally capped by state regulatory utility commissions (authorized ROE ~10.5-11.0%). Entergy has accelerated capital expenditures to $7.68B in 2025 (with multi-year plans exceeding $7B/yr for transmission, grid resilience, and load growth from data centers and Gulf Coast industrial facilities), significantly outstripping OCF of $5.15B and resulting in negative free cash flow. Consolidated long-term debt stands at $27.9B against $1.9B cash. EBIT of $3.20B covers interest expense of $1.34B by only 2.40x. While management has prudently de-risked the business by divesting merchant nuclear plants to focus on pure-play regulated utilities, the structural dependence on continuous capital market access violates Gate 6 peace-of-mind solvency criteria.

column14: State-granted exclusive geographic franchise monopoly for electric transmission and distribution across Kansas and Missouri (Evergy Metro, Evergy Missouri West, Evergy Kansas Central). Physical grid assets are unpermittable and uneconomic to duplicate, giving complete customer lock-in. Cost-of-service ratemaking provides steady formulaic return on invested rate base, but returns are legally capped by utility commissions (KCC and MPSC) at ~9.5% allowed ROE (resulting in 6-7% ROIC), with periodic regulatory lag on capital recovery.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet, REJECT). Regulated electric utility operating monopoly transmission and distribution networks in Kansas and Missouri under cost-of-service rate-base regulation. While possessing a durable franchise territory, returns on capital are structurally capped at 6-8% (5-year median GAAP ROIC 6.6%). Capital expenditures ($2.8B TTM, $22.5B 5-year plan) continuously exceed operating cash flow ($2.0B TTM), creating negative free cash flow before dividends. Balance sheet leverage is severe with $13.0B long-term debt against $855.6M net income (15.2x Net Debt / NI vs <=4.0x threshold) and interest coverage of 2.49x (vs >5.0x threshold), necessitating continuous reliance on the 'kindness of strangers' via debt issuance and ongoing $700M-$900M annual equity dilution.
column21: Multi-year financial history confirms structural utility capital dilution: GAAP ROIC has averaged 6.3%-6.7% across 2018-2025 (2025: 6.59%, median 6.59%), well below the 12% hurdle for quality compounding. FY2025 operating cash flow of $2,045.2M was overwhelmed by $2,796.9M in capex, generating -$751.7M in free cash flow before paying $613.1M in dividends. Long-term debt increased from $6.6B in 2018 to $13.04B in 2025, driving interest expense to $616.3M against EBIT of $1,532.9M (interest coverage 2.49x vs >5.0x standard). Net Debt / Net Income sits at 15.2x ($13,039.2M debt less $19.8M cash vs $855.6M net income). Planned 2026-2030 capex of $22.5B requires $700M-$900M annually in ATM equity dilution and continuous debt refinancing, failing Buffett's solvency and cash conversion criteria.

column14: Exclusive state-granted franchise territories across six major metropolitan regions (ComEd, PECO, BGE, Pepco, Delmarva, ACE) provide an insurmountable regulatory and physical monopoly over electric and gas transmission and distribution. Pricing power is formulaic via rate-base cost-of-service regulation with approved allowed ROEs (9.5-10%), though subject to regulatory lag and state political friction (e.g., Illinois ICC and Maryland PSC rate order pushbacks).
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). While Exelon possesses an unreplicable transmission and distribution monopoly with formulaic rate-base pricing power, it structurally fails the cash conversion and fortress balance sheet criteria. Heavy perpetual capex ($8.5B in 2025 vs $6.3B OCF) generates negative free cash flow, requiring constant debt issuance and reliance on capital markets. Massive debt burden of $49.4B against $2.8B net income (17.8x leverage) and capped ~5.5-6% ROIC result in chronic shareholder dilution.
